'I worked really hard and it paid off': Elation, nerves and proud parents as students get results

BBC News Thu, 13 Aug 2026 17:35:53 GMT

"I've worked really hard, I've tried and that's all I can do… and it's paid off", Emily, a student in Hartlepool said as she received her A-level results, admitting she "felt a bit sick" before finding out her grades.

She was just one of hundreds of thousands of young people to receive their A-level, Btec and T-level results across England, Wales and Northern Ireland on Thursday after weeks of waiting.

This year saw a record number of 18-year-olds accepted into university, with more than ever getting into their firm choice - although there are more of them in the population than in previous years.

Nervous, elated and tired students flocked to schools across the UK on Thursday to find out their grades, with many telling the BBC how they did and their hopes for the future.

Emily, who attended English Martyrs School and Sixth Form College, said she felt "sick" waking up on Thursday morning, but was happy with with her A*, A and B.

She said she's now looking forward to starting a degree apprenticeship to become a solicitor, a route she picked for the experience "now it's harder to get a job".

Anastasiia Sochka moved to Hartlepool from Ukraine with her mum, Victoria, in summer 2022 after Russia launched its full scale invasion.

Anastasiia told the BBC she initially struggled with the language barrier but was "so happy" to tell her dad, who is fighting in the Ukrainian army, that she achieved an A* in Russian, an A in psychology and a B in sociology.

"It was nice to be able to give him that good news because I wanted to make him happy. I miss him a lot," she added.

Anastasiia is now heading to Newcastle University and hopes to become a social worker.

"Lots of people are struggling in Ukraine now because of poverty due to the war, and I want to be able to help them," she said.

"Seeing what's happened has influenced me and changed my life perspective. I hope that by the time I graduate, the war will be over."

For some, the stress of the big day means all they can think about is finally getting some rest.

Civ, who is also heading to Newcastle University after getting two A*s and an A, said he plans to celebrate by heading back home and having a "lie-in".

He told the BBC he "might go out" later after getting some much needed post-results day sleep.

Michel's dad was overjoyed to discover his son earned an A*, A, A to book a place to study political economy at King's College London, beaming as he declared his son would be the "next prime minister".

"I'm so proud of him, so proud of everyone, his mates, it's amazing," he said before getting the crowd of students to cheer for his son.

In Canterbury, Kent, triplets Scarlett, Grace and Tabby Taylor said they were ecstatic for themselves and each other after getting into their first choice universities.

"It's proven to me I can do university and I will be able to succeed," Tabby said, who will be going to Bath Spa University.

"I can do what I want to do and get where I want to be," Scarlett added.

With the three of them heading to different parts of England to study, they are all looking forward to visiting each other in the months and years to come.

Scarlett added: "We will be able to see other places, it's so cool."

Some students, like 18-year-old on-call firefighter Bobi Jones, haven't had the time to worry about results day.

Bobi became one of the youngest crew members for the Mid and West Wales Fire and Rescue Service when he joined up last autumn while studying A-levels in business and sport as well as the Welsh Baccalaureate qualification.

"It's been a great experience," he said while admitting he "had plenty on his plate" as wildfires broke out in recent weeks.

Nick Basher, 19, beamed as he discovered he'd earned a merit in his T-level in digital production design and development.

T-levels - vocational qualifications for 16-19-year-olds in England - have grown in popularity in recent years as they offer a clear pathway to work in a difficult job market.

"I've been waiting a couple of months so there's been a little bit of nerves," he said.

Nick wasn't as nervous as some because he'd recently secured a full-time job at a solicitors working in their IT department.

"I am hoping to continue that within the company and look at whatever opportunities arise during that," he added.

For many students, results day may not have gone as planned, but that does not mean they are unable to continue in education, get an apprenticeship or find work.

If you only just miss out on the grades you need to get on to a university or college course, the admissions office might accept you anyway or offer you a place on a different course.

You could also try applying for a different place through the clearing process.

It may also be possible to re-sit some or all of your exams. Talk to your school or college if you want to explore this route.

Bonnie Tyler's classic hit spiked in streams during solar eclipse

BBC News Thu, 13 Aug 2026 17:07:42 GMT

As the biggest partial solar eclipse in nearly three decades took place, Bonnie Tyler's '80s hit could be heard throughout the village she once lived in.

With her instantly recognisable gravelly-voice and big, blonde hair, Gaynor Hopkins became an international sensation as Tyler with Total Eclipse of the Heart, and 43 years on it has cemented its place as one of the most famous power ballads of all time.

On Wednesday, people gathered all over the UK to enjoy the celestial event, and one of Tyler's friends heard the song playing throughout Mumbles, Swansea.

Spotify said Total Eclipse of the Heart almost doubled in streams on 12 August, with a 94% uplift in the UK and a 14% uplift globally.

Mal Pope, a musician and friend of Tyler's, watched the solar eclipse in Langland Bay, and like many, had the beloved Welsh singer - who died in July aged 75 - on his mind.

He said while walking around the area, he could hear children "singing along" to Total Eclipse of the Heart.

"It wasn't just the oldies who knew it the first time around. It's a classic song - it was really lovely hearing kids singing along with it."

He added: "Of course, because of the sad passing of Bonnie, she's in everybody's minds anyway."

Pope said there was going to be "a big procession" through the village on Saturday and a "tribute concert" on Sunday ahead of her funeral on 17 August.

"The whole village of Mumbles has got Bonnie on their minds. It just seems so ironic that of all the weeks for there to be a total eclipse, that it should be this week in Bonnie's very special, sad weeks."

Pope said Tyler would have "been belting out" her ballad, along with all the other people who were listening and singing along to her song during the solar eclipse.

"She had the most amazing voice, a great singer, and I'm sure she would have been smiling and thinking, 'isn't this lovely that people still remember this song', which was a big hit all around the world.

"Every time there's going to be a total eclipse, people are going to play the song on the spot, I'm sure, for generations to come."

A solar eclipse happens when the Moon moves between the Sun and Earth, blocking the Sun's light either partially or fully when viewed from Earth.

On Wednesday, the UK saw a partial solar eclipse, while other countries, such as parts of Spain and Portugal, enjoyed the spectacle of a total eclipse.

Pope added that he hoped people would take her musical legacy seriously now, and said the solar eclipse was a "fitting treat".

"It's like the sky came out in sympathy with us all here in Mumbles," he said.

Born Gaynor Hopkins in a council house in Neath, Tyler grew up with a love for music before she was discovered by talent scout Roger Bell in a Swansea club.

Tyler released her first single, Lost in France in 1977, but it was the release of Total Eclipse of the Heart five years later which changed her life.

The ballad spent two weeks at UK number one and four weeks in the US.

The iconic love song's music video surpassed 1.2 billion views on YouTube and has had over a billion streams on Spotify.

Spotify previously said it had paid out more than $1.4 million for streams of Tyler's catalogue in 2025.

The music platform said Total Eclipse of the Heart was one of a few "celestial" songs that saw a streaming spike in the UK on 12 August.

According to Spotify, the biggest increases in UK streams during the eclipse were:

Shannon Carragher, senior editor at Spotify, said: "It is always fascinating to see how major cultural events instantly reflect in what the UK is listening to.

"Cultural phenomena like the solar eclipse naturally bring people together and we instinctively look for the perfect soundtrack to share that moment."

Ahead of the solar eclipse, Tyler's McVitie's Jaffa Cakes TV advert also resurfaced - it was originally broadcast in 2023 when there was a partial lunar eclipse.

The nostalgic advert came after research revealed almost half (49%) of Brits did not understand how eclipses occurred.

In the video, Tyler uses a Jaffa Cake as a prop to describe the different types of eclipse.

She said: "There are three types of eclipse. You've got the lunar eclipse, the solar eclipse, and then there's the total eclipse of the heart.

"When the earth is situated between the moon and the sun it creates a shadow, and when it looks like someone has just taken a bite out of the moon. That's a partial lunar eclipse."

The grammy-nominated star had a string of other hits, including Holding out for a Hero and also represented the UK at the Eurovision Song Contest in 2013.

She was named in the Queen's last Birthday Honours list in 2022 and was awarded an MBE for her services to music by Prince William the following year.

Tyler died "unexpectedly" on 8 July, aged 75, at a Portugal hospital, "as a result of the illness that she was being treated for", her family said in a statement released on the star's official website.

At the time, tributes poured in from a host of friends and stars including Catherine Zeta-Jones, Bryan Adams and Rod Stewart.

Tyler's funeral service will take place on 17 August at 12:00 BST at St Mary's Church in Swansea.

It has since been confirmed that her coffin will be brought to her Mumbles home on 15 August at 15:30 BST.

People are invited to "pay their respects" by lining Newton Road at 15:15 BST.

Five key takeaways from results day 2026

BBC News Thu, 13 Aug 2026 16:49:28 GMT

Results for A-levels, T-levels, BTecs and other vocational qualifications are out.

And this year, they've come at a time when all eyes are on what teenagers decide to do next.

Universities are keen to get them through the door. As they grapple with their finances, they know that every filled seat in a lecture hall comes with tuition fee funding.

The new prime minister, meanwhile, wants to carve out clear routes into technical jobs that can rival the well-established path of A-levels and a university degree.

For teenagers, considerations about the immediate and long-term cost of university, as well as the availability of other options, are all in the mix.

Here are the standout things you need to know.

About 40% of 18-year-olds in England receive A-levels every summer, and this year top A-level results across the whole of England, Wales and Northern Ireland have risen for a third year running.

Overall, 28.5% of grades were marked at A* or A, up from 28.3% last year.

The results are still much lower than they were in 2020 and 2021, when exams were cancelled and results were based on teachers' assessments.

After that, there was a concerted effort to bring them back down. Grading in England returned to pre-pandemic levels in 2023 – prompting a big fall in top grades – while Wales and Northern Ireland followed suit in 2024.

The proportion of top grades across the three nations combined has been slightly creeping up since that drop in 2023.

The proportion of A-levels marked at A* and A was:

You can see how results were in your local area using the look-up tool below.

A record number of 18-year-olds in the UK have been accepted into university, according to the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas) - with more than ever getting into their first choice.

The steepest growth has been in acceptances to what Ucas calls "higher tariff" universities. These are the most selective institutions, like those in the Russell Group.

They have taken on 5.5% more UK 18-year-olds than last year, and many are still advertising courses in Clearing.

Nick Hillman, chief executive of the Higher Education Policy Institute, said a fall in the number of postgraduate international students had freed up resources for universities to teach more UK undergraduates, and the Russell Group stressed its members would "only admit students who show evidence of being able to succeed".

Still, four in 10 universities in England are expected to report a financial deficit in 2025-26, squeezed by a long-term freeze in domestic tuition fees and a fall in international student numbers. Taking on more UK students may offer some financial stability for those selective universities, but other institutions will be hoping to recruit more students through Clearing.

Jo Saxton, chief executive of Ucas, told the BBC the sheer amount of courses listed in Clearing meant teenagers could "absolutely still go to university in the autumn if that's what they would like to do".

That might be welcome news for some. While the raw number of 18-year-olds getting into their first choice has risen, there are more of them in the population than in previous years - and the actual percentage of 18-year-old offer-holders in England, Wales and Northern Ireland getting into their first choice has fallen from 82% to 79%.

Universities aren't the only ones worried about their finances. Teenagers, too, are concerned about the cost of going to university, and Saxton said many were using Clearing to find courses closer to home.

But ultimately, the percentage of UK 18-year-olds applying to university has remained stable, and worries about the long-term costs - with rising tuition fees and widespread criticism of the student loans system - do not appear to have put teenagers off.

This is the fifth year of T-level results in England, and the number of students getting grades has rocketed as their rollout continues.

More than 19,600 students received grades in 21 subjects this year, up from 11,900 students across 18 subjects last year.

This will be welcome news for the new prime minister, who says he wants pupils in England to be able to study technical subjects in addition to core academic learning from Year 10.

The pass rate increased slightly from 91.4%, according to last year's provisional results, to 92.6%. And the percentage of students achieving a merit or above grew from 65.3% to 68.9%.

The dropout rate remains high, though – and some students take longer than the standard two-years to complete the course. Around 77% of students who started their T-level in 2024, and were therefore expected to complete it this year, have received results.

T-levels are among the 300,000 grades for vocational and technical qualifications released today.

That's still much smaller than the number of A-level grades given out (more than 800,000 among 18-year-olds alone).

But there are indications that interest in technical education is on the rise. According to Ucas, engineering and technology subjects saw the biggest growth in university acceptances, up 16% from last year.

Technical education won't be the only thing standing out to Andy Burnham and his ministers today, especially after their recent meeting in No 10 North.

The gap between the highest- and lowest-performing regions in England has grown again.

In London, 32.7% of A-level grades were marked at A* or A. In the North East and the East Midlands, it was 23.1%.

That's a 9.6 percentage point gap – up from 9.2 last year, when the North East alone was the lowest-performing region. It's also the largest gap on record since the A* was introduced in 2010.

In fact, the gap between London and all other regions has widened since last year.

Henri Murison, chief executive of the Northern Powerhouse Partnership, said the regional gaps were driven by "persistent long-term disadvantage".

Chris Zarraga, director of Schools North East, said schools in different parts of England were "not operating on a level playing field".

He pointed out that the percentage of A* and A grades in the North East had grown, but London had "moved significantly further ahead", adding: "There is a structural divide in the circumstances and opportunities surrounding them."

But Myles McGinley, managing director of Cambridge OCR, said there were also "severe inequalities within the capital itself" between Richmond and Hounslow, for example, as well as between areas in the North East like Durham and Hartlepool.

More A* and A grades went to girls than boys this year – 137,000 compared to 120,900.

But more girls sit A-levels in the first place, and looking at the percentage of boys and girls getting these top grades suggests that boys are actually doing better.

This year, 28.9% of all grades given to boys were A*s and As, compared to 28% of grades given to girls.

It used to be the other round, and last year was the first year boys overtook girls in this respect since 2018. Now, that gap has widened.

Girls are still outperforming boys when you look at a broader range of grades, though.

For example, 79.8% grades given to girls were marked A* to C, compared to 76.8% of boys' grades.

Additional reporting by Phil Leake, Libby Rogers, Rob England, Isobel Cottam and Jess Carr

Honeytrap thieves jailed for killing men they had drugged

BBC News Thu, 13 Aug 2026 16:47:42 GMT

A couple who drugged men seeking sexual services in order to steal from them have been jailed for killing two men and poisoning others.

Adina Mihai and Madalin Dumitru admitted the manslaughter of Gary Mouat, 37, from Oxfordshire, and Malcolm King, 80, from Gloucestershire, in 2025 and 2024 respectively.

On the first day of their trial in June, the pair also each admitted two further counts of administering poison to surviving victims.

Mihai, 31, and Dumitru, 30, were both sentenced to 17 years in prison at Oxford Crown Court.

Mihai, who posed as a sex worker, and her partner Dumitru, arranged to meet men paying for services she had advertised online at their homes.

The court heard four had their alcoholic drinks spiked with the powerful sedative gamma-butyrolactone (GBL) so the pair could steal from them.

Two men died as a result, while two others - who cannot be named due to reporting restrictions - survived.

Julian Evans KC, prosecuting, said Dumitru would drop Mihai at the victim's home and wait nearby, apparently armed with weapons in case of trouble.

After encouraging the victim to drink the alcohol laced with GBL, Mihai would wait until they fell unconscious, before looking for property to steal, such as cash, aftershave, jewellery and expensive watches, Evans said.

He said the defendants, who previously lived in Birmingham before moving to Ilford, were "willing to act in this way out of greed".

Sentencing, Mrs Justice Brunner KC said the amount of GBL, commonly referred to as a date rape drug, given to the pair's victims was "haphazard".

She told them: "If you had stopped for a moment to consider the risks, as you should have done, you would have realised that you were creating a high risk of serious injury or death every time you administered that drug.

"If you had done the most cursory research you would know that GBL can be extremely toxic."

The judge added: "You left each victim alone in a state of deep unconsciousness, and a moment's thought could and should have led to the realisation that they might never come round."

The court heard Mihai first came to the UK from Romania to work in the sex trade, before leaving and returning again in 2023.

She advertised her sexual services on the online site VivaStreet, and would take cash deposits from victims ahead of meeting up.

Malcolm King had long-term heart conditions and was fitted with a pacemaker, and his death in August 2024 was initially treated as non-suspicious.

But after Gary Mouat died nearly a year later, detectives revisited the first case.

Jewellery, aftershave and a Rolex watch were also stolen from two further victims who subsequently contacted the police.

The couple were arrested when officers stopped a BMW with Dumitru driving and Mihai the front seat passenger.

Items belonging to some of the victims were recovered from the car, and Mihai's fingerprints were found on the wine glasses left behind in the men's homes.

A video statement made by Gary Mouat's eight-year-old son was played during the sentencing hearing.

He said: "My daddy was funny, silly, loving and a trickster, we always used to prank each other.

"Why did you have to kill my daddy, you could have just taken the money, he was really kind, he would have given it to you.

"He was my daddy and now he's gone.

"Ever since my dad died my life has been really tough. I miss him every day and will never get to see him again."

Jacky Seagroatt, Malcolm King's younger sister, said losing her brother had "devastated" her.

"He was not just my brother - he was someone I loved deeply and someone there for me when I need him most."

"The knowledge that two people have admitted responsibility for unlawfully killing my brother has brought some relief... however, it has not brought peace.

"What makes that even harder to bear is that Malcolm's wife, who loved him dearly, did not live long enough to see justice finally being done for him."

Are the UK's top universities really 'hoovering up' students?

BBC News Thu, 13 Aug 2026 16:43:34 GMT

A record number of UK 18-year-olds have been accepted into university this year, according to the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas).

But the biggest increase in acceptances was for the most selective, "higher-tariff" universities – such as those in the Russell Group.

Nick Hillman, chief executive of the Higher Education Policy Institute (Hepi), said the top institutions were "hoovering up all the crumbs" when it came to the top students, even if they had not met the grades they had been offered.

The Russell Group itself said there was "always some flexibility in admissions decisions", and that this "should not be confused with lowering standards".

The number of students accepted into higher-tariff universities in 2026 was 5.5% higher than last year.

By comparison, for medium-tariff universities - where students tend to get in with fewer Ucas points than the more selective universities - acceptances increased by 3.8%.

And acceptances at lower-tariff universities fell by 1.7% year-on-year.

The increase at the more selective universities comes at a time when the sector has been struggling financially as a whole, and questions have been raised about the importance of degrees and the cost of going to university.

"Universities are like every other institution, they want to be bigger and better next year," said Nick Hillman, chief executive of Hepi.

"If you can recruit good students, why wouldn't you?"

He said universities taking on more students meant less popular courses, such as modern languages, could be kept running, keeping staff redundancies at bay.

While there had been a "significant drop in international students" - who are largely postgraduates, and who pay higher fees - Hillman said universities were utilising their resources for UK undergraduates instead.

As it congratulated the 2026 cohort of new students, the Russell Group was quick to dampen down any questions that a boost in student numbers was a result of "lowering standards", and said it would "remain highly selective"

It said: "While there is always some flexibility in admissions decisions, this should not be confused with lowering standards. Our universities will only admit students who show evidence of being able to succeed on the course."

Duncan Ivison, president and vice chancellor at The University of Manchester, said students had been working hard to get the places they wanted and deserved.

"We're not cutting our standards," he said.

"We want our students not just to pass, but really flourish and do well. You can't admit students who aren't going to be able to take advantage of the opportunity that universities are offering."

The university said that, for the first time, it had received more than 100,000 applications this year – an increase of 13%.

A further 8,000 conversations were expected to take place through Clearing on results day alone.

For A-level student Stephen, from Carmel College in St Helens, results day turned into a "miraculous" morning after New College, Oxford, accepted him to study law despite him missing the grades he had been offered.

"When I opened my slip, I was initially really disappointed. I'd been made an offer of three As. I came out with ABB," he said.

"Then it was miraculous, I opened my Ucas form and I'd had my place confirmed.

"I'm absolutely over the moon."

It was a big relief for Niamh, too, who studies at the same college in the North West.

She told the BBC she had her heart set on studying midwifery at Edge Hill University in Ormskirk, Lancashire, but was turned down at the application stage and told she did not have the grades.

She had planned to go through Clearing and try her luck again, but was instead offered a place by the university about a month ago.

She said she was "really happy" and wanted to "empower women" and "leave an imprint on their lives" with her future career.

Universities UK, which represents 142 institutions, said the changes in student acceptance numbers was not necessarily as simple as the top universities grabbing as many students as they could by lowering grades.

Chief executive Vivienne Stern said the grade profiles accepted by different universities were "more or less identical to the pattern in previous years".

There are numerous reasons why students might be offered places with higher or lower grade requirements than average, she said, such as certain courses being under-subscribed.

While the financial situation of the higher education sector may have brought the issue to the fore, she said there were "checks and balances" in place.

"The important thing is we've got a system which regulates universities on outcomes," she said.

"You can recruit a student, but we're going to hold you to account. It's not in the interest to recruit a student who is not well equipped to succeed."

Hillman, from Hepi, said while universities were likely to be "breathing a sigh of relief" over the high student numbers, the true picture would only become clear once the new term begins.

LIV set to cancel season-ending Team Championship

BBC News Thu, 13 Aug 2026 16:36:15 GMT

Jon Rahm's future with LIV is reportedly in doubt

LIV Golf players have been warned that the season-ending Team Championship later this month is set to be cancelled, BBC Sport has been told.

Tickets for the event in Michigan cannot now be purchased online, with LIV's official website stating both ground passes and hospitality passes are "no longer available".

As first reported by the Telegraph,, external next week's tournament in Indiana looks increasingly likely to be the final event in the 2026 campaign.

However, LIV Golf is yet to make an official announcement, amid further reports that Jon Rahm could soon leave the league.

In July, former world number one Martin Kaymer said he felt it was "highly likely" the Team Championship would be cancelled, although last week Cameron Smith said he still expected the event to proceed, and that players "would be disappointed if it wasn't".

Last week, the series said it had secured an unnamed lead investor to keep the competition running in 2027 after the withdrawal of Saudi Arabian financial backing.

The Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF) said in April it would end its multibillion dollar bankrolling of the breakaway tour at the end of the season, plunging the future of the series into doubt.

LIV Golf secures unnamed lead investor for 2027

Tours form new alliance in latest blow to LIV Golf

Chief executive Scott O'Neil said a signed agreement with a new investor is in place and has been approved by the LIV Golf board, with the transaction expected to be completed in September. Until then, LIV bosses are said to be taking a disciplined approach to support its long-term sustainability and maintain operations.

No details of the amount of money that will be invested were announced. PIF has pumped in more than $5bn (£3.71bn) since the league launched in 2022.

O'Neil added LIV will make its players "majority equity holders" in the competition, calling it "a first for a major global sports league".

The LIV press release said the proposed deal with the lead investor is for "2027 and beyond".

The competition will reduce to 10 events from next season, with five in the United States and five held around the world.

There were 14 events planned for the 2026 season but in April, LIV postponed June's New Orleans competition amid questions over its future and has not announced a rescheduled date.

Last week, O'Neil said LIV was focused on "finishing the 2026 season strong", but made no explicit mention of the final two events scheduled this season, in Indianapolis from 23 August and the concluding Team Championship in Michigan from 30 August.

Alongside Rahm, major winners including Bryson DeChambeau, Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith, Martin Kaymer and Sergio Garcia remain part of the LIV roster after having left the PGA Tour.

American major champions Brooks Koepka and Patrick Reed rejoined the PGA Tour after it introduced a returning member programme.

Last week, when asked about the series' biggest stars, O'Neil said: "I think when you have a global game and you have 57 players from 21 countries and you're playing in 10 countries on five continents, how you define stars gets really interesting.

"So while I have all the time in the world for Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau, I think I'd be remiss in saying they're not only two of the biggest, best golfers on the planet, but I think they're some of the biggest stars in sports, let alone golf.

"Would certainly love them to come along for the ride and journey because they carry maybe more weight than anybody in the game and I have a lot of time for that."

In July, the PGA Tour and DP World Tour struck an alliance with the Asian Tour in another blow to LIV Golf.

LIV was founded in 2021 and launched the following year with 54-hole events, taking its name from the Roman numeral for 54.

However, it moved to the traditional 72-hole format for golf tournaments from this season.

Rashford, Mainoo & transfers - Carrick calls for more signings

BBC News Thu, 13 Aug 2026 16:21:51 GMT

This video can not be played

Michael Carrick won 12 out of his 17 games in charge of Manchester United last season

Manchester United boss Michael Carrick is determined to keep pushing to improve his squad this summer.

Carrick is about to begin his first full Premier League campaign in charge at Old Trafford.

He is acutely aware of the responsibilities that come with being the public face of such a worldwide institution, which he says it is a "privilege" to lead.

However, it also means having to address thorny issues with the media, which currently include a perceived lack of signings.

Carrick says he is delighted with United's business so far – they have spent £83m to sign Andrey Santos from Chelsea and Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa, with the out-of-contract Karl Darlow also joining as back-up goalkeeper.

However, with weaknesses at left-back and in central midfield, as they prepare for a return to the Champions League after a two-year absence, Carrick knows the work cannot stop now.

Because in a summer where his club missed out on key targets such as Elliot Anderson and Matheus Fernandes because they refused to match rival offers and are spending less than newly promoted Ipswich and Coventry, Carrick knows more transfer business needs to be done despite a desire to avoid the costly mistakes of the past.

"We want more, we need more, we keep looking for how we can do that," he said.

"Money's money, I get that. We feel like we have to be pushing for everything we're involved in, while being realistic of what the recent history's looked like over a period of time.

"For now, we've got to make the most of it, but we've got to push every boundary we can to be able to win again, basically.

"That's the challenge."

Michael Carrick signs autographs for Manchester United fans after the pre-season victory against Leeds at Croke Park

On a personal level, Carrick had an excellent day on Thursday as his daughter got the A-level grades she was hoping for.

He cut a relaxed figure, benefiting from a rare summer when his club have avoided draining trips further afield, instead travelling to Scandinavia for matches against Wrexham, Rosenborg, Atletico Madrid and Paris St-Germain, before facing Leeds in Dublin.

"I love the position I'm in," he said.

"There's the football side; the tactical, the training, putting the team together. Then there's the other side; being the face of it, leading it, trying to set the right messages, the right behaviours and right tone for what we want to look like as a football club.

"I never take anything that this position and this football club brings for granted."

This video can not be played

Carrick says he will treat Rashford like any other player despite being former team-mates

Carrick was given a number of opportunities to say Marcus Rashford will still be a United player when the transfer window closes on 1 September, but didn't take them.

"He's our player," he kept repeating.

It was also noticeable that in talking about the England forward, he was keen to stress Rashford was not the only player in his squad he had previously coached, managed or been a team-mate of given it has been highlighted as an area of strength in the player's reintroduction.

"It is not a unique situation at all and [we] treat him exactly like any other player," he said.

However, many supporters have not forgiven Rashford for his coolness towards United during loan spells with Aston Villa and Barcelona, where everyone expected him to be this season.

It is accepted even by those who know him there is a world of difference between the disinterested figure he became under Ruben Amorim and the fully motivated one who is widely accepted to be the best player to come through the club's academy since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

Ironically, Rashford's return to United colours is likely to be against Amorim's AC Milan in Wroclaw, Poland, on Saturday.

Carrick feels the 28-year-old still has a lot to offer.

"Football's got different directions," he said. "You've got to manage through the states to have a career for 10 or 15 years. It's never going to be smooth sailing.

"But you've got to keep moving forward. If you keep looking back too much, it doesn't do anyone any favours.

"It's been good to have Marcus around this week. He's our player. He's a good player, and he gives us something a little bit different."

Kobbie Mainoo was revitalised at United under Carrick during the second half of last season

Rashford was not the only England player to return to the United fold on Sunday evening.

Kobbie Mainoo also came back.

In a sense, it feels like back to square one for Carrick with the young midfielder.

When he took over from Amorim, after Darren Fletcher's two games in interim charge in January, he had to raise the confidence of a player of undoubted talent who had been virtually ignored by his boss.

At least Mainoo did come on as a substitute for Amorim in the Premier League last season. He didn't even do that for Thomas Tuchel's World Cup squad, even though it seemed England were crying out for his ball retaining abilities in the latter stages of the competition.

Carrick knows how Mainoo feels. He was similarly overlooked by Fabio Capello during the 2010 World Cup in South Africa.

Carrick spoke to Mainoo "through the World Cup" and says he has been "in great spirits" this week.

"I spoke to him all the way through the World Cup, not loads, but little bits," he said.

"It's challenging. From the outside we all see the glitz, the glamour and all the positive sides of football.

"But players are human beings. We all have our ups and downs. It's important we support each other.

"It was a good experience for Kobbie. It's a World Cup and that is a big step.

"He's still such a young man and he's achieved so much, so quickly. To be at the stage he's at is an achievement."

Person fined after using foghorn to wake sleeping polar bear

BBC News Thu, 13 Aug 2026 15:30:57 GMT

A person has been fined for using a foghorn to wake a sleeping polar bear in Norway's Svalbard archipelago, a local official said.

The incident happened earlier this month after someone sounded the alarm from onboard a vessel, which was sailing in a fjord in northwestern Svalbard - about 1,000 km (620 miles) from the North Pole.

On Thursday, a person - who has not been named - was fined 50,000 kroner (£3,890) over the incident, the governor of the territory confirmed.

Under local regulations in the region, "it is forbidden to needlessly disturb, attract or pursue a polar bear", which was declared a protected species in Svalbard in 1972.

About 250 polar bears were counted in the archipelago during the last scientific estimate, carried out in 2015.

In a statement, governor Lars Fause said when the vessel sailed past the animal "its occupants are said to have spotted a polar bear sleeping on land".

"A person on board then used the ship's foghorn, waking the animal, which moved to another location."

The individual has agreed to pay the fine.

It is not the first time people have been fined for disrupting animals in the Svalbard region.

In 2024, a tourist was fined 11,500 kroner (£900) for getting too close to a walrus.

The Svalbard Environment Act stipulates that all traffic on the archipelago must take place in a way that does not lead to unnecessary disturbance of local wildlife - which include polar bears, seals, whales, reindeer and arctic foxes.

Children in temporary accommodation hits record high

BBC News Thu, 13 Aug 2026 15:25:02 GMT

The number of homeless children in England living in temporary accommodation has risen 5% in a year to 177,530, according to new government figures.

January to March saw the 18th quarterly increase in a row, although the number of children living in B&Bs has fallen.

Meanwhile, the total number of households in temporary accommodation increased by nearly 4% in a year, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to introduce "the biggest council house-building programme since the postwar period".

Ronesha, 31, has been living in temporary accommodation with her two sons since 2024, after being made homeless following a no-fault eviction. She could not afford to rent privately and discovered that many social landlords wanted prospective tenants to have a guarantor.

The family was housed in a B&B for seven weeks - beyond the six-week limit - without proper cooking facilities or a fridge for her son's medication, she said, before being moved into their current accommodation.

"Living in temporary accommodation has taken a huge toll on my family," she said.

Ronesha, who lives in North London, is a registered carer for her younger child, who has type one diabetes and other complex needs. He has found the instability of being moved between temporary homes very difficult to cope with, she said.

His diabetes glucose monitor beeps in the night in the small flat, which wakes up her older son and has distracted him from his GCSE studies.

"He tried his best to do all the revision he could, but I felt really bad because there was nothing that I could do apart from giving alternatives like studying at a friend's house, or going to the library," Ronesha said.

"It was very difficult for him to study at home."

Section 21 "no-fault" evictions, where tenants can be evicted without giving a reason, are widely regarded as a key driver of homelessness, and were banned from May 2026.

But Ronesha said "Section 21 is not the problem", adding: "My issue is the government allowing landlords to skyrocket rental prices, which are not in line with salaries.

"It doesn't add up."

The Labour government pledged to build 1.5 million new homes in England over the course of this Parliament, but is currently not on course to meet that target.

"It is shameful that a record number of children are growing up without a home because decades of political failure have choked off the supply of genuinely affordable social homes," said Sarah Elliot, chief executive of housing charity Shelter.

"Right now, too many children are spending their childhoods in temporary accommodation that is barely fit for a one-night stay, let alone years on end.

"Whole families are crammed into B&Bs, hostels and tiny bedsits that are freezing and damp in the winter and boiling in the summer."

In his incoming speech as prime minister, Burnham suggested the UK was in the grip of a "housing crisis" and that he wanted to deliver "the biggest council house-building programme since the post-war period".

Shelter said it wanted him to use October's Budget to "kickstart the council house revolution he promised" by removing financial barriers that prevent councils from building more social rent homes.

The total number of households in B&B accommodation fell by almost a quarter in the year to March, with the number of households containing children living in B&Bs falling by half.

About 1,000 households with children had been in B&B accommodation for more than the six-week limit, although this represented a fall on a year earlier.

"While it's welcome that more households are being helped into a home and fewer families are living in bed and breakfast accommodation, these figures show there is still a long way to go, with record numbers stuck in temporary accommodation," Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said.

The government has also pledged an additional £340m to end rough sleeping.

How Premier League shirts will change with gambling sponsor ban

BBC News Thu, 13 Aug 2026 14:57:15 GMT

Nottingham Forest are yet to find a new principal sponsor after gambling deals were banned

Premier League shirts are going to look very different this season.

Twenty years after the door was opened for gambling companies to put their logos on the front of jerseys, it has been closed after clubs voluntarily voted to ban them.

For the past two campaigns, 11 of the 20 clubs have had their shirts adorned with the branding of some kind of betting firm - anything from online bookmakers to crypto casinos, sometimes who do not even operate in the UK.

It shows how finding a shirt sponsor today is very different to how it was in the 1980s, when corporate logos began to appear on kits regularly.

Teams used to attract local companies or foreign firms well-known on these shores. Think Draper Tools, Crown Paints, JVC and Sharp.

That all changed as the Premier League's global appeal mushroomed.

Sponsors could come from any place, and any sector, looking to target specific markets around the world.

As the market took off for the big six, it left the rest of the Premier League looking for the best deals - which came from gambling companies.

Eight Premier League clubs needed to find a new shirt sponsor this summer because of the gambling ban.

Nottingham Forest and Sunderland are still looking, as are Chelsea who have only briefly had a front-of-shirt sponsor in recent seasons.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that this could be down to clubs having greater expectations from their commercial deals.

"This is mainly due to the club's perception of its worth not being matched by that of sponsors themselves," Maguire said. "And the removal of gambling sponsors which has reduced supply.

"Chelsea in particular have struggled in recent seasons, as the club wants a long-term deal at a price that they consider reflects their current status as Fifa Club World Cup champions."

The club signed up with IFS, an AI technology company, for a few months last season - and that shows a trend.

Crystal Palace and Fulham have switched from gambling to technology and AI - to Temporal and ClickHouse respectively.

Premier League sponsorship has moved with the times. From tech, to alcohol, to gambling. As investment in AI companies grows, it is likely more names from this sphere appear on shirts.

Four Premier League clubs will have tech sponsors this season, with Ipswich and Manchester United alongside Palace and Fulham.

But finance is now the leading sector, sponsoring five of the 17 teams, with Everton having signed a deal with CMC Markets.

Other gambling deals have been replaced by sponsors from the fields of insurance, tourism and recruitment.

In the late 1970s, football clubs were actively searching for new revenue streams, but there had been resistance to front-of-shirt sponsorship - especially from TV companies who argued that it amounted to free advertising.

The Football Association and the Football League relented before the start of the 1979-80 season, but sponsors' logos still had to be removed for televised games and all cup ties.

Everton made league history when Hafnia, a Danish tinned meat company, was the first sponsor to appear on a shirt, followed days later by Liverpool, who had signed up with Japanese electronics firm Hitachi.

By 1983-84 the TV ban was scrapped, and all 22 top-flight clubs had deals.

The early years were dominated by emerging electronics companies such as JVC, Panasonic, Pioneer and Sharp.

In the first Premier League season in 1992-93, nine of the 22 clubs had technology sponsors, with Japanese companies accounting for five of them.

Ten sponsors were based in the UK, with seven within 100 miles of their club and four inside 10 miles. One club, Wimbledon, went through the full season without a shirt sponsor.

Today, only four teams have a UK sponsor. Three of those have their headquarters in London, more than 100 miles away from the relevant club.

Now only Ipswich have a local company, with Halo located 12 miles away in Stowmarket.

These days supporters may have to put company names into a search engine to discover what they do, and where they are from - whether that be American tech firm Snapdragon, South African energy drink KNOX Hydration or US artificial intelligence firms ClickHouse and Temporal.

Maguire explained how the value of these deals had soared, with commercial revenue having gone up "by nearly 4,000% from £58m to £2.4bn in 2024-25".

"As the Premier League's broadcasting footprint has increased so has the value of these deals," Maguire said.

"And one of the biggest elements of commercial revenues is front-of-shirt sponsorship deals."

By the mid-1990s, around a third of clubs were sponsored by alcohol brands.

This gradually phased out over time, with Everton's association with Thai brand Chang the last beer sponsor in 2016-17.

The real change came with the 2005 Gambling Act, which gave greater freedom for betting companies to put their names on the front of football shirts.

The explosion of gambling sponsorship began in 2006 with Tottenham's record £34m four-year deal with Mansion, an online gaming and casino platform.

Twenty years on, the big six are signing deals which dwarf that.

When Tottenham renewed their sponsorship deal with finance company AIA in 2019, it was worth £320m over eight years - at £40m a season, almost five times that of Mansion.

"There is no doubt that the big six clubs, as global brands in their own rights, have always been able to generate the highest fees," Maguire said.

"Manchester United's deal with Snapdragon is estimated to be worth about £60m a year, but at the other end of the spectrum a newly promoted club may struggle to get more than £5m or £6m."

Betting and casino companies still have greater advertising budgets than most other sectors, meaning they could link up with Premier League clubs outside the big six.

"This resulted in the proliferation of deals, nearly always with the 'other 14' clubs - Clubs who operate at much lower commercial fee levels than the global football brands," Maguire said.

By 2017-18 nine clubs had gambling companies on their shirts. For the past two seasons, it was up to 11.

Manchester United's training gear deal with a betting company is reported to be worth up to £20m a year

Clubs were given permission to put sponsors' logos on the back of shirts and the sleeves from the 2017-18 season, opening up another revenue stream.

It has proved lucrative and only served to drive a greater gap between the richest and the rest.

"The big six clubs are looking for a minimum of £10m per season, and can double this if there are secondary relationships with the sponsors," Maguire said.

"The other clubs may be willing to settle for amounts below £1m, although this may change from 2026-27 as gambling companies migrate from front-of-shirt deals."

While some clubs have transferred betting sponsors on to other parts of their apparel, it has not been widespread.

Betano has moved from Aston Villa's shirt to sleeve. Everton have done the same with Stake. com, though crypto casinos could be banned from the end of the season too.

Bournemouth, who have extended their stadium sponsorship with Vitality insurance to the front of their shirts, will still have betting advertising. MrQ casino will be on the sleeve, with bookmakers' SBK on the training wear.

Brentford, Crystal Palace, Fulham, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland have not, as yet, announced any new on-shirt gambling sponsorship.

Manchester United's pull has been shown by their training gear deal, which would be worth more than the front-of-shirt sponsorship of most clubs.

"Manchester United's deal with Betway is estimated to be worth up to £20m a year," Maguire said.

"Many of the smaller clubs do not have separate training kit sponsor deals because the level of interest in the club and potential merchandise sales do not warrant an arrangement, and the training kit is therefore bundled with the front-of-shirt deal."

Other clubs do have betting partners, with branding appearing inside grounds, online and across LED board around the pitch.

But only five of the 20 Premier League clubs have confirmed that there will be gambling logos somewhere on clothing.

The next battle ground could be cryptocurrency firms which are appearing on shirt sleeves.

BingX sponsors Chelsea and OKX has an sleeve agreement with Manchester City.

The Financial Conduct Authority has called them, external "questionable sponsorship deals with unauthorised financial firms".

Fans have spent the last 20 years walking around advertising betting companies on the front of their shirts. Could it be crypto currency exchanges next?

Who could replace White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt?

BBC News Thu, 13 Aug 2026 14:56:19 GMT

The departure of White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt will create a major opening in President Donald Trump's administration, and the guessing-game of who will replace her has already begun.

So far, the White House has not announced who will succeed Leavitt, and sources within and close to the administration said no decision has yet been made.

Leavitt has worked closely with Trump for years, and finding someone to take over could prove difficult. In announcing she would step down at the end of the month, Trump called Leavitt one of his "most trusted aides".

When Leavitt was on leave earlier this year, a series of high-ranking figures, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, gave press briefings, instead of a temporary substitute from her office. Some expect the White House to return to that system, at least temporarily.

But the complex job goes beyond the briefing room podium to include managing contentious relationships with the press, coordinating with other parts of the White House, and providing media advice to the president. The secretary also oversees an office that receives a significant amount of inquiries and requests on a daily basis.

Perhaps most importantly, Leavitt's replacement will also be expected to live up to Trump's expectations.

"It's not easy," a source close to the administration told the BBC. "That person will be very aware that he's watching every day."

Here's a look at a few of the potential candidates for the job.

Alina Habba was formerly President Trump's personal lawyer.

In December, she resigned as the top federal prosecutor in New Jersey, after a court battle over her eligibility to serve as US attorney for the state.

Trump selected Habba for the role of US attorney last year. When a district court rejected her nomination, Trump then installed her in a role allowing her to fill in on an acting basis.

During Trump's first few months back at the White House, Habba served as the president's counsellor. In announcing her appointment, Trump described Habba as "unwavering in her loyalty" and a "tireless advocate for justice".

Habba, 42, first joined Trump's personal legal team in 2021 after reportedly meeting him at his golf club in Bedminster, New Jersey.

She went on to represent Trump in his hush-money trial in New York in 2024, when he was convicted on 34 counts of falsifying business records. Trump has filed an appeal against that conviction.

Katie Miller is an influential conservative podcaster, media personality and former Trump staffer.

The 34-year-old is married to White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller - the conservative firebrand who set the president's hard-line immigration agenda in motion.

She served as press secretary to former Vice-President Mike Pence from 2019 to 2020, and then as his communications director from 2020 to 2021.

She was later the communications director for Doge, the cost-cutting initiative headed by billionaire Elon Musk also called the "Department of Government Efficiency".

Miller's podcast, launched last August, is targeted toward conservative women and busy mothers.

Anna Kelly is currently White House deputy press secretary and works under Leavitt.

The 29-year-old former beauty queen has represented the White House in the media.

She was previously the national press secretary for the Republican National Committee and worked for Representative Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin.

Sage Steele, a former television anchor and sportscaster, campaigned for Trump during the 2024 election.

The 53-year-old has emerged as a prominent conservative media figure and continued supporter of the president.

She has hosted several sports programs, including SportsCenter, First Take and the Scripps National Spelling Bee.

Steven Cheung is the White House's communications director and a long-time Trump adviser.

The spokesperson has been known for his combative approach with the media and fervent defence of the president.

Cheung joined Trump's 2016 campaign and later became the director of rapid response during his first term. He left the White House in 2018 and started a private firm that worked with Trump's 2020 campaign.

Prior to joining Trump's team, he headed communications for the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC).

After the announcement of Leavitt's departure, he posted a photo with her and congratulated her on "A job well done!"

He added: "Karoline has been the best teammate. She is fiercely loyal, unflappable, and a great person who serves the President with honor."

As a former assistant secretary for public affairs at the Department of Homeland Security, McLaughlin was known for ferociously defending the Trump administration's immigration policies on US airwaves.

She has maintained a low profile since leaving the role in February, but McLaughlin also has strong bona fides stretching back to the first Trump term, when she served in a variety of roles at the treasury and the State Department.

McLaughlin has been a political contributor for ABC News, and served as communications director for Ohio Governor Mike DeWine and for the short-lived presidential campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy.

Political commentator Scott Jennings has emerged as a fierce defender of the Trump administration on CNN, where he is a senior political contributor, earning him widespread praise from many of the president's supporters.

Once a critic of Trump, 48-year-old Jennings also has considerable experience in politics, having worked on four presidential campaigns.

He also worked on three of Kentucky Senator Mitch McConnell's campaigns, and is considered a close ally of the former party leader.

Trump has publicly praised Jennings, who last year published the book A Revolution of Common Sense: How Donald Trump Stormed Washington and Fought for Western Civilization.

"He's defending me all the time on CNN," Trump said at a rally in Michigan last year. "And he defends me really well, but he can't go too far because if he goes too far, he'll get fired."

Eclipse warning: The key signs you may have damaged your eyes

BBC News Thu, 13 Aug 2026 11:57:28 GMT

Eye experts are warning people to be on the alert for any signs their vision has been damaged by looking at the sun during Wednesday's eclipse.

The symptoms can include blurred vision, a central blind or dark spot and increased sensitivity to light.

After the previous total eclipse of the sun that was visible in the UK in 1999, around 70 people were left with damaged sight.

Many of them had spent less than a minute looking at the spectacle, without realising they were harming their eyes.

The danger comes because staring at an eclipse without protection can damage the retina, which sits at the back of the eye, and particularly those cells responsible for sharp central vision.

The sun is incredibly bright, even when partially obscured by the moon.

Normally if we stare at it, we wince and quickly look away.

But when it is darker, during an eclipse, that instinct may not kick in, even while our eyes are being damaged.

The bright light and ultraviolet radiation given off by the sun can lead to a condition known as "solar retinopathy".

And because the retina has no pain receptors, it's hard for people to notice the damage as it happens, so symptoms may only appear several hours later.

Leading up to the eclipse itself, experts were warning only genuine specially-designed solar eclipse glasses should be used, and that ordinary sunglasses or other devices were not enough to prevent potential damage.

Alexander Ionides, a consultant eye surgeon at Moorfields Eye Hospital in London says if you have damaged your eyes, the symptoms will start to come on within a few hours.

"It's a central spot in the visual field, whatever you're looking at, if you're looking at someone's face, or the writing of the page or the clock on the wall, you may have a distortion.

"It'll be a grey or a yellow or a dark spot right in the very centre of your vision.

"It doesn't hurt, there's no pain like what a burn might be considered to be like, and it can just very gradually come on."

Other symptoms to be aware of include:

Ionides says if you think you have damaged your eyes, you should seek urgent medical attention.

"There are different ways to get the eyes checked out in the UK, you can always go to a local optician, they're very well equipped now," he added.

"They can do retinal scans to look for any solar retinopathy, which is the damage to the retina from looking at the eclipse.

"And also they can refer you on to the local eye unit. There are local eye casualties as well. And most hospitals will have an eye doctor on call."

Because of the delay in symptoms developing it is not yet possible to say if anyone has experienced any damage to their eyes.

A partial eclipse like the one the UK experienced on Wednesday meant the sun was still pretty bright, so far fewer people may have tried to stare at it directly.

Ionides says compared to 1999, so far fewer people have contacted his hospital.

"Back in 1999, the switchboard and the casualty were inundated with many, many people coming along worried, or having had some damage.

"But so far, it's only the morning after, but at the moment there have been a lot fewer people contacting the hospital or coming along to casualty, which might mean that the message is getting out there, that it is damaging to look directly at the sun with the naked eye."

'I was blown away' - the fans who heard Phoebe Bridgers' unreleased album in a planetarium

BBC News Thu, 13 Aug 2026 05:23:45 GMT

What happens when a Grammy Award-winning artist, one of the most anticipated albums of the year and a planetarium collide?

This week the small city of Armagh found out.

It's been six years since songwriter Phoebe Bridgers last released an album, so the release of Lost Weekend on Friday marks, as The Guardian says, a "long-awaited return".

Since her last record, the critically acclaimed Punisher, she's recorded and toured with Grammy Award-winning supergroup boygenius, as well as navigating grief after the death of her father.

And now, in the days leading up to Lost Weekend's release, she's giving a handful of fans an "immersive" audio-visual experience at planetariums across the world.

Only two venues in the UK - Glasgow and Armagh - were chosen to take part.

The Lost Weekend Planetarium show combines curated, nocturnal scenes by National Geographic night-sky photographer Babak Tafreshi with the 16-track record.

The Armagh Planetarium hosted four, sold-out showings on Tuesday, and another four will be held on Thursday.

A phone free event, attendees have to put their devices into a pouch, which can only be opened by a magnet after the event is over.

Critics have described Lost Weekend - as a "daring exploration of love, grief and renewal," alternately spooky, hilarious, mysterious and sneakily moving and worth the wait as well as "staggering and stirring".

Some lyrics make reference to Bridgers' engagement, and eventual break-up, with Irish actor Paul Mescal, and the record is dedicated to her father, who died a few years ago.

Sisters Eibhlin and Emma were among the 80-strong crowd in the event's first screening.

The pair had an immediate one-word review: "Amazing."

"Before this, we had only heard one song so the whole rest of it was completely fresh and new and the visuals were amazing," Eiblin said.

"There were times I thought that the visuals linked really well to the music and the lyrics so it was just a really cool experience," Emma added.

However, time will tell whether it comes up top in their album rankings.

"I think you couldn't rank it after listening to it once, that's too hard. I need to focus harder next time to rank," Eibhlin explained.

Emma added: "I felt like it had a rockier, or even a folk sound to it which I really liked, that it was really cool.

"When it comes out properly then we can dissect the lyrics and see."

For fans like Kev, who were lucky enough to be at the event, the album's themes played well into the spatial experience.

"There's something both very human and very spacey about it, so I like that she married the two," he said.

"It was very calming, very emotive at the right time. There are songs on there that did really blow me away."

Armagh native and Bridgers fan Cathleen said she was "delighted" to see her hometown on the list of places showcasing the event.

"It's really cool, I don't think a lot of people would associate Armagh with contemporary, modern things, it's quite a historic town.

"So it's nice now we're getting recognised by a younger generation and younger artists."

Speaking before the showing, Cathleen explained why she could relate to most of Bridgers' music.

"Everyone's had those relationships and encounters," she said.

Also among those who were at Armagh Planetarium were Abbie and Scott, who had made the three-and-a-half hour journey from County Waterford.

"Sure, what else would you be at on a Tuesday night?" joked Scott.

The pair both have tickets to Bridgers sold-out run of shows in Dublin's 3Arena in November, but said the early listening event would be a good "preview".

"I relate to a lot of her songs," Abbie added. "I really like her song writing, and I think she's really cool."

Her relatable lyrics also brought friends Tara and Emma to the Planetarium for Tuesday's first showing.

"Her music is really powerful and it really helps connect people together," Tara said.

Emma agreed: "You can really understand the lyrics and it really shows the stages of growing up and life."

Speaking before the event, friends Emma, Bec and Arron were excited about hearing the long-awaited new songs, and didn't particularly mind that they couldn't have their phones out during the show.

"It's nice just to switch off and you're not going to have someone's camera in your face or a flash going off in a room and ruin it for you," Arron said.

"They were all scrambling at the start saying, 'Don't text me'," Bec joked.

"We've sent all of our SOS messages in case anybody's looking for us," Arron added.

Heather Alexander from Armagh Planetarium said there was a demand "never seen before" for the show, with phones ringing off the hook in the days before.

But, she added, it was an honour to be hosting it.

"It makes us feel so special because we're looking at all these other venues, like America, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and then there's Armagh, Northern Ireland," she said.

"It really puts us on the map to show that we are very keen to do collaborations like this, so if there's any other big stars out there that really want to do this type of immersive experience, we're all about it.

"We've just had the Fleadh in Belfast, we've shown that we're all about music and this event is just a little cherry on top for us."

Putin can no longer claim victory in Ukraine, Nobel Peace Prize winner tells BBC

BBC News Thu, 13 Aug 2026 04:55:58 GMT

At the Moscow offices of newspaper Novaya Gazeta, the corridors are silent.

There is an overwhelming sense of emptiness.

"There is no newspaper anymore," former chief editor Dmitry Muratov tells me in an exclusive interview, published on the BBC News YouTube channel.

Muratov, 64, co-founded Novaya Gazeta more than 30 years ago. It became the flagship for hard-hitting independent journalism in Russia, shining a light on human rights abuses and high-level corruption.

In 2021 Muratov was joint winner of the Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression." The Nobel Committee noted that "six of [Novaya Gazeta's] journalists have been killed, including Anna Politkovskaya who wrote revealing articles on the war in Chechnya."

It was recognition for courageous reporting.

But it didn't protect the paper.

"Putin issued a decree and the newspaper's printing presses were nationalised," Muratov explains. "Its registration was revoked."

Novaya Gazeta does retain a presence online. But only just: the authorities have blocked access to its website. It can only be accessed from abroad, or with the help of VPNs – virtual private networks used to circumvent restrictions.

The newspaper's difficulties reflect the broader crackdown on free speech in Russia which has accelerated since the Kremlin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Most opinion leaders have been declared 'foreign agents', 'extremists' or 'terrorists'. Several hundred," says Muratov.

"Figures vary, but at a conservative estimate, since the start of Russia's 'special military operation' [in Ukraine] at least 1,500 people are now in prison having spoken out against current state policy. That's three times more than during the savage days of the KGB in the USSR."

In his 1975 Nobel Peace Prize lecture dissident Andrei Sakharov listed the names of more than 120 political prisoners he was aware of in the Soviet Union. A decade later Amnesty International estimated more than 600 prisoners of conscience in the USSR.

What the Kremlin had assumed in 2022 would be a short, successful "military operation" has become the bloodiest conflict in Europe since World War Two.

Yet a confident President Vladimir Putin continues to predict victory for Russia.

"There will never be 'victory'," counters Muratov. "Because what has been going on for nearly five years – no matter how it ends – can no longer be considered a victory.

"It cannot be a victory when two Slavic nations have ripped a million people to shreds. Or more than a million."

"It seems to me that the situation with Ukraine now is this: you can destroy it, but you cannot conquer it. What do I mean by destroy? Continued escalation all the way to the use of a nuclear weapon."

Does he really believe the Kremlin leader would use nuclear weapons in this war?

"All those political experts who say 'Putin thinks this' or 'Putin is scared of that'…they're all charlatans," claims Muratov. "It's in the same league as astrology. Nobody knows what's going on in Vladimir Putin's head. And I don't know.

"I see things only as a journalist. I study big data. And since the beginning of the year the need to use nuclear weapons has been mentioned more than 500 times. When wackos say this, I pay no attention. But I've heard it discussed on state TV. And at the St Petersburg International Economic Forum, a state-run event, one of the speakers talked up the use of nuclear weapons as something favourable, something good."

When he announced the mass invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Putin spoke of "ensuring the security of Russia."

"Tell me, has security increased?" Muratov asks. "With Ukrainian drones now attacking warehouses of [Russia's largest online retailer] Wildberries; with the petrol crisis, the disruption to mobile internet, the political prisoners? Has security increased, or not?"

Despite opinion polls registering a fall in Putin's domestic approval ratings, Russia's president – Muratov believes - retains a tight grip on power.

"Sorry, I don't believe all this talk about a split among members of the elite, about secret conspiracies. The country is run by Vladimir Putin. They're frightened of him.

"And this fear is reinforced in every way by his main support base: the Federal Security Service (FSB)."

As critical as he is of his own government, he has few illusions about the West.

"[Putin] knows very well the true value of European leaders. On the one hand they talk to him about human rights. He laughs out loud because, with the other hand, they sign agreements – or used to sign agreements – with Russia on trading oil, gas, diamonds…all that stuff. When they talk to Putin about European values, he truly laughs out loud. He knows the true value of people who preached to him those values."

In Russia Muratov has been designated a "foreign agent", a label often used to punish critics of the Kremlin. "Foreign agents" have limited rights: they're banned from teaching, from taking part in elections; if they sell their flat, they can't access the assets. The label is also designed to stigmatise, to create the sense in society of an enemy within.

Yet the journalist appears reluctant to focus on the pressures he's under, preferring instead to highlight the plight of compatriots in prison.

"What worries me most right now is that no one in the world is interested in the political prisoners who were first to speak out against the land grab in our neighbouring country," Muratov explains.

He opens a folder and takes out a stack of large photographs: portraits of prisoners.

One shows four journalists - Antonina Favorskaya, Konstantin Gabov, Sergey Karelin and Artyom Kriger – convicted and jailed on extremism charges. They'd been accused of links to the anti-corruption organisation of the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny.

There's a photo of Alexei Gorinov: a city councillor jailed for "knowingly spreading false information" about the Russian military after he spoke out against the war in Ukraine.

"And here's a wonderful pianist, Pavel Kushnir," says Miratov. "An outstanding performer of Rachmaninoff and Schubert."

The musician was arrested after posting anti-war videos. Muratov holds up a second video.

"And this is him in his coffin."

Pavel Kushnir died in a pre-trial detention centre during a hunger strike. He was 39.

The stream of photos and prison stories highlights the dangers for individuals framed as opponents of those in power. It's a reminder of the risks that public criticism of the authorities and the war carry.

"Does being a Nobel Prize laureate give you at least some protection to say what you want?" I ask.

"This is not a question for me," replies Muratov. "Whenever you have the opportunity, ask the authorities that."

There is one more photo. From April.

"This is the newspaper's lawyer when she was waiting to get into the building. The police were searching our office. Thirteen hours it took. And they wouldn't let the lawyers in. Our managing editor Oleg Roldugin is now under house arrest."

Muratov paints a bleak picture of life in Russia for critics of the authorities.

Yet there are moments of hope.

"We live in a time when you stay quiet. But so many people support what we do. On the streets of Moscow, my colleagues and I hear only words of gratitude. They are spoken in a whisper. But what people think is very important."

Six ways to keep your home and yourself cool in hot weather

BBC News Mon, 22 Jun 2026 11:13:44 GMT

When temperatures soar, there are a number of simple things you can do to help keep your home and yourself cool.

Here are six practical tips from experts.

Open windows on opposite sides of the house to encourage air flow - releasing trapped warm air and allowing in cooler air.

Do this when the air temperature outside is cooler than inside, which tends to be overnight or in the early part of the day.

In flats which have windows on one side only, open doors and use a fan to encourage airflow.

Hot air rises within houses, so if you have loft vents or windows you can open them to release some of the heat.

The hot air can otherwise get trapped on the second floor, where you may be trying to sleep.

Extra insulation can also help keep heat out in the summer, as well as reducing your energy bills and usage in the winter.

In the heat of the day it is best to keep your windows shut and blinds or curtains closed - especially on the side of your home where the sun is shining.

Fans are a relatively cheap and energy efficient way to keep air moving and can help you stay cool.

Using a freestanding fan for a 24-hour period typically costs between 15p and 31p, according to the latest guidance from the Energy Saving Trust.

Putting the fan in front of an open window can encourage the fresh air from outside to be blown throughout the room - as long as it is cooler outside.

Placing ice cubes in front of the fan can cool the air being blown in your direction. You can use more than one fan to create a cross current.

Prof Mike Tipton of the University of Portsmouth says it is important to understand how the body works.

"Fanning the face improves thermal comfort most, but fanning the whole body helps lower body temperature more," he says.

Air conditioning is a much more expensive option than using fans. The Energy Saving Trust says 24 hours of continuous use costs between £4.84 – £6.

Ovens and cookers emit a lot of heat into the home during and after their use.

Sticking to cold foods such as salads - especially during the hottest times of the day - can stop unnecessary heat being generated.

Other appliances, such as washing machines and dishwashers, can also produce heat so try not to use them when it is hottest.

Heat exhaustion can also be brought on by high humidity - moisture in the air - so it is worth reducing humidity levels by:

Heat exhaustion is not usually serious as long as you can cool yourself down, but heatstroke is a medical emergency which requires immediate treatment.

Call 999 if you suspect someone has heatstroke.

Tepid showers can help to cool your body temperature, saving both money and energy. But Prof Tipton warns not to go too cold: "The trick is to try and get the skin as cool as possible whilst maintaining maximum blood flow to it.

"Too cold and the body will shut down blood to the skin and trap the heat in the body making it harder to get out."

Putting an ice pack or cold-water bottle on your body can achieve an instant feeling of relief. You may want to wrap it in a towel to avoid direct contact with your skin.

Your clothes can also really affect your body temperature.

Natural fibres like cotton and linen help to regulate body temperature and loose-fitting clothing allows room for the breeze to cool you down.

This is also why cotton bed sheets can help you sleep when hot air fills a room.

Air-conditioned public buildings such as libraries, leisure centres and shopping centres can also provide relief if your home is too hot.

Some local authorities have created a network of so-called "cool spaces" where the public can go, including London, Manchester and Bristol.
