As we go about our everyday lives, we’re constantly interacting with things made possible by mining – often without realising it. From the phones in our hands to the cars we drive, almost everything relies on core minerals and commodities that begin their journey in the earth. Along the way, there is a chance that leading heavy equipment manufacturer Komatsu has played a role.

This is also true of the Atlassian Williams F1 Team’s FW48 challenger. You may think a modern race car is just made of carbon fibre, but that is only part of the story. Beneath the surface of the machine lies a myriad of advanced materials across the powertrain, electronics, bodywork and chassis, each playing a vital role in the car’s design and performance at the highest level.

Unearthing performance

In the cockpit, the halo safety structure relies on titanium for its exceptional ability to withstand extreme loads. Magnesium, one of the lightest structural metals, is found in the wheel rims, helping to improve acceleration and overall handling. Nearby, iron, refined into steel, is used in selected fasteners, bolts and drivetrain components, delivering the necessary strength for high-load applications.

At the heart of the FW48’s electrified powertrain is the battery system. Lithium provides the high energy density required to deliver the electrical power that defines the sport’s new generation of power units. Alongside it, copper forms the backbone of the FW48’s electrical systems, carrying power and data between wiring, electronics and sensors.

In the engine and exhaust systems, lightweight and highly machinable aluminium helps reduce overall vehicle mass and efficiently dissipates heat from critical engine components. Meanwhile, nickel alloys retain their strength at temperatures exceeding 1,000°C, ensuring reliability in one of the harshest environments on the car.

From one pit to another

Facilitating the journey of these materials from the first cut into the earth to lights out on race day is a fleet of Komatsu mining machines working around the clock.

From 320XPC drills preparing blast holes, to PC9000 hydraulic excavators and 4100XPC electric rope shovels loading material, to 930E autonomous ultra-class, electric-drive haul trucks moving hundreds of tonnes in every load, Komatsu equipment helps uncover, move and process the resources that the world depends on.

Together with the incredible people behind every operation, Komatsu machines ensure that mining is performed safely and efficiently across the globe, 24 hours a day, seven days a week. This is just a snapshot of the global mining ecosystem of the advanced materials engineered into the Atlassian Williams F1 Team car. Behind every lap lies a story of innovation that starts deep beneath the earth – all made possible by the people and mining machines of companies like Komatsu.

“As a team, we never stop finding new ways to use materials, exploring different manufacturing methods to extract every last bit of performance. Komatsu is the same, and today they operate at the cutting edge of their industry.”

Running with a stroller seems to reduce the risk of injuries

New Scientist August 12, 2026

Running with a pram or stroller might make parents less susceptible to ankle pain and injuries to their calf muscles, foot arches and Achilles tendons. A survey of parents suggests there is a 37 per cent drop in injury risk with pram use. This may be partly due to changes in vertical forces – how much force our legs absorb with each step – when pushing a child.

“You get a little bit of a walker effect where you’re leaning and putting some weight on the stroller,” says Allison Altman Singles at Pennsylvania State University, who ran with a pram after the births of her two children. “That led me to wonder, you know, is this actually protective?”

Your running style changes when you’re short of sleep

Previous research suggests that people running with a pram tend to have shorter strides and slower speeds. They also lean forward more, with greater hip flexion and forward pelvic tilt. Last year, Altman Singles and her colleagues found there is a 16 per cent lower vertical impact force when running with a pram, but whether this affects injury risk was unclear.

Advertisement

To learn more, Altman Singles and her team analysed self-reported running and injury data from 196 parents who used any kind of pram on at least some of their runs while their children were younger than 3 years old. These individuals were compared against another 53 mothers or fathers who ran when their children were the same age, but without prams. All the participants had some running experience before becoming parents.

Free newsletter

The two groups of parents covered similar total distances and were relatively well matched in terms of factors like age, height and weight. But there were many more women than men in both groups, particularly the pram one.

Overall, 30 per cent of the non-pram runners reported having had running-related injuries, compared with 19 per cent of the pram runners. These included a higher incidence of ankle pain, calf muscle injury, plantar fasciitis (heel pain that occurs when the thick band of tissue on the bottom of the foot becomes irritated or inflamed) and Achilles tendinitis (injury of the Achilles tendon).

The slow-running movement, in which people meet for unhurried jogs, is booming – but don’t be fooled into thinking that if there’s no pain, there’s no gain

“Generally, stroller running involves rapid steps with short stride lengths,” says Cara Wall-Scheffler at Seattle Pacific University. “Although this can increase metabolic cost, it can also decrease the force production at each foot strike, which might explain some of these injury reductions.”

Wall-Scheffler says we should see this paper as a “great start” to understanding an important topic. However, future work should include a more balanced mix of men and women, she says. For instance, oestrogen and progesterone may affect the pliability of connective tissue, which could affect a woman’s injury risk.

Future studies should also collect injury-related data more regularly over time and could even investigate the effects of different pram-pushing styles, such as using one or two hands, says Wall-Scheffler.

PLoS One DOI: 10.1371/journal. pone.0354371

We should decide how AI shapes the future, not tech firms

New Scientist August 12, 2026

IT is said that history is written by the victors, but who gets to pen the future? For most of the 21st century, that authorial role has been played by tech wizards of Silicon Valley such as Steve Jobs, Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk. Today, they are joined in prophesising and proselytising by OpenAI and its competitors, who promise either a machine utopia or an AI apocalypse – and sometimes both.

As AI models encroach on ever more areas of human endeavour, it is easy to feel that, as mathematician Terence Tao puts it, we have lost control of the narrative. With OpenAI releasing multiple PhDs’ worth of results in one go, it is no wonder that Tao is calling for his colleagues to wrest back authority over what it means to be a mathematician.

Why I have changed my mind about AI and you should too

This tech-first control of the narrative is further illustrated by the disclosure OpenAI made last month that its AI models had unexpectedly hacked another firm, Hugging Face, during cybersecurity testing. Writing in apocalypse mode, OpenAI called this an “unprecedented cyber incident” and said the firm was taking steps to prevent it from happening again.

Advertisement

In subsequent weeks, other AI firms including Anthropic and Meta have made similar disclosures, suggesting such incidents are widespread across the industry. As the tech firms tell it, these are accidents, and they are now cleaning up their mess. But why are we allowing them to write the story?

AI models are building the future, but that doesn’t mean the rest of us must idly stand by

If a human employee of these companies had hacked another organisation, we would expect a criminal investigation. Uncertainty about the autonomy of AI models, fuelled by the AI firms themselves, seems to have avoided legal consequences thus far. If society was less willing to buy the AI narrative, the outcome could be very different.

At this point, it is hard to deny that the latest AI models are building the future. That doesn’t mean, however, that the rest of us must idly stand by and watch it happen. In the face of world-shaping technology, it should be the world that decides how it is used, not the tech firms.

‘Remarkable’ discovery upends our understanding of how brains store memories

New Scientist August 13, 2026

Our memories may persist even when half of the brain connections that store them are wiped out, according to a study in dormant mice. The “remarkable” discovery tells us more about how memory works and could one day reveal ways to improve it.

“Memories may be harder to break than we thought,” says Steve Ramirez at Boston University, who wasn’t involved in the study. “This absolutely, substantially advances our understanding of how memory works.”

What is a ‘normal’ memory slowdown, and when should I worry?

When we experience a stimulus, neurons in our sensory organs, like our eyes, transmit electrical signals to our brain. Neurons then process this information by firing electrical signals to each other via junctions called synapses.

Advertisement

These neurons, called engram neurons, encode information into a memory by forming new synapses and strengthening existing ones. Recalling a memory further bolsters these connections and our memory.

Many scientists think a memory persists as long as the specific pattern of synapses on the engram neurons encoding that memory is maintained. This is partly based on experiments that have used drugs or genetic tools to disrupt synapses on engram neurons, says Kazumasa Tanaka at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology in Japan.

Nelson Dellis credits techniques like the method of loci for his extraordinary memory. Now, brain scans have revealed the parts of his brain that this approach taps into, and how we can use it to improve our own recall

But recent studies suggest a memory persists even when these synapses are altered in location or number. This has called into question “what’s necessary and sufficient to have a memory preserved”, says George Dragoi at Yale University.

To address this, Tanaka and his colleagues took inspiration from hibernating animals. “Under hibernation, brain activity seems to drop significantly,” he says. “But studies in natural hibernators show that somehow those animals, after arousal in the spring, seem to remember their friends and the location of food they hid before hibernation.”

By examining how memory is retained during hibernation, a situation in which the brain changes dramatically, the researchers hoped to unpick basic principles by which the mammalian brain stores memories long term. “The [researchers] very cleverly and creatively get at the question of memory by using hibernation as a way to poke and prod at the brain,” says Ramirez.

They applied weak electric shocks to the feet of mice – which don’t naturally hibernate – while they were in a chamber that smelled of alcohol, creating a fearful memory associated with that scent. The next day, the mice froze in fear upon being placed in the same chamber, without receiving shocks.

The researchers induced an artificial state of hibernation in about half the mice for two days. This was done by injecting them with drugs that slow metabolism and placing them in a dark chamber.

Free newsletter

Five days later, mice that had artificially hibernated still froze when placed in the alcohol-smelling chamber. This was despite brain scans revealing that more than half of the synapses within the engram neurons in their hippocampus – a brain region crucial for memory – disappeared during hibernation. “Despite massive brain remodelling during hibernation, the memories were retained,” says Tanaka.

Dragoi says the findings are relevant to people, since prior research has shown that our brains store information very similarly to mice. “It tells us something about how our mammalian brains may work,” says Ramirez.

The team also found that the hibernating rodents’ brains retained synapses that clustered closely together on the surface of engram neurons, while those outside these clusters disappeared. This suggests that clustered synapses specifically are crucial for retaining memory in the brain, says Tanaka.

Non-clustered synapses that were wiped out by hibernation reappeared within a day post-hibernation, indicating that, while clustered engram synapses are necessary to retain the information within memories, the non-clustered synapses may be important for accessing memories, he says.

Women appear cognitively normal for almost three years longer than men after their brains start to develop Alzheimer’s disease, making it harder to diagnose and preventing early treatment

“This study is a remarkable step forward because it addresses a long-standing puzzle in memory research: how the brain retains long-term memories,” says Priyanka Rao-Ruiz at Vrije University Amsterdam in the Netherlands.

The team is exploring the molecular pathways through which clustered engram synapses store information and plans to dig into how non-clustered ones reappear, says Tanaka.

Targeting such pathways with drugs could even reveal ways to prevent or slow memory impairment, says Ramirez. “It gives hope that even in instances where information seems to be lost in the brain, whether it’s amnesia or Alzheimer’s disease, memory may nonetheless persist.”

Science DOI: 10.1126/science. aee7004

DNA reveals a society organised around women in pre-Roman Britain

New Scientist August 13, 2026

The DNA of more than 500 individuals who were buried in the north-east of England over a period of several centuries before the Roman invasion of Britain in AD 43 has been sequenced. It reveals a society organised around women, with large clans for which descent could be traced down the female line for up to nine generations, but where fathers were often absent from burial sites.

The study also reveals that some women had multiple male partners and shows a pattern of repeated unions between two maternal clans. “It’s revolutionary, and will totally change the way we think about the Iron Age,” says Rachel Pope at the University of Liverpool in the UK, who wasn’t involved in the study.

Archaeologists are unearthing the most powerful women who ever lived

It was suggested in the 1860s that early societies were female-led, but the idea was rejected by later anthropologists, who assumed male-led societies were the natural order. From the 1950s onwards, however, discoveries in Europe of lavish burials of ancient women showed that in some societies women could be of high status at the very least.

Advertisement

More recently, studies of ancient DNA have begun adding to the evidence. Last year a study of around 50 individuals buried in south-west England revealed that women remained in their ancestral homes while men moved around, a pattern known as matrilocality.

Now Ian Armit at the University of York, UK, and his colleagues have sequenced the DNA of around 500 individuals associated with the Arras culture, famed for its chariot burials. The remains of nearly 400 of these individuals were excavated by other archaeological teams at Wetwang Slack in the East Riding of Yorkshire, which was most active between the fourth and second centuries BC and is the largest known Iron Age burial ground in Britain. The rest came from nearby sites.

The Arras DNA also reveals a strong matrilocal pattern. Most of the women buried at Wetwang Slack also had close relatives buried there, such as a mother, for instance, but this was rarer for men. In a few cases, the team found direct evidence that a man originating from one site fathered children at another – in other words, that men moved around while women stayed put.

Flat head syndrome discovered in Iron Age skeletons

Matrilocality by itself doesn’t necessarily mean that women ruled a society. But it is generally associated with higher status and better conditions for women. An individual who leaves home to live with the family of a partner is reliant on that family and thus is in a weaker position than one who stays.

However, when the DNA evidence is combined with other evidence, it does point to societies where women could rule. “For Britain, the archaeological evidence supports a more equitable Iron Age than scholars had previously imagined, and some powerful women were certainly part of that,” says Pope. “From [bone injuries], we can even see now that some women were in combat with Rome.”

“Powerful Iron Age women abound in the texts: Onomaris, Boudica, Cartimandua, Celts with their women as judges,” she says. “Historians of the 1860s and 1870s believed in a largely matriarchal Iron Age until 1880s English anthropology asserted a patriarchal norm.”

Subscriber-only newsletter

That said, there was also regional diversity in how societies were organised, says Pope. Other DNA studies suggest that Iron Age societies in south-east England, for instance, weren’t matrilocal.

At least 12 of the Arras women had children with more than one man. This could reflect serial monogamy, the team members – who declined to be interviewed for this story – write in a preprint, but it could also reflect “polyandrous reproductive arrangements within a strongly female-line-centred social structure”. In other words, women could have had multiple husbands simultaneously, as some Roman sources claim was the case.

The team did find one case where a man had children with a woman and with her daughter, but this was exceptional.

Ancient Egyptians may have built a massive dam near the Red Pyramid

The genetics also show that individuals from the same maternal lineage avoided having children with each other. Because these people lived in small groups in which a large proportion of people were related, this must have been deliberate and based on knowledge of people’s ancestry. “[T]his avoidance demonstrates detailed knowledge of maternal-line affiliation across many generations and possibly hundreds of years,” the study concludes.

The exceptions to this were the three individuals – two male, one female – buried with chariots. “The individuals afforded chariot burials at Wetwang Slack stood apart by showing recurrent close kin unions, consistent with a reproductive strategy in which high status, identity and claims to particular forms of burial were concentrated within a restricted descent group,” the study says.

Genetic analysis of 1039 people buried in Britain between the Bronze Age and the Norman conquest highlights the impact of the Romans, Anglo-Saxons and Vikings on the island’s ancestry

All these lines of evidence point to a society organised around women rather than men, the researchers conclude. “[F]emale-line descent was not an incidental feature of Arras culture communities, but a central organising principle, as it may well have been across the communities of Iron Age Britain more broadly.”

“It is an excellent paper, closely argued and very rich in data and inference,” says Daniel Bradley at Trinity College Dublin in Ireland, who was part of the team that studied the 50 or so individuals buried in south-west England.

“We did notice a tendency for marriage across [maternal lineages] in our study, but the finding here of a sustained pattern of unions between two different maternal clan groups is really striking. It implies a deep knowledge of family histories – of which maternal social axis one belonged to – and perhaps of an alliance forming between them,” Bradley says.

Quantum entanglement is key to solving 250-year-old maths problem

New Scientist August 13, 2026

Quantum entanglement is key to solving a 250-year-old mathematical puzzle – and the discovery could ultimately help build quantum computers that are more resilient to errors.

In the 1700s, according to folklore, Russian Empress Catherine the Great posed a puzzle to the polymath Leonhard Euler. Could he find a way to arrange 36 military officers from six different regiments in a 6-by-6 grid so that in each row and each column, each officer belongs to a different rank and regiment? Euler concluded that no such arrangement exists, and more than a century later another mathematician, Gaston Tarry, rigorously proved this to be correct.

After another 100 years had passed, however, the “36 officers problem” got a second life. In 2022, Karol Życzkowski at Jagiellonian University in Poland and his colleagues showed that the problem could be solved after all – if it was made quantum.

Advertisement

Inside the company selling quantum entanglement

Now, Robin Simoens at Ghent University in Belgium and Simeon Ball at the Polytechnic University of Catalonia in Spain have built further on the 2022 work, identify the ingredient that was crucial for solving the problem: quantum entanglement.

The 36 officers problem is an example of a “Latin square”, or a square grid filled with symbols that each appear once per row and column. One famous example of a Latin square is a sudoku grid.

Życzkowski and his colleagues solved their quantum Latin square by letting each officer have a quantum mixture of ranks and regiments. For example, there could be an officer for whom it would be impossible to tell with complete certainty whether he was a captain of artillery or a major of cavalry because these options would be in a quantum superposition.

Subscriber-only newsletter

But their solution also contained an additional quantum ingredient. It required all 36 officers to be connected through the inextricable link of quantum entanglement. In fact, in solving Euler’s centuries-old problem, Życzkowski and his colleagues invented a new absolutely maximally entangled (AME) quantum state. Życzkowski says that this is equivalent to entangling four six-sided dice so much that after a person rolls two dice they can predict the outcome of rolling the remaining two.

Simoens and Ball wondered how much of this quantum correlation was really necessary. “We wanted to try to find a simpler solution that doesn’t use so much of the power of entanglement,” says Simoens.

He and Ball translated the problem of filling up the 6-by-6 grid into a specific type of mathematical graph. Then they used a computer algorithm to search through all iterations of this kind of graph, looking for a special feature that corresponded to a particular quantum state of the officers – one that would solve the problem through superposition alone, without requiring all that entanglement. But they discovered that such a solution doesn’t in fact exist.

“This shows that our solution is, in a sense, as simple as possible, since the effect of quantum entanglement is indispensable,” says Życzkowski.

Quantum computing firm QuEra says it plans to make a fault-tolerant quantum computer and offer it to users through the cloud in 2028, which will require a real leap in engineering

The discovery may have practical value for quantum computing.

Jamie Vicary at the University of Cambridge, who co-invented quantum Latin squares, says that when AMEs are made with a quantum computer’s qubits, they can act as error-correcting codes, or states that protect the qubits from making errors during computation – which is vital if quantum computers are to have practical applications.

But how to create the best error-correcting codes is an open question, says Vicary. This means that insights into what makes them work are extremely valuable. In his view, it isn’t surprising that entanglement has proved to be a key feature. “Entanglement is really the most profound driving force of new structural phenomena quantum theory can provide,” he says.

Simoens says that he and Ball are now studying solutions of the 7-by-7 Latin square problem that are not classical, but genuinely quantum.

Physical Review Letters DOI: 10.1103/hxzf-nmpx

Fate of the AMOC may depend on how quickly CO2 rises

New Scientist August 13, 2026

The fate of a critical ocean current may depend more on how fast our planet heats up than the temperature level we ultimately end up with.

Earth could warm by more than 5°C above pre-industrial levels but still enjoy a functional Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), so long as this warming happens very slowly. But very fast warming, similar to the current rate, could push the AMOC towards collapse at just 2°C above pre-industrial levels.

Mysterious ‘cold blob’ in the Atlantic suggests the AMOC is weakening

René van Westen at the University of Utrecht in the Netherlands and his colleagues used a state-of-the-art climate model to simulate the stability of the AMOC under three different rates of warming. The first scenario modelled a very slow increase of carbon dioxide concentrations of 0.5 parts per million each year; the second a rate five times faster; and the final scenario a rate 10 times faster, which is comparable to today’s rate.

Advertisement

The team found that, under very slow rates, the AMOC remained stable beyond 5°C of warming. “We were very surprised by this result,” says van Westen.

But under current rates, the AMOC collapses at about 2°C of warming. Unless the world dramatically reduces its emissions, this could happen around 2060, says van Westen. “We need to consider that this is a scenario that can develop over the upcoming decades if we remain at these warming rates.”

The modelling indicates the AMOC’s stability “is not controlled by some magical temperature level”, he says, but “by how fast the climate is warming”.

The loss of Antarctica’s doomsday glacier would transform our planet. Now scientists are revealing the secrets of this remotest of places, and asking the question: is its demise inevitable?

The AMOC carries warm, salty water from the Gulf of Mexico towards the north Atlantic Ocean, where it cools and sinks, flowing back south along the ocean floor.

Without the AMOC, much of Europe would suffer a 10 to 30°C drop in wintertime temperatures, while rainfall patterns around the world would shift dramatically, with catastrophic consequences.

To drive the flow of the current, surface water around Greenland must sink into the deep ocean. This depends on the surface water cooling and becoming dense enough to descend into the deep ocean. “There needs to be some kind of density overlap between the interior of your ocean and the surface,” says van Westen. “That’s the only way to have a very strong AMOC.”

Free newsletter

But under fast rates of warming, surface waters become warmer and lose density far faster than the deep ocean, leaving the ocean layers stratified and unable to effectively mix.

Keeping the warming at a slow pace allows both the surface water and the deep water of the ocean to change at roughly the same pace, says van Westen. “The whole ocean can keep up.”

The findings suggest that a dramatic slowdown in the rate of CO2 pollution could rescue the AMOC from collapse, even if the world doesn’t manage to achieve net-zero emissions in the medium term.

For decades, the oceans have absorbed much of the excess heat caused by greenhouse gases. The latest observations suggest they are reaching their limits, so how worried should we be?

But translating results from a climate model to the real world is tricky. For example, the model doesn’t account for factors such as the melting of the Greenland ice sheet and the effect of other greenhouse gas emissions like methane.

“Higher-complexity models vary a lot in AMOC behaviour and have biases that affect AMOC stability, so we can’t yet take this as a clear-cut, real-world projection,” says David Armstrong McKay at the University of Sussex, UK.

But the main message is clear, he stresses: “It still shows, though, just how much pressure the ocean is being put under by continued fossil fuel burning, and underlines that the faster these emissions fall, the better the chance of avoiding any potential nasty surprise from the AMOC.”

“What this study shows is that slowing the rate of CO2 increase immediately is perhaps more crucial for averting future AMOC weakening than limiting the total amount of CO2 we emit,” says Camille Hankel at the University of Washington. For policy-makers, she says it could mean that “spreading out our total emissions in time would be more favourable for maintaining a strong AMOC”.

Mammal ancestors were giving birth to live young 236 million years ago

New Scientist August 13, 2026

Creatures that bridged the gap between reptiles and mammals may have been bearing live young 90 million years earlier than we thought.

One of the hallmarks of all mammals apart from monotremes – echidnas and the platypus – is that they give birth to live young. This “viviparity” contrasts with the “oviparity” seen most other vertebrates, in which females lay eggs that hatch outside their bodies.

One long-standing question has been whether creatures known as cynodonts, which emerged around 260 million years ago during the Permian geological period and are directly ancestral to all mammals, laid eggs or gave birth to live young, as no evidence of their reproduction has been discovered either way.

Advertisement

Extraordinary ichthyosaur fossil shows its last meal was a pterosaur

“Whether mammalian ancestors were oviparous or viviparous has been considered a mystery,” says Leandro Gaetano at Argentina’s National Scientific and Technical Research Council. “We had no clues on how or when one of the most distinctive traits of the majority of present-day mammals, viviparity, evolved in the mammalian lineage.”

This has now changed, thanks to a chance observation made during a postgraduate class at the University of Buenos Aires in Argentina. The students were examining a fossil of Chiniquodon theotonicus, a cynodont that lived 236 million years ago and was unearthed in the Talampaya National Park in north-western Argentina in 2011. Part of the analysis involved using a microscope to examine thin slices taken from one of the ancient animal’s leg bones. At that point, the class noticed a curious growth line inside the bone.

Gaetano and his colleagues investigated further and eventually concluded that this line, analogous to a tree’s growth ring, recorded the moment that the ancient mammal relative went through a growth spurt after its birth.

Fossil fruits show flowering plants flourished in time of dinosaurs

The researchers reconstructed how large the leg bone and the animal itself would have been when the growth line formed. They calculated that the animal would have weighed 1.68 kilograms at that point. When the animal died as a full-grown adult, it was just shy of 12 kilograms.

This gave the researchers a ratio of newborn to adult size in the ancient animal. They then compared this figure to similar ratios obtained from a wide variety of modern animals: 1869 mammals, 2619 non-avian reptiles and 782 birds.

“We were amazed to find that Chiniquodon grouped with extant placental mammals,” says Gaetano.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Egg-laying animal groups produce young that are far smaller than adults when they hatch, he says.

For example, some species of large birds have newly hatched young that are just 0.002 per cent of adult body mass, whereas placental mammals often give birth to young that are over 20 per cent of the size of their parents.

“Only placental mammals produce relatively large newborns, whereas reptile and bird hatchlings are comparatively very small,” says Gaetano. “Hence, we propose that [the] Chiniquodon theotonicus reproductive strategy was most similar to that of placental mammals.”

Mike Benton at the University of Bristol in the UK says the findings are convincing.

Millions of fossil whale bones found in deep-ocean ‘necropolis’

“Further, as they argue, the apparent absence or rarity of actual eggs of any kind in the Permian and Triassic has always been puzzling – the so-called amniote egg gap,” he says.

Oliver Griffith at Macquarie University in Sydney says his gut reaction is to be sceptical of the claim of live birth, as we have only indirect evidence. But he is impressed that, in the absence of any direct fossil evidence, the team is still trying to solve the puzzle.

“We may never get any of the kind of direct evidence that solves themystery, for example a fossilised mammalian egg or a fossil mother duringpregnancy,” he says. “So it is kind of cool that they’re taking a different approach to trying to find an answer to that question.”

New Zealand Herald August 13, 2026

Christopher Luxon is due to make a policy announcement this morning as he addresses South Island business leaders.

The leaders are putting politicians on the spot today – demanding answers on investment in the region.

Around 640 business and political leaders are at the first South Island Election Conference in Christchurch, including Prime Minister Luxon, Act’s David Seymour and Labour’s Chris Hipkins.

The conference, presented by Business Canterbury, kicked off at the Christchurch Convention Centre Te Pae at 9.30am.

“From what we understand, it’s to be the biggest business election conference in New Zealand, and I think that speaks volumes, too, about the real interest in the South Island and the role that we can play in growing our contribution to the New Zealand economy,” Business Canterbury chief executive Leeann Watson said.

“We’re really excited to be hosting ... we’ve got 640 people coming along, and I think that in itself is a real demonstration of the very real interest in how the South Island can take a larger role in contributing to the New Zealand economy.”

The programme began with Luxon giving an address, followed by a panel discussing all things economy, including productivity, innovation, economic agenda and tax settings.

Hipkins will address attendees before a workforce panel about immigration, health and safety, industrial relations and education.

The last item on the programme is a South Island infrastructure debate between National Minister Chris Bishop and Labour’s Kieran McAnulty.

Earlier this week, a new report revealed that only $1 of every $9 of Government roading funds gets spent in the South Island.

The report confirmed that the South Island accounts for almost a quarter of the country’s population, 22% of gross domestic product (GDP), a third of export goods and 40% of international visitor spending.

However, the region receives only 11% of transport spending.

Earlier this year Business Canterbury joined with the seven other South Island Chambers of Commerce to launch a shared election policy platform and called on all political parties to back the South Island as a driver of New Zealand’s next phase of economic growth.

The manifesto, Growing New Zealand from the South: A Policy Platform for Election 2026, sets out a shared vision for “unlocking investment, productivity and sustainable growth across the South Island economy, while providing political parties with a clear and actionable blueprint for supporting regional business success”.

Representing around 7,000 businesses, the combined chambers set what they described as an “ambitious” goal – lifting South Island GDP per capita to at least $130,000 by 2035 and positioning the South Island above the national average in living standards and economic performance.

Watson said the reason for holding the conference was “really clear”.

“We want to make sure that those who are in the next government – and in fact all of the political parties that play a role in shaping our future – really understand that backing the South Island is a way to driving New Zealand’s economic prosperity.

“You know, we’ve got so many opportunities here and what we want to do is really highlight what those opportunities are and what is needed from the government in order to realise those opportunities.

“So our message has been really simple and really clear – if New Zealand wants stronger productivity, they want higher incomes and greater resilience, then backing the South Island and backing its growth is one of the smartest investments that they can make.”

Watson said the conference would be “well structured” and there was “good representation” from the main political parties.

“We’ll be asking the hard questions,” she promised.

“We’ll be really focusing them in on what some of the policy platforms mean specifically for the South Island.

“We don’t want generic policy comments. We actually want them to demonstrate how well they understand and how well they are committed to investing in the future of the South Island.”

Watson said the conference was a way for those wanting to be in power after the upcoming election to share their views – and for South Islanders to “hold them to account”.

“It’s not just all over after the conference tomorrow,” she said.

“It’ll be a very strong advocacy platform for Business Canterbury and the other chambers of commerce across the South Island, to use in their ongoing engagement in partnership with the government.”

New Zealand’s top butchers face off at National Butchery Awards

New Zealand Herald August 13, 2026

Winners of the Master Butcher Challenge: Bryce Gyde (left), Luka Young and Calum Sutherland, pictured in front of their gallery-like display of gourmet meat cuts. Photo / RNZ, Lucy Xia

By Lucy Xia of RNZ

From carcasses up to 60 kilograms hanging on steel racks to gourmet meat platters infused with herbs and spices and decorated with edible flowers.

Spectators and supporters were in for a visual feast as 24 of New Zealand’s top butchers and apprentices faced off in the 2026 National Butchery Awards on Thursday night, run by Retail Meat New Zealand.

Competing butchers had two hours to do boning, trimming, cutting and marinating before presenting their final labour of love in mock storefronts, ready to sell in a silent auction.

They had to impress eight judges, including a chef, with their technique, craftsmanship, immaculate presentation of their final products, and show that meat was cut in a way that meant it could be cooked well.

North Auckland butcher Bryce Gyde appeared to be in a flow state as he seasoned a premium lamb shoulder.

“I’ve got garlic and rosemary in it, and I’m about to top it with a chicken stock diamond, so what that does is, when you cook it, it actually melts and infuses all that nice chicken stock into these lamb shoulders when you slow-cook them,” he said.

Gyde, along with his teammates Luka Young and Calum Sutherland, were crowned the winning team of the Master Butcher Challenge, the category for the most experienced butchers.

Rhys Tamanui from Waipawa Butchery in Hawke’s Bay won the under-35 young butchers category, and Te Awamutu’s Cody Burbery scooped the apprentice of the year award.

One of the judges, Brian Everton, said they were looking for the skill of removing the bones so as not to damage the cut and cause tough meat.

He said waste minimisation was also one of the criteria considered.

“It’s all about utilisation; it’s getting the best value out of the carcass, out of the cut that you got, so it’s the way that you make sure that you don’t have waste.

“Because every little mistake or little bit of meat only ends up in trimming, which ends up in mince, which is lower value.”

The competition was not short of innovative spins, including meat presented as art pieces, alongside adaptations of famous paintings such as Starry Night, Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.

A twist on the usual pork and apple sauce tradition, a platter of maple syrup-infused apples, stuffed with pork and topped with pork lard, caught the eye of head judge Peter Martin.

“When that cooks, the rendered pork fat is going to melt down through that pork as it’s cooking, and you’ll get the sweetness of the apple that’s contained it; you’ll end up with something yummy and delicious,” Martin said as he observed the work of Whangarei butcher Chloe Steel.

Twenty-four-year-old Mya Wilson Hiraka recently completed her final exams for her three-year apprenticeship and is now a qualified butcher.

This is her second time at the National Butchery Awards, after winning the best pork product category last year.

Hiraka made 21 products from the raw meat she was given, including a pork shoulder, lamb leg, two chickens and beef rump, to scoop the emerging talent award at Thursday’s competition.

“My biggest thing, becoming a butcher and wanting to do all those things and showcase my talent, is to inspire the younger generation to do the same, and whatever you put your mind to, you can go far in it,” she said.

“I never thought butchery could take you around the world, but it can, and that’s where I wanna head.”

Part of her goal is to compete in the World Butchers’ Challenge in Australia in two years.

She said butchery also allowed her to give back to her home community in Ōpononi.

“Giving back to my community, whānau, the ones who’ve supported me, being a butcher, go up to the marae for tangihanga, funerals, and I’m able to get into the back room and help cut up the carcass, and that’s very rewarding.”

Martin said the butchery trade continued to draw in young talent.

“Butchers are really relaxed; we don’t have the temperament of a chef, we don’t have the 2am starts of a baker. People who like working with their hands and like a physical aspect to the job they do are really attracted to this industry.”

Martin, who works for an agency that provides industry training and apprenticeships, said job prospects had been strong for the butchery trade.

“One of the most frequent calls we get is, ‘Do you know of a qualified butcher who would look to come and work for me?’. Something’s really interesting: carpenters [during] economic downturn, their jobs disappear; people eat, and that doesn’t really face a downturn.”

Northland rescue groups demand action over sale of 1-week-old puppies

Animal Rescue puppy foster co-ordinator Katrina Harman wants the SPCA to take action against people selling puppies that are too young.

Northland animal welfare and rescue groups are calling for action to stop puppies as young as 1 to 2 weeks old being taken from their mothers and sold near the Kaitāia community market.

They also want to debunk widespread myths about dog desexing in Far North communities to help stem the flow of unwanted dogs that end up being dumped or euthanised.

Donna Doolittle’s Animal Rescue puppy foster co-ordinator Katrina Harman said animal rescue groups want to take legal action, but their hands were tied.

She said the SPCA - the only charity in New Zealand with statutory powers under the Animal Welfare Act - should be doing more, particularly when the issue had been repeatedly reported to them.

“People ring them, and they get nothing, so they come to us.”

Last week, the Northern Advocate reported puppies that barely had their eyes open were being sold for $50 each in a carpark near the Saturday Kaitāia market.

The SPCA said it had been making inquiries into the alleged sale of underage puppies.

“At this stage, the owner remains unidentified despite numerous attempts to locate them, and we encourage anyone with further information to ... contact their nearest SPCA centre.”

Harman said the sellers took advantage of busy market days but because they weren’t actually in the market, the organisers couldn’t do anything.

“All we can do is support people,” she said.

“If they [people with unwanted litters] reach out to us for help we can help, they don’t have to be dumping or selling them.”

Under animal welfare rules, puppies must be able to feed independently and be in good health when made available for sale or rehoming, unless they have been orphaned.

Bay of Islands Watchdogs co-ordinator Leonie Exel said an overwhelming number of people are getting litters of puppies from their dogs.

The case of puppies being sold in Kaitāia was “tragic ignorance”, she said.

“You can’t just hand out vulnerable puppies.

“Give them to a rescue or look after them yourselves; if you want a dog to have puppies you have to look after them.

“We’ve got to do something about it; we’ve got to get breeder regulations.”

Apart from high euthanasia rates in the Far North, there is an ongoing problem of stray and roaming dogs attacking people, pets, and livestock.

Animal rescue groups have long been calling for mandatory desexing to stop unwanted dogs, with education about responsible dog ownership.

The Far North District Council has not directly answered questions about whether mandatory desexing would be introduced.

While not committing to mandatory desexing, the council says it wants to reduce financial barriers to desexing and supports reforms that could include penalties for owners who do not desex their dogs.

Exel – who also wants to stop puppies being sold on social media – said there are many myths people in the Far North believe about de-sexing.

“A lot of people think that a bitch needs one litter before she’s spayed to keep her healthy and happy – that’s false.

“Many farmers and pig hunters believe if their dog is desexed it will make the dog less effective or change their personality. That’s also untrue.

“Breeding puppies for profit is not okay.”

A severe thunderstorm warning has been lifted for Northland, but thunderstorms may return to parts of the North Island today, MetService head of weather news Heather Keats says.

“A severe thunderstorm sparked up just before 6am ... it moved through quite quickly, but we are going to continue to see the chance of thunderstorms across the day, this morning and this afternoon for the Far North”, Keats told Ryan Bridge TODAY.

Northern Bay of Plenty and Gisborne could also be in line for thunderstorms today, she said.

Northlanders were earlier being warned of possible surface or flash flooding around streams, gullies and urban areas and “extremely hazardous” driving conditions.

Conditions could still be dangerous after the storm had passed, according to National Emergency Management Agency advice shared by MetService.

“During and after the storm you should also beware of fallen trees and power lines [and] avoid streams and drains as you may be swept away in flash flooding,” that advice says.

Contact the NZ Herald newsroom

Coromandel Peninsula and parts of Bay of Plenty have already copped heavy overnight falls, with more than 36mm of rain falling in six hours at Whangamatā, and 21mm at Waihī, Keats said.

Heavy falls were also recorded in parts of Northland, with 20mm of rain in an hour at Purerua and surrounding areas, MetService wrote on X.

Parts of the North Island are forecast to be battered by heavy rain this weekend, as a front sweeps up the country, bringing colder temperatures and a risk of frosts.

MetService meteorologist Alwyn Bakker told the Herald the weekend’s weather would grow increasingly unsettled before easing off into early next week.

“It’s going to get quite wet on the east coast of the North Island.”

Several heavy rain warnings and watches will be in place throughout today for eastern parts of the country, with more potentially on the way.

“That’s more in the kind of ‘we might need to put a watch out’ territory rather than ‘lots of exciting stuff happening, everybody prepare now’.”

The Bay of Plenty about and east of Kawerau is under watch until 9am, while Gisborne, north of Tolaga Bay, is under a heavy rain warning until 8pm.

“We had a trough over most of the country yesterday, a low approaching the upper North Island from the Tasman Sea. All of that’s going to be moving eastwards today.”

Another front will build in the south later today and shift upwards across the country over the course of the weekend.

Temperatures are expected to be above average today but will begin to drop as strong southerlies move in on Sunday and Monday.

A high of 18C in Auckland today will drop to 15C on Sunday, with Christchurch and Dunedin plunging from the mid-teens today to 9C on Sunday.

In the capital, today’s high of 14C will be replaced by a chilly 9C on Sunday.

Keats told Ryan Bridge TODAY the front moving up the South Island could bring snow to the “higher passes” of the island.

“We are likely to see some more watches and warnings issued for the rain for the eastern side of the North Island, road warnings for snow, and possibly some gale southerly strong wind watches for places like Wellington up to southern Taranaki, and even maybe some of the Marlborough Sounds as well.

“So that’s for the weekend and that southerly flow will drop temperatures again.”

Bakker said there was likely to be a risk of frosts for a lot of the country, although the incoming chilly weather wasn’t expected to match the intensity of the recent cold snap.

Auckland will fall from 16C tomorrow to 13C on Monday, with the frost risk beginning in the South Island before “gradually” moving northwards.

“There’s better news further off on the horizon”, Bakker said.

“It’s looking like we’ll be looking reasonably ridgy next week, so that’s more of those clearer skies, colder days kind of thing, but we’ve got a bunch of wet weather to get through first.”

Tony Randle’s family pay tribute to clever and caring Wellington City Councillor after unexpected death

New Zealand Herald August 13, 2026

In the Wellington City Council chamber, Tony Randle’s blazer hangs over his empty seat, with flowers, a framed photo and his calculator placed beside his nameplate. Photo / Mark Mitchell

The “devastated” family of Wellington City Councillor Tony Randle have paid tribute to a “dedicated father, husband, son, brother and friend”.

The 65-year-old died over the weekend in what Mayor Andrew Little described as a “complete shock” to the council.

Randle’s mother Daphne, told the Herald he would be remembered as “a very good eldest brother to his siblings, diligent in his responsibility as an eldest son”.

She described her son as a wonderful, clever and caring man, and said he had recently spent 10 days with the family in his hometown of Alexandra before travelling to the UK during the recent council break.

“He was especially good to Dad and I on a very regular basis,” she said.

“It’s just a loss, such a loss,” Randle’s younger sister Sher said.

She said the family had been honoured to see the outpouring of tributes from community members, media figures, and politicians across the aisle.

“He was the one that helped keep the family together and communicated,” she said.

“It’s important that we remember the good things and try and emulate what he does and carry on really.

“He was a type of politician that focused on the facts and the numbers and didn’t get into personal issues or calling people names or character assassinations, which is a shame that we’ve lost him from politics to be fair, we need more of that.”

Randle was admitted to hospital with stomach pains on Friday and was expected to be discharged, but suffered heart-related complications and died on Sunday, his sister said.

His death has been referred to the coroner.

In a further statement, his family said they were “devastated”, describing Randle as “very committed to the Wellington community, especially the Northern suburbs, where he lived for more than 30 years”.

In the council chamber, Randle’s blazer hangs over his empty seat, with flowers, a framed photo and his calculator placed beside his nameplate.

“He is going to leave a real hole in presence around this table for time to come,” Deputy Mayor and fellow Northern Ward councillor Ben McNulty said at the council’s first briefing on Tuesday since Randle’s death.

“The business of a city doesn’t stop, even with the loss of one of us around this table, I’m grappling with that a little bit, I’m sure everyone else is as well, but knowing Tony I’m also sure he would expect us to continue,” McNulty said.

“Tony was a colleague, he was a friend, and we’re going to miss him dearly,” he said.

Randle’s death means a byelection for his Northern Ward seat.

A Wellington City Council spokesman said plans for a byelection would be announced in the coming weeks, but it is required to be held before the end of the year.

A memorial service for Randle is being held at 1pm this Saturday, August 15, at Wellington’s Tākina convention centre.

In lieu of flowers, the family has asked people consider donating to the Johnsonville Trust in Tony’s name, as an organisation he “cared deeply about”, that provides community grants to individuals and groups in the Northern suburbs.

Ethan Manera is a Wellington-based journalist covering Wellington issues, local politics and business in the capital. He can be emailed at ethan. manera@nzme. co. nz.

A man died after being shot by police during an incident at Sylvia Park mall in Auckland’s Mt Wellington.

Police say the man earlier stole an air rifle at Gun City in Penrose at 2pm, sparking a chase.

A white Suzuki Swift was seen driving erratically towards Mount Wellington Highway.

The car became stranded at an intersection outside Sylvia Park before the man fled on foot.

Police say he headed towards an entrance into the shopping centre, and was shot while in possession of the air rifle.

First aid was provided, but he was pronounced dead at the scene.

At a stand-up yesterday evening, Superintendent Sunny Patel said the man was on bail.

'We don't know what his intent would have been,' Patel said.

The man who was fatally shot by police outside Sylvia Park yesterday reportedly grabbed an air rifle from Gun City as it was being shown to him by staff.

Gun City owner David Tipple told Stuff the man then ran from the Penrose store, with three staff members chasing after him.

One staff member got close, but the man managed to get away in a car.

“Our call to the police led the police helicopter to the car rapidly,” Tipple told Stuff.

The gun was unloaded and no pellets were stolen from the store, Tipple said.

Superintendent Sunny Patel told media yesterday that the man was known to police and was on bail.

He was not wanted by police and had not breached his bail conditions.

"Should his bail conditions have been different?" Tipple said.

“It’s tragic that we have lost a human being. I believe we all have the potential a to contribute positively to society.”

A worker from Gun City Penrose told the Herald that the store is open as usual today.

Superintendent Sunny Patel said the officer who fatally shot the armed man outside Sylvia Park yesterday afternoon is being provided with support.

"We've put support in place for the officer concerned and that support will be ongoing," Patel told media last night.

"No one comes to work and expects this kind of result. Our staff work very, very hard on a daily basis to make sure the community is safe, and this is the last thing that they want to experience."

Patel said he was happy with police response times to the incident.

Police urged anyone with phone or dashcam footage of the incident to come forward.

Photos by Sylvie Whinray.

Seeing an offender with a gun heading for a crowded shopping mall is “probably a police officer’s worst nightmare”, Police Minister Mark Mitchell says.

He told Ryan Bridge TODAY he did not know the details of the man shot dead by police at Sylvia Park in Auckland yesterday as he was running toward the mall with a gun.

“Obviously my thoughts are with the family of the deceased but I want to acknowledge our police officers who quite simply have done an outstanding job [in what was] a very very tough situation.”

Mitchell, a former police officer, said officers had to make tactical decisions very quickly, and public safety was always front of mind.

“No police officer gets up in the morning wanting to be put in the situation that they faced yesterday – but it's incumbent upon them to act quickly and protect members of the public and that appears exactly what they've done.”

Asked if there were concerns about security at Gun City, Mitchell said two separate investigations – one internal to police and one through the Independent Police Conduct Authority – would look at how the man got into the gun shop and took a firearm.

The gun store owners and employees were responsible for having control measures in place for dealing with customers and the handling of firearms, he said.

Some workers and customers at Sylvia Park were left in the dark for almost an hour with many thinking “a gunman was on the loose”.

A worker, who didn’t want to be named, said a customer “staring blankly” came running into a store with a child.

When asked if they needed help, the customer said “there’s been a shooting” and was trying to hide.

Workers quickly shut the doors and attempted to contact security and mall management several times, but didn’t hear anything until close to an hour later. Three different stores reported similar experiences.

A customer who was in the Forever New clothing store told the Herald “we ran for cover” when the shots rang out.

“We had no idea what was going on … this store was very close to the shooting but we had no idea of the circumstances. We thought that perhaps a gunman was on the loose.”

They said staff “were just incredible” and grabbed everyone in the store, locked the front doors and took them into a back room to hide.

“After [about] 25 minutes we came out of the back room and saw cops everywhere with rifles. Unfortunately no one would speak to us … I wish we had known that the shots were from the cops and not someone on a rampage.”

They said it was a “terrifying experience”, but was grateful the person with the gun wasn’t able to use it inside the mall.

Kiwi Property, which owns and manages Sylvia Park, said it didn’t communicate what was going on to shop workers and customers inside the mall until “police confirmed the situation was contained”.

Workers and shoppers had expressed concern about being “terrified” and being left in the dark for almost an hour as gunshots were heard inside the mall.

“During any emergency incident, we take our lead from police and emergency services, and we do not communicate unverified information that could create further confusion or concern,” a Kiwi Property spokesperson told the Herald.

“As soon as police confirmed the situation was contained, the site was safe, and there was no ongoing threat to the public, we issued an alert to our tenant database.

“Our centre management team also checked in directly with those tenants closest to the incident, including stores that had been temporarily locked down.”

Police said they were alerted about 2pm after an air rifle was stolen from Gun City in Penrose.

The offender fled in a white Suzuki Swift as police units were dispatched.

The police eagle helicopter was deployed to the area and located the vehicle travelling near Sylvia Park.

The car was tracked travelling into the Pakuranga area, where it entered the carpark at Pakuranga Plaza before exiting and driving "erratically" towards Panmure.

Police said the vehicle was spiked but continued towards the Mount Wellington Highway, before being stranded at an intersection outside Sylvia Park.

At about 2.50pm, the man fled on foot carrying the air rifle and headed towards an entrance of the shopping centre.

He was confronted by police underneath an overpass and was shot.

First aid was immediately provided but the man was pronounced deceased at the scene.

Police said a critical incident investigation is underway after yesterday afternoon's fatal shooting at Sylvia Park.

"Our investigation is still in the very early stages of piecing together all the events," Superintendent Sunny Patel said.

A man, who earlier stole an air rifle at Gun City in Penrose about 2pm before heading to Sylvia Park, died after being shot by police outside the entrance to the mall.

Patel said determining whether the air rifle was loaded and the decision to shoot the man will form part of police's ongoing investigation.

"There's a critical incident investigation that has commenced within place. The Independent Police Conduct Authority have been notified and they will be carrying out their own investigation. And so that's one part of the ongoing investigations."

Witnesses described the chaos that unfolded at Sylvia Park yesterday as a man was fatally shot by police during an incident outside the mall in Auckland’s Mt Wellington.

Multiple gunshots were heard as part of the mall went into lockdown about 3pm.

A significant amount of police and ambulance staff were outside the mall.

One shopper told the Herald they saw a man approaching the shopping centre with what appeared to be a firearm.

“I couldn’t see him after that, but I heard three gunshots,” he said.

A witness told Newstalk ZB: “It was five or six shots ... I thought that’s not a car backfiring.

“I heard the sirens going and saw half a dozen police cars.”

He said he went to the train platform to warn people.

“I said to everyone, ‘there’s an active shooter at the mall so I wouldn’t go over there if I were you’.

”I was stopping people going in there, I needed a new pair of shoes, but not that desperately.”

Another witness, Nick, told Newstalk ZB he was driving through the complex when he saw “cops everywhere”.

”There appeared to be a hatchback car that looked like it had crashed into the middle island. I didn’t know if that had anything to do with the active shooter.

“There were millions of police everywhere, lots of guns.”

Beetle-borne fungi pose biosecurity risk to forests and orchards

New Zealand Herald August 13, 2026

The black pine beetle (Hylastes ater).

Bark and ambrosia beetles are acting as tiny taxis for fungi across New Zealand, giving researchers valuable clues about how these organisms travel through forests and crops.

To understand whether plant disease-causing fungi are being moved this way, scientists at Bioeconomy Science Institute Maiangi Taiao are identifying the species carried on beetles found in New Zealand forests and orchards.

“While a lot is known about the beetles, less is known about the fungi that travel with them,” task lead Darryl Herron said.

Since 2024, researchers across the Bioeconomy Science Institute, including teams from Lincoln, Rotorua, Ruakura, Auckland and Motueka, have been collaborating to trap bark and ambrosia beetles across New Zealand and analyse the fungi they carry, through projects funded by Better Border Biosecurity (B3) and Zespri.

By combining expertise and sampling capability across teams and sites, this work has revealed a broad range of fungal associates linked to native and introduced beetle species.

While most of these fungi are common plant associates, the team has detected species with the potential to disrupt plantation forestry, horticulture and native ecosystems if conditions change or new beetle species arrive.

The work includes assessing potential risks to native bush, urban environments and botanical collections and monitoring beetle activity in and around orchards, where new associations and increased aggressiveness in the beetle-fungal system could pose future threats.

Bark and ambrosia beetles tunnel into trees and interact with fungi in different ways.

The latter carry and cultivate specific fungi, while the former pick up a more mixed assortment.

Together, they’re associated with a wide range of woody plants across plantation forests, orchards, urban areas and the native estate.

Their rapid breeding ability means beetle numbers can rise quickly – so their fungal passengers are never short of taxis.

“It’s often these fungi that cause the greatest harm,” Herron said.

“Some fungal species block a tree’s ability to move water and nutrients, weaken natural defences or accelerate disease, particularly when trees are already stressed by drought, age or harvesting activity.

“By identifying these fungal ‘passengers’, we’re building a clearer picture of the microscopic communities being moved across New Zealand and which beetles are more important to focus on from a biosecurity perspective.

“This helps us assess whether these beetles have the potential to facilitate the movement of fungi not currently established in New Zealand.”

Overseas, certain beetle-fungus partnerships have caused extensive forest dieback.

“Our focus is understanding what risks exist here before those impacts occur,” Herron said.

“If we know which beetles can carry damaging fungi and where they’re moving, we can respond faster and reduce the risk to forests and export markets.”

The research also contributes valuable information to national surveillance efforts led by the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) and industry partners, including the Forest Owners Association, alongside other research programmes.

Understanding fungal diversity carried by these tiny beetle taxis could help refine risk modelling tools, guide where and how surveillance and monitoring are most effective and strengthen post-border surveillance.

Together, these investments support New Zealand’s ability to stay ahead of emerging biosecurity risk, helping protect forests, horticulture and ecosystems and the industries and communities that depend on them.

“Maintaining strong biosecurity pathways is critical for protecting plantation forestry and export markets,” Herron said.

Because bark and ambrosia beetles can occasionally arrive in wood packaging and untreated wood products brought into New Zealand, sector and public awareness remains vital.

Anyone noticing dying trees accompanied by significant insect activity is asked to report it to the Ministry for Primary Industries or email the Bioeconomy Science Institute (fhdiagnostics@scionresearch. com) with a clear photo of the damage and insect activity, and the GPS co-ordinates or address.

Almost 20 years on, Peking Duk have made their debut album. Why now?

Sydney Morning Herald August 14, 2026

As AI slop takes over the local dance charts, Reuben Styles and Adam Hyde are still doing it the right way.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

When Adam Hyde closes his eyes and pictures the Australia he loves, he’s not really thinking about a beach. “There’s an ashtray with heaps of cigs in it,” he explains. “There’s a beer that’s almost done but it’s really hot. There’s a shitty speaker somewhere and there’s all these characters, from all walks of life, and they all seem to get along.”

Hyde’s Peking Duk bandmate Reuben Styles nods across the table from him. “We want to write a love letter to all the caravan resorts out there,” Styles continues. “The places that are such beautiful parts of your childhood that you took a little bit for granted. You think of a trailer park in the American sense. It sounds trashy as, but we call them caravan resorts. It’s paradise.”

Styles takes a sip of his Coke. “Shout out to the beach caravan resorts of Jervis Bay,” he smiles, forever a Canberran.

The cigs aren’t exactly overflowing in the Imperial Hotel in Paddington, where Hyde and Styles are sitting in the middle of a vast, empty front bar on a Monday afternoon. We’re sitting here because nearly 20 years after becoming best friends in a Canberra skate park and forming one of Australia’s most popular dance acts, Peking Duk are finally releasing their debut album, Paradise. The first and most obvious question to ask is, why now?

“I think it’s more of a why not,” Styles answers. “We’ve done about 16 years now of Duk just doing singles. Whenever you feel like things are getting a little bit repetitive in any sense, shaking it up and trying something totally new just makes the whole thing f---ing exciting again.”

“I think the era that we came up in, we were just making beats for clubs,” Hyde adds. “There was no calling for an album necessarily. It was like, ‘just make the track, put out the track’. And then we kind of found ourselves … not trapped – that’s very dramatic – but we found ourselves stuck in this rhythm. And once these songs found some skerricks of success, we were kind of like, ‘Okay, well, we should keep that going’. We were bound to the structure of drop a single, do a tour. It became a bit of a machine that we created ourselves.”

That machine gifted them great success. A scan over their CV reveals multiple ARIA award wins and nominations for bounding festival-fillers like 2014’s High and 2016’s Stranger; a fistful of Hottest 100 placements; sold-out tour after sold-out tour. Their brand of spiralling, supercharged EDM, born from the scrappy clubs in Canberra (shout out Block 33, say the pair) and the heyday of Sydney’s Kings Cross, helped define Australian dance in the 2010s. For year after year, the duo would drop one or two big-hitting singles and then crisscross the country in what seemed like endless loops.

“Every single you drop then fortifies the prison you’ve made around yourself,” Styles laughs. “When you’re doing just one or two singles a year, you’re really hoping for some type of result from the single. I feel like the second we got into album mode, it just made us completely unthink ‘Is it going to do well or not?’ It just made us think of, ‘Is it sick or not?’. We f---ed off the whole rule book.”

“I should add,” Hyde jumps in. “There was a long period of time where there was somebody in our team that made things very hard for us to move forward, in many ways. I don’t want to shit on anyone, but there was somebody that we had to farewell in order to move forward. I think in hindsight, just sitting here now, candidly speaking, it’s like that was a big thing that held us in our own constraints of like, ‘It’s got to be like this. Picture perfect, Peking Duk!’”

The duo don’t elaborate about the team member they farewelled, except to add it feels like they now have the keys to their own car back. “We’re stealing our own car and doing burnouts,” Hyde smiles.

Stretching across 14 tracks and featuring an extensive guest list that includes Killer Mike, Matt Corby, Phantogram, Rico Nasty and Kah-Lo, Paradise feels polished and focused. Rather than building a Frankensteinian monster of offcuts from over the years, the duo went into sessions in LA with a clean slate, determined to build something fresh.

The album loosely wraps around the concept of a pirate ship sailing into paradise – where paradise is an empty metaverse of being famous, being seen. Its best tracks, like Forever with Phantogram and Let Go with Matt Corby, take on this dreamy, somewhat melancholy air.

After 16 years as Peking Duk, the project is no longer their sole focus: Hyde is now arguably better known around the country as Keli Holiday thanks to the success of 2025 track Dancing2, while Styles has been busy flirting with alt-country as Y. O. G. A. While they’re steadfast that both ventures feed the creative fire rather than extinguishing it, they admit it’s led to some awkward moments with festivals. “Promoters will try and do a cheeky thing, where they’ll book Reuben and then book me and will say ‘Oh you’re both in, we’ve got some decks here!’,” Hyde laughs. “But God bless them, they’ve got a hard job, I guess.”

In the week leading up to our chat, the local music industry has been tearing itself apart over the number-one song on the Australian airplay charts. Josh Fawaz’s Madonna cover, Like A Prayer, reportedly used generative AI tools in its construction. Fawaz has since added AI credits to the track. Styles laughs in disbelief.

“I can’t believe it,” he says. “I landed in Australia three days ago just to find out the number one song played on Australian radio is AI vocals… I wonder what the average person listening to [radio station] KIIS, for example, how they feel about the song or if they’re just like, ‘Oh yeah, don’t mind’? Would you have dinner at a restaurant on your birthday if you knew there was no human cooking your steak?”

“To me, it’s like, do you want perfect? If you want perfect, go get it,” Hyde adds. “But music and art and romance, love and hate, it’s so far from perfect. The longing is the most crucial part of the experience. If you lose that, it kills everything. The whole thing … it’s heartbreaking. Even if you were to program a bot to make it more imperfect, then it’s like, what are we doing?!”

We’re sitting not too far from the Hordern Pavilion, where the young pair would attend hard-style raves as teens. Their lives are a little different now: Styles will soon head off to have some quality time with his child; he excitedly talks about the new bike he’s bought them. “I had a kid and got daggy,” Styles smiles, reflecting on their 20-year-long friendship. “Adam went to LA and got sexy.”

“There are moments when we’re drunk and we put our arms around each other and cry,” says Hyde. “And I think that’s f---ing awesome. To have a bond like that, that’s truly special.”

Peking Duk’s debut album Paradise is out now. Their national Paradise Tour includes shows at Brisbane’s The Tivoli on October 17, Sydney’s Roundhouse on November 7, and Melbourne’s The Timber Yard on November 27.

Polls close in Clacton byelection where Nigel Farage faces slew of fringe candidates

The Guardian Thu, 13 Aug 2026 21:37:58 GMT

Longest ballot in UK voting history features likes of Count Binface and Howling Laud Hope alongside Reform leader

Polls have closed in Clacton, where thousands of residents in the Essex seat voted in a ballot featuring Nigel Farage and a range of novelty and fringe candidates led by Count Binface.

The Reform UK leader resigned as the MP for Clacton at the start of July and forced a byelection in an attempt to address complaints over a deepening scandal about gifts he received.

He is expected to face a formal investigation by the parliamentary standards watchdog, which was opened in May after the Guardian revealed he had received a £5m personal gift from Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based crypto billionaire, in April 2024.

Farage has denied the gift amounted to an inducement to run for office, insisting it was personal in nature. He has given a series of explanations for the gift, including that it was for his security and a reward for Brexit.

The inquiry will look into allegations Farage was financially supported by the crypto gambler and convicted fraudster George Cottrell, a close friend, after the Sunday Times reported that Cottrell’s support included security and social media staff who worked on Farage’s online content in the year before he was elected.

Reform UK claimed that was a “baseless and contrived story” and that no parliamentary rules had been broken.

The inquiry, which was suspended on 8 July after Farage’s decision to force a byelection, could restart as soon as Friday if he is re-elected.

If parliament imposes sanctions for failing to declare the gifts, he may be removed from the House of Commons and face a second byelection.

All of the main parties have boycotted the byelection, announcing they would not stand candidates for a “media circus” and a “vanity project”. Instead, Count Binface, the self-declared “entirely independent space warrior” created by the comedian Jon Harvey, stepped into the void.

A record number of candidates are seeking election, presenting voters with the longest ballot paper in British electoral history.

Among the 34 candidates on the ballot paper are independents, the actor and rightwing political activist Laurence Fox and three figures from the Monster Raving Loony party: Howling Laud Hope, Baron Von Thunderclap and Nick the Incredible Flying Brick.

As well as the town of Clacton-on-Sea, the constituency comprises rural villages, farmland and several seaside towns and villages including Frinton, Walton-on-the-Naze and Jaywick, which last year was named the most deprived neighbourhood in England for the fourth consecutive time since 2010.

The three polls that Jaywick topped before 2025 were published in 2010, 2015 and 2019.

According to figures from the Office for National Statistics, the population of Clacton is older than the average in England. A third of working-age people are economically inactive, compared with fewer than one in five in the east of England. Of Clacton residents who voted in the 2016 Brexit referendum, 70% favoured leave.

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

After standing in multiple British elections since 1994, Farage was elected to the Commons as the member for Clacton in 2024. He won the seat with a majority of 8,400, taking 46.2% of the vote. The Conservatives came second and Labour third.

The previous record for the largest number of candidates in a constituency election was held by the Haltemprice and Howden byelection in East Yorkshire in July 2008, which featured 26 candidates. It took place after Tory David Davis resigned his seat and stood again as a protest over the issue of civil liberties.

The result may be seen as a benchmark to measure Farage’s relative success in this byelection. Davis won 72% of the vote in the election – which Labour and the Liberal Democrats did not contest – up from 47.5% at the 2005 general election, with a majority of 15,355.

Farage’s critics argue that his standing as a contender to be the next prime minister has taken a serious hit as a result of the byelection, with much of the Reform leader’s time and energy spent in the Essex constituency.

Last summer Farage was able to dominate the news agenda while the leaders of other main parties took summer holidays, helming seven press conferences in six weeks.

This year he held his first press briefing on 3 August, his first national press conference since May. He has not appeared keen to debate with Binface or the other 32 candidates.
