Edinburgh international film festival showcases a Scottish industry in rude health

The Guardian Thu, 13 Aug 2026 17:05:30 GMT

This year’s festival is superpowered by a strong year for Scottish cinema, showing it can thrive under the ‘four dimensional perpetual catch-22’ of global ambitions

Borges, ballet and BDSM: Peter Bradshaw’s 10 must-see movies at Edinburgh international film festival

Now that its disastrous collapse and speedy rebirth is a trauma slowly receding in the rear-view mirror, the Edinburgh international film festival can set its sights on bigger things. Apart from its traditional role providing a showcase for the best of current world cinema, the festival has an ace up its sleeve for 2026: the undeniable confidence and conspicuous achievement of its home film industry in Scotland. Just as Cannes likes to give a decent amount of houseroom to favoured French directors, and Sundance sees at least part of its job to talk up US independent cinema, Edinburgh acts as a vector for Scottish film-makers to gain valuable exposure and get their work in front of significant festival audiences. Inevitably, some years are harder than others, but Edinburgh’s 2026 edition feels stronger than it has been for years.

The festival’s opening gala slot, traditionally a local film, has been given to The Incomer, a surreal comedy starring Domhnall Gleeson and set Scotland’s far north, and which picked up a major award at the Sundance festival earlier this year. Among a clutch of strong films are Borges and Me, based on Jay Parini’s memoir of escorting author Jorge Luis Borges on a trip around the Highlands; and The Education of Jane Cumming, the extraordinary true life story of the 19th-century Edinburgh schoolkeeper who inspired The Children’s Hour. Scottish artist Douglas Gordon is the focus of a new documentary, Douglas Gordon by Douglas Gordon, while Scottish Ballet perform in These Violent Delights, a film rendering their dance version of Romeo and Juliet. Past glories are due to live again with a 30th anniversary screening of junkie classic Trainspotting (with the added bonus of a live club night featuring a DJ set from Irvine Welsh).

Paul Ridd, the festival director, is aware of the potential minefield of sticking up for Scottish cinema. “It’s great to have all those movies in the mix, these films deserve to be at the big table. But we never want to think we’ve got to promote this stuff. What we want to avoid is the sense that there’s any film in our lineup that is in there for any other reason than it’s just top quality. We’re not quota driven. It’s always about the quality. And I’m just very happy that there’s such a wealth of great Scottish work to showcase.”

Ridd points to the influence of Screen Scotland, the state-and-lottery funded agency founded in 2018 that was designed to act as a specialist funding unit for Scottish film. “All these great films are testament to what the whole organisation has been doing to put those film-makers and those films on the map.” The recent appointment of Screen Scotland’s executive director Isabel Davis as head of the British Film Institute’s £20m film-making fund – itself seen as a vote of confidence in the way the Scottish film industry has evolved.

Davis, who takes up her new post in October, is clear that increased and targeted project development has been vital. “We were put together with the notion that really good creative development support was going to be the key to all of that film-making success, and it has paid off. It takes years, project by project. It means giving tough love to people on scripts, saying that things could be better, pushing people to be more ambitious – and then backing that up with more development support and then production support.”

Festival success is a major marker, and the fact that seven Scottish films were selected for Sundance earlier this year was a major cause for celebration; as well as The Incomer, the picks included and The Story of Documentary Film (The 1980s), the newest in a stream of film-history essays from critic-turned-film-maker Mark Cousins – who is described by Davis as “the gift that keeps on giving” as far as the Scottish film industry is concerned. Conversely the recent Scottish film that appears to elicit the most fervent admiration from across the Scottish industry is the most hyperlocal of all: Everybody to Kenmure Street, documentary about the mobilisation of local activists to prevent the arrest of two men by immigration enforcement officials. Davis says “it’s just connected to people so far beyond Scotland, it’s unbelievable.”

Producer Ken Petrie, whose new film Sunny Dancer is releasing UK cinemas this week, is one of the new generation of Scottish film-makers who have benefited from Screen Scotland’s involvement, but says the going is still tough. “You know, it’s always been a hard business. It’s never been so hard or expensive to make something that has so little financial reward. The whole value chain of the film industry at the moment is a challenge, especially for independent producers.”

Petrie, who started out as a special effects technician on projects such as The Wolfman, Robin Hood and World War Z, says that, for him at least, the challenge is to avoid staying too close to home. “Scotland is in a good place, but I think we need to have a bit more courage to try to really blossom on to the global stage. The question for me is: how do you make that stuff that’s going to travel internationally, entertain Scotland and the UK, but also the rest of the world?”

He adds: “The ugly fact is the UK film business is centred in London. I don’t know if it’s possible that people can live and work in Scotland in isolation and be able to build global companies. I’m trying to make stuff for global audiences, so surely you have to go and find out what the global marketplace is saying.”

On the other hand, Petrie is concerned that Scotland’s record as an international production base – which has seen projects of the calibre of Spiderman: Brand New Day, The Odyssey, Frankenstein and The Buccaneers shoot in the country – may be hampered by Westminster over the level of subsidy it can offer to attract these productions. “Should we be trying to grow more in Scotland? It’s like a kind of four-dimensional perpetual catch-22.

“I mean, Scotland’s an exciting place. Everybody loves the Scots. Certainly when I’m out in the marketplace that’s what comes across. There’s a lot of goodwill out there towards Scotland. I try to always be an optimistic realist and I think that’s what we need to be in Scotland at the moment.”

Edinburgh international film festival starts on 13 August and runs until 19 August.

Fake sex worker and accomplice jailed for fatally spiking men’s drinks

The Guardian Thu, 13 Aug 2026 16:47:27 GMT

Adina Mihai and Madalin Dumitru from Essex jailed for 17 years for drugging four men to steal from them, two of whom died

A woman who posed as a sex worker and administered a deadly amount of sedative to two men has been jailed for 17 years, along with her accomplice.

Adina Mihai, 31, and her partner Madalin Dumitru, 30, who arranged for her to meet men at their homes, drugged their victims to steal from them.

She spiked the glasses of wine of four men with the sedative gamma-butyrolactone (GBL). Two, Malcolm King, 80, of Gloucestershire, and Gary Mouat, 36, of Oxfordshire, died.

Jailing Mihai and Dumitru, from Ilford, Essex, at Oxford crown court, Mrs Justice Brunner said: “Your intention was to incapacitate each victim making them deeply unconscious.

“The administration of the drug was haphazard and depended on the strength of each batch, the amount put into drinks, and the amount they drunk.

“If you had stopped for a moment to consider the risks, as you should have done, you would have realised that it carried a high risk of serious injury or death at the very moment you administered that drug. If you had done the most cursory research, you would know that GBL can be extremely toxic.”

The pair pleaded guilty to two charges of manslaughter and to administering poison to the two survivors, who cannot be identified.

Julian Evans KC, prosecuting, said: “While Dumitru waited nearby, Mihai would enter the victim’s home. There, she would persuade the victim to drink alcohol laced with GBL.

“Once the victim was unconscious, Mihai would look for property to steal. Then she would rejoin Dumitru, leaving the victim alone and unconscious.”

No sexual services were provided but the pair worked on the premise that victims would not report what had happened to the police out of embarrassment.

The court heard Mihai advertised online and the couple would take cash deposits before meeting the men. When their victims fell unconscious, she would steal watches, jewellery, aftershave and cash.

In a victim personal statement, Mouat’s son, aged eight, said the defendants had ruined his life.

He asked the couple: “Why did you have to kill my dad, you could have just taken the money, he was really kind, he would have given it to you.

“He was my dad and now he’s gone. I miss him every day and will never get to see him again. I will never be able to get another dad and that makes me feel so sad. You have ruined my life and all the plans we had to do things together. My family is destroyed now.”

King’s daughter, Caroline, said: “When my father was killed, the defendants did not only end his future. They stole mine as well.”

His younger sister, Jacky Seagroatt, said: “What haunts me every day is the way he died. I might have been able to come to terms with losing my brother if he had died naturally or as the result of a tragic accident. I cannot stop imagining what he went through or how frightened he may have been.”

Charles White, the senior crown prosecutor with the CPS, described the case as “unique”.

No other deaths, poisonings or thefts have been linked to the pair but police are keeping an open mind about the possibility of other victims.

Food Standards Agency should do more in the fight against ultra-processed foods

The Guardian Thu, 13 Aug 2026 16:38:57 GMT

Felicity Lawrence’s alarming piece on ultra-processed foods (Why are ultra-processed food firms panicking and suing? Because they know time is running out, 7 August) made no mention of the UK’s Food Standards Agency, whose primary statutory objective is to protect public health from risks arising from the consumption of food.

The FSA is an independent, non-ministerial government department. Its advice to ministers, and guidance to consumers, is informed by the most up-to-date scientific evidence, free of political or commercial considerations.

As Lawrence pointed out, food manufacturers see government action as a threat. And regulation is surely the most effective way to control profit-oriented companies, many of which pay little regard to the possible negative impact of their products until compelled to do so.

The FSA last published guidance to consumers on ultra-processed foods in February 2025. Given that “the science on harm caused by foods high in fat, salt and sugar is now settled”, it is perhaps time for it to consider updating this guidance and also whether to recommend government intervention. Mike PenderCardiff

The Jason Arday affair must not spell the end for diversity. Here’s how – and why – we should defend it

The Guardian Thu, 13 Aug 2026 16:37:30 GMT

The scandal has given succour to the same old rightwing attacks on D&I, but companies that do it properly raise standards rather than lowering them

This has not been a good fortnight for the concept of diversity and inclusion. The fallout from the Jason Arday affair has been an all-out attack, by the rightwing media and political classes, on institutional efforts to reduce inequality.

Arday was the Black academic who, in a fanfare of publicity, had been appointed a professor at Cambridge University in 2023. At the time, British institutions were still struggling to address the widespread issues of systemic racism thrown up by the murder of George Floyd three years earlier.

Last month Arday faced allegations of plagiarism over his PhD thesis, and amid massive scrutiny he resigned last week. Cambridge University has now announced an independent inquiry into its appointment procedures, but many academics already believe that Arday was given the job more for his remarkable backstory than for his academic ability. Arday was, they felt, not at the level you would expect for a professorial chair at such an elite institution. But he was the man who said he couldn’t talk till he was 11, and couldn’t read till he was 18; who had run 30 marathons in 35 days, the last third of them with a leg fracture. What an amazing story. Arday gathered headlines and media appearances. He became a walking advert for how an institution with such a poor record on diversity had progressed so far. Or had it?

I’ve been promoting diversity and inclusion for more than 25 years, and one of the stock responses I often hear is: “I’d love our organisation to be more diverse, but we don’t want to lower standards.” It trips off the tongue so smoothly, always accompanied by an apologetic faux-empathetic shrug.

Yet the response completely misunderstands what diversity and inclusion is about. If it meant lowering standards I’d never waste my time pushing it. Who could possibly believe in making their organisation worse? D&I is not about making a moral point that you believe in equality (though you should); it’s not about performing an act of charity because you feel sorry for poor, excluded minorities (though you might); it’s not even about a business case in the expectation of making more money (though you also might).

The point of D&I is that you bring people into your organisation with different life experiences and perspectives; you value them and listen to them (that’s why it’s called “inclusion”); and the outcome is that you make more informed decisions, so that your organisation better serves its customers. This may or may not translate into profits, but it definitely makes you better, and able to spot changing trends and changing patterns of behaviour more quickly.

Opening up your hiring to more diverse communities leads to more competition and therefore higher standards.

This is also why it’s important to make the distinction between positive action and positive discrimination.

Positive action is inclusive and offers training or short-term experiences to underrepresented groups, helping to level the playing field before they apply for permanent jobs. Positive discrimination (commonly referred to as quotas), excludes people from job applications, reduces the numbers who are able to apply, and therefore lowers standards.

Positive discrimination has always been illegal in the UK; its US equivalent, “affirmative action” was legal but provoked a huge backlash and is now in effect outlawed. Positive discrimination also leads to minorities in any organisation having doubt cast on their position, that somehow they’re second rate, the “diversity hire”.

The backlash over the Arday appointment has cast this shadow once again over a whole swathe of Black academics. Many of them are now furious at what Cambridge did. If the university had wanted to open the door for a Black professor, there are dozens of academics at the right level. The difference is that they wouldn’t have been such a PR hit. The message they’ve taken from Cambridge is that, if you’re Black, you only get a top job if you have a superhuman backstory. Level playing field? Really?

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

If Cambridge really were an inclusive institution it wouldn’t have been looking for the “quick fix” that the Arday appointment gave it: a superficial symbol that everything here is OK. Instead it would have been examining its recruitment processes, the retention and promotion rates of its minority academics, to see where the problems were and what could be done. Cambridge would ask: how can we identify true potential and what kind of support can we offer people from underrepresented groups to ensure they thrive in the institution? (This applies just as much to women, working-class people and those with disabilities.)

The past 18 months, since Donald Trump regained the US presidency, have seen huge political efforts to turn the clock back on equality and racial justice. Many companies have stood firm; but some have caved in and ditched their policies. The difference is that some understand why diversity and inclusion matters, and some don’t: there is ample evidence that diverse organisations perform better.

So what should be the lesson for progressives who believe in equality? If, after the past few weeks’ headlines, any institution feels under renewed pressure to ditch its diversity policies, the correct response is: “But we don’t want to lower our standards.”

Joseph Harker is the Guardian’s senior editor, diversity and development

Ukrainian cathedrals, Gaza’s archives, Iranian squares – modern war is systematically erasing human history

The Guardian Thu, 13 Aug 2026 16:04:12 GMT

It is not enough now for war to kill, it must eradicate a people’s cherished and precious heritage too

Wars may not take summer holidays, but they do sometimes see exhaustion. As drones race back and forth across Ukraine and the strait of Hormuz, a grim stalemate seems to have invaded the earth beneath. Aerial bombardment knows limited resistance and even less victory or defeat. Ukraine, Russia, Israel, Iran and their allies seem able to defy diplomacy and drop bombs on each other for ever.

At which point the outside world can merely count some of the costs. Vladimir Putin’s known desire to eliminate Ukraine’s historical identity has led to its cultural devastation. Two weeks ago Unesco reported the destruction or dereliction of 545 of its historic buildings, including 156 religious sites and 43 museums. The attempted eradication of what Putin himself claims to be an intrinsic part of Russia’s own history is sickening.

Russia’s bombing of Kyiv’s Pechersk Lavra complex and the Dormition cathedral, coupled with shattering the magnificent St Sophia cathedral, are comparable to Ukraine bombing the Kremlin. So, too, is the attack on a cathedral and a museum in Odesa, and the destruction of a theatre in Mariupol. These are defining monuments of Ukraine’s past. Yet their dereliction has received little publicity in the west.

Meanwhile in Iran the beautiful city of Isfahan might surely have been spared Donald Trump’s egotistic bomb-fest. Not so. A Reuters survey in June found the historic Naqsh-e Jahan Square, the Jameh mosque and the governor’s palace partially destroyed. In Tehran, the Persian royal palace of Golestan has been badly damaged. Unesco reports of an attack on an 1,800-year-old fortress that embraced a prehistoric settlement reputedly 63,000 years old.

The most savage consequence of the collapse of order in the Middle East is the reported damage or destruction of over 80% of the buildings in Gaza. The ancient city of Gaza itself is now largely rubble. Bombed by Israel are the medieval Great Omari mosque and the church of St Porphyrius, dating from the fifth century and one of Christianity’s most ancient sites.

Gaza’s archives have been destroyed. The Omari mosque’s library and the adjacent cultural centre, whose thousands of ancient documents had survived the Crusades, have reportedly been lost. The Al Qarara museum was bombed from the air and then bulldozed to the ground. A people’s entire past has been deliberately eradicated.

As for Israel’s war on Lebanon, it culminated in June in what appeared to be the gratuitous bombing of the ancient port of Tyre. This included an attack on the site of the Roman hippodrome. The 1,000-year-old fortress of Beaufort was also damaged. The past is clearly without privilege.

Aerial wars are unlike ground ones. Soldiers with guns have targets. So, we are constantly told, do modern missiles, but that does not explain the US bombing of an Iranian girls’ school in February. The reality is that bombers are casual because they are near invulnerable, while their victims appear small and anonymous. Bombers do not conquer territory or secure surrender. They are manifestations of leadership machismo.

In the allied invasion of Italy in 1943-45, individual British and American officers were known to take steps to protect its monuments from destruction. As a result Italy’s ancient cities survived to a degree that Germany’s did not. In the aftermath, sincere efforts were made to evolve rules of war, including respect for cultural and historic monuments. War was still seen as a contest of professionals, not of cultures.

The result was The Hague Convention of 1954 and the Convention for the Protection of Cultural Property in 1972. But recent years, in which we’ve seen a collapse of global governance, have left The Hague convention a paper tiger, like that other supposed discipline, the UN’s International Court of Justice. Victory today appears to lie in destroying an enemy’s identity and morale as much as in killing its people. When the Islamic State ruined much of the Iraqi city of Mosul in 2014, it set about eliminating all traces of its past. Trump’s threat to Iran, that “a whole civilisation will die tonight”, showed an equally primitive approach to conflict. It hardly warned his bombers to spare the mosques of Isfahan.

Of international bodies, Unesco is active in keeping a record of the fate of cultural heritage worldwide, but a record is just a record. Its listing of Russia’s and Israel’s devastation of their hated foes is like watching a historic tragedy unfold in real time. We might almost prefer it to happen behind our backs.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

One thing the outside world can do is help those seeking to help themselves. Thus the World Monuments Fund’s Crisis Response Program is invaluable. It sends aid, advice and materials to war zones, almost before the bombs have stopped falling. It was present in Mosul and its Ukraine Response Fund has many projects (26 of which are completed) helping to protect and stabilise bombed buildings, one day perhaps to restore them.

As the west continues to meddle in foreign wars, perhaps this is the least that some of us can do. One of humanity’s deepest obligations is to its past. That past knows no national boundaries.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

Michael Carrick has stated that Manchester United will not make a £100m signing this summer due to their finances, with the manager also insisting that Marcus Rashford “is our player” despite the forward and club preferring him to depart.

In the current window United have invested a total of £85m on Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos but have never spent £100m on a single transfer.

This is in contrast to Manchester City, Tottenham, Liverpool, Arsenal, and Chelsea, the rest of the traditional big six, who have all spent £100m-plus on a player in recent years.

Carrick was asked how United can compete. “Money’s money. I get that,” said the manager. “It’s still about football and that’s where the competition lies. What we feel naturally as a group is to try and win games. So there’s a lot that goes into that, but certainly the situation is what it is as well, whether that’s finances or whatever.”

Carrick guided United to third last season and was asked why the money from Champions League qualification cannot be invested in expensive elite players.

“To be honest, I haven’t got the answers for that. We’re working with pushing everything that we can to make the best of it,” he said. “For now, we’ve got to make the most of it, push everything in every boundary that we can to be able to win again, basically.”

Youri Tielemans has apologised to Aston Villa after saying he joined Manchester United because they are a bigger club than his former team.

Tielemans made a £35m move to Old Trafford in July, when United triggered a release clause in his Villa contract. The Belgium midfielder helped Villa end their 30-year trophy drought by winning the Europa League last season, but Tielemans had no qualms about joining United, who finished one spot above fourth-placed Villa in the Premier League last season.

"There are clubs above Villa, and Manchester United is one of them," he said on Wednesday – before taking to social media on Thursday to make peace with his former club.

"Never meant for my words in the press yesterday to offend anyone or the institution of Aston Villa Football Club, which I massively respect and I’m grateful for the past three years," the 29-year-old wrote on Instagram.

The 45-year-old was asked whether United can win the title without any players worth £100m or more in the squad.

Carrick said: “A little bit depends on what position that is and what you’ve got and the dynamics you need at certain points. Sometimes you do need that if it’s the right player. Again, it’s not purely on money. Obviously over time we need to be pushing to look to enhance the squad. So, yeah, 100% we need to do that.

“We’ve done really good business. So we’re delighted with that [but] we want more, we need more, we keep looking for how we can do that, so that never stops.”

Rashford joined the squad at their County Kildare training camp base on Sunday following a post-World Cup break. The 28-year-old has been on loan the past season and a half at Barcelona and Aston Villa respectively, due to a breakdown in his relationship with the club’s executive and the former United head coach Ruben Amorim.

UK records hottest day of year as fifth summer heatwave reaches peak

The Guardian Thu, 13 Aug 2026 15:48:53 GMT

Kew Gardens in London hits 38.1C and 40C-plus recorded in parts of Europe with continent trapped under heat dome

Europe heatwave – latest updates

The UK has recorded its hottest day of the year so far with a provisional temperature of 38.1C in southern England as Europe sweltered under a major heat dome.

As temperatures on the continent surpassed 40C at the peak of the summer’s fifth heatwave, the thermometer at Kew Gardens in west London on Thursday surpassed the previous high of 38C on 28 June, the Met Office said.

In France, which has recorded 17 days of extreme heat – one of the longest periods ever – Bordeaux reached 39C and Nantes 37C, Paris was on 37C and Montpellier 35C. In Spain, a maximum of 42.4C was recorded at Miranda de Ebro, prompting fresh fears of wildfires in the two countries.

In the UK, Charlwood in Surrey recorded 37.1C, the second highest August maximum temperature since 2003. Teddington in London reached 36.1C, Pershore College in Worcestershire 36C, and temperatures in Wales reached 35C, according to provisional Met Office figures.

An amber extreme weather warning was issued on Thursday across east and south-east England, including London, the Midlands, north-west England, south-west England and parts of Yorkshire and Humber.

An extreme heat alert warning of significant impacts on health and social care services across the whole of England is in place until 9pm on Friday.

The Met Office has said this summer is on course to be the UK’s hottest since records began, with 2026 likely to be the first year in which the country has recorded four separate days with temperatures of 36C or above.

Spain has broken its burned area record for this time of year, data published by the European forest fire information system on Thursday shows, while in France, the area burned had already by the third week of July surpassed that of any full year on record. Fire weather in the EU since the start of the year has been more severe than ever before.

The fires in many regions have been exacerbated by unusually dry conditions as heatwaves sap moisture from plants.

Firefighters in the UK continued to tackle a blaze in the New Forest in Hampshire. In the West Midlands, at least six homes were damaged and four people were taken to hospital for treatment because of an extensive grassfire near Stourbridge golf course. About 60 firefighters were sent to the scene, while the area’s town hall was set up to receive those fleeing their homes.

“The apocalyptic scenes in Norton and across Stourbridge are sadly just a taste of what is to come if we don’t act,” said local councillor Andrew Tromans.

Across parts of eastern and southern Scotland, there were warnings about a very high risk of wildfires. With record dry conditions in July and a dry start to August, nearly three-quarters of England and the whole of Wales are in drought, heaping pressure on water resources for households, agriculture and the environment.

In mainland Europe, record-low water flows on the Danube have deprived thermal power plants of cooling water and forced some to reduce output as electricity demand for cooling grows. Romania on Thursday stopped the second of two reactors in its only nuclear power plant, which supplies about a fifth of the country’s electricity. The plant’s director told Agence France-Presse he did not foresee a restart within the next 10 days.

In neighbouring Hungary, one of a number of central European countries to break national heat records last week, engineers have resorted to laying stones to boost the water level of the Danube by the Paks nuclear power plant, which avoided a full shutdown in July but is producing only 25% of its usual output, up from 10% earlier this month. The prime minister, Péter Magyar, said work was proceeding at a rapid pace on Thursday.

Sign up to Down to Earth

after newsletter promotion

The human-driven climate crisis is primarily the result of burning fossil fuels, which releases greenhouse gases that trap heat, raising temperatures. The extra heat alters the planet’s water cycle and energy balance, making extreme events such as heatwaves, heavy downpours and severe drought significantly more frequent and intense.

People in the UK and Europe have felt the effects of extreme heat throughout the summer. Julia King, the peer who chairs the adaptation work of the Climate Change Committee, an independent advisory body to the UK government, has said extreme weather “gets worse from here” until net zero is reached.

Doctors consider heat a “silent killer” because it greatly increases mortality rates while only occasionally being listed as the direct cause of death. In Germany, where meteorologists have issued heat warnings for a swathe of the west of the country for Friday, public health officials estimate that 12,500 people have died as a result of the heat so far this summer. More than 9,000 of these deaths occurred in an severely hot week in late June, when a national temperature record of 41.7C was set in eastern Brandenburg.

NHS staff working in A&E departments across England have experienced their busiest summer ever, health leaders said. The Royal College of Nursing said its members were working in inhumane conditions, “dripping with sweat from head to toe” during the record-breaking heat.

The RCN became the latest union to speak of unsafe working conditions for many members in hospital wards and care homes as the number of days of 30C-plus heat in the UK reached a record 35.

Extreme heat has driven a surge in attendance at A&E departments over the summer, with more than 2.4 million patients attending each month in May, June and July – the three highest monthly totals ever recorded.

The water industry regulator, Ofwat, said it would allow water companies in England and Wales to increase bills to spend £3.4bn more than planned to meet supply demands, including for the building of new homes and datacentres.

The Guardian has reported how Labour’s target of building 1.5m homes by the end of this parliament has come up against the reality of water scarcity in many of the areas where most development is planned.

We saw crescent circles of light shifting on the cardboard as the moon moved across the sun – it looked like scales. The Lakers have become a poker chip for some of the most powerful men in America

The Guardian Thu, 13 Aug 2026 15:12:26 GMT

One of the most famous teams in the world is about to change hands for the second time in less than a year for more than $12bn. Will anyone push back?

One of the most brutal lessons we must learn as fans is that the team we shed blood, sweat and tears for is seen by those who own it as just one of many assets. That gap has never felt as wide as it does this week. On Wednesday, ESPN reported that the Los Angeles Lakers are set to change hands, for the second time in 10 months, for $12.5bn, a sum that would be a record for any North American sports team. (The deal must be approved by the NBA’s board of governors before it can go through.) The buyers aren’t diehards who saved up every penny like the good Dr Jerry Buss in the 1970s. Those days are gone. If and when the deal is approved, the new owners will be venture capitalist Josh Kushner and his business partner, Bob Iger. Kushner is the younger brother of Jared Kushner, the titleless Wormtongue to Donald Trump’s Saruman. Iger used to run Disney. These men have connections across the political world and influence in every corner of the American empire. A franchise woven into a city’s identity should never become an asset vastly wealthy people move around like a chip around a poker table. But that is exactly what the Lakers are about to become. The way the deal came together should terrify anyone who still thinks sports belong to the fans.

Mark Walter took control of the team from the Buss family last October at a valuation of roughly $10bn. Now he is set to cash out around $2bn richer. That’s not how this is supposed to work. The old guard, like Buss, used to guard their NBA teams like heirlooms and pass them down. Walter is set to flip the team after less than a year.

He has other issues to deal with. Bloomberg reported in July that Manhattan prosecutors want to know whether two insurers that Walter controls, Delaware Life Insurance Co and Clear Spring Life and Annuity Co, concealed that their private-credit books were secretly propping up his other businesses. The SEC opened its own line of inquery, and the loans at issue reportedly run near $16bn. (A spokesperson for Walter’s company, TWG Global, told the Wall Street Journal that “Mark Walter and TWG have always acted in good faith, and those who have done business with Mark know him as honest and straightforward.”) Insurance made Walter rich long before basketball did, and TWG Global still owns slices of MLB’s Dodgers, the WNBA’s Sparks, Chelsea, the Professional Women’s Hockey League and Cadillac’s Formula 1 team.

The Lakers’ buyers also know that sports can generate huge returns to add to their already vast wealth. Starting in 2009 at the age of 24, Kushner built Thrive Capital into a firm now worth more than $60bn. He shoved his way into Instagram’s 2012 round at a $500m valuation days before Facebook paid $1bn for it, then rode early bets on OpenAI, Stripe, Spotify, GitHub and Skims. He owns a piece of the Miami Heat that league conflict rules will force him to shed before he can run the Lakers. And he founded Thrive Eternal to buy long-term positions in sports, media and entertainment. (Its first big move was a stake in MLB’s San Francisco Giants.)

Iger, the former Disney CEO, took control of the NWSL’s Angel City FC in 2024 alongside his wife, Willow Bay, and he’s also a Thrive partner. Now, Kushner and Iger are set to add one of America’s most important cultural touchstones to their portfolio.

The timing of Kushner’s deal may not be random either. Fifa said in late July it would hive off its commercial arm into a new company, Fifa Forward Enterprises, and sell 20% to a Thrive Eternal-led group for $4.2bn. But Europe torched the plan. Uefa convened an emergency summit and threatened to have all 55 members boycott every Fifa competition until the deal died. Negotiations ended within a week. Then Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee, proposed an inquiry into whether Fifa handing prized assets to a fund run by the president’s relative crossed an ethical line. “Over the last few weeks, Fifa’s cozy relationship to Donald Trump has been floating to the top of the swamp of quid pro quo corruption in which the Trump Administration is swimming,” Raskin said in a statement to the Guardian. “But now we see where all the bribes, kickbacks and sweetheart deals have been leading.”

So Kushner pivoted to the NBA, where venture capital is more welcome. In fact, the other 29 owners have a direct financial stake in blessing the sale. The paper value of every team just surged with news that Kushner and Iger are willing to pay $12.5bn for an NBA franchise. Teams are no longer cherished possessions to grow and share with fans; they’re assets that can be snapped up by the ultra-wealthy – franchises are now too expensive for the merely very rich to buy – and sold on at a vast profit down the road.

But the proposed Lakers deal isn’t just about how wealth has changed sports. It’s also about how one family has moved into every part of American life. The Kushners keep ending up on the title of the most coveted assets on the planet, and the connective tissue is proximity to power. Trump campaigned on burning down exactly this kind of arrangement. Josh is the younger brother of Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump’s husband, and a senior adviser during Donald Trump’s first term. Jared is now a Special Envoy for Peace and helped negotiate the recent ceasefire with Iran. Their father, Charles Kushner, pleaded guilty in 2005 to 18 counts – among them illegal campaign contributions, tax evasion and witness tampering – and was sentenced to two years in prison. Trump pardoned him in 2020, and today he represents the United States as ambassador to France, a job he holds despite not speaking French.

after newsletter promotion

Some seem to think Josh Kushner’s moves are more acceptable because he’s a registered Democrat who told Forbes in 2017 that liberal values shaped him. He didn’t vote for Trump, and after 2016, he reportedly went company by company through his portfolio, telling founders he couldn’t get them anything from the administration. His wife, Karlie Kloss, publicly split with her in-laws in 2021, writing that honoring a legitimate election is patriotic and inciting violence is not. All that may be true, but Josh Kushner’s views on climate change or gay marriage or foreign aid aren’t the point. It’s the concentration of power in the hands of a few that is the most troubling.

Politics, extreme wealth and sports are headed for a collision. Athletes and fans are the last line of defense against the owners. And they can fight back – look at how NFL players in 2020 forced league commissioner Roger Goodell into an apology over how he handled athlete protests; or how NBA players threatened to boycott the season the same year over the police shooting of Jacob Blake; or how the proposal for a European Super League in soccer was abandoned after backlash from fans in 2021. But those were actions against leagues and governing bodies. Whether athletes have the motivation to take on the billionaires who pay their wages is another question altogether.

Girls, in turn, spread the good word about him. To this day, fans still shout “Your dad is gay!” at him in the street, a call-back to the moment when Elijah tartly advises Hannah that she might want to fine-tune her gaydar.

It is an older, gentler, salt-and-pepper-bearded Rannells who stars in the comedy-drama Miss You, Love You. He plays Jamie, a personal assistant arriving in Albuquerque, New Mexico, to shepherd the spiky and recently widowed Diane (Allison Janney) through the initial weeks after her husband’s death from Parkinson’s. As it dawns on them that Diane’s son – Jamie’s employer – may not make it to his stepfather’s funeral, these strangers navigate their way through the grey area of their flung-together friendship.

Initially, Jamie struggles to retain composure in the face of Diane’s gale-force disdain, as she picks and pecks at his every word. “I was just trying to keep up with what Allison was doing,” says Rannells, who is wearing a silvery-grey shirt and running a hand through his chestnut quiff. He knew Janney from starring together in the comic thriller Another Simple Favor, but nothing prepared him for being harangued by her during the new film’s extended takes. “She is relentless. She goes and goes and goes. All her years on The West Wing really prepped her.”

Rannells is hardly low-energy himself. Whether in his impish US television appearances, collected in YouTube compilations with titles such as “andrew rannells being a little TOO ICONIC on talk shows”, or in his shopping-mall song-and-dance number as an incorrigible Juilliard graduate in Ryan Murphy’s The Prom, he is all razzle-dazzle. “Yeah, I’m usually in that position,” he concedes. “It was fun this time to be on the other side of it and to feel what it’s like to get pushed around and bullied.”

It is a few weeks before his 48th birthday and Rannells is speaking on a video call from the home in Los Angeles he shares with the actor Tuc Watkins and the latter’s twin teenage children. The room behind him is blurred, so it is impossible to identify the three paintings on the wall, but since Rannells put his stylish Manhattan apartment on the market last year for nearly $2.5m (£1.8m), Dogs Playing Poker is unlikely to be among them.

He and Watkins met on the 2018 Broadway revival of the pre-Stonewall chamber-piece The Boys in the Band. Their first kiss was in character. “We would end each show making out on stage. Ten minutes of us rolling around while Jim Parsons was crying.” They hooked up but didn’t start dating until a year later, when the cast reconvened for Murphy’s Netflix version. “We turned a showmance into a relationship,” he says with a little twitch of the eyebrow.

Given his success, it is natural to assume that Rannells’ performance as Jamie in Miss You, Love You was based on his own experience of having PAs. On the contrary, he says – he has never hired one. This may make him something of an outlier in Hollywood. “One of my closest friends has an assistant. At times, I’m closer to the assistant than I am to him.” Why has Rannells resisted? “Maybe it comes from years of working in theatre. I got in the habit of doing things for myself. To relinquish that control now would be, I think, hard for me.”

Knowing when and how to ask for help is one of the lessons that Jamie must learn in the film. Rannells can sympathise. “You are raised in the midwest to take care of your own problems: don’t make waves, fix it, move on. Sometimes I do myself a disservice by not asking for what I need. I’m getting better at it. But I’ve certainly seen it abused. A lot of actors take advantage of people and I don’t want to be that person.”

He grew up next door to a children’s theatre in Omaha, Nebraska, and took drama classes from a young age. Performing soon began to pay: from 13 to 31, he was a prolific voice actor in cartoons including Pokémon and Yu-Gi-Oh!. That spilled over into his burgeoning stage career: at 21, he toured the US in Pokémon Live!. “In retrospect, [I] would rather have done a snuff film or porn,” he said later.

His big, gay New York life was under way by then. He came out to his parents shortly before leaving home to study drama at 19. “My family was mostly – what’s the best way to say this? – not shocked,” he wrote in Too Much Is Not Enough: A Memoir of Fumbling Toward Adulthood. That 2019 book also revealed, in a chapter entitled It’s Never the Priest You Want to Kiss, that he had been sexually assaulted as a teenager by a Catholic priest.

“My mum accepted my sexuality,” he says. “My dad said: ‘I don’t think you have to be this way, but I love you.’ I was like: ‘Eh, that’s not exactly what I wanted to hear, but whatever.’” A few months later, his father reached a different conclusion. “He said: ‘I realise you’ve always been this way and I’m sorry I said that.’” Hadn’t his dad introduced him to 1940s musicals from a young age? “Exactly! It was his fault.”

Coming out was relatively plain sailing, but there was a crisis ahead. When Rannells was 22, he brought a date back to his apartment. In the bathroom later, he checked the phone messages he had been ignoring for the previous few hours and found that his family had been frantically trying to reach him. His father was in a coma; a few days later, he died.

That night, with its intermingling of sex, intimacy and mortality, left an impression on Rannells. In 2017, he wrote about the awkwardness of being consoled in this devastating moment by a naked man he hardly knew: “After I hung up, he tried to hug me: ‘What happened?’ I wanted to shout: ‘Clearly nothing good! Put on some pants!’”

That essay inspired him to write and direct How Do You Remember Me?, his half-hour contribution to the Amazon series Modern Love. In the screen version, he highlights the disparity that exists between separate recollections of identical events. “I’m sure that guy has gone off and told that story, especially as I’ve become successful,” he says. “And I’m sure it’s mostly the same as mine – but also pretty different.”

Rannells had his own experience of seeing the familiar from a revealing new angle when he read Dunham’s recent memoir, Famesick. Its tales of behind-the-scenes horrors on Girls include the allegedly hostile behaviour of Adam Driver, who Dunham claims berated her for forgetting her lines before hurling a chair at the wall next to her. “That book is a great example of seeing things differently,” Rannells says. “Girls was my first TV job and when I showed up on set I saw the fun, exciting part. At times, Lena would open up to me and I’d read things in the press that were untrue or unfair. But the book was hard to read as someone who is close to her now. I felt terrible that I wasn’t a better friend.”

What could he have done? “Been more available. I let a lot of shit slide because so much was happening. I had a break-up, then a new relationship. I was doing The Book of Mormon eight times a week and working on Girls.” He left to shoot 22 episodes of Murphy’s 2012 gay-dads sitcom, The New Normal, before returning to Girls when The New Normal was cancelled. “Of course, there was another part of reading her book,” he says. “I was, like: ‘Why didn’t she talk about me more?’” Joking he might be, but there is a Reddit thread on that very topic. “I would like to say I started that thread, but I did not,” he says. The eyebrow twitches again. Did he or didn’t he? As ever with Rannells, you are left with a tantalising question mark.

Miss You, Love You is on HBO Max in the UK and Ireland, the US and Australia

Do I really need air conditioning in the UK? The best portable aircon tested – plus the pros, cons and alternatives

The Guardian Thu, 13 Aug 2026 14:54:03 GMT

As hotter summers become the norm, home aircon can feel increasingly tempting. We put six units to the test for cooling power, noise and energy use – and explain what you need to know before buying

How to sleep in a heatwave Can air conditioning be green?

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Tell people you’re testing air conditioning, and the truth soon comes out: far more people have aircon than you’d ever imagine. It’s a guilty secret, the home improvement equivalent of Botox or weight loss jabs – everyone notices the results, but nobody admits to the method. Most portable aircons are in bedrooms, hidden away from visitors, so they’re easy to keep secret. And while friends with aircon don’t suddenly look younger or slimmer, they do look suspiciously well rested during a heatwave, while you’ve spent the night tossing and turning.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

So if you’re using an aircon unit, why have it in the bedroom? Warm air rises, so upstairs bedrooms can be the hottest by the end of the day, making for restless nights. And if your bedroom is in a loft conversion, it’s even worse: the roof absorbs the sun’s heat all day before radiating it back into the room after dark.

Most UK homes are built to retain heat, not shed it. Cooling an entire home is difficult and expensive, but a single aircon unit can make at least one room – and a good night’s sleep – more achievable.

So, should you get aircon? And if you do, should you feel guilty about it? Yes and no. It depends on how you power it, whether the machine is built to last, and whether you really need it.

We are in a climate crisis. This year’s hot summer hasn’t been a blip. In fact, extreme heat and flooding will worsen in the coming years. We got into this mess by burning fossil fuels, and we continue to do so, so the carbon footprint of your cooling matters. You could be making the problem worse by opting to have air conditioning. Unless you’re on a renewable tariff – or even better, producing itself yourself with solar panels – electricity use accelerates climate breakdown. (If you are looking to move to a renewable tariff, it’s worth researching those that invest most in renewables.)

Before you buy, read the “What you need to know” section at the bottom of this page on the global warming potential (GWP) of refrigerants. These are used in air-conditioning units, as well as fridges, freezers, heat pumps and other appliances that move heat. Some refrigerants have a global warming impact hundreds, or even thousands, of times greater than the same amount of CO2 if they escape into the atmosphere.

We were facing our fifth heatwave of the year at the time of writing, and unsurprisingly, portable air conditioning units had been in high demand. None of the options I’ve recommended is currently in stock, with the first restock due in late November, and many more expected in March 2027. If you want a good-quality, well-recommended unit that’s built to last, bear that in mind. So take your time: these units are big investments built to last, and there’s lots to consider.

Fans

There are cheaper (and greener) alternatives to air conditioning, including fans and evaporative air coolers, both of which I’ve tested for the Filter. Fans don’t actually lower a room’s temperature; they simply move air across your skin, helping sweat evaporate and making you feel cooler, like a breeze on a hot day.

If you decide to go with a fan, buy a good one (my favourite, the Lume, is now on preorder for delivery from 31 August). Cheap models are often noisy, with much of that noise being wasted energy. A well-engineered fan is noticeably quieter and more effective.

As you might have already discovered, fans and air coolers often sell out during hot weather, especially the good ones. If you find a model you like on preorder, it’s usually worth reserving it. Sadly, we’re likely to see more heatwaves.

Air coolers

Evaporative air coolers work by drawing warm air through water-soaked pads. As the water evaporates, it absorbs heat, cooling the air by a degree or two, before it’s blown back into the room. The result isn’t the fridge-like chill of an air conditioner, but a gentler cooling effect – like a sea breeze on a hot day. The trade-off is that the fans built into evaporative coolers are often less powerful, so you don’t get the strong blast of air that you get from a standard fan.

Importantly, evaporative coolers (sometimes known as swamp coolers) humidify your air, so aren’t a good option if you have damp and mould problems. They’re designed to be used with doors open and fresh air circulating. Many of the ones I recommend are now out of stock, but my favourite portable option, the Morphy Richards Flexi Freeze, was available at the time of writing.

Keeping cool without electricity

There are natural ways to cool your home, too. The problem is that most houses in the UK have been designed to retain heat, not cope with prolonged hot weather. In countries where super-hot summers are the norm, homes are often built with high-thermal-mass walls, which warm up and cool down slowly, and external shutters that block the sun from entering through windows.

We’ve written in depth about alternative ways to keep your home cool this summer. Closing and covering windows can keep out hot air and block solar heat by day – then opening them in the evening lets cooler air into your home, flushing out not just warm air but also the heat stored in your walls.

If your home has windows on opposite sides, open both in the evening so cool air can blow through. If you live on more than one level, open windows upstairs and downstairs in the evening. Warm air will rise out of the top windows and will be replaced by cooler air that’s drawn in at the lower level.

There are valid reasons to own air conditioning, even during a climate crisis. Older people, young children and those with health conditions are more vulnerable to extreme heat, and some homes are simply much harder to keep cool.

Like any appliance, an air conditioner has two main sources of carbon emissions: the CO2 generated from manufacturing and disposing of it (known as “embodied carbon” ) and the CO2 generated to power it over its lifetime.

To reduce its overall impact, buy a unit that’s built to last, from a trusted brand with a long warranty, rather than the cheapest model you can find. A longer-lasting unit spreads its embodied carbon over many more years. Buying secondhand also reduces the impact, extending the life of an existing unit.

But the biggest difference you can make is how you power your air conditioning. If you’re on a 100% renewable electricity tariff, then running it shouldn’t require burning fossil fuels (again, it pays to do your research here). Better still, if you have solar panels and a home battery, you can run aircon using electricity you’ve generated yourself. It’s a significant investment, but one that’s becoming increasingly attractive as fuel prices rise and solar panels and batteries get cheaper.

Be aware that if you’re on a standard electricity tariff, the mix of fuels used to power your home will depend on the time of day. Around the middle of the day, electricity is typically supplied by a higher share of renewables. When demand peaks, typically in the early evening, gas-fired power plants are more likely to be brought online to meet it.

So, if you can, run your aircon outside these evening peak hours. Use shutters, curtains, open windows and other natural cooling methods first, then use air conditioning for a short time before bed to take the edge off.

I’ve tested portable air conditioners here, but for a full rundown on the types available, see the “What you need to know” section at the end of this article.

I’m a veteran, award-winning consumer tech journalist with decades of experience testing gadgets. I’m also a menopausal woman in her 50s, who honestly can’t recall the last time she felt cold – which may explain the appeal of wild swimming at this age. Oh, and I have a degree in engineering. Between the three, I’m well qualified to put these portable air conditioners through their paces, both from a scientific and personal perspective.

Unsurprisingly, air-conditioning units have been hard to come by this summer, with many sold out, and review samples also in short supply. I focused on units that are going to be restocked and tested six, with details of stock levels and replenishment dates included, where available.

Where possible, I tested units in the same 14 sq metre room with average ceiling height, and with doors and double-glazed windows closed, so it was the warmest room in the house. I opened a casement window for the hose.

The only exception was the Midea PortaSplit. Its unusual design pairs an indoor unit with a rather heavy outdoor unit that remains permanently connected by refrigerant lines, so you can’t separate the two. As I couldn’t lift the outdoor unit through a window, I tested it in a larger 37 sq metre room with a sliding door – which was the only suitable space available.

To test performance, I measured each unit’s power consumption at maximum draw with a plug-in energy meter, although since air conditioners cycle on and off, they don’t use that level of power all the time. The highest settings’ noise levels were recorded using a sound meter app from one metre away, and I measured each unit’s size.

I also monitored room temperature with a thermometer placed on the opposite side of the room. This measured how much each unit cooled the whole room, rather than the cold air coming from the vent.

Finally, I judged each air conditioner on how effective the cooling felt, how annoying I found the noise and how easy the controls were to use. I also considered the design, how easily each unit could be stored over winter and, of course, its price. Note that all models come with remote controls and on castors.

All of the aircon units that weren’t collected by the manufacturers after testing were donated to charity. Some went to Furnishing Futures, a charity that creates fully furnished homes for women and children who have survived domestic abuse. And some went to Lowri House in Hackney, London, which provides safe, short-term accommodation for homeless patients leaving hospital, with support from the homeless and inclusion health charity Pathway.

after newsletter promotion

Currently out of stock; stock due 27 November

This 10,000 BTU air conditioner is from the popular MeacoCool (MC) range. There are also Pro and CH models that offer a companion app and heating.

It’s A-rated for energy efficiency and designed for a medium room. The controls and display sit on the top at an angle, so you can see them from a distance. This is welcome, as the remote control is pretty basic, and there’s no companion app.

It uses R290 (propane) refrigerant, which has a low global warming potential of 3.3 (for more information on this, see the “What you need to know” section at the end of the page).

Why we love itOn test, this was simply the best and fastest at cooling. It brought the temperature down by 3C in 15 minutes and 6C in two hours.

The design is simple. For example, you have to manually open the louvres (the angled grilles on the front) and point them where you want the cold air directed. By directing them downwards, it created a cooling breeze on the floor and on my legs, which I found made everything feel cool.

It also has a fan and dehumidifier. The sleep mode dimmed the display but didn’t immediately make it quieter, instead gradually increasing the target temperature by a couple of degrees throughout the night.

It’s a shame that … the remote doesn’t have a display.

Dimensions: 32 x 32 x 74cm (WDH)Weight: 26kgBTU: 10,000Room size: medium (up to 28m²)Warranty: three yearsMeasured power use on top setting: 890W Peak noise level on test: 60dB

Currently out of stock

The Dimplex Eco IQ has a really handy app featuring controls such as a 24-hour timer. It uses R290 (propane) refrigerant, which has a low global warming potential of 3.3.

Why we love itThe unit looks classy, and is pretty compact considering it’s powerful enough for a large room. It offers 12,000 BTU, plus wifi and app control. This means you can control it from your Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant smart speaker if you want to control your aircon by voice.

The cooling is impressive. It cooled the room by 1.5C in 15 minutes and 5C in two hours.

I found the Dimplex a bit loud, though. It may measure the same number of decibels as others, but it has a fairly deep hum and a slight rattle, like the noise you hear from a fridge. This makes sense because, like a fridge, it uses a compressor and a refrigerant. The noise measured 60dB at its loudest (similar to a conversation – so you’ll definitely hear it, but you can learn to ignore it), and this went down to 55dB on sleep mode. However, I found the noise worth it for the cooling on a hot day.

It’s a shame that … it’s loud. The remote control is also basic, to the point of looking a little cheap. It lacks a display, which is a shame because the unit’s display and controls are on top and so can’t be seen from across the room. You can always use the app, though.

Dimensions: 29 x 34 x 70cm (WDH) Weight: 23.8kgBTU: 12,000Room size: large (up to 35m²)Warranty: one year, extended to two if registered within 28 daysMeasured power use on top setting: 1,400WPeak noise level on test: 60dB

And now for something completely different. This “portable split” air conditioner has an indoor and outdoor unit, connected with refrigerant pipes. The pipes are 2.5 metres long and have a 6 x 2.7cm cross-section, instead of the usual 15cm diameter air hose.

The units can’t be detached from each other because the pipes are full of refrigerant (R32, global warming potential 675), so it’s suitable only if you’re able to put the outdoor unit outside and close the door to leave a 2.7cm gap. Alternatively, you can mount the outdoor unit outside permanently if you’re able to accommodate space for the pipes. I found it easiest to bring it back inside when not in use: it stores neatly on top of the indoor unit. It also comes with a kit for sealing out hot air and a window lock, consisting of two fittings to stick on to the frame with Velcro to connect them, which keeps your window gap narrow.

It’s large and heavy: you wouldn’t carry it up and down stairs, although it wheels around OK. If you’d struggle to get the 32.5kg indoor unit and 9.9kg outdoor unit into place, you may find JoyBuy’s £35 installation service good value; they’ll unpack it and bring it to the right room in your home. They’ll even mount it on the no-drill-required brackets if you have a suitable window.

Why we love itIt’s much quieter than a “monobloc” one-piece portable aircon unit and could be a permanent fix for renters in modern flats. If you can bring it up to your flat in a lift and have a balcony on which to put the outdoor unit, you’re winning. And it offers year-round service: it’s an efficient A++-rated air conditioner and also an A+-rated heater.

And despite its bulk, it’s good-looking. Controls are intuitive, and there are three displays: one on top with the controls, one on the front showing the target temperature, and one on the remote control. You can also control it via the app and add Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant voice control.

It cooled the room during testing, and the dog approved of its cooling prowess, but comparing figures would be like comparing apples and oranges: the room I tested it in was considerably larger.

If the Midea suits your home – a back door or a balcony really – it’s a good option.

It’s a shame that … it’s only suitable for homes that can accommodate its pipes.

This 9,000 BTU air conditioner is a good all-rounder for medium-sized rooms. It’s also a fan and dehumidifier, and Devola also offers a version with heating.

It comes in black or white. I tested the black (known as the DVAC09CB; the white is DVAC09CW), and found the matching hose and accessories were a nice touch. It uses R290 (propane), which has a low global warming potential of 3.3.

The remote is simple, without a display, and the unit’s controls and display are on top, so you can’t see them from the other side of the room. The app paired easily, however, and it meant I could clearly see and control the mode and target temperature. You can also use the app to schedule and to pair with Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant for voice control.

Why we love itThe unit looks good and is lightweight enough to lift. And the cooling feels powerful for its size. It reduced the room temperature only a little in the first 15 minutes, but it had dropped by 2C after an hour and 3C after two hours.

I didn’t find the noise too annoying, either. The sound is reminiscent of a fan with the added deeper hum of a compressor: I could get used to it. The sleep button had no immediate impact on noise, simply dimming the display, but it gradually reduces cooling through the night to save energy.

It was immediately cooling, but performance was so-so: the temperature dropped 1C within 15 minutes and 3.5C after two hours. As with many others here, it uses R290 (propane), which has a low global warming potential of 3.3.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s loud. It measured 60dB, like several others, but I found its deep hum annoying and had to turn up the TV.

Currently out of stock

Best for: small rooms

This has the lowest cooling capacity (7,500 BTU) on test, so it’s suitable only for small rooms up to 14 sq metre. The 1.5m hose was too short to reach my high window, too (meaning I had to test all of the monobloc air conditioners on top of a desk, to be sure of a fair test, even though most come with 1.8m hoses).

It’s small but has decent features, including a front display, companion app and voice control via Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant, and the remote control features a display. Cooling was impressive considering its size: the temperature dropped 1.5C within 15 minutes and 3.5C after two hours. I liked the flat, magnetic area on top for storing the remote control, too.

Sound is a deep hum, although it’s a bit quieter on sleep mode. As with others here, it uses R290 (propane), which has a low global warming potential of 3.3.

It didn’t make the final cut because … for only a little more, you can buy the Meaco MC10000, which offers much better cooling.

Dimensions: 39 x 36 x 63cm (WDH); weight: 22.5kg; BTU: 7,500; room size: small (up to 14m²); warranty: two years; measured power use on top setting: 755W; peak noise level on test: 55dB

Here I’ve tested portable air conditioners. These are freestanding units with an exhaust hose that carries hot air through an open window. They’re designed to cool a single room and can be packed away at the end of summer. They need to be positioned close to an opening window and a power socket.

Most are “monobloc” all-in-one designs that sit on castors and are portable, in that they can be wheeled from one room to another. However, they’re not light, so moving them between floors is another matter entirely.

Another option is a “split” air-conditioning unit, which is a permanently installed system with two separate units. The indoor unit is usually mounted high on a wall and blows cool air into the room. The other unit sits outside the home (on a roof or hanging off the wall), with pipes and electrical cables connecting the two. These systems tend to be more expensive but much quieter.

This test also features a portable split air conditioner, which is a hybrid between a portable aircon unit and a fixed split system. This, too, has two units, but the outdoor one is more compact, and the pipe is thin and more flexible, making it easier to move around. It works well on the ground floor, where you can safely put the external compressor unit outside on the ground, which also makes it quieter. Using it upstairs would require the use of brackets outside, which makes it rather less portable.

Air conditioners use the same tech as air-source heat pumps. By compressing and expanding a refrigerant, they move heat from one place to another. In cooling mode, they pump heat out of your home; in heating mode, they bring heat in. If you’re installing a permanent split system, go for a reversible model so you can use it to cool your home in the summer and heat it in winter.

I haven’t carried out a group test of split aircon units because they require professional installation, but I have tested the Bosch Climate 3000i 3.5kW (from £2,420) from Boxt. It cools a room quickly and also works as a heater, air purifier and dehumidifier, doing four jobs without taking up any floor space.

For each aircon unit here, I’ve measured its power use on the top setting, in watts (W). Electricity costs are in kilowatt hours (kWh). If, for example, you were using a 900W aircon for an hour, it would use 900Wh. Divide by 1,000 to convert it to kilowatt hours: 0.9kWh.

The energy price cap for 1 July to 30 September 2026 is 26.11p a kWh. So that’s the price to use 1kWh of energy. Multiply 26.11p by 0.9kWh, and you’ll discover it costs 23p an hour to run a 900W portable aircon unit. It’s not a fortune if you use it sparingly, but fans are much cheaper to run: the winner of my fans test cost less than a penny an hour.

An air conditioner’s British Thermal Unit (BTU) rating indicates its cooling capacity. The higher the BTU rating, the larger the room it can cool. There are online BTU calculators where you can input your room measurements to find out the BTU you need. Above, I’ve given a maximum floor space for the models reviewed, assuming an average ceiling height of 2.5 metres.

An undersized air conditioner will struggle, meaning it’s more likely to be on constantly and at higher risk of breakdown, so it’s important not to buy a unit that’s underpowered for your space. On the other hand, getting a more powerful unit than you need means it will be more expensive and larger than necessary. Make sure to measure your room and get a unit with the right BTU or only slightly more than you need on paper. For example, if you’re not sure which room it will be used in, buy a unit that suits your largest bedroom.

When you poke the flexible hose out of the window to remove hot air, you’ll want to seal the rest of the window. How you do this depends on the type of window. I have hinged, casement windows, so I used sticky-backed Velcro to make a line around the window opening and then attached a fabric cover, with zips to open a hole to poke the hose through. Most air conditioners come with two window kits: the other is an adjustable solid cover for sash and other sliding windows.

All the units on test have two- or three-year warranties. I’m a big fan of long product lifespans, as the “embodied carbon” used in your unit’s manufacture and shipping also matters, alongside the electricity it uses to cool you. The longer you can get your unit to last, the better. To give yours its best chance of a long life, clean or replace the air filters regularly, dry it out on the fan-only mode before winter storage, and store upright.

Global warming potential (GWP) is a measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps in the atmosphere over time, relative to carbon dioxide – CO2 has a GWP of 1. This matters if the refrigerant leaks or is disposed of unsafely. Propane, used in many of these models, has a low GWP of 3.3 and is climate-friendly compared with refrigerants with a GWP measured in hundreds or thousands.

If your old aircon works, try to find it a good home on a local swap site or street WhatsApp. If it’s not working, check your council website or Recycle Your Electricals. Electrical items don’t belong in general waste and, like fridges, air conditioners contain a refrigerant that needs to be removed by a specialist. If it’s allowed to leak into the atmosphere, it contributes to global warming as a greenhouse gas (which is where its GWP, above, comes in).

For more, read readers’ top tips for beating the heat this summer and our roundup of the best folding fans

Caramel Quin is a journalist specialising in consumer technology. She prides herself on real-world testing and plain language. Her pet hates are jargon, pointless products and overcomplicated instruction manuals. Caramel is an engineering graduate who has won awards for communicating hi-tech subjects to normal people. When she’s not testing gadgets, she’s feeding pets (16 beasts at the time of writing) or pottering at the allotment

Man, 102, dies after alleged assault in south Wales pub

The Guardian Thu, 13 Aug 2026 13:59:59 GMT

Phillip Ormerod was taken to hospital after the incident in the Crow’s Nest in Cwmbran and later died of his injuries

A 102-year-old man has died of his injuries after allegedly being assaulted at a pub in south Wales.

Phillip Ormerod, of Cwmbran in the Welsh valleys, was taken to hospital after the incident at the Crow’s Nest pub on 1 August. Gwent police said on Thursday that he had since died.

A 56-year-old man from Llanelli was arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm in connection with the case. He has been released but remains under investigation.

The senior investigating officer, DCI Shelley Comley, said: “We understand the public interest in this incident but want to remind people that not only is this an active criminal investigation but there is a family at the heart of it processing the loss of a loved one.

“Please consider the impact that inaccurate or speculative comments – particularly online commentary – could have on them and the ongoing investigation as a whole.”

Emergency services were called to the Crow’s Nest at about 10.25pm on the night of the incident after Ormerod had fallen from a stage.

According to reports, he had walked up three steps on to the stage where the Llanelli-based band SuperHans were playing to ask for the volume to be turned down when he was knocked over.

Ormerod reportedly suffered critical injuries after falling backwards and hitting the floor.

His son, Robert Ormerod, told the Press Association his father had lived in the Llanyrafon neighbourhood for decades and was a popular regular at the Crow’s Nest, where younger people would buy drinks for him.

The great-grandfather was a draughtsman before he retired. He lived alone after the death of his wife 40 years ago and was recently diagnosed with dementia.

Ormerod said: “I feel sad – even though he could be difficult because of his age and dementia, still, you get used to him being around. Even though I suppose he wouldn’t go on forever, he would’ve carried on I think for a bit.”

Gwent police have appealed for anyone who was in the pub between 10pm and 11pm on the night of the incident to get in touch directly or via Crimestoppers.

RSC postpones Othello while leading actor Sharon D Clarke has cancer treatment

The Guardian Thu, 13 Aug 2026 12:35:24 GMT

Radical reimagining of Shakespeare play was due to run at Swan theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon from 13 February to 3 April 2027

The Royal Shakespeare Company has announced that it will postpone its radical production of Othello starring Sharon D Clarke, while the Olivier-winning actor undergoes treatment for cancer.

The production, directed by Monique Touko, was scheduled to run from 13 February to 3 April 2027 at the Swan theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon. Clarke, 60, is best known for her role as Lola Griffin in the BBC medical drama Holby City, as well as for her theatrical performances in Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom and Caroline, or Change.

In a statement on Thursday, Clarke said: “I would like to thank all the beautiful people at the RSC for their understanding, love, support and healing energy. Othello will be my north star as I undergo treatment.”

She added that she, her family and wife – the writer and director Susie McKenna – had been “overwhelmed, humbled and buoyed by the tidal wave of love that we have received and are so blessed to have an army of strength and support to hold us up. Love and thanks to my beautiful people.”

The RSC said anyone with tickets to see Clarke in Othello would be automatically refunded and a replacement production period would be announced at a later date.

Touko, whose recent work has included Marie & Rosetta at @sohoplace and Jaja’s African Hair Braiding at the Lyric Hammersmith, said: “On behalf of the entire creative team, we send Sharon all the love for her ongoing treatment and recovery.

“As a director, I have been incredibly blessed to collaborate with Sharon on this major reframing of Shakespeare’s tragedy, which reimagines Shakespeare’s Othello through the lens of misogynoir. Sharon is the ultimate collaborator. Her generosity and passion for this project continues to astound me and I look forward to us coming back together when the time is right to share this production with the world.”

The RSC described the show as “set in a climate-threatened future in which a Black lesbian holds a seat of power”.

It said it “re-imagines Shakespeare’s 400-year-old story through the lens of misogynoir, as an unsanctioned marriage perilously crosses boundaries of race, sex and status, allowing jealousy, suspicion and malign intent to close in.”

The RSC’s co-artistic directors, Daniel Evans and Tamara Harvey, said Clarke’s casting as Othello was integral to Touko’s adaptation, “which is why we have taken the difficult decision to postpone, to give Sharon the time and space she needs to undertake treatment”.
