A bungled bomb plot in Poland exposed a spy – but whose spy was he?

The Guardian Thu, 13 Aug 2026 04:00:49 GMT

When exiled Russian opposition campaigner Igor Rogov was accused of working for the Kremlin, his friends were shocked. Could this young activist have really been an undercover agent?

The summer issue of the Long Read magazine is out now. Click here to order

The police came for Igor Rogov because someone had mailed him a bomb-making kit. The eclectic mix of items – a chrome vacuum flask, a pair of marker pens, a power bank and a bottle of antifreeze fluid – might have seemed innocuous to an untrained eye, but Poland was on high alert in July 2024. Two months previously, a shopping mall in Warsaw had burned down in an arson attack; an Ikea in neighbouring Lithuania was also set on fire. Authorities believed it was a sabotage campaign masterminded by Russia’s intelligence services, intended to sow panic and undermine support for Ukraine. They feared it was only a matter of time before the Kremlin escalated further.

A security officer at the parcel company’s warehouse was suspicious enough about the package to call in the authorities, who arrived with sniffer dogs and special equipment. X-rays of the marker pens showed they had 1980s Soviet-produced detonators concealed inside, while the flask had a false bottom containing a sachet of metallic powder. The power bank appeared to have been tampered with in some way, and a probe of the bottled liquid showed it contained a highly volatile nitroglycerine solution. With the right expertise, the items could be turned into a powerful bomb.

Police ascertained that Rogov, the parcel’s addressee, was a 27-year-old Russian political activist, who in the past had campaigned for the opposition leader Alexei Navalny and other anti-Kremlin groups. He had fled Russia two years previously, fearing arrest for his activities, and been granted asylum in Poland. He won a scholarship to attend university in Sosnowiec, an industrial city in the south-west of the country. His wife, Irina Rogova, followed him to Poland and also enrolled at the university; the couple lived in a student dormitory. It was there that authorities arrested him.

Rogov’s phone, when searched, contained photographs of urban scenes in the vicinity of Sosnowiec overlaid with red arrows, apparently indicating places to hide or retrieve items. One photo was of a gas pipeline on the outskirts of town, an appealing potential target for a Russian bomb attack. The chance discovery of the package, it seemed, had led authorities to a participant, perhaps even a coordinator, of Russia’s sabotage campaign against Poland, living under deep cover as a brave opponent to the Kremlin.

More than a year later, in October 2025, Polish authorities revealed they were also accusing Rogov of longstanding collaboration with the FSB, Russia’s feared security service. This suggested that his whole career as an anti-Kremlin activist might have been a cover story for his FSB work. When the case came to court, however, the judge closed proceedings to the public and press on national security grounds, fuelling further speculation and rumours about what exactly Rogov had done – especially among Russia’s exiled political opposition, where infighting, suspicions and accusations are commonplace.

Although Rogov’s trial was closed, I discovered thousands of pages of documents about him and his wife in the court papers of a related case. (Some of the files were previously reported on by the Polish news site Wirtualna Polska). Those files, as well as interviews in several countries with intelligence sources and with those who knew Rogov, helped piece together a tale of exile and espionage that involved blackmail, deception and a marital crisis with dramatic consequences. (In accordance with Polish law, people mentioned in court files are identified in this story by first name only, except where they have given their consent to be interviewed and named in full. Rogov and his wife are named as they have already been widely identified as protagonists in the case.)

Many who knew Rogov were shocked by his arrest. They described their friend as likable, easy-going and somewhat hapless, and struggled to imagine him as a cunning superspy, or a bomb courier with a secret life blowing up European cities on behalf of Vladimir Putin. “This is a guy who once accidentally sent half-naked photos to the group chat,” said Milia Kashapova, who was Rogov’s campaign manager when he stood in city council elections back in Russia and worked with him at close quarters for several months. “It’s hard for me to believe that all that time he was playing a double game, that he didn’t once come unstuck. If he was really collaborating all along, well, then I’d have to say that Igor Rogov is a genius.”

At the beginning, the only thing Polish investigators had on Rogov was the fact that someone had mailed him the suspicious package. In his first jail interrogations, Rogov maintained it was all a big misunderstanding. He denied any knowledge of the package’s contents and insisted he would never have knowingly done anything to harm his new homeland. “I’m very grateful to Poland for taking me in and I’m ready to help you in any way I can,” he told investigators.

Rogov gave his version of how his name had come to be on the package. His friend Emil, also a Russian opposition activist, had told him that a contact was bringing a parcel from Ukraine and needed someone in Poland to leave it with. Emil said the package contained “presents from Ukraine” and Rogov said he would be fine to pick it up. Some days later he received a call from a woman who introduced herself as Kristina. “I’ve got a package for you from Diesel,” she told him, adding that she had just arrived in Kraków from Ukraine. Rogov had no idea who Diesel was, but assumed this was the package Emil had asked him about. He told Kristina he was away visiting friends, but gave her his address in Sosnowiec and explained how she could mail it to him using a courier service.

Polish authorities soon identified Kristina as a Ukrainian model from Odesa and put out an international arrest warrant for her. She was detained in late August at Amsterdam airport, just before boarding a plane to the US. Once delivered to Polish custody, she explained her side of the parcel story. “Diesel” was her old acquaintance – the nickname was because he worked with secondhand cars. He had found out she was planning to drive to Poland and asked if she might take a package with her. “He said he needed to distribute this stuff to poor people and was helping women and families,” Kristina told investigators. “I did think it was a weird set of things, but Diesel is a pretty weird guy.”

Kristina told investigators that Diesel had put the flask, power bank and other items in her Mercedes before she embarked on the long drive to Kraków. There, she had a rendezvous with a Czech businessman who had offered to pay her €3,000 if she would spend a week with him at a luxury hotel. She ate oysters and drank champagne with the Czech, though at night they retired to separate bedrooms, the case files suggest.

After she bade farewell to her new Czech friend, Kristina remembered the package. She was meant to hand it off in person, but when she called the number Diesel had given her, the man on the other end – Rogov – told her to send it via parcel courier instead. She retrieved the empty shoebox from a pair of €500 Golden Goose sneakers the Czech had bought her and filled the box with Diesel’s items. Then she wrapped it in paper and took the package to a bank of automated parcel lockers as instructed by Rogov.

Having addressed the package, she shoved it into a locker that was a shade too small, causing the packaging to tear. That damage meant the courier company opened the parcel when it reached their sorting facility, discovered the suspicious contents and raised the alarm. This set in train the arrests of Rogov and Kristina. Had she picked a larger locker, the package might have gone undetected and the bomb been assembled and detonated. But by whom? Rogov, or someone else? And on whose orders?

In the days after she sent the package, but before she was arrested, Kristina said she received a call from Diesel’s number. “I’m going to speak. You listen and stay quiet,” said a male voice she did not recognise. He told her the person she had mailed the package to had been detained, and that if she were also detained, she should invent a story about how she had come by the package. “All the correspondence between you and Diesel has been erased; don’t mention Diesel to anyone,” said the man.

The mysterious Diesel was emerging as the key to the parcel plot. Could he be a Russian agent working in Ukraine? Polish authorities had already arrested several Ukrainians recruited by Moscow to carry out arson in Poland, and it was possible that Diesel was part of a Russian sabotage ring with Rogov, using easy access to explosives in Ukraine to source the raw materials before they were assembled and detonated in Poland. Polish authorities issued an international arrest warrant for Diesel and one for Emil, who had told Rogov about the package.

Whoever Diesel was working for, one thing became clear as the questioning continued: Kristina knew nothing about the parcel’s purpose or final destination. In one of her interrogations, as investigators scrolled through her phone demanding ever more details of her encounters with various men in her contacts list, she lost her cool and asked them how this could possibly be relevant to the matter at hand. “All you’ve managed to achieve through your investigations is to prove that I’m a breaker of men’s hearts,” she told them.

Kristina was released in summer 2025, after a brief trial in which the prosecutor accepted that she had carried the items without realising they were dangerous and agreed to soften the charges. She was sentenced to time already served – 304 days – and fined. She did not respond to my requests for further comment.

As for Rogov, it was starting to look as if he, too, could be a tangential player in the bomb plot. He insisted he knew nothing of Diesel, and that the package had his name on it only because he had agreed to help out Emil. The biggest red flag suggesting he might be lying was the set of photographs of various urban scenes in Sosnowiec, marked with arrows, found on his phone. But he had a convincing explanation for that, too. He had sometimes ordered recreational drugs via a Telegram bot, he admitted, and would receive a photo of the pickup location with an arrow marking the drop spot. The only reason some of the locations were close to pipelines or other infrastructure was because these were desolate, empty places where hiding or retrieving a package would draw less attention, he said.

The investigation, which had initially seemed like it would uncover a major Kremlin terror plot against Europe, was not going to plan. There was no proven link to Russia, and the only two arrests were of a clueless Ukrainian model and a young Russian who was apparently guilty only of the occasional purchase of recreational drugs.

But something else was about to come to light about Rogov. Polish investigators were to learn that he had been credibly accused of working for the FSB for years, spying on his friends and colleagues in the Russian opposition. The source of the accusations made them hard to dismiss: it was Rogov’s wife, Irina.

Igor met Irina when they were teenagers. They were both studying veterinary medicine in Saransk, a drab city about 500km (310 miles) south-east of Moscow, where they lived their whole lives before emigrating. Rogov had a cheeky smile and easygoing demeanour that made him friends easily. He got into activism as a student, though to start with he was mostly drawn to local environmental issues. He was then one of thousands of young Russians who helped out with Navalny’s ill-fated attempt to stand against Putin in the 2018 presidential election, and he later became part of Open Russia, the opposition movement set up by the exiled oligarch Mikhail Khodorkovsky.

Rogov won respect in opposition circles after an incident in Minsk, in neighbouring Belarus, in August 2020, when Alexander Lukashenko, a close ally of Putin, declared victory after a rigged presidential election. Protesters took to the streets and Lukashenko launched a violent crackdown. Rogov was in Minsk as part of an informal monitoring mission organised by Open Russia. On the second evening of protests, Rogov and a fellow activist, Artem Vazhenkov, got caught up in an ambush outside a shopping mall. Black-clad riot police grabbed anyone they could lay their hands on and tossed them into armoured trucks; Rogov and Vazhenkov ended up at Minsk’s notorious Okrestina jail with hundreds of others. They were kept in a courtyard, hands tied and face-down on the ground, then moved to a packed cell holding about 40 men. “There was no attempt to get any information, like in Russian prisons. They just beat you for the hell of it,” Vazhenkov told me. The riot police broke Rogov’s ribs and fingers and left his body covered in bruises. The repeated kicks to his head in custody gave him migraines that recurred for years.

After three days of beatings, Rogov was released and deported to Russia. At the Open Russia office back in Moscow, he alternated between laughing and crying as he recounted the ordeal, still moving gingerly from the bruises. “We sent him to a holiday guesthouse for a couple of weeks to recover,” said Andrei Pivovarov, Open Russia’s executive director at the time.

A few weeks later, Igor and Irina, then 23 and 24 years old, got married in Saransk. Vazhenkov, who attended, said it was a “typical Russian wedding”, with vodka, toasts and lots of dancing. Rogov also became more active in Open Russia; the organisation felt partly responsible for the Minsk debacle and supported him to become the official head of their Saransk branch. But a few months later, Open Russia officially dissolved itself, because its designation as “undesirable” by Russian authorities meant activists could be arrested just for being linked to it. So when Rogov ran for a seat on Saransk’s city council in the summer of 2021, he stood as an independent candidate. Getting registered to stand, even in such a low-level vote, required organised and sustained campaigning. Milia Kashapova, a 26-year-old activist formerly associated with Open Russia, moved to Saransk for a few months to be his campaign manager.

The campaign was low-budget – Kashapova lived in the apartment of Rogov’s grandmother – but inventive. They spent long days canvassing on the streets and made Instagram reels featuring Igor and Irina’s cats. In the evenings they sat in bars, often with Irina, and discussed strategy. The police showed up at most public events to intimidate supporters, but this was standard practice in Russian regional politics, and Rogov ploughed on. He and his team went door-to-door, promising those who agreed to hear them out that, if elected, he would bring a breath of fresh air into the corrupt city council. In a campaign post on Telegram, he posted a picture of him and Irina with one of the cats, accompanied by the slogan: “Love and fidelity are the foundations of my family.”

When polling day came, Rogov won 16% of the vote in his district, finishing third behind two broadly pro-Kremlin candidates. He thanked his supporters and announced that he planned to launch several court cases to protest against procedural violations. “Think this is the end? It’s just the beginning,” he wrote on his Telegram channel. But in the following weeks, with a political crackdown on opposition groups under way, the Rogovs decided to leave Russia. They went to Georgia, then to Poland, after winning scholarships on a programme for Russian opposition activists. They arrived in Sosnowiec on 28 February 2022, four days after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Over the next few months, Russia would take a dramatic turn for the worse, as wartime censorship laws kicked in. Henceforth there would be only two choices for most political opponents: jail or exile.

The Rogovs’ new home was a boxy room in a student dormitory, where their neighbour was Danila Buzanov, another exiled Russian activist. Buzanov had spent several years working as a Navalny coordinator in Balakovo, a gritty industrial town known for its nuclear power plant. He had done multiple stints in jail and fled Russia in late 2021, packing a bag and slipping out of the country overnight after police showed up at his mother’s house with another arrest warrant for him.

Buzanov was also starting a new life from scratch in Sosnowiec, and he bonded with Igor and Irina over stories from Russia. “Igor was just a solid, straightforward guy, always joking, always pleasant to talk to, just like the kind of friends I had back at home, the ones I knew since school,” Buzanov told me. The trio’s closeness was amplified by the living arrangements: they shared a bathroom and a kettle, and the doors to their bedrooms were usually left open so the cats – which Irina had managed to exfiltrate from Russia – could roam freely.

Rogov always seemed to have money to go out and socialise. “Absolutely any meeting, with anyone, he was always there, always ready to have a beer and talk,” said Buzanov. Irina worked long hours doing manicures at a beauty salon to supplement her miserly university stipend – but Igor had no job. When Buzanov asked him where the money came from, he said he had sold his car before leaving Russia and was living off the proceeds. Rogov was also ever-present at the political demonstrations organised in nearby Katowice, where the small community of Russian exiles would gather to protest against the war in Ukraine or commemorate the death of Navalny in a Russian jail. Irina rarely joined. “She was completely apolitical; she’d rather go clubbing than go to a rally,” said Buzanov.

Over time, the psychological pressures of a life in exile began to take their toll on the Rogovs’ marriage. Irina found Igor distant and moody, and he was increasingly using recreational drugs. One of the dormitory’s administrative staff later described him in a police interview as a “nice polite boy” who was “rather hapless and seemed as though he wasn’t very good at dealing with things”. The couple’s arguments got progressively worse, and at some point Irina moved out to a room on a different floor, taking the cats with her. Igor grew a moustache and started working out more. He began spending time with another Russian exile studying at the university, named Polina. In April 2023, Irina walked in and caught him and Polina having sex on their old bed. She shouted at them and stormed out. A few minutes later, Buzanov’s phone buzzed with a Telegram message from Irina: “Did you know that Igor has been informing on you and others to the FSB?”

Irina sent a similar message to a group chat of her husband’s old political contacts from Russia, and within minutes, Igor’s phone was lighting up with queries that could be loosely summarised as: “WTF?” After a frenzied discussion between the couple, Igor persuaded Irina to give him her phone and he unsent her message. Later, she and Igor both messaged the group to say it had been a bad joke, apologising for any confusion. But Rogov swiftly confessed to his neighbour, Buzanov: “He was close to tears, and he didn’t try to justify himself, he just began apologising. ‘I’m so sorry, I was forced to do it,’ that sort of thing,” Buzanov told me. Too shocked to ask many follow-up questions, Buzanov put a password on his laptop and warned other friends to be careful around Rogov.

The marriage crisis put Irina in a difficult position, as her Polish residence permit was tied to Igor’s asylum status. She was furious that the whole dormitory knew about his affair, and told him he had humiliated her and ruined her life. She even discussed with friends whether it would be safe for her to move back to Russia, given that she had never directly been involved in opposition politics, and had once gone back to Saransk for a short trip to visit relatives without encountering any problems. But she was still in Sosnowiec in July 2024, when Igor was arrested.

When the news broke, the friends from the group chat assumed it was confirmation that Irina had been telling the truth about Rogov’s FSB collaboration, and that Polish authorities had found out. In reality, for the first few months of his detention, investigators were focused only on the explosive parcel, and had no idea about anything else.

From the files I was given access to, it is not clear how Polish authorities first became aware of Rogov’s alleged FSB links – whether Igor confessed, Irina told them or information was volunteered by someone in the group chat. But on 13 November 2024, roughly four months after Rogov was arrested, investigators added a second charge to his file: along with the charges linked to the explosive, he was also now under investigation for espionage. On the same day, Polish authorities arrested Irina, grabbing her as she crossed the street in Sosnowiec and accusing her of being her husband’s accomplice. Through a series of interrogations of both, the story of Rogov’s collaboration came into focus.

Rogov said he had been recruited during his university years, before he even started out in opposition politics, by a local Saransk FSB officer he knew as Yevgeny. To start with, he was proud of the collaboration, believing the FSB to be a patriotic organisation and grateful for the small amount of extra income it provided. After some time, Yevgeny gave Rogov a burner phone, and told him to keep it hidden at home; it would be their way of communicating. Irina was suspicious of these conversations, and demanded to know who Igor was speaking to so regularly on the secret phone. At first, he told her it was “a person who helps me with studies, deals with various bureaucratic issues and helps me financially”. Later, he confessed that he had been recruited by the FSB. He never told her the details of his conversations with Yevgeny, he claimed, and she never pushed. “It was enough for her to know it wasn’t another woman,” he said.

It is not clear from the files if the initial impulse to get involved in opposition politics came from Rogov or from Yevgeny, but once Rogov started his political activism, the FSB man pushed his recruit to make as many contacts as possible. “I was supposed to keep doing the things I wanted to: climb up the ladder in opposition circles, meet new people, help people, and then at the end tell the FSB about everything,” Rogov recounted. Whenever he came back from a trip to an opposition conference in Moscow or abroad, he told Irina he needed to spend some time working up a report to pass to Yevgeny.

The ideal scenario, Yevgeny told Rogov, would be if on one of these trips abroad, he was approached and pitched by a western intelligence agency. “The point was, I was supposed to become a double agent,” said Rogov. That plan never worked out, but it suggests Yevgeny had big plans for his agent. In every Russian region, one European intelligence official told me, there were numerous FSB operatives focused on infiltrating opposition groups, and these officers would look for ways to elevate their cases beyond local interest. “The low-level officer who did the recruitment will be trying to prove himself by pushing the case as far as possible,” said the source.

This may also explain Rogov’s trip to Minsk in August 2020. A report detailing the mood on the Belarusian streets would have been attractive currency for Yevgeny, an FSB man in the provinces, with his superiors in Moscow. Irina had begged Igor not to go, as they were due to be married a few weeks later, but after several conversations with Yevgeny on his burner phone, Rogov had told her he had no choice.

A few days after Rogov left for Minsk, he went dark. There were widespread reports of mass arrests, and Irina was in such a panic that she retrieved the burner phone and called the single number saved in it. When a man picked up, she said: “I’m Igor’s fiance and I know he talks to someone on this phone. I know that Igor went to Belarus because of you, and I need to find out what happened to him.” The man on the other end said little, then hung up. Soon after, Belarusian authorities released Rogov. It is not clear whether the FSB intervened with Minsk to facilitate his liberty, but his fellow activist Vazhenkov, who was detained at the same time, was not freed for another two days.

When Rogov returned, shaken and bruised from the beatings in Minsk, he was angry with Irina for contacting Yevgeny. He told her she should not poke her nose into his business and that she should never use the secret phone again. Then he hid it somewhere she could not find it.

In the months after Minsk, Rogov could sense that Yevgeny was delighted as he rose to prominence in the local opposition scene, he recalled. But he also claimed to have become genuinely engaged in the opposition struggle, and regretted he had ever agreed to collaborate. “If I had a choice I wouldn’t have done it … but to function in politics and maintain relationships I had to pass information on, because [Yevgeny] could have made everything impossible with one click of his fingers,” he said. On one occasion, when Rogov was at a hospital appointment for his migraines, he was presented with a military draft notice. When he discussed it with Yevgeny, the FSB man suggested he could make it go away. “Yevgeny knew everything about me and he blackmailed me … I had no choice, I felt under constant psychological pressure,” Rogov claimed. It was not clear from the files whether Yevgeny supported or had input into Rogov’s 2021 city council run, nor was it clear whether Rogov continued to receive regular payments from the FSB.

In Rogov’s telling, when he arrived in Poland in February 2022, he thought he had finally escaped Yevgeny’s clutches. He broke off contact, he claimed, and was focused on building a new life in Poland. But three months later, he got a message from an unknown number on Telegram and guessed immediately it was Yevgeny. “In a very veiled way he asked me to bring him some car parts, and I knew that he was demanding I pass on information,” Rogov told investigators. He ignored the message, but Yevgeny kept sending new ones. “Each of his messages caused huge stress for me, because I had family in Russia and I was really afraid of that,” he said. Rogov claimed that his father, still in Saransk, had been approached and told he could be mobilised into the army to fight in Ukraine, even though he was over 50 and should not have been eligible. Rogov assumed it was Yevgeny cranking up the pressure.

Eventually, Rogov said, he collected some fairly mundane information about Buzanov and a few other exiled opposition activists he knew, wrote it up into a Word document, and put it on a USB stick that he gave to Irina, who was taking a trip to Russia in summer 2022 to visit her parents. “I was convinced that the information could not really harm people, that this data could be partially found on the internet,” he claimed to his interrogators. Rogov said he had hoped the information transfer would placate Yevgeny, and also that he believed it could have been useful insurance for Irina: if she was given any trouble by Russian border guards for her links to opposition figures, she could say she was carrying important information for the FSB. (Irina claimed he did not tell her what was on the stick or who it was for until after she arrived in Russia.)

In the end, Irina entered Russia with no trouble. Back in Saransk, she visited the couple’s old apartment, which was now empty, and on her husband’s instructions, retrieved his old burner phone from the back of a kitchen cupboard, where it had remained undisturbed since their emigration. She charged it and called the one number saved in its contacts, as Igor had ordered her to, but there was no reply. She left Russia without handing over the USB stick. When she returned to Poland, she asked her husband if he was still in touch with Yevgeny. “He said no, and that he doesn’t want to maintain contact with him but he doesn’t know how to get out of it,” she said.

Some months later, around the time the marriage started disintegrating, Rogov got a message from another of Yevgeny’s alias accounts. By now, the couple’s asylum papers had come through and Rogov said he had been ready to start a new life, without Russian politics and without the FSB. “I wrote back saying I don’t work in politics any more and I won’t be passing any more information,” he said.

Later in 2023, Vazhenkov – the activist who had also been arrested in Minsk – visited Rogov in Sosnowiec and found his old friend to be a changed man. “We hardly discussed politics … he said he’s no longer political, he’s focused on studying hard. And he was really upset about the breakup with Irina,” Vazhenkov told me. Irina seemed to be adjusting better, having apparently moved on from the dark period immediately after the separation: “She had a lot of plans and she had learned good Polish.”

But neither Igor nor Irina would get to live the new lives they had envisioned. Before long, both were in jail. Last month, three years after Rogov claimed he had broken off contact with Yevgeny and two years after his arrest, a court in Sosnowiec sentenced him to seven years for espionage. Irina was sentenced to three years for aiding him by taking the USB stick to Russia.

The trial was held behind closed doors, and even information about how the defendants pleaded is classified. But lawyers for Igor and Irina told me they were planning appeals. Both lawyers said they would have preferred an open trial, suggesting that if the public knew the facts of the case, they might be less inclined to view the couple as Kremlin superspies. “It’s a shame my client’s case couldn’t be looked at in a more transparent and nuanced way,” said Irina’s lawyer, Katarzyna Matejczyk. However, at a time when Moscow is waging war in Ukraine and organising sabotage attacks in Europe, Polish authorities have little time for shades of grey when it comes to Russian spying. “In the current geopolitical situation, there is no chance of any verdict other than a conviction,” she said.

There was one remaining loose end – the explosive package that had set the whole story in motion. Rogov was found guilty on charges relating to the package, but there were few details in the short public verdict. Jacek Dobrzyński, a spokesperson for the Polish minister who coordinates the country’s security services, told me the parcel’s trail had led back to Moscow. “There is no doubt that this was a Russian plot orchestrated by the Russian secret services,” he said.

However, something did not quite add up. The court files I was able to see yielded no evidence of a Russian link and in fact pointed to a different possibility. During the investigation, one source told Polish authorities they believed “Diesel”, the Odesa car salesman who had given the package to the model Kristina to bring to Poland, actually had links to Ukrainian military intelligence.

This suggested the package might not have been a Russian bomb after all, but a Ukrainian one, transiting Poland and eventually destined for Russia. Since 2022, Kyiv has been running its own campaign of sabotage inside Russia, targeting military officials or pro-war cheerleaders. The latest such attack came this month, when an improvised bomb exploded in a Moscow restaurant during the birthday celebrations of a Russian army general. Three people were killed. My Ukrainian intelligence sources claimed no knowledge of the package sent to Rogov, but one said Kyiv’s sabotage campaign was a delicate issue with allies and usually organised behind their backs: “Almost every European country agrees that it’s legitimate for us to do this, but almost none of them want to cooperate on it.”

The person who could best solve the puzzle of the package, I thought, was the man who sent it, the mysterious Diesel – real name Yuriy Kovalenko. Finding him was easier than expected: he replied to my Facebook messages and agreed to meet at the offices of his lawyer in Odesa, on condition that she also be present. When we met, he was wearing a shell-suit jacket, blue jeans and New Balance trainers, and a kippah – he had rediscovered his Jewish identity in recent years, he said. He told me his nickname was due to his longstanding love of cars, but that these days most people just called him Yuriy.

Kovalenko told me he made a living by importing, fixing up and selling secondhand cars. He categorically denied any links to the Russian intelligence services. He also denied links to the Ukrainian services, but made it clear through his answers that he believed the explosive package had been Ukrainian, not Russian. The final destination was meant to be Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave that borders Poland, he said. However, he insisted he had only found this out later, and that he, too, had been merely a link in a chain of unsuspecting couriers. He claimed he had been given the collection of items by a friend who “possibly had some kind of link” with Ukrainian intelligence services. That friend, he said, asked him to send some items to Poland, so he asked an old acquaintance in the Russian opposition, Emil, if he knew anyone reliable there. Emil gave him Rogov’s name.

Kovalenko was evasive on the specifics: he refused to give further details about the person who supposedly gave him the package and he would not say how he knew the explosives were bound for Kaliningrad. Nor could he explain how they were meant to get there. In addition to his lawyer, he was accompanied to the interview by a man who sat silently next to him and did not introduce himself, claiming to be there “by chance” when asked.

In the shadow world of intelligence games and sabotage plots, it can be hard to discern where the true loyalties of each individual player lie. To add a final complication to the tale, Emil is suspected by many former colleagues in the Russian opposition of being an FSB informer just like Rogov. The full story of the bomb and its various couriers might be lost to history, but the very fact that Ukraine has not arrested Kovalenko, given Poland warned Kyiv of his role in the bomb plot and requested his extradition, points in the direction of the explosives being Ukrainian, not Russian.

And if that is indeed the case, it would be a further strange twist in the story of Igor Rogov, making him at once a Russian FSB informant and a would-be Ukrainian bomb courier.

In the two years since Rogov’s arrest, his old roommate Buzanov has been conflicted over what to think about his former friend. At the start, he felt sorry for Rogov and wrote him letters in prison. Then he was angry that Rogov’s treachery had led to Irina also being jailed, simply for carrying the USB stick into Russia. He also fears the story could prompt unfounded doubts, among Polish authorities or his friends, about his own loyalties. “Our biographies are so similar, and that’s uncomfortable,” he said, as we chatted in a cafe in a city not far from Sosnowiec. Many of Rogov’s friends rejected my interview requests, saying they did not want to be linked publicly to a convicted spy, but Buzanov was happy to talk for hours, keen to show he had nothing to hide.

This is one of the most damaging consequences of Rogov’s collaboration: it has intensified suspicions about Kremlin infiltration among the thousands of Russian opposition and civil society activists who have fled the country in recent years. These suspicions further corrode the effectiveness of the exiled opposition, already weak and divided, as they struggle to remain relevant from their new homes in Warsaw, Berlin or Vilnius.

Rogov was certainly not the only one among their ranks to have been recruited. “I am convinced there were hundreds of us,” a former FSB informant in Navalny’s organisation told the Guardian in 2022. Increasing the sense of paranoia among the opposition is likely part of the FSB strategy in making these recruits in the first place. Kashapova, Rogov’s former campaign manager, told me she used to brush off concerns about infiltration but had become “suspicious of everything and everyone” since Rogov’s arrest.

If the FSB’s goals are clear, Rogov’s motivations remain more elusive. From the testimony I saw, it is hard to say for sure just how reluctant his cooperation was, where his real loyalties lay or whether the information he passed on caused anyone real harm. His friends, without access even to that testimony, have drawn a range of conclusions: some refuse to believe the charges, others accept he may have been an informant but presume he was subjected to unbearable pressure by the FSB, while a third group are furious at him and believe there can be no excuses for collaboration. None can quite square the idea of Rogov as a long-term FSB plant with the young man they thought they knew.

Buzanov, who testified as a witness at the trial, imagines Rogov’s collaboration was likely down to his trademark poor decision-making, which had always got him into scrapes. He is convinced that Rogov was genuinely against Putin, but suspects he was so weak-willed that he was co-opted into working for the FSB, thinking he could make some money without doing anyone much harm. In the same vein, he assumes, Rogov agreed to receive the suspicious package without asking too many questions. “I don’t think he’s some superspy, sent on a special mission to Poland,” he said. “I think he’s just a fool.”

Additional reporting by Ada Petriczko

I got married in the Vegas of Europe. It was the most romantic 20 minutes of my life

The Guardian Thu, 13 Aug 2026 04:00:49 GMT

Post-Brexit visa rules and faceless pen-pushers were keeping me and my partner apart. But love finds a way

Consider your ideal wedding. You may picture religious pageantry, majestic domes and the auspicious light of the Divine beaming on a white dress. Maybe you see friends dancing on a pub’s veranda, cheering for you in front of a town hall, or anywhere really – the people you love are there, and it’s all that matters.

What you are probably not picturing is a meet-up with Chris and Mitch, two complete strangers waiting for you and your future spouse by a nondescript fountain in the middle of Copenhagen. Judging by my soon-to-be-wife’s bewildered laugh throughout the entire 20 minutes of our wedding, this is not what she was picturing either. Should I add that neither of us is Danish, or lives in Denmark?

My wife, who is attached to her privacy and thus will remain “my wife” for the purpose of this piece, is British-Polish, and made her life in the UK. I am French. Brexit means Brexit. To live happily ever after under the same London roof, we had to prove our commitment to the relevant authorities.

Our immigration adviser – an odd but knowledgable fellow – was unsubtle about it. On a Zoom call about a year ago, he mimed a rifle being reloaded. To end our long-distance relationship and build a life together, it was time for a shotgun wedding.

But while love doesn’t wait, administrations around Europe like to take their sweet time. Marrying in Britain required a “fiance visa”, which would have allowed me to stay in the UK while waiting to get married, but not to work, making it financially unviable. Doing it in my home country would have required dealing with French bureaucracy – you can appreciate why we ruled that out. If only there was a simple way to marry abroad, we thought.

A single Google search was enough to find an agency called Marry Abroad Simply.

Despite the hundreds of five-star reviews praising “excellent communication”, “genuine kindness” and a “completely stress-free experience”, I couldn’t shake the feeling that getting wed with Marry Abroad Simply was a bit like going for a haircut to a salon named Best Haircuts. One would hope for a bit more mystique.

But so be it – I dialled the WhatsApp number on the website and mumbled something to the effect of: “Hello, I’d like to marry my partner as soon as possible, please.” Instead of saying, “Sounds a bit dodgy, love”, a charming woman called Leanne laid out her fast-and-furious pitch.

Plan A, she said, was Gibraltar, the easiest option when it comes to paperwork. However, the marriage certificate can take a few weeks to arrive in the post. Plan B was Denmark, but city halls were crowded, so we would need to pay extra for a quicker ceremony in the park. Finally, she added, “I can get you married in Georgia in a couple of weeks.”

We opted for a compromise between speed and familiarity, and picked the “Copenhagen Express” package.

Denmark, we found out in the process, is the Vegas of Europe. Thanks to its lenient, multilingual administration, couples from around the world flock to the Scandinavian kingdom to elope. The trend started more than a decade ago, with Germans crossing the border to marry their partner from outside the Schengen area. It’s not a bad business: international couples bring about 120m kroner (about £13.7m) to the economy every year.

Leanne, who spoke to me after our blitz wedding, reckons her company helps 150 couples in Denmark every month. She often deals with cases more complex than ours, such as same-sex unions where one spouse comes from a country still denying them their rights. A former government document specialist, in 2013 she joined this industry specialising in quick, fuss-free wedding planning.

Our own wedding attained summits of fusslessness you wouldn’t believe. The day before, our suitcases barely unpacked, we got to Copenhagen city hall, where the civil registrar desk also serves as a gift shop. We queued with other couples to prove our identity to the Danish government. Fake bouquets were displayed on a table next to a sign saying “Flowers (for rent) on your wedding day”.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

We passed on the offer and the next morning rushed to the flower shop at Copenhagen train station. The white and purple bouquet my partner chose would look splendid under the grey Danish sky. With our prêt-à-porter suit and dress, she was gorgeous and I was dapper enough. We were ready to walk down the aisle.

After a 15-minute stroll through Copenhagen’s Latin Quarter, under the gaze of curious tourists and blase locals, we arrived at our venue: the gardens of the Royal Library. It’s a nice but unassuming park in the heart of the city. We had no guests, as you can imagine, and Marry Abroad Simply procured us Chris and Mitch.

Chris and Mitch – bless them – were our professional and only witnesses. They introduced us to our officiant, a mild-mannered gentleman named Jesper. We then stood awkwardly in front of the building that housed centuries of Danish literature. Jesper gave a brief speech about how we, too, were writing the first page of our common book. Listening to the sniffs on the video Chris took of that moment, I believe he shed a tear. But Leanne since told me they could do several of these a day, so he may just have had a cold.

We were so engrossed in the absurdity of the situation that we didn’t pay that much attention to Jesper’s speech. We said our vows, exchanged our rings, and kissed under the golf clap of onlookers. After some pictures, including a selfie with the gang, we crouched down on a bench to sign the papers. My wife and I were married.

You might find this unromantic, but I couldn’t disagree more. Throughout our Danish escapade, we kept bumping into other couples roaming in and around city hall. We could often guess from their looks and their accents that they were there for reasons similar to us. They were lovers seeking to tear down the borders erected between them, to prove their most intimate devotion to faceless pen-pushers.

That day was for us against the world. It was a day of boldness and belief in a bright future. To my readers longing for marriage, I say: forget bridesmaids, distant cousins and nervy photographers. What I wish for you is to marry abroad simply.

Jules Darmanin is a French journalist

Judge Dismisses Federal Government’s Antisemitism Case Against Harvard

The New York Times August 13, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The government argued the university had not done enough to combat antisemitism during campus protests. A judge called the incidents “isolated and episodic.”

By Mark Arsenault

A federal judge in Boston on Thursday dismissed the Trump administration’s antisemitism lawsuit against Harvard University, dealing a blow to the government’s efforts to force the school to make a deal.

The lawsuit was part of a broader pressure campaign to force the university to comply with a variety of government demands on issues that include its handling of antisemitism and race in admissions.

Judge Richard G. Stearns of the U. S. District Court in Massachusetts granted Harvard’s motion to throw out the case, saying that the antisemitic incidents cited in the administration’s March lawsuit were “too isolated and episodic” to show that Harvard is breaking the law.

In its lawsuit, filed in the spring, the Trump administration had accused the university of turning “a blind eye to antisemitism and discrimination against Jews and Israelis.” The administration said that Harvard had allowed anti-Israel protesters to violate school rules “with impunity” after the war in Gaza began in 2023.

A spokesman for Harvard declined to comment. The Trump administration did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Thursday.

The administration accused Harvard of violating Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which bans discrimination in programs that receive federal money.

The lawsuit stated that Jewish and Israeli students had been subject to “hostility, harassment and intimidation,” during a time when students were holding pro-Palestinian protests.

It cited a conflict from 2023 in which a Jewish student trying to film a “die-in” at Harvard was surrounded by protesters, who tried to block his camera with scarves and jostled him. The lawsuit repeatedly cited the report of a task force Harvard created to investigate episodes of antisemitism.

The university argued in a June brief that Harvard for several years had “engaged in sustained, institution-wide efforts to identify and address antisemitism on campus.”

Judge Stearns sided with Harvard in his ruling, noting that the Trump administration’s lawsuit focused mostly on incidents during the 2023-24 school year.

The antisemitic incidents cited by the administration do not support “a plausible inference that any institutionalized noncompliance with Title VI persists at Harvard to this day,” the judge wrote.

The Trump administration in its lawsuit sought the right to deny federal grants to Harvard. But the judge said the law was designed to force a school into compliance, not to penalize it.

Carl Tobias, a professor at the University of Richmond School of Law, said the ruling for Harvard was “rather narrow” and may be appealed. He expects the Trump administration will continue to pressure colleges and universities through the courts.

The administration and the Justice Department seem to have “focused on Harvard as the major private school target, but a number of other private and some public schools have been, and seem to remain, in D. O. J.’s cross hairs,” he said.

But Samuel Bagenstos, a University of Michigan law professor, said the ruling “eliminates any realistic chance that the Trump administration can use a Title VI investigation to coerce Harvard.”

The government has proved “very creative” in devising ways to pressure the university, he said, though “at some point, the folks in the Trump administration will surely realize that they look as ridiculous as Wile E. Coyote trying to catch the Road Runner.”

The Brandeis Center, a Jewish civil rights group, argued that the judge’s reasoning could create a legal standard that would make it harder for the government to win civil rights cases in the future. Instead of just showing that an institution had refused to fix a violation, the government would have to also show subsequent violations, the group’s chairman, Kenneth L. Marcus, said in a statement. That would set a much higher bar for cases, said Mr. Marcus, who was an education official in the first Trump administration.

Other Trump-Harvard litigation continues to grind through federal courts, mostly out of sight, as the two sides build lengthy records of briefs and legal arguments.

Another Boston federal judge ruled in September that the Trump administration had improperly frozen grants to Harvard. The administration said it had done so in response to the school’s tolerating harassment of Jewish students.

The Trump administration appealed, and the case is progressing. In a legal filing this spring, the president’s lawyers sought to show Harvard’s “long, sordid history of antisemitism” by citing Judah Monis, a Jew hired as a professor of Hebrew some 300 years ago, who had to convert to Christianity to join the faculty. That injustice was in 1722, decades before the Declaration of Independence.

In July, more than 10,000 alumni, from members of the Class of 1950 to the Class of 2026, filed a brief in support of Harvard, arguing that “universities like Harvard can only manifest their mission, values, and foundational principles if they can operate with academic freedom.”

Harvard’s battles with the Trump administration have broader implications for the federal government’s relationship with higher education. Many universities rely heavily on federal financial support to conduct research on cancer treatments, agriculture and other topics.

In late July, more than three dozen schools filed a legal brief supporting Harvard, saying that cutting research money to universities “jeopardizes American innovation and economic growth by severely limiting their ability to play their vital, longstanding roles in expanding scientific knowledge.”

Harvard and the government are also in a legal battle after the Trump administration tried to stop Harvard from hosting international students. A federal judge ruled in Harvard’s favor in June 2025. The government is appealing.

Mark Arsenault covers higher education for The Times.

Appeals Court Sidesteps Key Question Over Trump’s Use of Wartime Law

The New York Times August 13, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

The court dismissed a case over the Alien Enemies Act in a messy conclusion to a long-running legal battle that had seemed destined to end up before the Supreme Court.

By Alan Feuer

For nearly a year, the American Civil Liberties Union has been waiting for an answer to a legal question arising from one of the earliest pillars of the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration agenda. Could President Trump use the sweeping powers of an 18th-century wartime law to summarily deport people accused of belonging to a Venezuelan street gang?

In September, a three-judge panel of the conservative federal appeals court in New Orleans provided a response, rejecting Mr. Trump’s use of the law, the Alien Enemies Act, after finding that the American homeland was not under invasion by the gang, Tren de Aragua.

On Thursday, however, the full court, which had been mulling the question ever since, made the unusual decision to dismiss the case altogether because of what amounted to a legal technicality. The judges ruled that because the government had already expelled the three Venezuelan men who filed the original lawsuit challenging Mr. Trump through traditional immigration methods, there were no longer any plaintiffs — and so no longer any case.

The surprise move by the U. S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit was a messy — and somewhat baffling — conclusion to the leading case in a long-running and multipronged legal battle that had seemed destined to end up in a showdown at the Supreme Court. But now the issues that both the A. C. L. U. and the Justice Department have been waiting to be decided will — at least for the moment — remain unresolved.

The case involving the Alien Enemies Act, which has been used only a handful of times since it was passed in 1798, reaches back to March 2025. Mr. Trump issued a proclamation drawing on its broad authority to round up and remove members of a hostile nation in times of declared war or during an invasion or predatory incursion of the United States.

The target was dozens of Venezuelan men accused of belonging to Tren de Aragua, which Mr. Trump claimed had invaded the country through the process of illegal immigration. He further asserted that members of the gang were not mere criminals but were working in coordination with the hostile government of Venezuela, which was led at the time by Nicolás Maduro, the former president who is now in American custody and facing drug charges in New York.

Several lower courts, including the three-judge panel of the Fifth Circuit, rejected the president’s assertions, rebuffing the idea that immigration, even at a large scale, was synonymous with a military breach of U. S. borders.

“A country’s encouraging its residents and citizens to enter this country illegally is not the modern-day equivalent of sending an armed, organized force to occupy, to disrupt or to otherwise harm the United States,” Judge Leslie H. Southwick wrote for the panel’s majority at the time. “There is no finding that this mass immigration was an armed, organized force or forces.”

There was an expectation that the full Fifth Circuit, one of the most conservative courts in the country, would quickly overturn the panel and grant Mr. Trump the authority to use the Alien Enemies Act to expel the Venezuelans from the country. But after convening all of its 17 active-status judges for what is known as an en banc hearing in January, the court remained unusually silent — that is, until Thursday when it issued a pair of rulings.

The first rejected a compromise solution to the problem arising from the expulsion of the plaintiffs in the case, which both the A. C. L. U. and the government had embraced. The two sides agreed that the easiest way forward was simply to introduce new plaintiffs from the larger class of Venezuelans who had challenged the law and continue on to a decision on the underlying issues.

The second ruling, building on the first, tossed out the case in its entirety.

“Given the lack of any named petitioners to whom we could grant relief in this appeal, and given that this case has never and does not now feature any class, we conclude that the appeal is moot,” the court’s majority wrote.

Lee Gelernt, a lawyer for the A. C. L. U. who argued in front of the Fifth Circuit, said that the injunction issued by the three-judge panel remained in effect, protecting immigrants in Texas, where the case began, from being deported under the Alien Enemies Act.

“Perhaps the administration will now consider revoking the alien enemies proclamation given the overwhelming view of courts around the country that using this wartime authority during peacetime is flatly unlawful,” he said.

The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment.

In many ways, the decision by the full appeals court raised more questions than it answered.

It remained unclear, for instance, whether Mr. Trump would keep up the fight to use the Alien Enemies Act given that his administration managed to deport the three named plaintiffs in the Fifth Circuit case through normal means largely without dispute.

It was also unclear what would happen to the other cases in other states that have also challenged the use of the law. The case in the Fifth Circuit was supposed to have been the one that arrived first in the Supreme Court for a final ruling on the president’s wartime powers declaration.

Other cases — in New York, for example — were essentially on hold, awaiting a decision in New Orleans. Now those cases will start moving forward again, though it remains unclear which one will take the lead.

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

The Nuns Who Took Over an Assisted Living Center

The New York Times August 13, 2026

As convents are closing all over, the sisters are facing the end of their lives together — and they have brought the party to an assisted living center in the suburbs.

Having sold their convent, the Sisters of Divine Compassion (from left, Sister Joanne Fallon, Sister Mary Stephen Healey, Sister Mary Alice O’Brien, and Sister Jane Keegan) now gather at the Wartburg home in Mount Vernon, N. Y. Credit...

Supported by

By John Leland

Photographs by Roshni Khatri

It was happy hour at the assisted living building, with snacks and a live entertainer, and Sister Stephen was doing her best to be happy. She clapped along to “Hello, Dolly!”

About 20 women and one man sat in a brightly lit activity room, some in wheelchairs. Here, happy hour comes every Friday at 2 p. m.

“You’re a sister?” a woman asked Sister Stephen. “You don’t look like a sister.”

“Well, what does a sister look like?” the sister asked. The woman did not have an answer. What does a sister look like?

“I’m going to get up and dance in a minute,” Sister Stephen said. At age 96, after two knee replacements, she is limited in her dance steps. But get up she did, using her walker for support, and swayed to “Save the Last Dance for Me.”

Still, she felt something was missing. For starters, there was no white wine.

“Only red,” said Sister Mary Martin, taking orders around the room.

But more than that, where were all the other sisters?

Sister Stephen looked around the room with some bafflement.

“It’s funny,” she said, surprised by what she saw. “Most of the people in this room now are not nuns.”

Because usually, she said, there were more. A lot more. Through a confluence of forces, the center has become one of the last places in New York where you can find an abundance of nuns.

In the mid-1960s, America was home to more than 180,000 Roman Catholic nuns; now there are only about 35,000, with an average age of over 80. Congregations have had to sell or close their convents, forcing these older sisters to find new places to live.

For many in the New York area, that has turned out to be an unlikely place: a Lutheran care center called Wartburg. Founded in 1866 as a farm school and home for Civil War orphans, the center spreads across 34 acres in Mount Vernon, N. Y., with care options ranging from independent living to skilled nursing and memory care.

Since the first wave of about 30 nuns from the Dominican Sisters of Hope, a congregation in Newburgh, N. Y., arrived in 2009, the number of sisters in the center has swelled to about 80, more than one-third of the residents.

“When the cardinal was here last year,” said David Gentner, the president of Wartburg, “he said there’s more consecrated women religious on this campus than anywhere in the archdiocese.”

The sisters at Wartburg, now mostly in their 80s and 90s, belong to a cohort of women who took their vows in the decades after the World War II in numbers never seen before or since. It was a boom time for American religion, when churches saw record attendance and the words “under God” were added to the Pledge of Allegiance. The sisters staffed schools and hospitals and social service providers; they marched for peace or against hunger. And they watched their numbers steadily diminish in the following decades, as fewer and fewer women followed them.

Now, as they navigate their own final chapters, they are also contemplating the end of their congregations, a process known as coming to completion. And they may be witnessing the end of sisterhood itself.

“In 10 years, children will not know what a nun is — was,” Sister Stephen said, correcting herself. “They’ll be gone.”

Yet to spend time among the sisters at Wartburg is to see a promising vision of old age: collective, purposeful, grounded in service to others — and above all, accepting of change. Having long ago taken vows forsaking so much of the world’s strivings, the sisters are perhaps uniquely prepared for the losses and separations of old age.

“Even just the fact of an elevator, we’re not used to,” said Sister Stephen, who ran a Catholic school for 59 years before she retired last year at 95. It was a warm March afternoon, and her small studio apartment in Wartburg’s assisted living building was decorated in paper shamrocks for St. Patrick’s Day. “I never lived like this before, to be honest,” she said. “I mean, three meals a day, your apartment is cleaned. I never had all this before. In fact, there’s too much, I say sometimes. But it’s OK.”

On a recent evening, the sister, whose full name is Mary Stephen Healey, had a question about the other sisters at Wartburg. She was talking with four members from her congregation, the Religious of Divine Compassion, or Sisters of Divine Compassion. The congregation, which once had almost 300 sisters, now has only 40, with a median age of 84, and no new novices entering. Of the 40 still living, 23 are at Wartburg.

The reason so many were missing from the happy hour, it turned out, was that they were at a funeral.

The “Divines,” as some at Wartburg have called them, had never lived among sisters from other orders. Now their neighbors at the center included sisters from seven other congregations, as well as lay people.

“How do you think we’re perceived here by the rest of the sisters?” Sister Stephen asked.

“I think we’re kind of an outgoing, very compassionate, social, fun group,” said Sister Mary Alice O’Brien, 81. Sister Mary Alice described herself, playfully, as “a high introvert.” She has a reputation as a particularly spirited presence at happy hour. “Truthfully,” she said, “I think we’ve brought life to the place.”

All insisted that there was no rivalry, friendly or otherwise, among the orders.

Absolutely not, Sister Stephen said. “Though I do think we’re unusual.”

The Sisters of Divine Compassion were founded in 1886 to serve the population of poor immigrant girls, many Irish or Italian, then arriving in New York City. Later the order shifted its focus to education.

Sister Stephen, whose name at birth was Clare, was born in the Bronx and attended Catholic schools, though she was asked to leave kindergarten after throwing peas at a nun. “I was always in trouble,” she said, not contrite at the admission. After her mother died when she was 10, she moved to a boarding school run by the Sisters of Divine Compassion in White Plains, N. Y.

She entered the order and moved into the convent at age 18, she said, because she was so moved by the sisters who taught her, and started teaching before she even finished college, a common practice in the 1950s and ’60s. As she taught, she returned to school for a bachelor’s degree and then a master’s.

When she arrived at Wartburg last July, she had a ready-made community of women who shared her experience and her congregation’s charism, or founding mission. Across the hall was Sister Joanne Fallon, 86, who worked with Sister Stephen for more than 50 years, teaching first and then fourth grade. They had retired together last spring, the last two sisters in their school, and the last two at the convent, which the order was turning into a community center.

For Wartburg, the influx of sisters has been a plus, said Mr. Gentner, the president. They’re the unpaid outreach workers, social hubs in a center where isolation and despair are always risks. Many only recently stopped working; Sister Stephen still teaches Spanish at her old school, driving there three days a week over two heavily trafficked highways. “They’re vital, they’re educated, they’re service-oriented,” Mr. Gentner said.

What they do is not dramatic, but in a community of older adults who have had to leave their homes and neighbors, a commitment to service and compassion can go a long way.

Sister Mary Martin Delahanty, 87, who worked as a teacher and school principal until she was 81, makes a point to welcome all new residents and visit those who are bedbound or frail, offering Communion and companionship. She serves drinks and snacks at happy hour.

Three years ago, other sisters from her order, the Dominican Sisters of Hope, urged her to move to Wartburg. “I said, Who’s paying for it?” she said, with a dry Massachusetts accent and the fatalistic humor that comes of being a Mets fan. “They said: ‘The community. So come on.’”

At Wartburg, she found her purpose in doing simple things for other residents, whether sisters or lay people. “I like to sit with people and talk to them and fool around with them,” she said. “That’s me. If they’re sad or lonely I’ll say, ‘Come on, you’re better than that.’”

The sisters’ move to Wartburg, like so much in New York, began with real estate. “We were paying for these big properties that we had, and we were finding that it wasn’t going to be sustainable,” said Sister Laura Donovan, 76, president of the Sisters of Divine Compassion. “And canonically, we’re responsible for every sister till the last sister dies.”

For 125 years, the congregation owned a 16-acre campus in White Plains, with a high school, college, convent and chapel. But as the order shrank, and the sisters’ medical needs grew, they sold it to a real estate developer for a reported $16.3 million in 2016.

They chose Wartburg, in part, because it wasn’t too luxurious, as “that was inappropriate to us for our vows,” said Sister Laura, who does not live at the center herself. The congregation pays for the sisters’ accommodations, which range from just over $5,000 a month for an independent living cottage to $11,845 a month for an all-inclusive apartment. (There is also a subsidized building for low-income residents.)

Sister Mary Alice had taught at the high school in White Plains until the congregation closed it in 2015. At the time, she was living with another sister — a “brilliant woman,” she said, who had been a university dean — who had early onset dementia and needed someone to care for her

Though she was not ready to give up teaching, she said, she decided that her next assignment was caring for her friend with Alzheimer’s, first in the apartment they shared, then — when the stairs became too much for Sister Mary Alice — in Wartburg. Now, Sister Mary Alice regularly visits her friend at a nearby skilled nursing home, where the woman no longer recognizes her.

There were advantages to living with sisters from other communities and with lay people, she said.

“More and more we see ourselves as one powerhouse of service and kindness and compassion and mercy,” she said. “When all the communities were larger, that maybe facilitated being separate, but now we see ourselves as sisters, and we have these common values and common goals and common beliefs for compassion in the world, peace in the world.”

Another Friday, another happy hour. Sister Jane sat with two lay women, both widows. Sister Mary Alice sat a little farther back at a table with other sisters, some from different congregations. Again, some sisters, including Sister Stephen, were missing because of a funeral.

Again, no white wine.

“Only red,” Sister Mary Martin said.

I asked the sisters if they had ever had any doubts or regrets about choosing their vocation. On a previous visit, Sister Stephen had said that she used to wish that she had a child. But over the years the children had changed, the world they inhabited had changed. “Now I wake up in the morning and say, Oh, thank you, God,” she said.

Sister Jane thought she had doubts at some point, but now she could not remember them. “I didn’t choose this” she said. “I had a whole lot of things I wanted to do with my life when I was a young person. I wanted to fly a plane like Amelia Earhart. I wanted to be a drummer in a band. So that’s how I know it was God saying no. And I haven’t flown a plane yet.”

Sister Mary Alice sang along to “Day-O” and “Can’t Help Falling in Love.”

Finally, during the Johnny Cash song “Ring of Fire” — not the holiest of songs — she walked over to a man in a wheelchair, one of the few men in the room, and danced beside him, holding his hand so he could move as well, even in his chair.

This, too, was part of her charism, what gave her life meaning and purpose in this stage, she said. “I mean, it just takes a little bit to put a smile on a person’s face,” Sister Mary Alice said. “And to me, that’s beautiful. That’s of God. That’s of the spirit. I feel I’m still giving and in service to other people.”

And in the end, sisters adapt. They had absorbed so much over the years, from Vatican II to Smart Boards in the classroom, incorporating all into their mission. Wartburg was just one more adaptation.

“I’m here because it’s my journey to the Lord,” Sister Stephen said. “I’m getting ready. I’m only 96 and I so have a few more years, probably. I think that this is where I’m to be, and this is the beginning of my journey.”

After the happy hour, Sister Jane found a quiet seat overlooking the lawn. She worried about another woman who looked like she might be disoriented walking nearby.

She regretted that she could no longer march in demonstrations, she said. At a monthly Peace Prayer the day before, a number of sisters had lamented that their canes and walkers now limited them to making phone calls or writing letters.

Yet there were also compensations. “I enjoyed my red today,” she said. “I don’t usually drink red, but it didn’t matter. It’s not what’s in the glass that’s important. It’s what’s in the spirit that we share.”

On my second or third visit, the sisters dropped the bomb: “You have to come back for happy hour.” I’ve spent plenty of time in facilities like Wartburg, both as a reporter and a son. Too often, residents are lonely and adrift, living out their last years with no clear sense of purpose. The sisters showed another way to thrive in old age — a blueprint we could all learn from.

John Leland is a reporter covering life in New York City for The Times.

Female Afghans Erased From Public Life in Five Years of Taliban Rule

The New York Times August 13, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Decrees restricting women’s rights to study, work, travel and act independently now threaten to damage Afghanistan permanently, experts say.

By Ephrat Livni

The Taliban regained control of Afghanistan five years ago this week, returning to power after two decades and restoring an Islamic government that had severely restricted women’s rights.

In those few years, women and girls have been systematically erased from most public life, experts say. And, some add, the limitations imposed on half the population could hobble Afghanistan far into the future.

The harsh restrictions on women and girls are a return to conditions that prevailed the previous time the Taliban controlled Afghanistan, in the late 1990s. More than 160 decrees have been issued targeting women and girls, barring them from secondary and higher education and restricting their employment, movement, dress, speech and decision-making.

“No other country in modern times has dismantled the rights of half its population through law, policy and practice to the same extent,” the United Nations agency on women said on Wednesday. “At the same time, overlapping humanitarian and economic crises and deepening poverty are also having a disproportionate impact on women and girls.”

The official restrictions have reinforced social pressures, and many women say their communities increasingly press them to conform, a new U. N. Women report found, based on recent surveys. “Half a decade of escalating restrictions has narrowed where Afghan women can go, what they can do and how they can live,” it said. “The results are alarming.”

The agency surveyed about 5,000 Afghans in rural and urban communities this past spring and last year, asking women and men about life under the Taliban. There were some similarities in the genders’ answers — but some very stark differences as well.

Many Afghans surveyed expressed disappointment with the course of their lives in recent years. Still, women reported levels of isolation and distress that suggest a growing mental health crisis, the U. N. report said.

More than half of men surveyed — about 55 percent — said their lives were worse than they had expected they would be before August 2021, compared with 65 percent of women who reported a similar sentiment. But their reasoning was starkly different.

Male respondents reported frustration with a lack of economic opportunities, while many women also blamed reduced access to education, for themselves or their children, and rules restricting women’s jobs and lives.

“By closing off education and many forms of employment, these restrictions compound the economic pressures already felt by most women,” the U. N. report said, noting the “profound personal toll” the situation has had on women in Afghanistan. Many women reported rising stress, worry and pressure, “consistent with wider evidence of deteriorating mental health,” it added.

The report highlights the isolation many Afghan women now experience as a result of the restrictions. A vast majority of the women surveyed — 90 percent — said they must have a male family member’s permission to leave the house. And more than half said they went out only once or twice a month. Among male survey respondents, more than 95 percent reported leaving their homes daily.

Women and girls’ adherence to the new Taliban rules is increasingly reinforced by people around them, like relatives and neighbors. The U. N. report noted that nearly 40 percent of women surveyed this year said they felt more pressure than before to tailor their behavior for fear that those they know will report them for inappropriate dress, speech or actions.

“The Taliban have extended state control deep into the private sphere by transforming patriarchal norms into legal obligations and conscripting families into the enforcement of their ideology,” Belquis Ahmadi, a human rights lawyer and expert on Afghanistan, formerly at the United States Institute of Peace, wrote in a recent report on Taliban rule.

Human rights experts say that the crisis for women in Afghanistan has reached a critical point.

Afghanistan is the only country in the world to formally prohibit access to education for girls and women beyond the primary level. The longer women and girls are excluded from schools, institutions and public life, the more entrenched the restrictive system becomes, the further behind they fall and the fewer models there are, making their ability to recover ever less likely, jeopardizing the country’s long-term prospects.

“As a new generation of girls grows without an education, their future becomes increasingly dark,” UNESCO wrote in a statement this week, calling for the full restoration of the right to education for Afghan girls and women.

Ms. Ahmadi wrote in her analysis, “Behind every Taliban decree is a human story: a university student packing away her books, a teacher dismissed from the profession she loves, a judge forced into hiding, a doctor prevented from treating patients, an entrepreneur closing her business, or a young girl asking her parents why she is no longer allowed to learn while her brother walks freely to school.”

She argues that the international community must speak up for the silenced.

“The greatest danger facing Afghanistan today is not only that 20 million women and girls are being systematically erased from public life,” Ms. Ahmadi wrote. “It is that the world is slowly learning to live with it.”

Ephrat Livni is a Times reporter covering news around the world. She is based in New York.
