Trump Gives Green Light to U. S. Companies to Aim Hacks at Cybercriminals

The New York Times August 13, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The practice would align the United States more closely with countries like China and Russia, where spy agencies have long relied on private-sector hackers to help with national security missions.

By Dustin Volz

Dustin Volz covers cybersecurity and intelligence from the Washington bureau.

The Trump administration is encouraging American companies to conduct their own cyberattacks against criminal hackers, a move that White House officials say will help address digital scourges like ransomware but that some former officials and security experts warn could lead to chaos.

Under a national security memorandum that President Trump signed late Wednesday, select companies would work with the Justice and Homeland Security Departments to strike foreign cybercriminal groups with hacks under certain conditions. The attacks would allow both surveillance of the criminal networks and specific types of hacking operations that could lead to disruption, manipulation or destruction of information systems and networks, including virtual and physical infrastructure.

It was not clear which companies, if any, would sign up, but the move is a sharp pivot from decades of cybersecurity policy across Republican and Democratic administrations that generally prioritized improving corporate defenses and confined offensive cyberoperations to the U. S. military and intelligence agencies. It adds detail to a shift that Trump officials had teased in general terms for months.

The concept of giving the private sector a more direct role in offensive cyberactions has been around for years. But it has never before been publicly endorsed by a presidential administration, in part because of concerns that doing so could provoke more cyberconflict, raise novel questions of liability and international legal exposure for U. S. firms, and have unforeseen — and potentially escalatory — consequences. The new memorandum does not directly address many of those concerns, though it states that the policy is meant to tap into the “ingenuity of the private sector” to stem the ever rising costs of cyberattacks.

Rather than permit a free-for-all on the digital battlefield, however, the conduct that U. S. companies can engage in is intended to be relatively circumscribed. Participating companies must first be vetted to be included in the program, sign a contract with the government that includes $1 million fines for violations, and receive written approval from officials at the Justice and Homeland Security Departments before proceeding with an attack. The policy will not authorize attacks that are likely to lead to loss of life, serious injury or “rise to the level of use of force or armed attack under international law,” though former officials and experts said precisely calibrating offensive cyberoperations is sometimes as much an art as a science.

The White House did not respond to questions about the memorandum other than to say operations would be “based on intelligence.” The Trump administration did not brief reporters on the order ahead of its release late Wednesday.

Amanda Naylor, director of cyberpolicy at the National Security Council, which helped draft the memo along with the Office of the National Cyber Director, said in a LinkedIn post that the memo would “give the United States new tools to protect Americans from cybercrime and fraud.”

But many former officials and some security executives expressed worry that the new approach could be difficult to enact and risked complicating the already unpredictable world of modern cyberwarfare. Among other issues, it appeared that the approved companies could potentially take actions that exceed the authorities granted to the government’s own security agencies, a former senior U. S. intelligence official said.

Mr. Trump’s executive action contains a classified annex laying out a process to deconflict private-sector hacking with the federal government’s own operations. The memo also specifies that attacks will be limited to transnational criminal organizations that are considered separate from a foreign government “unless clear intelligence exists establishing such connection.”

Nick Carr, the threat intelligence lead at Microsoft and a former cybersecurity official, said in a social media post that his biggest concern was “just how difficult attribution in criminal operations is, and how few organizations can repeatably do it right,” including government agencies. He added, however, that the order could improve those efforts.

Still, it is often murky whether a criminal hacking group, such as a Russian-speaking gang of cyberthieves, has ties to a foreign power or at times does work for a spy agency on the side. Michael Garcia, who served as the associate chief of policy at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency until departing in June, said that while attribution had improved over the years, it still was not perfect and that “obfuscation is still a hell of a tactic.”

Some former officials said the order sought to address a growing and unsustainable problem that was probably only going to become worse in the short term with artificial intelligence.

“The current pace of cyberoperations is unsustainable for just the military,” said Mieke Eoyang, a former Pentagon official who oversaw military cyberweapon use during the Biden administration.

Ms. Eoyang, now a visiting professor at Carnegie Mellon University, said the memo’s success would hinge on the classified procedures for vetting firms and approving targets. She added that the existing process for approving military cyberoperations, developed during the first Trump administration, was “onerous, but it took into consideration collateral consequences and deconfliction.”

To some extent, the new order would align the United States more with some of its chief cyberantagonists, including China and Russia, where spy agencies have long relied on contract hackers working in the private sector to further their national security missions, in part to afford the state plausible deniability. U. S. defense technology companies also support the National Security Agency and U. S. Cyber Command, but that relationship usually involves supplying hacking tools, cyberintelligence and tradecraft to the U. S. intelligence community and military, rather than engaging directly in cyberoperations.

Dakota Cary, an expert on China’s hacking ecosystem, said that historically Beijing had copied various cybersecurity policies from the United States, but that the new Trump policy was a reversal of that arrangement.

“In many ways, China’s hacking prowess now stems from the fact that they copied our education system,” said Mr. Cary, an adviser at the U. S. cybersecurity company SentinelOne. “Now it seems the U. S. is interested in copying China’s system for deputizing private-sector hackers.”

Given all its complexities, it was not clear what companies might participate in the program, which some lawyers said appeared to contain substantial risk.

“This approach from the government presents novel questions for publicly traded companies in the sector: Even if they engage in ‘hack back’ activities under U. S. government cover or direction, how will they manage the increased operational risk to their business and customers, and how and when will they disclose it?” said Vanessa Le, a partner at Latham & Watkins who advises companies on geopolitical risk.

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

Kennedy Center Board Decides to Inscribe Trump’s Name on Building

The New York Times August 13, 2026

Trump Remakes Washington

Advertisement

Supported by

The vote to add “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” is an aggressive test of a judge’s order to remove his name.

By Julia Jacobs

The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted on Thursday to inscribe President Trump’s name on the building beneath the main signage, according to two people with direct knowledge of the proceedings, aggressively testing a federal judge’s order.

According to the resolution approved by the Trump-allied board, the inscription underneath the institution’s name would read: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.” The board’s decision, which directs officials to act by “all legal means,” came shortly after it voted to move forward with Mr. Trump’s plan to shutter the building for renovations.

The president’s name was added to the building last year, but the judge ordered the letters taken down, finding that only Congress had the authority to change the institution’s name. The center removed Mr. Trump’s name in June but is appealing the ruling.

The move appeared to attempt to find a creative workaround to a provision in the federal law governing the Kennedy Center that says “no additional memorials or plaques in the nature of memorials shall be designated or installed in the public areas.”

In Thursday’s resolution, the board directed officials to honor Mr. Trump for bringing the center back “from the brink of disaster,” presenting a series of possibilities that included naming the center’s grounds the “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”

“It is hereby resolved,” the measure said, “that the center desires to recognize and honor President Trump’s existential and unprecedented contributions to the survival of the center by all legal means.”

Both decisions will be subject to the scrutiny of the judge who, in response to a lawsuit from a Democratic lawmaker, found that the board had been “derelict” in considering the closure plan before approving it originally. Mr. Trump announced in February that the center would close for two years, with the objective of transforming what he called a “tired, broken and dilapidated” institution.

The board voted on Thursday to close the Kennedy Center’s main building while keeping a newer addition to the campus, known as the Reach, open for limited programming and to operate as an active memorial to John F. Kennedy.

Representative Joyce Beatty, a Democrat from Ohio and an ex officio member of the center’s board who sued the center, said in a statement that the resolutions were part of a “transparent effort to circumvent the court’s ruling.”

In a phone interview after the votes, Paolo Zampolli, a former modeling agent and a longtime Trump ally who sits on the board, said the trustees acted out of a desire to make the Kennedy Center more of a sought-after sightseeing destination. His goal for the inscription of Mr. Trump’s name is to make it “as big as it can get,” he said.

Ahead of the meeting, the board was presented with a 163-page plan for a $250 million “renewal” project that includes structural repair work, new marble floors, $11.8 million in “acoustical improvements” and a plan to temporarily move the famous 3,000-pound bronze bust of Kennedy to another building on campus. The judge had said in his order that the board had a legal obligation to maintain the facility as a memorial to Kennedy.

The approved resolution noted that the decision to close was made based on an “independent and objective analysis” of possible options by an outside consulting firm, which determined that keeping the main building open during renovations would be significantly more costly. It notes that the board was “fully committed” to continue arts and educational programming during the closure and maintain the “historic and architecturally significant nature” of the building.

Mr. Trump, the board’s chairman, called into the meeting, which was held remotely, and criticized those opposed to his closure plan, according to the people with direct knowledge of the proceedings.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who was tapped by the president to help oversee the Kennedy Center, strongly endorsed the plan, the people said, at one point crediting the president, a developer by trade, with an ability to keep construction projects on schedule and on budget.

After Mr. Trump announced the closure plan this year, the board quickly agreed. But Judge Christopher R. Cooper of Federal District Court in Washington temporarily blocked the closure, ruling that the original vote had been “ill-informed and seemingly preordained.” In his order in May, the judge wrote that the center’s trustees had a legal obligation to seriously consider the potential consequences of shuttering Washington’s pre-eminent performing arts venue.

Mr. Trump lashed out at the judge following his decision and said it would be “dangerous” to keep the center open. Center officials later assured the judge that they were following his order and further scrutinizing the decision, culminating in the meeting on Thursday.

Judge Cooper will soon review the board’s resolution to consider whether the trustees, in his view, performed enough due diligence ahead of the vote.

“The board will be expected to prepare itself with sufficient information to make a considered, independent decision,” the judge wrote in the May order, “taking account of its obligation to both maintain and operate a premiere arts venue and its solemn duty to memorialize a fallen president.”

For weeks, the future of the Kennedy Center has been in limbo, with a largely bare performance calendar.

Broadway touring shows, typically a major source of ticket revenue, have gone elsewhere. The National Symphony Orchestra, the center’s resident ensemble, has yet to announce a season that typically opens in late September. And employees at the center, which already executed rounds of layoffs, remain unsure about their futures.

The resolution approved by the board noted that during the closure, the orchestra would perform at outside venues, and the Kennedy Center Honors, the institution’s marquee event, would also be held off-site.

Ahead of the meeting, trustees were provided with a comparison of two scenarios for renovations by an outside consultant. Both the consultant and the construction management firm, JLL, raised safety and cost concerns that they said would arise from keeping the building open during a phased renovation.

The proposal by JLL said the project would address chronic leaks, replace outdated equipment and redesign parts of the interior. Changes would include new furniture, a new coffee shop, electronic ticketing kiosks and $7 million in public restroom renovations. The target for reopening would be summer of 2028.

It was unclear immediately after the meeting, which was not public, whether the center intends to pursue the exact construction plan laid out in the report.

Over the past year and a half, the Kennedy Center has struggled with an exodus of audience members, employees and artists unwilling to be involved with what they now view as a political arm of the White House. The backlash was particularly strong late last year, when the board voted to change the institution’s name to the Trump-Kennedy Center. New letters were added to the building’s marble facade the next day.

Judge Cooper ruled that changing the center’s name required approval from Congress, which dedicated the institution to Kennedy in 1964, shortly after he was assassinated. Before the center removed “Trump” from the building, it also installed a towering matrix of scaffolding, covered in tarps, that obscures much of the current signage.

Many of the board members are staunch Trump allies, such as Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff; Dan Scavino, a Trump adviser; and Allison Lutnick, a former lawyer who is married to the commerce secretary.

In an interview in June at a Kennedy Center event to honor the comedian Bill Maher, Mr. Lutnick said Mr. Trump asked him to get involved to make sure the board’s processes were in line with the court’s expectations.

“He asked me to help him make sure everything is organized,” Mr. Lutnick said, “so that when judges consider what the board is doing, that it’s done perfectly.”

Matt Floca, the center’s executive director, has argued that a full closure would be the most efficient and responsible way to execute sorely needed renovations using the $257 million allotted by Congress last year. In a report for the board, Delta Consulting Group, which was hired to compare different scenarios for renovations, said that if the center pursued a phased construction process over four years, the congressional appropriation would cover less than half of the estimated costs.

Outside arts administrators have suggested the financial realities for cultural organizations are far different from what the board is projecting, saying institutions typically do anything possible to avoid closure so they do not lose ticket revenue and donors. Ms. Beatty’s lawsuit questioned the true reasoning for the closure plans, arguing that it may be an effort to mask a financial downturn stemming from the president’s takeover.

The Kennedy Center has until next week to share its plan with Judge Cooper.

Julia Jacobs is an arts and culture reporter who often covers legal issues for The Times.

Luigi Mangione Is Expected to Plead Guilty in Federal Court

The New York Times August 13, 2026

Luigi Mangione Cases

Advertisement

Supported by

He is charged with stalking resulting in the death of an executive, but the specifics of his plea were unclear. A murder trial in state court is set for next month.

By Benjamin WeiserDevlin Barrett and Hurubie Meko

Luigi Mangione is expected to plead guilty on Friday in Manhattan federal court, where he faces charges of stalking resulting in the death of a health insurance executive in 2024, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

Mr. Mangione was set to go on trial in federal court in January for the stalking charges in connection with the killing of Brian Thompson, the chief executive of UnitedHealthcare, charges that carry a potential life sentence. Mr. Mangione is not charged with murder in the federal case. The two people spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the ongoing talks, which could fall apart before or even during a scheduled hearing in federal court on Friday.

The potential plea in the federal case comes less than a month before Mr. Mangione, 28, is scheduled to go on trial on a state murder charge on Sept. 8 for Mr. Thompson’s killing.

Mr. Mangione’s legal team did not respond to a request for comment. When asked at an unrelated news conference on Wednesday about a potential plea, Jamie McDonald, the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan, said there was a court conference scheduled for Friday, adding, “That’s all we can say at this time.”

Mr. Mangione has pleaded not guilty to all charges against him, in both federal and state court.

Mr. Thompson’s killing on one of the most congested patches of America — Midtown Manhattan — and the five-day manhunt that followed riveted the country, leaving many people horrified, but others rallying to support a gunman who some saw as protesting the nation’s health insurance industry.

It was unclear what charges Mr. Mangione would plead guilty to on Friday, and he could reverse his decision at the last minute, even during the court hearing itself.

The impact of a federal plea on Mr. Mangione’s state murder case also remains in question. His lawyers could seek dismissal of the state charges on double jeopardy grounds, which bars someone from being tried twice for the same offense — arguments the Manhattan district attorney’s office is likely to vigorously oppose.

Both the federal and state cases have narrowed over time. In January, the federal judge, Margaret Garnett, dismissed two other charges in Mr. Mangione’s federal case, including one that carried a potential death penalty if he was convicted.

Last year the judge overseeing the state case, Gregory Carro, dismissed a state terrorism count, saying the evidence behind it was “legally insufficient.” The remaining state charges include second-degree murder, which could lead to a possible sentence of 25 years to life.

When Mr. Mangione was first charged in federal court during the last weeks of President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s term, the U. S. attorney’s office said it expected the office of the Manhattan district attorney, Alvin Bragg, to try the state case first. But shortly after Mr. Trump took office, his Justice Department signaled it would accelerate the pace, announcing quickly it would seek the death penalty for Mr. Mangione, a decision that usually takes many months to make.

Since then, the state and federal prosecutors have seemingly been jockeying to try Mr. Mangione first.

If the federal plea happens on Friday, legal experts say, Mr. Bragg’s office could argue that it can still prosecute Mr. Mangione because the state charges addresses a different harm — murder — than the federal stalking case.

Mr. Bragg’s office raised the double jeopardy issue last month after news reports surfaced about the possibility of a federal guilty plea.

A state prosecutor, Joel Seidemann, suggested in a July 2 letter to Justice Carro that Mr. Bragg’s office would object if a proposed federal guilty plea “would operate to defeat a just outcome in the state prosecution.”

Mr. Seidemann said the district attorney’s office would want Judge Garnett, to “consider that fact in deciding whether to accept that plea.” He said the office had advised Mr. Mangione’s federal prosecutors and his defense team of its position.

“Any guilty pleas in these matters must account for the seriousness of defendant’s offenses, the loss of an innocent life, the impact of those crimes on the victim’s family,” Mr. Seidemann wrote in the letter.

Mr. Mangione’s defense team, led by Karen Friedman Agnifilo, argued from almost the moment he was charged by state and federal authorities in December 2024 that the dual prosecutions violated his rights.

In a motion filed in Manhattan State Supreme Court, the defense called the parallel prosecutions “so constitutionally fraught that we are hard-pressed to find precedent for such an unprecedented situation.”

“The state and federal prosecutions relate to identical facts,” the lawyers wrote, adding that the offices were “trying to get two bites at the apple to convict Mr. Mangione.”

Benjamin Weiser is a Times reporter covering the federal courts and U. S. attorney’s office in Manhattan, and the justice system more broadly.

Devlin Barrett covers the Justice Department and the F. B. I. for The Times.

Hurubie Meko is a Times reporter covering criminal justice in New York, with a focus on the Manhattan district attorney's office and state courts.

Connections Coach

Democratic Socialists are capturing more votes than ever before — even as they run up against the limits of their appeal.

Credit... Photo illustration by Lisa Sheehan

Supported by

By Charles Homans

Charles Homans talked to more than 30 D. S. A. candidates, organizers, members and volunteers in New York, Chicago, Michigan and Wisconsin.

It was the Democratic Party’s “Summer of Socialism,” as an email from the Republican National Committee cheerfully called it that morning, and Ashik Siddique, a co-chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, was standing on a chair outside a bar, rallying the comrades.

“Zohran’s race is a big proof of concept,” Siddique told the crowd, which had gathered in Chicago on the last day of July for a D. S. A. organizing summit. Many of the hundred or so members assembled around him had volunteered for the campaign of Zohran Mamdani, the recently elected New York City mayor and D. S. A. stalwart. “We can scale that up all over the country over the next year and a half,” Siddique said.

The D. S. A. is not generally an organization of outsize personalities; its leaders tend to exude a self-effacing, slightly dorky enthusiasm. As Siddique, a 38-year-old former environmental organizer from New York, mustered the troops on the bar patio, he resembled the lead volunteer at a particularly enthusiastic Sunday-afternoon park cleanup event, pointing people to the spare rakes and garbage bags, and not the leader of an organization that was presiding over what has been arguably the most remarkable season in the history of American socialism.

As recently as 2011, socialism was so taboo in the United States that PolitiFact could observe, uncontroversially, that “the S-word is overwhelmingly considered a toxic label in American politics.” But since Senator Bernie Sanders’s 2016 presidential run, and even more so since Mamdani’s mayoral win last year, this has changed significantly.

This July, a CNN poll found that a full third of Democratic and Democratic-leaning adults identify themselves as democratic socialists. And they are voting like it.

D. S. A.-backed candidates have won five congressional primaries since June for solidly Democratic seats in New York, Philadelphia, Detroit and Denver — two of them upsets of long-serving incumbents. A D. S. A. er is poised to be the next mayor of Washington. Another is in a runoff for mayor of Los Angeles.

The narrow loss this month of Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist candidate for governor running in Wisconsin’s Democratic primary with local D. S. A. chapters’ endorsements, disappointed many on the left. But it was also a signal about the potency of new socialist politics: Even without the backing of national D. S. A. leaders and politicians, her campaign came within a few thousand votes of beating a rival enthusiastically supported by the state’s Democratic governor.

In 2015, the D. S. A., the largest socialist organization in the country (though not a political party), could claim fewer than 7,000 members, most of them inactive. In early July, Siddique announced, the group had reached 120,000 members, making it larger than any organized socialist movement in American history — even in the early-20th-century heyday of the Socialist Party of America.

“I try not to be a superstitious person, looking for omens or signals,” Siddique went on, “but the day we hit 120,000 members, surpassing the historic Socialist Party, was the Fourth of July.”

“U. S. A.! U. S. A.! U. S. A.!” someone shouted. The comrades chanted along for a few beats, then trailed off into slightly uncomfortable laughter.

It has been a little less than a decade since supporters of Sanders’s 2016 presidential campaign dusted off the D. S. A., a minor heirloom from a long-gone era of the American left, and refashioned it as a vehicle for taking on what they viewed as a complacent and compromised Democratic establishment. Since then, that establishment has observed the D. S. A. with wary curiosity, like an oil tanker captain squinting through binoculars at a band of pirates approaching from a great distance on a slow and iffy-looking fishing pontoon.

“Yes, you had the A. O. C. victory” — Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s 2018 upset in a New York congressional race — “and some other Squad stuff, but the D. S. A. really wasn’t, you know, a major player,” Jonathan Cowan, president of the centrist Democratic think tank Third Way, told me. But the organization’s winning streak, starting with Mamdani, has snapped the Democratic Party to attention. Those who oppose the D. S. A., Representative Tom Suozzi, a Democrat from Long Island, told me, “have been wringing our hands at cocktail parties. Nobody’s been getting organized. And we have to get organized.”

Some prominent liberal Democrats have argued for welcoming democratic socialists and pursuing “addition, not subtraction,” as Gov. Gavin Newsom of California told a podcaster in July. But moderates maintain that there can be no compromise with a movement whose national platform calls for abolishing prisons and the United States Senate, and which frankly views the Democratic Party not as a coalitional partner but as a means to an end.

Cowan likens the D. S. A. to Trump’s MAGA movement: an insurrection that Republicans first dismissed, then accommodated and finally were devoured by. “They pose, in my view, a mortal threat to the Democratic Party,” he told me.

Third Way, which spent heavily against Sanders’s campaigns in 2016 and 2020, announced in August that it would invest $15 million in a project to counter the D. S. A.’s rise. Otherwise, Cowan fears, a D. S. A.-aligned candidate like Ocasio-Cortez could mount a credible challenge for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028: “a reprise of Bernie 2016, 2020, but successfully this time.”

On this, many socialists agree. “Zohran’s campaign showed us the power that we have — and the power people have come here to take,” Diana Moreno, a D. S. A. assemblywoman from Queens, told me at the bar in Chicago, where a contingent of D. S. A. ers had gathered to discuss how to organize for an Ocasio-Cortez presidential run. “Now, it’s like, we’re heading for the moon, baby!”

On one level, the D. S. A.’s appeal in a guillotine-curious moment in American politics is obvious enough. “People really don’t like Donald Trump, according to the polls, and they really don’t like the Democratic Party,” John Nichols, executive editor of The Nation and co-author of a book with Sanders, told me. “D. S. A. comes along and says: ‘We’re different. We don’t like Trump, and we’re not particularly satisfied with the Democratic Party.’”

The D. S. A.’s membership amounts to less than 0.3 percent of registered Democrats, and its wins, even this year, fall far short of recent right-wing upheavals like MAGA and the Tea Party. But like those movements, the D. S. A. is a sort of black light illuminating the failures of the party it has taken as a host.

It has produced talents like Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani at a time when Democratic leaders’ approval ratings, and the party’s, are dismally underwater. Its politicians have won voters on issues like data-center construction and the war in Gaza, where more mainstream Democrats have been slow to grasp major shifts in the electorate or are paralyzed by the commitments of the party’s donor class and interest groups. Its grass-roots volunteers have helped the organization’s candidates beat much better-funded rivals and at times promoted simpatico (if not socialist) progressives like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate race.

But the D. S. A. is also a movement with no demonstrated ability to expand the Democratic majorities it would need to implement even the most modest elements of its platform in a country where 57 percent of people, according to a Gallup Poll last August, still view socialism negatively. The internal factions that have gathered under its capacious definition of democratic socialism — “a system where ordinary people have a real voice in our workplaces, neighborhoods and society” — range from slightly left of progressive to outright communist, and they are deeply divided on whether working within Democratic politics is even a desirable strategy, or rather a betrayal of the full revolutionary promise of their movement.

Its leaders view a presidential run by a popular D. S. A. politician with excitement but also trepidation. “There are people who feel like it would force a crisis and potentially help destroy our organization,” Siddique told me, “because we couldn’t deal with the contradictions.”

On an evening in early July, a couple of hundred New York socialists descended on a bar in Crown Heights, a Brooklyn neighborhood on the frontier of the Brooklyn and Queens districts known as the Commie Corridor, where the D. S. A. gained one of its first significant beachheads in Democratic politics in the late 2010s. At the bar, the wine was orange, the beer was Narragansett and the arak was Palestinian.

“Chelsea!” someone called out. I turned to see a newly arrived Chelsea Manning, the former Army intelligence analyst who served seven years in prison for leaking classified military and diplomatic files to Julian Assange, exchanging hugs with other guests. Manning has lately become a fixture of the New York D. S. A. chapter’s parties, where she occasionally plays D. J.

The party that night was a fund-raiser hosted by the influential socialist podcaster Daniel Denvir, along with a number of prominent New York D. S. A. activists and politicians, for David Morales, a socialist candidate for mayor in Providence, R. I.

The terroir of the D. S. A. varies from city to city. Events hosted by N. Y. C.-D. S. A., by far the organization’s largest chapter, feel like parties for a fashionable new literary journal, heavy on writer types with stick-and-poke tattoos and Ivy League diplomas stashed in Bushwick closets. Some of the bigger Midwestern chapters are more of a bartenders-and-bike-mechanics scene, while elsewhere there are strong notes of the intense left-liberal online fervor of 2020 — a boom year in D. S. A. recruitment — embodied by the social workers and librarians who are still on Bluesky yelling at people to wear masks. (In order to attend the Chicago summit, I was asked, for the first time in years, to submit proof of a negative Covid test.)

All of these subcultures are consistent with the findings of the D. S. A.’s last member survey, in 2021, whose respondents were by their own account overwhelmingly white, college-educated and urban. This is not a portrait of the working class the D. S. A. professes to champion — though the many critics who have noted this tend to misunderstand the D. S. A.’s project. The group seeks less to capture the working class, as it is usually understood in American politics, than to redefine it.

Its dream is a country where enviably paid union autoworkers, marginally employed immigrant Uber drivers, downwardly mobile graduate students and even comfortably middle-class professionals whose fortunes are more precarious than their parents’ are united by shared aspirations (health care, affordable housing), a shared view of who is standing in the way of them (billionaires, landlords, imperialists) and at least a bumper-sticker-level agreement about what is to be done. (Tax the rich. Abolish ICE. Free Palestine.)

Observed at close range, however, the D. S. A. feels less like a class expression than a cultural one. Offline communities built around shared interests — the sort once found in bowling alleys, all-ages punk-rock venues, church basements or radical bookstores — are rare now, and D. S. A. chapters fill this role. They offer not just a different politics but a different model for what participating in politics means. Chapter operations are heavily D. I. Y. affairs, which adds a giddy unreality to their victories, as if a group of college friends started a record label in their dorm room and somehow ended up using it to unseat an eight-term congressman. “It becomes a thing that you do to meet your friends — and to make friends,” Shua Sanchez, a 36-year-old organizer with the Milwaukee chapter, told me.

Even Democratic strategists who are wary of the group’s growing influence in the party grant that they have figured out something that the mainstream of the party now struggles to organically produce. “They’re real civic engagement,” said Adam Jentleson, a former staff member of Harry Reid’s and John Fetterman’s and president of the Searchlight Institute, a new Democratic think tank that is trying to drag the party away from the cultural politics of the 2020 era. “We don’t have Elks Clubs anymore. We don’t have union halls anymore, really. But we have these 50 people in a room discussing Robert’s Rules of Order. We shouldn’t let them determine the direction of the party, but we shouldn’t chase them out of the tent.”

There are recent antecedents to this in left-liberal politics — and not just the 2016 Sanders campaign. More than one D. S. A. er confided to me that their formative experience with grass-roots politics was the conventionally liberal 2008 candidacy of Barack Obama, whose two million volunteers, organized through Obama for America, propelled his campaign from long shot to the White House. Many Obama volunteers felt they were building a progressive force bigger than his presidency and were disappointed when Obama’s advisers shunted the volunteers off into the Democratic National Committee as a highly managed cheerleading operation for his administration.

“I knocked doors for Obama!” Sanchez, the Milwaukee D. S. A. organizer, told me. “And they never asked me to do anything again after that.” Megan Romer, the D. S. A.’s other national co-chair, who phone-banked for Obama in 2008, said that for the D. S. A., the experience had been “instructive”: “Like, how did that get dissolved? How did that get co-opted? Because there was organic energy.”

Renée Paradis, an election lawyer and a onetime progressive Democrat, also worked for Obama’s campaign, in 2008, and joined the D. S. A. immediately after Trump’s inauguration in 2017. “I was like, This elite theory of change is just absolutely inadequate to this problem,” she told me at the Brooklyn party.

Paradis worked on Ocasio-Cortez’s 2018 campaign, which more than any other introduced the political and media class to the D. S. A. The group’s organizers, however, generally regard Mamdani’s election last fall as more significant. “What’s different about Zohran,” Denvir, the podcast host, told me, “is that Zohran is a cadre member of N. Y. C.-D. S. A.” Unlike Ocasio-Cortez, who joined the organization around the time she started running for Congress, Mamdani spent years volunteering for and managing campaigns for other D. S. A. candidates before he ran himself.

Mamdani demonstrated his commitment after arriving in Gracie Mansion with his endorsements in New York’s congressional races, backing two D. S. A.-endorsed candidates, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, who won their primaries and will almost certainly win seats in November. This was a vision of an organization that didn’t just endorse politicians but produced them organically from its own rank and file, turning out candidates who saw themselves as part of its ongoing project.

“This would be really a foolish, silly, vain project if we just elected socialists for the sake of it,” Julia Salazar, a D. S. A. state senator, told the crowd in Brooklyn. “We elect socialists to build this movement, to build power together.”

“It feels like a moment of immense possibility,” Paradis, the election lawyer, told me. On this point, though, the D. S. A. was not entirely unified. As we talked, she was checking her phone. On social media, Rhode Island D. S. A. ers were fuming at the New Yorkers for participating in a fund-raiser for Morales, whom the state chapter refused to endorse. Although Morales was a socialist, the chapter was led by hard-liners who unendorsed him three years earlier for voting to re-elect the Democratic state house speaker.

These conflicts are not uncommon in the D. S. A. Decision making in the organization resides mostly at the level of its often fractious local chapters. The more moderate of those chapters, like New York, in turn sometimes find themselves at odds with the national organization, where more radical elements often have a loud voice.

For instance, although Ocasio-Cortez is endorsed by the New York chapter, the national D. S. A. has recently withheld its endorsement over what it views as insufficient commitment to several aspects of the D. S. A.’s program. The two national co-chairs are actively divided over her future. Siddique is involved in efforts to draft her for the 2028 presidential race, but Romer told me she is “a little bit skeptical of how committed A. O. C. is to D. S. A.”

These disagreements are partly structural and partly historical. The D. S. A. is an organization whose membership has mostly arrived in the heat of political crises and then has had to figure out what, exactly, they are doing together.

The D. S. A. was founded in 1982 by Michael Harrington, an influential midcentury public intellectual and activist who organized alongside the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and wrote a book, “The Other America,” that inspired the Johnson administration’s “war on poverty.” Harrington, who died in 1989, was also the heir to the legacy of organized socialism in the United States — although at the time of his inheritance, there was not much left of it.

The Socialist Party of America, founded in 1901, was a prominent force in the early 20th century, fusing the agrarian populism that rose up in opposition to the inequality and corruption of the Gilded Age with radical elements of the labor movement and new Marxist thinking from Europe. Its membership included figures like Jack London, Helen Keller and W. E. B. Du Bois. At various points in the 1900s and 1910s, Socialists held seats in state legislatures, as well as the administrations of more than 30 towns and cities from New York to North Dakota to California.

When Eugene V. Debs ran as the Socialist candidate for president in 1912, he won 6 percent of the vote. Socialists saw his campaign as the beginning of an ascent. In fact, it was the peak. The party’s opposition to American involvement in World War I led to some of its leaders’ being prosecuted under the Sedition Act by Woodrow Wilson’s administration. When Debs ran for president again in 1920, it was from prison.

But the Socialist Party also fell victim to more prosaic, and often self-inflicted, misfortunes. Few of its politicians elected during the boom years managed to stay in office for more than one term. The party fell into an acrimonious factional struggle — then as now, a chronic left-wing habit — and in the 1920s, it lost much of its membership to the new American Communist Party, which was both more radical and better organized.

The socialists’ most popular ideas, meanwhile, were co-opted by progressive politicians, most fatefully Franklin D. Roosevelt, whose New Deal took an economic agenda that democratic socialists advanced in other countries and packaged it as Democratic policy. After the New Deal, the Democratic Party became the hegemonic power in American politics. The Socialist Party became a footnote.

By the time Harrington became chairman in 1968, the Socialists were a party in name only, whose political commitments would, to a 21st-century socialist, appear incongruous. They supported civil rights and labor but having split bitterly with their erstwhile comrades over the authoritarian direction taken by the Soviet Union, they were also fiercely anti-Communist and often hawkish in Cold War foreign policy. (Some would soon break from the left entirely, becoming the first generation of neoconservatives.) Unable to win electorally, the party had shifted toward cultivating influence within the Democratic Party through union leaders and sympathetic politicos.

But when the Democratic coalition cracked up in the late 1960s and ’70s, Harrington somehow managed to step on every resulting shard. He fell out almost immediately with the New Left. “We thought he was far too right-wing,” recalls the political historian Michael Kazin, at the time a member of Students for a Democratic Society. “He didn’t like revolution.” He also didn’t like Jimmy Carter, whom he viewed as unacceptably conservative, and backed Senator Ted Kennedy’s failed challenge in the 1980 primary. Two years later, locked out of the Democratic establishment and shocked by the Reagan Revolution, Harrington assembled the remnants of two earlier left-wing organizations into a new group, the Democratic Socialists of America.

“In the early ’80s, D. S. A. was basically meaningless,” said Kazin, who joined around that time. The group drew a modest membership of older Harringtonites and refugees from the New Left, like Kazin, who had been chastened by the movement’s post-1968 collapse amid political violence and ideological esotericism and were now willing to consider what Harrington called “the left wing of the possible.” But what was possible, in the ’80s, was not much.

The first inklings of the D. S. A.’s more promising second act came during Obama’s presidency. Though not a leftist, Obama drew an energy that in another time would very likely have found its way to more left-wing causes, attracting volunteers who saw him as an antiwar protest candidate or were simply captivated by the prospect of electing America’s first Black president. Taking office with a governing trifecta amid a crippling financial crisis, he also seemed to represent the first opportunity in decades to enact an ambitious progressive policy agenda.

But as hopes of a new New Deal receded in 2009 and 2010, the left soured on Obama. The first major expression of discontent, in late 2011, was Occupy Wall Street. The protest movement’s encampment in Manhattan’s Zuccotti Park happened to be a few blocks from D. S. A. headquarters, and a handful of members made a pilgrimage to the occupation, marching behind a red banner. But the protest’s most profound impact on the D. S. A. was an indirect one. “Without Occupy,” David Duhalde, later the D. S. A.’s deputy director, told me, “there’s no Bernie Sanders.”

The entrance of Sanders, a self-identified democratic socialist (though not a D. S. A. member), into Democratic presidential politics was a historical pivot point in the American left. His gambit was as audacious as it was obvious: What if, instead of just railing against the two-party system, as left-wing activists had for decades, you actually tried to win by its own rules? Although he lost, his unexpectedly strong performance opened up a universe of possibilities.

These were most clearly articulated days after Trump’s election in an article in Jacobin, a buzzy newish socialist magazine aligned with the D. S. A., titled “A Blueprint for a New Party.” One of the magazine’s editors, Seth Ackerman, called for “a national political organization that would have chapters at the state and local levels, a binding program, a leadership accountable to its members and electoral candidates nominated at all levels throughout the country.”

This organization would, in effect, be a political party — but unlike the Green Party, with its dogmatic insistence on running on its own ballot line, it would be pragmatic about the two-party system. Its candidates would operate on the Sanders model, running independently when it made sense and in Democratic primaries when it did not. They would be within the Democratic Party but not of it; their real allegiance would be to a “truly democratic party” outside the system.

As it happened, a vehicle for this vision already existed, and the supporters of Sanders’s campaign, gathering offline and on social media, soon found it. On the eve of the 2016 election, the D. S. A. had 6,400 members. By the end of 2017, it had nearly 30,000.

“In 2017, there was a lot of trial and error,” Siddique, a Sanders-campaign volunteer who joined the D. S. A.’s Washington chapter that year, told me. “We were all just figuring out, What is socialism?” Siddique went on. “What is organizing? What are we doing here?”

Siddique and Romer, the organization’s national co-chairs, are now often summoned onto cable news shows to affirm the D. S. A.’s most radical positions, but they are not really movement leaders in a conventional sense. The national organization works to extract some semblance of consensus from its disparate chapters and caucuses — which, over the past decade, have sometimes heatedly debated the answers to those initial questions. Sanders’s campaign, out of which most of the new arrivals came, offered some points of policy agreement (Medicare for all) and some broad inclinations (fighting oligarchy) but plenty of blank spots, and fissures opened up quickly enough.

The splits were often generational in an organization whose median member age, after 2016, dropped suddenly to 33 from 68, according to its surveys. The new arrivals were mostly too young to remember the Soviet Union, and some — including Romer — proudly announced themselves to be Marxist-Leninists, which appalled the anti-Communist oldheads. The organization’s fast-proliferating new internal coalitions included a Communist Caucus.

On foreign policy, the new D. S. A.’s members mostly settled for a sort of all-purpose opposition to American imperialism and militarism — including U. S. membership in NATO, which the organization sees as “primarily an aggressive force,” Romer said. It continues to oppose arming Ukraine. “Do we want to go to war with Russia?” Romer asked. “Does that feel like a good idea to anybody?”

But one foreign-policy issue above all preoccupied the new members: the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. One of them was Olivia Katbi, who joined the D. S. A. the day after the 2016 election in Portland, Ore., where she soon became co-chair of a new D. S. A. chapter.

“A lot of us who joined, myself included, were kind of new to politics,” Katbi, a 34-year-old high school track coach in Portland, told me. But Katbi, who is Syrian American and has Palestinian family members, had taken an interest in the Palestinian liberation movement several years earlier after attending a rally for the cause in Chicago. “That really opened my eyes about Palestine — and B. D. S.”

The then-decade-old Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement calls on governments and institutions to pressure Israel to end its occupation of the Palestinian territories, expand the rights of Palestinian citizens and give Palestinian refugees the right to return. It had become a tenet of the broader left-wing activist milieu that gathered itself within the D. S. A. in 2017. At the organization’s convention that year, Katbi and several other members put forward a resolution for the D. S. A. to endorse B. D. S. When it passed, supporters erupted into cheers, waved a Palestinian flag and began chanting, “From the river to the sea/Palestine will be free.”

The D. S. A.’s founding cohort included many friends of the Israeli left, like Harrington, who considered himself a Zionist. This gave the B. D. S. resolution, like much of Israeli-Palestinian politics in America, a sort of Oedipal resonance: It was an act of breaking from the organization’s Harringtonite past and pointing it toward a more radical future.

But the issue opened up subtler divisions within the organization’s younger majority, which became visible in 2021, when Jamaal Bowman, a D. S. A.-endorsed New York freshman congressman and member of the organization, voted for additional funding for Israel’s missile-defense system and visited the country with a liberal Zionist organization. A D. S. A. working group dedicated to the B. D. S. issue, which had drawn the organization’s dedicated pro-Palestinian activists, reacted furiously, leading more than 50 local chapters in calling for Bowman’s expulsion.

The D. S. A.’s main governing entity, the national political committee, condemned Bowman but refused to expel him. The spat continued until the D. S. A.’s next biennial convention, in August 2023, when the committee succeeded in passing a resolution dissolving the B. D. S. working group.

These tensions exploded after Hamas fighters mounted an attack on Israeli military installations and civilians on Oct. 7. The statement the national D. S. A. issued that day allowed that “we unequivocally condemn the killing of all civilians” but argued that “today’s events are a direct result of Israel’s apartheid regime”; it also called on members to “take to the streets to join a protest for peace and against funding the Israeli state.” That day, N. Y. C.-D. S. A. promoted on its official X account a rally hosted by a coalition of other organizations (though not the D. S. A. itself), proclaiming the group “in solidarity with the Palestinian people and their right to resist 75 years of occupation and apartheid.”

In the ensuing blowback, even some politicians allied with the group distanced themselves, and 24 prominent old-guard members announced their resignations. But in the coming weeks, as Israel launched its counterattack in Gaza, the D. S. A. faced an uprising on its other flank, too. Members of the organization’s disbanded B. D. S. working group staged a sit-in at the Washington office of Sanders, who had denounced both the Hamas attack and Israel’s reprisal, and shortly after announced that the group was leaving the D. S. A. entirely, reconstituting itself as an independent organization. The D. S. A., they claimed, was no longer “a safe space for our members to organize.”

The moment, Siddique told me, “felt like a massive crisis for the organization.” When I asked him whether there was consensus within the D. S. A. about the Oct. 7 attacks, he replied carefully: “I think we’re a big-tent organization. There’s always a very wide array of perspectives.”

But the duration and brutality of Israel’s invasion of Gaza has largely resolved the dispute in the pro-Palestinian vanguard’s favor. When the working group’s leaders reformed themselves within the D. S. A. last year, as a new coalition with the stated aim of building the organization “into a mass revolutionary force” that “advances anti-imperialist politics with Palestine as our compass,” they met with little opposition.

Still, the more pragmatic D. S. A. ers I met spoke of the hard-line activists with exasperation. Part of this was genuine disagreement — the view that, as one of them put it to me eye-rollingly, “you don’t actually have to ‘hand it to Hamas.’” But even some of the most pro-Palestinian voices in the D. S. A. considered the working group’s posturing unhelpful to the cause, if not openly nihilistic. “It’s really hard to organize with people who seem to hate the organization we’re organizing in,” Olivia Katbi wrote on X.

The conflict maps loosely onto a new kind of generational division in the D. S. A. Nearly a decade into the organization’s rebirth, the members who joined immediately out of the Sanders 2016 moment, organized around the project of winning electoral power, have mostly replaced the Harringtonites as the organization’s graying old guard. And they have increasingly found themselves defending that project against more recently arrived activists — the pro-Palestinian vanguard and various far-left factions — who see electoral politics as a cop-out, a delusional diversion from the true business of revolution.

More than once, I heard these activists described by other D. S. A. ers as “ultras” — an old Marxist pejorative for the far fringe of the left, the radicals who threatened to devour or derail movements. Ultras blew apart the New Left of the 1960s, and witnessing the explosion at close range had led many early D. S. A. ers to join the organization, with its sober-minded vision of change. Now their successors were learning the same lesson.

D. S. A. pragmatists believe that the organization’s electoral successes have helped settle some of these internal arguments in their favor. Its string of recent wins, from Mamdani to its congressional upsets this summer, have brought it attention that labor organizing and demonstrating have not, forcing the political mainstream to take the group seriously. But the D. S. A. itself has, in truth, not always been the principal driver of these wins. Its bottom-up structure — the national organization can back only candidates already endorsed by local chapters — and internal disagreements have made it slow to capitalize on the same shifts in politics that it has anticipated.

This is particularly true when it comes to Israel, on which Democratic voters, and especially young voters, have shifted sharply pro-Palestinian since the Israeli invasion of Gaza. This shift has led the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the influential pro-Israel lobbying group better known as AIPAC, to wade aggressively into Democratic primaries. Its efforts have drawn a furious counterattack from Justice Democrats: a political action committee that, like the reinvigorated D. S. A., emerged from the 2016 Sanders campaign and works on behalf of left-wing congressional candidates.

Three of the D. S. A.’s five 2026 primary victories in national races were candidates endorsed and in some cases recruited by Justice Democrats to punch back at AIPAC-backed incumbents, who were only later endorsed by the D. S. A. Two of the three candidates, Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York and Melat Kiros in Colorado, are pro-Palestinian activists who just recently joined the socialist organization.

What the D. S. A. has been able to give these candidates is a grass-roots army: canvassers and phone bankers who can provide a valuable edge. On a hot and humid Sunday afternoon in July, Cara Tobe, an organizer with the D. S. A.’s Detroit chapter, was knocking on doors across several neighborhoods on behalf of a congressional candidate named Donavan McKinney, a Justice Democrats recruit challenging an AIPAC-backed Democratic incumbent, Representative Shri Thanedar, whom he would defeat two weeks later.

McKinney, a Black union organizer and state representative with family roots in the auto industry, had been a D. S. A. member since 2019 and was practiced in pitching its merits to prospective constituents in a plurality-Black, lower-income district. “A livable wage, to be able to work one job, to not only make ends meet but have some disposable income, benefits to take care of your family and a retirement to look forward to: That. Is. Socialism,” he told me. But the D. S. A.’s Detroit chapter decided to back him only many months into the race, to the frustration of supporters like Tobe.

Tobe, a 37-year-old Wisconsin native, wore a D. S. A. T-shirt and a “TEAM ZOHRAN” hat; like many D. S. A. ers, she had volunteered with Mamdani’s campaign in New York. In her doorstep conversations, she would talk up McKinney and mention the D. S. A. as a sort of if-you’re-curious aside.

The voters, all registered Democrats, sometimes took note and sometimes did not. The ones who recognized the D. S. A.’s name seemed to regard it positively. “D. S. A. is going to save this country,” a bookish-looking man in his 50s told her.

“Next year’s definitely going to be interesting,” Tobe told me as she made her way between houses. “We’ve never really had this many people going into Congress.” A member of the D. S. A.’s pragmatic camp, she believes these victories have pushed the organization in that camp’s direction. “It’s like, OK, we’re building a party,” she said.

The D. S. A.’s primary wins are likely to bring the group’s congressional contingent to seven members. That is far fewer than the several dozen that the Tea Party captured in its breakout year of 2010, but it is enough to upgrade its caucus from what is currently a duo — Ocasio-Cortez and Michigan’s Rashida Tlaib, who was also elected in 2018 — to a bloc.

Hakeem Jeffries, the Brooklyn-born, dispassionately tactical Democratic leader in the House, has a mutually antagonistic relationship with the D. S. A., which one of his advisers called “Team Gentrification” in last year’s mayoral race. But if Democrats return to the House next year with a narrow majority, “he needs all of our votes to be speaker,” said Chris Rabb, the D. S. A.-backed Democratic nominee in Pennsylvania’s third congressional district.

But transforming the government requires controlling not just a party but a majority. The compromise stimulus packages and health care legislation that Democrats passed under Obama, which D. S. A. ers now consider insufficient half-measures, required decisive numerical advantages in both chambers that neither party has seen since. “A political party exists for the purpose of gaining power, and then using that power to do good things in governing,” Cowan, the Third Way president, told me. Neither the D. S. A. nor Justice Democrats, Cowan points out, have flipped a single congressional seat from red to blue; their wins have simply pushed already-Democratic districts further left. If they couldn’t win the majorities they needed to enact their vision for the country, Cowan asked, “what the hell is the D. S. A. good for, then?”

This is one reason the next presidential election looms so large for both the D. S. A. and its intraparty enemies. Both anticipate that the Democratic presidential primary will feature a D. S. A.-aligned candidate like Ocasio-Cortez, whose presidential ambitions are a matter of intense speculation. (Through her staff, she declined to comment for this article.)

To the D. S. A., contesting the presidency at the nadir of the Democratic Party’s popularity, and at the height of the organization’s own, is an opportunity — and also, in all likelihood, a necessity. The most radical paradigm shifts in American governance, from F. D. R. to Reagan to Trump, have required a head of state’s unique power to make once-marginal political ideas — from the progressive welfare state to free-market conservatism to right-wing authoritarianism — mainstream, to acclimatize even disengaged citizens to the previously unthinkable.

The Democratic Party’s moderates and many of its reformers fear that a D. S. A. candidacy would extend Republican control of the country at a genuinely existential moment, dividing the party and, if it succeeded, sending the Democrats into a general election with the S-word hanging around their neck: a label that remains anathema to a majority of American voters.

Socialists counter that as a general election matter, socialism’s popularity is unproven, because it is untested. Few people would have imagined that a socialist could win 43 percent of the Democratic primary vote in a presidential election, after all, before Sanders. And a socialist Democratic candidate running in a competitive general election remains a theoretical proposition — which was why, for several weeks in July and August, Francesca Hong suddenly became a figure of great significance in American politics.

Hong, a state assemblywoman and chef from Madison, was a relatively recent convert to the D. S. A.; she told me that she didn’t know much about the organization until 2020, when the group’s small Madison chapter endorsed a friend with whom she was campaigning during her first race. Running for governor this year, she became an early progressive favorite but was not a dominant presence in the race until mid-July, when her closest rival dropped out over campaign-finance irregularities — making Hong, overnight, the top Democratic contender.

If a democratic socialist could win a Democratic governor’s race anywhere, it might have been Wisconsin, a state with a deep progressive political culture and one of the last redoubts of the old Socialist Party; its largest city, Milwaukee, had Socialist mayors throughout the first half of the 20th century. Wisconsin is also a stubbornly purple state, and a Hong victory would have set up a clarifying test of socialism’s potential, and limits, in American politics.

Shua Sanchez, the Milwaukee D. S. A. organizer, likened the possibility of her winning to Obama’s upset in the Iowa caucuses in 2008. If Hong could “show that a socialist woman of color can win in a state like Wisconsin,” he said, “that opens the door to someone like A. O. C. winning a presidential race.”

When I caught up with Hong in late July, the state’s mainstream Democrats were in the midst of a panic. David Crowley, the county executive of Milwaukee, who had dropped out of the race days earlier, had hastily re-entered it, with the immediate endorsement of Gov. Tony Evers. “I think when you fight power, power fights you back,” Hong told me as we rode back to Madison from a campaign stop in Baraboo. “People are inherently afraid of change, sometimes, when it means a change to your influence, right?”

Some powers, however, seemed happy enough to have Hong in the race. Republican groups were in the midst of spending around $4 million on TV ads spotlighting Hong’s progressive agenda. This reflected a bipartisan conventional wisdom that Hong — a dogged campaigner but an unpracticed retail politician with a lot of unexploded ordnance in her social media posts from the fever season of 2020 and 2021 — would be an enviable opponent for Republicans.

Hong had initially broken out from the Democratic field with her sharply defined positions on new issues like data center construction. But as she went from outsider curiosity to heavily scrutinized front-runner, she struggled to defend herself instead on old positions: past exhortations to abolish the police, a tweet calling to “cancel Thanksgiving.” Evers, asked whether Hong could beat the Republican candidate, Tom Tiffany, said, “Probably not.”

The drama had strangely little to do with Hong’s socialism per se. Her old statements weren’t all that particular to the D. S. A.; they were part of the broader progressive sprint to the far edge of social-justice politics in the first Trump term, in which many mainstream Democrats, too, had participated. Asked about Hong’s statements on ABC’s “This Week,” Ocasio-Cortez responded, “Woke 1 was crazy” — a popular shrug of a self-absolving catchphrase among Democrats that, as it happens, originated with a D. S. A. City Council member in New York. Still, Ocasio-Cortez did not endorse Hong, nor did Sanders — and nor did the national D. S. A.

On the Wisconsin primary election night of Aug. 11, Hong’s supporters packed into a music venue in Madison. On the edge of the mostly millennial and Gen Z crowd, Barbara Clark and Patty Elson were taking in the scene. Clark, a 72-year-old retired public-school teacher, and Elson, an 80-year-old retired real estate agent, were, as they were quick to point out, well outside of the crowd’s demographic; they were the kind of well-dressed, genial baby boomers I encountered more frequently in liberal Resistance contexts, at post-Women’s March kaffeeklatsches and No Kings rallies.

“I think a lot of older people are afraid,” Clark told me. She had worked for years on Democratic campaigns, including managing a local office for the Obama campaign in 2008 and volunteering for his re-election in 2012. “Now, I can’t do that anymore,” she said.

I asked Clark whether she now considered herself a Democrat, a democratic socialist or both. “I don’t know what I think of myself as anymore,” she said. “I mean, I was a Democrat. I really was. A straight Democrat.”

“The party has shriveled up,” Elson said. “They haven’t done a thing because of that corporate money. It’s keeping them in line.”

The early returns were starting to come in, and they were much closer than the last polls, which had Hong up by double digits. The supporters’ ebullience acquired an anxious edge. When Hong appeared late in the night, she spoke elegiacally about “how we’re going to win together in November — and for Novembers to come.” When the final ballots were counted, she had lost to Crowley by several thousand votes.

Just before midnight, I ran into Clark and Elson again on their way out. I asked them what they thought had happened. “He got a lot of the Democratic money people,” Clark said of Crowley.

“I think she would’ve won,” Elson said, her voice quavering. The future was so close. But now, once again, they would have to wait.

But from another angle, Hong’s loss was a kind of victory for the D. S. A: A socialist candidate whom even the socialists had been hesitant about had come remarkably close to winning a major statewide election and would be spared the blame for a loss, if it occurred, in November.

When I suggested this reading to Siddique, the national co-chair, he demurred, allowing only that Hong’s run “had really raised everyone’s expectations.” The margin had been small, he emphasized, “and now we have way more data now about how far we can get with our existing strength — and what more can happen going forward.” The movement had fallen short of proving what it claimed was possible. But that only meant it still was.

The rise of the D. S. A. and its tensions with the Democratic Party have fascinated me for some time. I was excited to have the opportunity this summer to get out and talk to the group's members, candidates, voters and critics across several states to understand where this movement came from and where it could be going.

Source images for photo illustration: MJ iceberg/Adobe Stock; Sapphire/Adobe Stock

Charles Homans is a reporter for The Times and The Times Magazine, covering national politics.

Hamas Has No More Cards to Play

The New York Times August 13, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Muhammad Shehada

Mr. Shehada is a Palestinian analyst and a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations.

After five months of daunting negotiations with President Trump’s Board of Peace, Hamas agreed last month to a road map under which it and other armed Palestinian groups would decommission their heavy weapons and give up security control in Gaza. Hamas also agreed to step down from governing Gaza and accept the deployment of an international stabilization force. In return, Israel would halt airstrikes, withdraw its troops from Gaza and allow the devastated enclave to be rebuilt.

Hamas’s agreement represented a fragile opportunity to break out of an otherwise intractable deadlock. The rejection of the plan by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel on Sunday is a setback for Israelis who want peace and security, and for Palestinians in Gaza who want relief from the cruel and painful conditions imposed by Israel. It is the latest example of Israel’s inability to say yes.

There is a narrow window to pressure Israel to change its mind and lock in Hamas’s compromise. Once Hamas’s disarming and Israel’s withdrawal took place, it would become impossible for Hamas to renege. The world would blame it for giving Mr. Netanyahu a pretext to collapse the deal and resume Israel’s military campaign.

In rejecting the peace plan, Mr. Netanyahu said Israel would not begin to withdraw until the Palestinian groups completed their disarmament. But Hamas is unlikely to accept that. It believes it would lose all leverage in the negotiations, and may have difficulty convincing its entire rank-and-file membership to disarm immediately, instead of in phases, without something in return.

One sign Hamas might be serious about giving up its weapons is that, aside from an alleged incident of a sole projectile being fired and landing inside Gaza itself, it and other armed groups have apparently not fired a rocket at Israel since the original cease-fire took effect in October. They have shown this restraint despite the fact that Israel has killed over 1,000 Palestinians in Gaza in that time, including Hamas’s top military leaders.

This unusual holding back could very well indicate that Hamas has no better cards left to play. Armed resistance in Gaza has reached its limit and has exhausted the rationales that sustained it. Well before the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas’s deputy leader, Saleh al-Arouri, admitted as much in 2020, according to a leaked phone conversation. “Frankly, armed resistance failed to create change,” he said. “The resistance presented heroic examples and fought honorable wars, but the blockade wasn’t broken, the political reality didn’t change and none of the land was liberated.”

When Hamas fired hundreds of improvised projectiles on Israel in 2021, purportedly to deter Israel’s escalation in East Jerusalem, Sheikh Jarrah and the West Bank, a cease-fire was reached, only to result in a sharp escalation of Israel’s military raids and settler violence in the West Bank. The years 2022 and 2023 became two of the deadliest on record in the West Bank.

The Oct. 7 attack failed to ignite the Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar’s dream of a multifront war in which Israel would be overwhelmed by assaults from Gaza, Lebanon, Syria, Iran, Iraq and Yemen along with popular uprisings in the West Bank, inside Israel and in neighboring countries. Instead, it led to an Israeli offensive that killed more than 70,000 people and destroyed most of the Gaza Strip. Some Hamas officials have suggested openly and privately that Oct. 7 was a strategic mistake and that they failed to take into consideration the severity of Israel’s reaction.

Palestinian factions such as Hamas, which defined themselves for decades by the ideology of armed resistance, have been looking for a face-saving way out, figures close to Hamas have told me. Hamas leaders like Khaled Meshaal have been sending the message that Gazans have done their part in contributing to the Palestinian cause and paid the heaviest price, and should now be allowed to recover and heal.

Sensitive messaging is crucial to avoid mistakes made in other decommissioning experiences, like in Colombia, where a significant number of former FARC militants defected and joined cartels or created new gangs. For example, disarming for a group dedicated to armed resistance must be framed as a transition, not a surrender. That is why the Board of Peace’s road map for Gaza tries to avoid the spectacle of defeat, surrender or forfeiting of the right to armed resistance by using the language of “storing” rather than “destroying” weapons, and by placing a Palestinian police force in charge of the process rather than Israel or other external parties.

A better idea needs to fill the vacuum created by suspending Palestinian armed resistance. The appeal of violence has not historically increased support for Hamas. Hamas benefited instead from the failure of nonviolent options or their undermining, whether diplomacy, protests, advocacy or legal pressure.

Northern Ireland’s experience shows that decommissioning can eventually be successful only if coupled with a genuine political process leading to lasting peace, in this case a credible path toward Palestinian self-determination and statehood. Mr. Trump’s plan gestures toward this as a possibility in the indefinite future, but that is not enough.

Mr. Netanyahu’s insistence on Hamas’s disarmament before any Israeli troop withdrawal from Gaza is detached from reality. Israel’s military path has been proven futile. After over two years pulverizing Gaza, with heavier bombing than Dresden or Hamburg during World War II, Israel has failed to destroy Hamas. An extensive study on militant groups found that only 7 percent were defeated militarily, while 43 percent disbanded through a transition to a political process, dialogue and conversion to unarmed politics.

Israel’s argument that the road map would allow Hamas to regroup for another Oct. 7 is a scare tactic rather than a serious assessment. Surprise was a decisive element in making the attack possible, not the superior firepower of a militia against one of the world’s most powerful militaries. As the Israeli journalist Nir Gontarz noted, it was more about “the stupidity, arrogance and negligence of the Israeli Army and government, than about sophistication and danger on the part of Hamas.” What are the chances of another Oct. 7 today when the surprise element is lost?

Mr. Netanyahu’s obstructionism is most likely mainly about his political survival ahead of Israeli elections. A group of Mr. Netanyahu’s government ministers joined a march last month calling for the rebuilding of illegal settlements in Gaza. His defense minister last month announced plans to build such settlements in Gaza and bragged, “Today, there is no Shajaiye, no Jabaliya,” referring to the Gaza City neighborhood and Gazan city. “All these terrible places that you remember don’t exist.” That’s why withdrawal or reconstruction would, for Mr. Netanyahu, constitute political suicide.

America’s political leaders should not indulge Mr. Netanyahu’s argument that he is constrained by Israel’s domestic politics. They should say: We, too, have our own domestic political calculations, regional interests and international standing to worry about, and we will not let you endanger them to save yourself from a reckoning with your people.

Muhammad Shehada is a Palestinian analyst and a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations.
