Even at a time of anti-immigration politics, there has never been a richer variety of Mexican restaurants in the United States.

Chalupas at Chalupas Poblanas El Tlecuile’s, in Queens, N. Y. Credit... Lisa Corson for The New York Times

Supported by

By Bill Esparza and Brett Anderson

In reporting this story, Bill Esparza and Brett Anderson visited dozens of Mexican restaurants across the country over the course of a year.

Along the old path of Route 66, America’s mother road, the drive-ins and lunch joints of Oklahoma City look a bit different from the picture postcards in nearby souvenir shops.

In the state that gave us Sonic Drive-In, the carhop craze of the 1950s and ’60s has long since withered as customers preferred to drive-through to satisfy their fast-food fix. But in recent years, the strip of Western Avenue has been revitalized by another kind of menu: Instead of burgers and shakes, you’ll find superspecific varieties of tacos, tortas de albañil, traditional Mexican stews and tostadas de pollo.

El Primo Loco, a grilled chicken drive-through (right next door to a Sonic, as it happens) offers a tostada Siberia, made famous by its namesake restaurant in Monterrey. Hang a right onto Southwest 29th Street and you’ll find a paleta and bionicos dessert shop, a panadería and a Mexico City-inspired torta spot that’s a tribute to the beloved TV character El Chavo.

Bookending the scene are the markets La Aguascalientes Mercado de Carnes and La Aguascalientes Super Market, which feature dishes rare outside Aguascalientes, one of Mexico’s smallest states.

In a former drive-through oil change shop, Crudoolandia sells ceviches and aguachiles alongside Clamato cups and beers for customers to mix into micheladas to drink, well, anywhere but there (per local liquor laws).

“We’ve always wanted to capture that Mazatlán, Sinaloa vibe,” said Nancy Soto-Hallman, who opened the spot with her husband in 2012. “Of course, we don’t have seafood as delicious as Mazatlán’s — it’s one of the cities with the best seafood in Mexico. But we wanted to copy that style — the banda Sinaloense-style, the festive atmosphere.”

A little piece of Mazatlán in O. K. C.? A generation ago, that notion may have sounded unlikely. In 1980, fewer than 10,000 people of Mexican descent lived in the metro area. Today, that number is about 180,000, nearly 12 percent of the population. And the variety of culinary offerings across the city reflects the size and regional backgrounds of that community. The Mexican food scene here is booming, and Oklahoma City is hardly an outlier.

In the past 50 years or so, the population of people of Mexican descent in the United States grew nearly fivefold, from about 8.5 million to more than 39 million. And according to a Pew Research Center analysis in 2024, one out of 10 restaurants in the United States serves Mexican dishes, and about 85 percent of all counties have at least one Mexican restaurant.

That means a vast array of regional Mexican food can be found across the country, from the Gulf Coast to the Pacific Northwest. There are pocket-size food scenes in New Haven, Conn.; Charlotte, N. C.; and the Armourdale neighborhood of Kansas City, Kan.

Eleven Mexican restaurants in the United States received Michelin stars this year, including Californios in San Francisco, the only Mexican restaurant anywhere in the world to get three stars.

In just the last 15 years, the American palate has expanded well beyond combo plates and game-night nachos. Mexican food in America today is a dynamic cuisine all its own, created by Mexicans and Mexican Americans apart from Mexico — and as American as any food.

But there is a jarring split-screen. Just as Mexican food is flourishing in the United States, so are nativist politics. Latin Americans, including Mexicans and Mexican Americans working in hospitality, have been swept up in aggressive deportation campaigns that have been a pillar of President Trump’s second term.

The paradox is not lost on Gustavo Arellano, a columnist for the Los Angeles Times and the author of “Taco USA: How Mexican Food Conquered America.”

“Basically Mexican food now is where Italian food was in the ’90s,” Mr. Arellano said. “You had chefs showing people that there was all of this regional variety.”

He pointed to birria tacos as an example. They are a staple in Zacatecas, where his parents are from, but he never saw them in restaurants, even in Southern California, until the mid-2010s. Not long after that, he came across a list of the best places to find them in Boston, not historically a hotbed of Mexican culture. “I could never have imagined a day where such a regional specialty would become not just ubiquitous, but a cliché,” Mr. Arellano said.

“From the moment Americans tasted Mexican food, they have never wanted to move on from it,” he said. At the same time, he added, “You have the continuation of Mexican immigration into this country, but also the spread of Mexican people to where they were not before. Where there are more Mexicans, you are going to see a backlash. History has taught us this.”

The story of Mexican food in the United States really began with the American annexations of the Mexican territory that became much of the U. S. Southwest. In his book, Mr. Arellano chronicled the rise, starting in the 1800s, of Mexican purveyors like the Chili Queens of San Antonio and tamale wagons in Los Angeles. In the decades that followed, Mexican American cuisine evolved to cater to the brief lunch breaks of blue-collar crowds.

Entrepreneurs of Mexican descent began to serve generous, one-plate, multicourse meals — wet burritos, stuffed sopaipillas and cheesy enchiladas. By the 1980s, Mexican food was widespread, the margarita emerged as one of America’s most beloved cocktails and American corporations like Frito-Lay and Pace Picante made tortilla chips and salsa ubiquitous.

In the 1980s and ’90s, Oaxacan immigrants went to California to work in great numbers. Most were Indigenous, and they formed a large population and culture of transnational people known as Oaxacacalifornia. Lugya’h, Casa Gish Bac and Comedor Tenchita are just a few examples of restaurants that carry on the legacy of Oaxacan immigrants who helped make moles, tlayudas and quesillo famous in the United States.

This sharing of Indigenous traditions and stories through food also set an example for other Mexican immigrants to showcase dishes from their own regions, be it plate-size tacos placeros in New York, chorreadas in Compton or birria estilo Aguascalientes in Oklahoma City.

Today, there are thousands of Mexican restaurants in Los Angeles, where the cost of living is among the highest in the nation. So, like many other Americans, Mexican immigrants and their descendants have looked elsewhere for work and more affordable housing.

That’s what brought Salvador Alamilla’s family to Idaho. Mr. Alamilla started cooking at a Tex-Mex restaurant in Boise called On the Border — “avocado fries, taquitos, every fried thing that you can think of” — working his way up from dishwasher to several cooking positions.

When he opened his own restaurant, Amano, in Caldwell, Idaho, Mr. Alamilla wanted to hew to the foods his family used to make in Michoacán, in southwest Mexico. That meant short ribs, and lamb shanks roasted for 12 or more hours in an underground oven like the one his grandfather used. The distinctive wood-smoke flavors of the region are married to a depth of spice, “the way we grew up eating.” He’s even slow roasting papayas and guavas for a smoky, fruity cocktail.

The move was a bit of a gamble. “Because we are not in the L. A. Arts District, we didn’t start off with that ready audience,” said Mr. Alamilla, the restaurant’s chef and co-owner. “But over the years, I brought the community along with us on our ride.”

Turning diners on to such regional specifics would have been difficult for Mexican chefs a generation ago, particularly in Idaho, he said.

“There was different pressures to try to assimilate, because the food that they were eating in the back was probably different than the food they were serving,” he said. “But for us, as their kids, because we grew up here, maybe we’ve been a little bit more privileged, we feel like we can be ourselves more, or at least we want to be ourselves.”

The tensions of the political moment weigh on Mr. Alamilla, whose parents brought him to the United States as a 5-year-old using another child’s papers. He did not become a documented permanent resident until high school. In a town the size of Caldwell, he said, it’s not hard to know your neighbor’s views. He sometimes looks out at the dining room and sees people who he knows support the ICE deportation campaign.

“It gives me a lot of sadness,” he said, “that the same people who want our people to be deported are the same people that are enjoying a chile colorado.”

At 7:30 on an overcast Sunday evening in March, the line was 40 deep at El Volcancito, one of the busiest tacos al pastor stands in East Charlotte, N. C. The stand is near the impressive Pulga Rodeo, a Mexican flea market teeming with regional cuisine, including Mexico City-style quesadillas at Los Machetes and soursop ice cream at Don Ruby.

Standing at the trompo, a standing spit of roasting pork, the taquero Daniel González said he honed his craft in Los Angeles’s competitive street-food scene at a chain of tacos al pastor vendors that are among the best in Southern California. “I was at La Güera out there in Los Angeles,” said Mr. González, smiling with pride as he turned the trompo to cook his mound of marinated pork.

As Mr. Gonzalez flicked small chunks of pineapple from atop the vertical spit and caught them on corn tortillas lined with strips of freshly carved pork, a woman in line exclaimed that they were just like the ones in Los Angeles, a sentiment echoed by many on TikTok.

Crowding around the salsa bar and huddling onto patches of grass to eat tacos standing up, locals debate whether Charlotte’s best al pastor is at El Volcancito, El Nazareno, Tacos El Regio, Compa Tacos or La Cumbre. But the fact that there is such a debate — in a county that had fewer than 7,000 Hispanic residents, according to the 1990 census — tells much of the story. Today, that population is around 60,000.

Maria Hernández, who owns El Volcancito, said she doesn’t mind the healthy competition. In the local al pastor scene, “el sol sale para todos,” she said — “the sun shines for everyone.”

The budding culinary renaissance has reconnected many Mexican American chefs with their home country’s cuisine. Gustavo Romero built his career cooking Italian after immigrating to the United States as a teenager from Hidalgo, Mexico. The first time he cooked Mexican food professionally was in 2017, at Calavera, a Oaxacan restaurant in Oakland, Calif.

“I understood more about myself through the process,” he said.

The experience led Mr. Romero to start Nixta Tortilleria with his wife, Kate, in Minneapolis, in 2020. Oro by Nixta, a full-service restaurant, followed three years later. Customers come from across the metro area to visit the side-by-side storefronts in northeast Minneapolis, both fueled by Mr. Romero’s passion for heirloom Mexican corn.

“We started treating the tortilla the way you treat a baguette,” Mr. Romero said.

Carlos Salgado helped create the surge of American chefs learning to nixtamalize heirloom Mexican corn to make tortillas in the traditional, labor-intensive way in his 10 years cooking at Taco Maria, in Orange County, Calif. The chef and his wife, Emilie Coulson Salgado, closed the Michelin-starred restaurant in 2023, and moved to Ms. Salgado’s native Door County, Wis.

La Sirena, their new restaurant, is finishing its second summer in Ephraim, population roughly 400. Wind blew in off nearby Eagle Harbor in late May, as diners filled the 22-seat restaurant for the evening’s featured dish: arrachera con mole negro, made with Wisconsin Wagyu and served with warm heirloom corn tortillas.

Door County, where the Hispanic and Latino population is around 4 percent, is a long way from Southern California. But Mr. Salgado said he’s as inspired as he ever has been to cook world-class Mexican food.

“It’s not an exaggeration to say that we wanted nothing less than to substantiate this example of brown excellence in a place that maybe hadn’t seen it before,” he said, “kind of like Taco Maria did 15 years ago.”

If rural Wisconsin and East Charlotte seem like unexpected places for remarkable Mexican food, until fairly recently New York City may have been just as surprising. But today, the well-worn line that “there is no good Mexican food in New York” says more about the speaker than the city.

“Before, you would see these large menus with enchiladas, burritos, tortas, tacos and all of that,” said Tania Apolinar, a co-owner of Carnitas Ramirez in the East Village. Now one perfect dish is plenty, whether it’s her own carnitas from Michoacán, flour tortillas from Sonora at Border Town or chalupas from Puebla Chalupas Poblanas El Tlecuile.

One of the more vibrant concentrations is at Sunset Park Plaza, a makeshift mercado that on weekends occupies a vacant parking lot in southwestern Brooklyn. Sonia Cortés started the Sunset Park Plaza in 2025, after another outdoor market in the neighborhood was dismantled by local officials. Ms. Cortes, an organizer, was selling pozole from a pushcart when police restrictions forced her to pivot.

In 2024, Ms. Cortes and other vendors rented the space, where they now operate under tented stalls, rain or shine. “Why not create a safe space where vendors could work, support their families and share their culture without having to worry about being moved from the streets?” Ms. Cortes said.

The market is now home to 10 vendors, each with a different specialty. One stand offers mammoth tacos placeros, spilling over with rice, beans and chiles rellenos. Another toasts Oaxacan tlayudas over an improvised grill in wire fish baskets. It’s a cross-section of Mexican cooking that exists nowhere else in the city, where everyone sips home-brew tepache, a pre-colonial pineapple beverage served from coolers with a heavy ladle.

“It’s like having a little piece of Mexico,” Ms. Cortes said.

Luke Fortney contributed reporting.

Bill Esparza and I crossed the country in search of the people and places, from taco trucks to tasting menu counters, that have made Mexican cuisine in the U. S. better than it ever has been — a dynamic cuisine all its own and as American as any food. The country-wide renaissance that brought us to this golden age unfolded against a backdrop of rising nativist politics that has impacted the lives of everyone we came across. Our story reflects this split-screen.

Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. Get regular updates from New York Times Cooking, with recipe suggestions, cooking tips and shopping advice.

Brett Anderson is a food reporter for The Times, based in New Orleans.

A City Mobilizes Against a Stubborn Health Threat: Mosquitoes

The New York Times August 13, 2026

The city of Belém in northern Brazil was overwhelmed by an outbreak of dengue two years ago. An all-out municipal effort has reduced cases and may offer lessons to American cities.

The city of Belém in northern Brazil was overwhelmed by an outbreak of dengue two years ago. An all-out municipal effort has reduced cases and may offer lessons to American cities.

A health worker discarding water from a larvicide dissemination unit in Belém, Brazil, last month. Credit...

Supported by

By Apoorva Mandavilli

Photographs and Video by Alessandro Falco

Reporting from Belém, Brazil

It’s been 10 years, but Paulo Gomes still vividly remembers the terror he felt that his wife, Lucirene, would never return from the hospital, that she would die instead of the dengue she contracted from a mosquito bite, her body racked with fever and excruciating pain.

She did come home, after 15 days, and recovered fully after several more months. But the experience forever changed how Mr. Gomes thought about mosquitoes.

Mr. Gomes, now 65, is an eager participant in an aggressive campaign by Belém, the northern Brazilian city where he lives on the edge of a rain forest, to reduce mosquitoes and the health dangers they bring.

Municipal workers have counseled him that mosquitoes breed in standing water and thrive in musty, moist spaces. He fills the swimming pool in the backyard every Friday for his grandchildren who live nearby, but drains it religiously every Sunday after they leave.

He and his wife keep their veranda scrupulously clean and uncluttered, just a tricycle in one corner, a hammock in another — and, since last summer, a plastic bucket that is a centerpiece in Belém’s multipronged strategy against mosquitoes.

The size of a small trash can, it offers just the sort of dark, watery cavity a female mosquito might seek to lay eggs. But it contains larvicide, a chemical that kills young mosquitoes, and when she lands inside she becomes coated with it. When she flies away, she will spread it to other breeding sites, typically within a quarter-mile radius. Last year, Belém distributed 5,000 units in the parts of the city hit hardest by dengue.

At the moment, mosquitoes are a bigger menace in Belém and the rest of Brazil than in the United States or Europe, but the warming planet is expanding their range. Most cases of dengue, malaria and chikungunya in those places were contracted during travel abroad, but locally acquired cases are occurring more frequently. In 2024, the United States recorded nearly 3,800 cases of dengue, more than 100 of them locally acquired. About a third of the patients were hospitalized, and six died.

“The climate crisis is a public health crisis,” Dr. Alexandre Padilha, Brazil’s health minister, said in an interview.

“It’s not a coincidence” that during its Group of 20 presidency, Brazil championed new initiatives to combat climate-driven diseases like dengue, Dr. Padilha said. “We have a lot to learn and also to teach many regions in the U. S. A. about how to face the impact of climate change,” he said.

Forged by bitter experience, Brazil has embraced new techniques to combat mosquitoes. Most of them are environmentally friendly, including building the world’s largest “mosquito factory,” a facility that produces mosquitoes containing Wolbachia, a bacterium that blocks dengue and other viruses. The Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes are then released in communities to breed and pass the bacteria to the next generation.

Tackling mosquitoes requires more than gee-whiz science. Municipal departments will need to beef up their vector control divisions and budgets, doctors must be trained to recognize and treat the diseases, and the general public will need education on protecting itself.

“It’s important for other countries to get ready for the possibility of having more and more cases happening, and train all the layers of the society,” said Luciano Moreira, the chief executive of Wolbito do Brasil, a joint venture between the nonprofit World Mosquito Program and the Brazilian government.

“It’s not just something like the government just goes there and sprays,” he said. “It’s part of a movement.”

Locals like to say Belém has only two seasons — one in which it rains every day, and one when it rains all day.

The city is a gateway to the mighty Amazon, and it is edged by lush, muddy rainforest. Mango trees and their fallen fruit line the streets, luring insects with their sweet sticky scent. Small puddles of water — on the sidewalks, in stacked tires and in trash cans — offer mosquitoes the perfect nurseries to grow millions more of themselves.

For decades, Belém residents have been under attack by Aedes aegypti, the type of mosquito that carries dengue, Zika and chikungunya — so much so that in 2018, a city park installed a large fiberglass statue of the insect. (Aedes aegypti is also found in many parts of the United States, including Florida, Texas and California.)

Climate change has allowed these mosquitoes to multiply faster, intensifying the threats they carry. In 2024, dengue infected more than 10 million people in Brazil and killed more than 6,000. There might have been even more deaths if doctors in Brazil did not know how to recognize and treat the disease promptly, said Moises Silva, a microbiologist at the ⁠Federal University of Pará in Belém.

Brazil’s toll that year was about four times the previous number, and in Belém, it was about seven times higher, flooding the city’s hospitals and forcing a reckoning. City officials adopted myriad methods in response, from increasing common-sense solutions like garbage disposal and treatment of sewage to collaborating with academic scientists like Dr. Silva.

It was Dr. Silva who petitioned the health minister to include Belém in the list of 10 cities that would try out the special larvicide dispensing buckets, and to fund training and equipment for city workers.

Dr. Silva and his colleagues looked at the distribution of dengue cases across the city. They also factored in data from the city’s entomology lab on mosquito larvae and egg traps to gauge the size of the population that season.

Based on those two streams of information, they identified the most vulnerable areas, down to the street level, many of them in low-income neighborhoods and favelas, that would benefit from the units.

Unlike mosquito traps that kill females, the larvicide units, which cost less than $2 each, use the females to spread the chemical to breeding spots that would be hard for humans to find, Dr. Silva said. “We’re using the mosquito against the mosquito,” he said. “That’s the smart thing about the trap.”

The city also trained the workers to educate residents in the low-income areas on ways to keep mosquitoes at bay, to recognize dengue symptoms and to head to the hospital at the signs of severe illness. High fever, headache and vomiting can be mistaken for signs of many other diseases. But dengue also produces intense muscle and joint pain, which earned the disease the moniker “breakbone fever,” and may progress to leaky blood vessels and death if left untreated.

“Back in the day, there was a lot of focus in the wealthier area, so the center of the town, and so we spread that out,” Igor Normando, Belém’s mayor, said in an interview.

Because of these efforts, he said, mosquito-borne diseases in the city dropped by 70 percent last season.

“The success of this program was a result of the fact that we didn’t just focus on one specific thing,” Mr. Normando said. “We didn’t only focus on education and only rubbish collection and only this or that.”

A core part of Belém’s strategy is its community outreach. Of the city’s more than 1,000 workers in the health department, about a third are focused on limiting mosquito populations. (By contrast, Bay County, Fla., a coastal area of comparable size, has 15 full-time employees in its mosquito control division.)

Many of Belém’s so-called vector control agents go door to door, reminding residents about ways to keep their premises insect-free, keeping water containers covered and mopping up wet spots after the day’s inevitable rainfall. The houses that have the larvicide dissemination units get a monthly visit to replenish supplies and to ensure that the containers have not been refashioned to pot plants or to launder clothes.

On a sweltering day last month, workers on door-to-door rounds discovered that one homeowner’s grandson had thrown the container away when cleaning, not realizing its purpose. Another family hid the container behind two bicycles, to prevent their dogs from getting to it.

As a shirtless Mr. Gomes tried to stay cool in the unrelenting heat, Elizabete Reis, the city agent, inspected the bucket in his veranda for mosquito larvae — there were none — then dumped the water and refilled it. She then added a fresh mesh strip coated with the larvicide, which sticks to female mosquitoes as they land on the strip to lay eggs.

Mr. Gomes said he was “fascinated” to hear that Belém was ahead of many American cities in adopting this approach. “We imagine that this would be something that you would already have, and we always expect these solutions to be coming from the U. S., not for us to be exporting them,” he said.

Most cities in the United States still rely on aerial or truck spraying to control mosquitoes, dispatching the trucks after dusk and warning citizens to stay indoors. The pesticides can cause dizziness, nausea and skin irritation in some people, trigger seizures in some pets and wipe out beneficial insects like bees and butterflies. Brazil, too, initially relied heavily on spraying, but by the early 2000s, the mosquitoes had begun to show signs of resistance to the chemicals. Cities like Belém now resort to fogging — which produces a fine mist rather than the big droplets from sprays — only during outbreaks.

“We cannot just ban the use of insecticides, but we need to use them in a more rational way,” said Dr. Moreira of Wolbito do Brasil. Ideally, insecticides would become part of a larger strategy, to be used mainly during outbreaks, he said, “so that’s what Brazil is doing.”

In 2016, amid widespread insecticide resistance, Brazil’s health ministry convened experts to brainstorm new solutions, including breeding mosquitoes containing Wolbachia bacteria. Wolbachia is an environmentally harmless solution, naturally present in about half of all insects. The technological marvel here was in introducing the bacteria into Aedes aegypti.

The approach is now part of the country’s mosquito-control strategy in 16 cities, but the government plans to expand that number to nearly 80 by the end of next year, Dr. Moreira said.

Belém is not yet on the list to release Wolbachia mosquitoes; it may do so after reducing the numbers with other methods first. But for some residents, the city’s strategy of distributing larvicide units has already brought back unexpected magic.

Filipe Borges, 63, recalled that when Belém sent trucks to fumigate his neighborhood decades ago, the electric blue Amazonian butterflies of his childhood disappeared. But now, he said, there are noticeably fewer mosquitoes in his yard, and yet “the butterflies are back.”

Apoorva Mandavilli reports on science and global health for The Times, with a focus on infectious diseases and pandemics and the public health agencies that try to manage them.

How Thanksgiving Became Political: Francesca Hong’s Tweets Explained

The New York Times August 13, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Ahead of Wisconsin’s Democratic primary for governor, a past tweet by the assemblywoman that called for the holiday to be canceled was resurfaced.

By Alisha Haridasani Gupta

For months, polls indicated that Francesca Hong, a chef and a democratic socialist state lawmaker, was the clear front-runner in the Democratic primary for governor in Wisconsin.

So when Hong narrowly lost to her opponent David Crowley on Tuesday, some in the political world pointed to Thanksgiving. Or rather, a six-year-old, now-deleted social media post from Hong dismissing the cherished American holiday and saying it glorified colonialism.

“Cancel Thanksgiving,” she wrote in the post on X. “Should have done this in 1621.”

Though a number of factors led to the election’s outcome, and as establishment Democrats have pushed the party to focus on courting moderates, Hong’s comment on the holiday sent political pundits and strategists into a frenzy. A debate ensued around whether reframing the quintessential American holiday was too radical an idea in the current political landscape.

Hong’s comment resurfaced in the days leading up to the election in a swing state and came alongside her other takes on almost every holiday: She also seemingly dislikes Valentine’s Day, the Fourth of July and Halloween and using Christmas trees as computer screen backgrounds.

All of which became rich fodder for her political opponents and the right-wing media, feeding into Republicans’ longstanding gripe that liberals, with their progressive interpretations, are ruining all holidays. The conservative National Review magazine named Hong the “Grinch of all holidays” and Senator Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas, claimed on X that Democrats like Hong “openly hate America.”

Even Democrats tried to distance themselves from the blast radius; in an interview with ABC’s “This Week,” Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a figurehead of progressive politics, labeled the Thanksgiving comment, along with Hong’s other posts, as an example of outdated and ineffective “Woke 1.0” — a strand of left-wing political discourse that emerged around 2020, as the country grappled with social justice issues, like racial inequality and the Black Lives Matter movement.

Hong tried to walk back those posts, saying in an interview with Politico that she “had some hot takes, some bad takes.” In an interview with CNN last week, she responded to a question about her Thanksgiving statements by referring to her experience as a chef, saying that anything that brings people around a table to talk is “a good thing.”

But, she added, “Thanksgiving is also a time that is incredibly painful for many people in our communities.”

The reaction to Hong’s Thanksgiving post is emblematic of a broader reckoning among many Americans with the country’s checkered history.

Popular depictions of Thanksgiving trace the fabled autumnal tradition back to a three-day feast in 1621 between Pilgrims, who arrived in Massachusetts from Plymouth, England, and members of the Indigenous Wampanoag tribe to celebrate a successful harvest. Over two centuries after that shared meal, in 1863, President Abraham Lincoln proclaimed Thanksgiving Day a national holiday.

Some Americans, especially on the left, have questioned the accuracy of that lore, saying it glosses over massacre, war, exploitation and slavery.

Schools across the country have rethought how they teach students the history of Thanksgiving, and even “Saturday Night Live” has produced sketches that poke fun at the holiday, including one starring Will Ferrell and Maya Rudolph that reimagines the first Thanksgiving meal as tense, rather than friendly.

Still, a vast majority of Americans still celebrate the holiday, a Pew Research Center survey found in 2024. Thanksgiving remains a federal holiday, and organizations are unlikely to change how it is observed.

The Thanksgiving debate is reminiscent of debates around the decisions in many states and communities to celebrate Indigenous Peoples’ Day either alongside or instead of Columbus Day as a way to acknowledge the people who were already living in North America thousands of years before the Italian navigator arrived.

A similar debate bubbled up before President Joseph R. Biden Jr. signed legislation in 2021 that designated Juneteenth — the annual commemoration of the end of slavery in the United States — a federal holiday.

Alisha Haridasani Gupta is a Times reporter covering style and pop culture.

Our favorite choices for seafood from Sonora, carnitas from Michoacán, chalupas from Pueblo and so much more.

Credit...

Supported by

There has never been a better time for Mexican food in the United States. A culinary renaissance over the last 15 years has expanded the American palate well beyond Tex-Mex, tacos and game-night nachos.

Mexican and Mexican American chefs have brought their cooking, in all of its regionality and specificity, to nearly every corner of the country. You’ll find it in large cities like Chicago and Philadelphia, but also in towns like Ephraim, Wis., where the population could fit inside an urban high school.

For more than a year, our team of reporters, editors and photographers have traveled the country in search of our favorites. This list is not an attempt to rank the best Mexican restaurants. It is, rather, a mosaic of great places to eat, from food trucks to corner restaurants to tasting-menu counters. We hope it tells an expansive story about Mexican cooking in America today — a dynamic cuisine all its own, and as American as any food.

New Orleans

Ana Castro, who owns Acamaya with her sister, Lydia, folds pristine local crab together with collard greens and chochoyotes (masa dumplings); slips sweet, cheese-crusted shrimp into costra tacos; and serves blackened drum Veracruz-style, in a stew of tomatoes and olives. This is not a forced hybridization of New Orleans and Mexican cuisine. It’s the work of a gifted chef cooking what she knows, using the most attractive ingredients available — which, in Southeast Louisiana, means seafood from the Gulf of Mexico. Acamaya, open just two years, is one of New Orleans’s best restaurants. And the Castro sisters now have a sister restaurant, Casimiro, a Mexican breakfast and lunch spot that opened a few blocks away in the spring. BRETT ANDERSON

Save to your restaurant list:

Oklahoma City

A pair of midsize Mexican markets bookend the vibrant Mexican food scene that runs along La 29 in Oklahoma City, a shopping hub for local Central Americans and Mexicans, especially those from Aguascalientes, one of the smallest states in Mexico. Inside the store, overfilled aisles of sundries are encircled by a vibrant panadería case, a carnicería, a window for check cashing and money transfers, and a kitchen behind steamer trays of Mexican stews. The most coveted item comes out of a small commercial oven that produces fresh birotes, the Aguascalientes-style roll and traditional vehicle for the state sandwich, torta de albañil. The market’s fresh versions are slit open on one end and stuffed with a ham cold cut, pickled jalapeño and crema Mexicana until it leaks out the opening — a little taste of home for the city’s Hidrocálidos. BILL ESPARZA

Save to your restaurant list:

Nashville

Edgar Victoria’s career was actually jump-started after he was laid off. Joblessness is what led him to build a local following cooking at concession stands, pop-ups and food trucks. The chef became easier to find last year, after opening Alebrije, his first brick-and-mortar restaurant. Mr. Victoria uses heirloom corn for the restaurant’s housemade tamales, tostadas, sopes and tortillas that are foundational to the street food in his native Mexico City. His unassuming restaurant on the second floor of an East Nashville strip mall is one of the Southeast’s best taquerías. BRETT ANDERSON

Save to your restaurant list:

Denver

By the time you finish reading this sentence, Johnny Curiel may well have opened another restaurant. On a several-year hot streak that many chefs can only dream of, he started with this pocket-size ode to the fondas his family runs in Guadalajara. Named for his mother, Alma, the restaurant is refined, contemporary and deeply satisfying. Tucking into dishes like duck carnitas and the agave-roasted sweet potato leaves you feeling both impressed and welcomed by Mr. Curiel. This year, he opened Milpero, a 16-seat tasting-menu restaurant, a further sign of his belief in the power and potential of Mexican cuisine. BRIAN GALLAGHER

Save to your restaurant list:

Philadelphia

At Amá, chips and salsa aren’t a humble starter. Broad, crackling tostadas made with heirloom corn arrive with six salsas drawing on flavors from across Mexico, like Baja’s creamy smoked-cashew salsa or a fiery burned-habanero salsa negra from the Yucatán. The chef Frankie Ramírez left Mexico City for Philadelphia at 16 and spent two decades in other chefs’ kitchens before opening Amá in 2025. While Mexican restaurants here have long been shaped by Puebla, the home state of many local families, Mr. Ramírez offers a broad taste of the country’s extraordinary regional variety. There’s coal-blistered Oaxacan tlayudas, fall-apart Jalisco-style lamb-neck birria with brick red consomé, and, inspired by the Pacific Coast, a whole octopus charred over a custom wood-fired grill. REGAN STEPHENS

Save to your restaurant list:

Caldwell, Idaho

The chef Salvador Alamilla, who owns the restaurant with his wife, Rebecca, is from Michoacán by way of Santa Ana, Calif. He brings the spirit of both places to the menu. The tortillas are made in-house with the Indigenous technique of nixtamalization, and in a nod to Southern California, the L. A. Birria Tacos have a particularly rich consomé. But the meats that emerge from the depths of the oak-fired barbaoca pits outside are Mr. Alamilla’s Michoacan magic. The smoke and spice on short ribs or lamb shanks and belly are worth a detour to the Idaho prairie. BRIAN GALLAGHER

Save to your restaurant list:

Washington, D. C.

Born in Chihuahua, Mexico, and raised in El Paso, Irabién Christian imbues Amparo Fondita’s food with his painterly eye and impressive command of Mexico’s vast palette of flavors and recipes. Savory-sweet mole manchamanteles cover enmoladas filled with turkey poached in duck fat. Sopecitos arrive disassembled on a platter rimmed with fixings, including fresh-fried blue corn masa cakes so flavorful, tender and warm you’ll be tempted to eat them alone, like breakfast biscuits. While Mr. Christian’s kitchen operates at the cutting edge, his convivial restaurant functions as a place to drop into for a restorative bowl of brick-red pozole, or a round of margaritas and queso frito, which the menu helpfully describes as Oaxacan cheese curds. BRETT ANDERSON

Save to your restaurant list:

Phoenix

The enticing waft of burning mesquite will coax you in the door at this small-but-mighty Sonoran steakhouse. If you’re lucky, you can follow it all the way to the seat at the end of the bar closest to the grill, where you can watch the chef René Andrade commune with the coals. Not surprisingly, the bone-in New York strip and rib-eye are the stars of the short menu, but the skill and smoke make their way into every dish, so don’t neglect the grilled chicken or especially the embered elote with spicy lime crema. BRIAN GALLAGHER

Save to your restaurant list:

Richmond, Calif.

Omar Mejía comes from a proud family of barbacoyeros, and just like many of his fellow Bay Area construction workers from Mexico, he has many talents. As more construction workers from his native state of Hidalgo arrived in the area, he began to sell barbacoa on the weekends at the Richmond Pulga, a bustling swap meet. Mr. Mejía’s family recipes include tender pit-roasted lamb, delicious consomé and regional salsas such as a salsa verde that includes xoconostle (prickly pear), and chinicuiles (grubs). The best day to go is on Sunday, when he also serves pancita blanca, a rare offal dish, and occasionally, ximbo, a whole spatchcocked chicken wrapped in maguey leaves that’s slathered in adobo and covered with pork rinds and nopales before the package is lowered into the pit. It’s a dish from Actopán, Hidalgo, that’s found a home in the Bay Area. BILL ESPARZA

Save to your restaurant list:

Chicago

Carrying a recipe that goes back generations in Ocotlán, Jalisco, Ruben Reyes opened this classic birrieria in 1973. Today, it is run by his son, Andres Reyes, and the cafeteria-style tables and chairs still surround an elevated counter where the taquero prepares orders. And the menu has not changed — it’s just oven-roasted goat and well-seasoned consomé served with corn tortillas and condiments. It wasn’t a compromise to add crowd-pleasing quesabirrias, the only innovation over decades for a taquería that has consistently given Chicago a birrieria that’s like visiting a mercado in Jalisco. BILL ESPARZA

Save to your restaurant list:

Tucson, Ariz.

In Arizona, the separate specialties of Sonora carne asada and Sonoran hot dogs are both under the same roof. Opened in 1994 by Benjamin and Karel Galaz from Nacozari, Sonora, the festive pub-style restaurant complete with wood furnishings offers mesquite-grilled carne asada, and caramelos (carne asada with melted cheese), both served in flour tortillas. The loaded Sonoran hot dog comes in a sweet bun that’s topped with beans, grilled onions, diced tomatoes and fresh onions, and mustard, mayonnaise and a housemade jalapeño salsa. There’s even a traditional caldo de queso at the Sonoran-style taquería that’s made in America. BILL ESPARZA

Save to your restaurant list:

Seguin, Texas

Burnt Bean’s Texas barbecue is outstanding. The lines attest to that, as do the accolades, including being named the state’s best barbecue joint by Texas Monthly in 2025. It’s also accurate to say the restaurant simply serves the food of South Texas. Ernest Servantes, Burnt Bean’s co-pitmaster and co-owner (along with David Kirkland), grew up in Uvalde eating barbecue with guacamole, pico de gallo and tortillas. You’ll find all of that at Burnt Bean, along with specials like tortilla soup and, on weekends, a brunch roster of menudo, barbacoa tacos and brisket huevos rancheros. You could call it Tex-Mex barbecue, but it’s just how barbecue is eaten in a state whose Mexican border is more than 1,200 miles long. BRETT ANDERSON

Save to your restaurant list:

San Francisco

The chef Val Cantú and his team fashion mesmerizing “aha” moments with each plate on the tasting menu here, while still keeping faith with the Mexican dishes they reference. The ceviche is made with Monterey Bay abalone and accompanied in its shell with kombu and a shaved ice made from fermented carrot juice. The fish taco is served on a duvet-soft sourdough tortilla that wraps around a perfectly battered and fried piece of local black cod, and topped with huitlacoche and corn crema. Each of the dozen or so courses manages such virtuosity in its own way. There is a reason (so many, in fact) that Californios is the only Mexican restaurant in the world to hold three Michelin stars. BRIAN GALLAGHER

Save to your restaurant list:

Springdale, Ark.

Ricardo Palos began serving tacos one day a week at his family’s butcher shop, which opened in 1996. The frequency increased as diners learned that Mr. Palos was nearly as handy with a grill as he is with a butcher’s knife. He still makes chorizo, carnitas and an array of chicharrones from the pigs he breaks down every week, drawing on skills he learned from Mexican butchers while growing up in Chicago. The modest Arkansas storefront is a longtime source of sustenance and solace for local Latinos and, in more recent years, Marshallese, drawn to northwest Arkansas for jobs at local chicken processors. Carnitas are Hermanos’s best seller and Mr. Palos’s specialty. But he will cook tacos with whatever you fancy — including prime sirloin and house-cured cecina — from the butcher’s case. BRETT ANDERSON

Save to your restaurant list:

New York City

No restaurant on the Eastern Seaboard offers carnitas in as many variations as Carnitas Ramirez in the East Village of Manhattan. Head, shoulders, knees and toes: All end up in the bubbling copper cauldron, or cazo, along with slippery ribbons of skin, crunchy ears and crumbles of brain destined for palm-size tacos. Knowing a little Spanish helps, since ordering happens at the steam table and all cuts are listed by their traditional names. The difference between maciza and matriz? There’s no better place to find out. LUKE FORTNEY

Save to your restaurant list:

NEW YORK CITY

Weekend nights, Cleotilde Juárez Ramírez commands a patch of sidewalk in Corona, part of a stretch of Queens that is home to the largest concentration of New Yorkers of Mexican descent. Her simple setup: a comal the size of a satellite dish over a brazier. In goes a scoop of lard, then eight corn tortillas, fanned out and briskly dressed with onions, salsas rojo and verde, and ragged strips of beef. For $10 you get the whole stack, warm and supple, to be chased by cafe de olla from a terra-cotta mug. Street vendors lead uncertain lives, and Ms. Ramírez has had to shift around the neighborhood a number of times, even briefly running a storefront. Undeterred, she keeps going. LIGAYA MISHAN

Save to your restaurant list:

Santa Fe, N. M.

Santa Fe is not short on pork preparations. But the carnitas, adobada and al pastor coming out of this unassuming food truck are particularly noteworthy. A mixed taco plate is a good way to eat through the selections. Be warned (or enticed) that the accompanying blistered jalapeños have not succumbed to the broad milding of those chiles elsewhere. The Luis Mix breakfast burrito is a superlative version of the form. Stuffed with chorizo, bacon, Polish sausage, eggs, potato, cheese and green chile, it’s an ideal meal for you … and your whole family. BRIAN GALLAGHER

Save to your restaurant list:

Denver

The chef José Avila, a native of Mexico City, is a savant when it comes to the fortifying hominy soup in the restaurant’s name. The pozole negro, in particular, is a formidable sight — rich and restorative in the way the world’s great soups are. Do not discount the guisados, though, a whole genre of stews and braises, which can be ordered as tacos or costras (basically disks of griddled cheese that play the role of tortillas). The menu has a slate of more than a dozen, but the huachinango, red snapper with pineapple butter and citrus slaw, is hard to forget. BRIAN GALLAGHER

Save to your restaurant list:

New Haven, Conn.

The view from the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 goes from banal to spectacular as you careen around City Point and two dozen food trucks come into view. The first vendors to inhabit this stretch of Long Wharf Drive, later named Food Truck Paradise by city officials, sold American hot dogs and flowers. These days, they are seriously outnumbered by catering trucks grilling Puerto Rican pinchos and salsa-soaked tortas ahogadas, the flags of their home countries flapping in the offshore breeze. Tricked-out bebidas are a specialty of … well, everyone. Take your pick from mangonadas, avocado slushies and Shirley Temple agua frescas, then grab a seat along the waterfront as traffic rushes by. LUKE FORTNEY

Save to your restaurant list:

San Antonio

Garcia’s has been a family affair since Julio and Yolanda Garcia opened it in 1962, along with Julio’s parents, Guadalupe and Nicolasa. The restaurant moved across the street in 1970, to a narrow property that used to hold a rail-car diner, which seems apt. In the hands of the founder’s children — John, Andy, Sandra and Julio Jr. — Garcia’s is what an idealized American diner looks like in this part of the country: housemade salsas, tortillas instead of toast and plates of nourishing food at prices that explain why some customers visit multiple times a day. Mexican No. 1, a regulars’ favorite, brings together two enchiladas, one gravy-smothered tamale, rice, beans and a crispy taco for $11.99. The 65-seat restaurant is also something of a pioneer. With Andy Garcia as pitmaster, Garcia’s has been serving house-smoked brisket wrapped in tortillas for over 20 years. BRETT ANDERSON

Save to your restaurant list:

Chicago

Chicago is a gorditas town. You can find amazing variations from Aguascalientes, Zacatecas and Durango, like the ones at this beloved family restaurant with a warm inviting interior of brick wall panels and decorative ceiling tiles. The attentive staff checks in often, and your gorditas arrive fast. Regional Mexican stews like chicharrón prensado come in your choice of red or green salsas, as do deshebrada (shredded beef) and asado. Gorditas filled with smoky chile pasados and queso, or unctuous asiento, unrefined lard, are just some of the more than 20 fillings on the menu that bring a little bit of the Durangan city of Santiago Papasquiaro to the Midwest. BILL ESPARZA

Save to your restaurant list:

Houston

Hugo’s opened in 2002, 18 years after the chef and co-owner, Hugo Ortega, arrived in Texas as a teenager, illegally. He jumped off a moving train in San Antonio and ultimately landed in Houston, where he got a job as a dishwasher at a restaurant owned by Tracy Vaught, now his wife and business partner. (He has since become a naturalized citizen.) Hugo’s, the couple’s first restaurant together, introduced Houston to regionally distinctive cuisine that was more expansive and refined than what Texans then widely understood as “interior Mexican” cooking. Aged into a fine-dining lion in the cradle of Tex-Mex, Hugo’s still features longtime staples like banana leaf-wrapped cabrito, grilled octopus and sautéed chapulines, not to mention mezcals and Mexican wine. Today, the restaurant’s mostly Mexican employees provide warm, white-tablecloth service — “Can I bring you a stand for your cowboy hat, ma’am?” — to regulars in rhinestones and families marking milestones. BRETT ANDERSON

Save to your restaurant list:

Portland, Ore.

The burritos here have their fans, and like everything on the menu they are certainly a worthy order. But the chef Manny Lopez’s Yucatecan specialties are the way to go. The panuchos and salbutes are great topped with any of the options, but the cochinita pibil, citrusy slow-roasted pork, should be the first move. The relleno negro and menudo soups aren’t always available, but if they are, make sure to get both. Shared small plates are a cliché at a certain kind of restaurant, but here they are truly the best way to try as much of the menu as possible. BRIAN GALLAGHER

Save to your restaurant list:

Los Angeles

Alfonso Martinez started Poncho’s Tlayudas outside the offices of the Comunidades Indígenas en Liderazgo with a vision for Oaxacan food and community in Los Angeles. His new place is one of the highlights inside Maydan Market, where the dinner menu has greatly expanded with memelas, turkey in mole and traditional black bean tamales. But you can’t leave without trying the moronga; the recipe and technique for this delicate and delicious blood sausage, flecked with onion, yerba buena and dried chiles, has been passed down like a family heirloom, and it really is a local treasure. TEJAL RAO

Save to your restaurant list:

Phoenix

The competition for “best Mexican restaurant under a shade structure in a parking lot” can be a stiff one in the Southwest. But Mariscos el Profe must be a contender. Seafood isn’t the first thing that comes to mind when you hear “Arizona,” but the state is just across the border from Sonora and its lime-and-chile-kissed mariscos traditions. At this food truck, the mixed seafood Ceviche Es Lo Que Hay! is a fitting introduction to the piquant maritime flavors of marinated marlin, salt-cured sea bass and tender octopus. But don’t neglect the terrestrial pleasures of the rib-eye aguachile. BRIAN GALLAGHER

Save to your restaurant list:

Los Angeles

Across the United States, the cuisine of small-town Mexico has made its mark, but perhaps most notably with what Raul Ortega’s shrimp tacos have done for San Juan de Los Lagos, Jalisco. Mr. Ortega’s white taco truck has been parked along Olympic Boulevard in the Boyle Heights neighborhood for decades. From there, the legend of this taco has spread. Originally a Lenten dish of shrimp, it’s deep fried inside a corn tortilla and finished with a tomato salsa mixed with raw cabbage. The salsa is poured over and a spoon-cut avocado slice crowns the taco. When visitors ask where to go if they can hit only one taquería in Los Angeles, Mariscos Jalisco is the answer. BILL ESPARZA

Save to your restaurant list:

Albuquerque

This is New Mexico, so naturally red and green chile are on offer at this down-home spot, which opened in 1963 — and both are exemplary. But the carne adovada, an even more specific specialty of the state, is the must-order. Strips of pork are marinated then baked in red chile sauce, and the results are earthy, spicy and faintly vegetal in perfect proportion. The dish comes in various iterations — enchilada, chimichanga and omelet among them — but the turnover made with Cheddar and a fried flour tortilla is the best bet. If more meat is needed, the New Mexico-style chicharrones are the salted fatty pork cubes of your dreams. BRIAN GALLAGHER

Save to your restaurant list:

Los Angeles

The first thing you notice is the line out the door, which is for Gilberto Cetina’s extraordinary mariscos at Holbox (and yes, I’m sorry to report that those aguachiles and tostadas are worth the wait, as is a reservation for the tasting menu). But this former garment factory in South Los Angeles, a development project of the Esperanza Community Housing Corporation, is home to a half-dozen interconnected restaurants and an unreasonable amount of talent, hospitality and sheer deliciousness that draw Angelenos from every walk of life. Fátima Juárez had a vision for Komal, which is both a neighborhood molino, grinding heirloom corn varieties from Mexico to make fresh masa, and a kitchen that specializes in snacky antojitos and carefully calibrated salsas made with both great ingredients and finesse. TEJAL RAO

Save to your restaurant list:

CHICAGO

For most of living memory, Midwest Mexican has been a euphemism for Mexican food prepared by and for white Midwesterners. Diana Dávila shredded that narrative. Lengua in peanut salsa was one of the first hits on the menu at Mi Tocaya, which she opened in 2017, an early signal that the chef relished challenging her audience. Ms. Dávila’s career began in her parents’ suburban Chicago taquería and lifted off after attending Susana Trilling’s Seasons of My Heart Cooking School in Oaxaca. Channeling that experience, she continues to innovate at her cheerful, uncompromising antojería in the Midwest’s most Mexican city. BRETT ANDERSON

Save to your restaurant list:

Portland, Ore.

When Polo Bañuelos and Carlos Reynosa, partners and native Angelenos, opened their pop-up, they made it their mission to serve down-home East L. A. Chicano food in line with their vegan lifestyle in the Pacific Northwest. Now a vibrant restaurant full of Chicano iconography in a rainbow of pastels, Mis Tacones serves remarkable Mexican food that happens to be vegan. It’s almost inexplicable how delicious dishes like the nachos — topped with al pastor seitan, cashew cream and vegan beans — can be. And the plump, lightly golden chimichanga called la Chimi is served with evident pride and attention. BILL ESPARZA

Save to your restaurant list:

Austin, Texas

Edgar Rico and Sara Mardanbigi’s taquería is like no other that you’ll find in this taco-packed town. There is fish sauce in the salsa crudo, and furikake dusts the tuna tostadas. The sholeh zard is inspired by the Iranian dessert Ms. Mardanbigi grew up eating, blended with elements of the arroz con leche from Mr. Rico’s Mexican American childhood. Nixta is justifiably known for its tortillas — Mr. Rico makes masa using heirloom corn and nixtamalization. The reservations-only tasting menu, served Thursday through Saturday, further showcases the couple’s stunning creativity and ambition. But most of the time Nixta remains what it always has been: a counter taquería of the utmost excellence. PRIYA KRISHNA

Save to your restaurant list:

Minneapolis

Gustavo Romero is from Mexico, but established himself as a chef cooking Italian cuisine in Florida, Chicago and the Bay Area. He started cooking Mexican food after following Kate, his wife and business partner, to Minneapolis. The Romeros raised the bar for quality Mexican cuisine locally with the tortillería they opened during the pandemic, serving tacos off an ironing board on the sidewalk. Oro by Nixta, which opened in 2023, advances that project considerably. Mr. Romero channels his passion for nixtamalized heirloom corn into a masa-focused menu fleshed out with braised and roasted meats, in-season produce and an impressive array of moles and salsas. The ambitious but unpretentious restaurant is one of the reasons Northeast Minneapolis is among the country’s most alluring neighborhoods for dining. BRETT ANDERSON

Save to your restaurant list:

Kansas City, Kan.

The Armourdale neighborhood became one of the Midwest’s foundational Mexican American communities in the early 20th century, when immigrants were drawn to the abundant meatpacking and railroad jobs along the Kansas River. A visit to the area is incomplete without lunch at El Pollo Rey. The vibe is Kansas City barbecue meets Northwestern Mexico. The aroma of spatchcocked, Sinaloa-style chicken, drifting off the restaurant’s hickory wood-fired grills, hits you before you walk in. The chicken is served with taco fixings: tortillas, pickled onions, charro beans, fresh salsa. You can order a half or whole bird. And you will want some of the saucy, foil-wrapped Buffalo wings, the only other thing on the menu. BRETT ANDERSON

Save to your restaurant list:

Ephraim, Wis.

Eagle Harbor is a short walk from the doorstep of La Sirena’s. Peninsula State Park is in the distance, and the immensity of Lake Michigan looms in the mist. That splendor is core to the appeal of the restaurant Carlos Salgado and Emilie Coulson Salgado opened last year after moving to Emilie’s hometown. Ephraim (population roughly 400) is far from Orange County, Calif., where the couple ran the trailblazing Taco María. That restaurant’s ethos is reoriented at La Sirena most vividly in the summer, when tourism peaks along with a local harvest rich of sweet corn and sour cherries, ramps and morels. It’s all integrated on a tasting menu with premium ingredients from Mr. Salgado’s native Mexico, including heirloom corn. But this 22-seat restaurant is open year-round. Locals by now know to be on the lookout for Mr. Salgado’s exemplary Caesar salad, because the menu changes with the seasons, just as Ephraim does. BRETT ANDERSON

Save to your restaurant list:

NEW YORK CITY

Beyond the Belt Parkway overpass, in the industrial sprawl of southwest Brooklyn, more than a dozen street vendors squeeze into a vacant parking lot — right next to the full-sized crane — transforming it into Sunset Park Plaza. There’s music, coolers of home-brew tepache (made from fermented pineapple rinds) and never enough folding chairs to go around. Everything is gloriously improvised. The bean-slathered Oaxacan tlayudas are toasted over charcoal in fish baskets. The crimson seafood cocktails arrive in domed plastic slushie cups. And it’s impossible to try everything in one visit. Fortunately, every weekend, the plaza roars back to life. LUKE FORTNEY

Save to your restaurant list:

Charlotte, N. C.

Amazing tacos al pastor might be unexpected in Charlotte, N. C., but the gifted Indigenous Mixe taqueros know no borders. María Hernández, the owner, recruits the taqueros from Oaxaca and Los Angeles to make perfect layered strips of marinated pork sliced from an impressive, shapely trompo onto toasted corn tortillas. A line 50 or so deep forms before opening. A Latino crowd that includes Central and South Americans, along with Mexicans from different states, comes together at the salsa bar to dress their tacos, excited that a taquería “just like they have in Los Angeles” is now easy to find in Charlotte, a new al pastor capital. BILL ESPARZA

Save to your restaurant list:

El Paso

This strip-mall taquería — the sophomore effort of the owners Emiliano and Kristal Marentes, who own the acclaimed restaurant Elemi — opened quietly this past winter, but its tacos came out swinging. The restaurant excels at every style of taco on offer. The standout is the al pastor, whose pork is sliced while partially frozen to give it an even thickness, then arranged on the trompo so that the tips get crunchy and caramelized, but the meat stays juicy and slicked with fat. The tortillas, elastic and blanket-like, are never more than a few hours off the comal, and the bracing salsas taste like they’re made with the same exacting attention to detail. El Paso has long been one of the country’s great taco towns. Elemi shows there’s always room for more excitement. PRIYA KRISHNA

Save to your restaurant list:

Central Falls, R. I.

Diego Alcantar opened Tuxpan Taqueria, named for the Michoacán town where he was born, in 2022 with his mother, María, the restaurant’s chef. They serve standout tacos, gorditas and, in the early summer, fried quesadillas filled with squash blossoms grown in narrow cinder-block beds outside. But you can’t visit Tuxpan taquería without ordering a sandwich. The house signature is a drippily seductive chicken Milanesa torta crossed with chilaquiles verde. Like the other tortas, it’s served with a slice of bacon on top, and the bun is a locally baked Portuguese roll. All are paradigmatic Mexican American sandwiches in this historically working-class, majority Latin American New England town. BRETT ANDERSON

Save to your restaurant list:

Oceanside, Calif.

When the chef Roberto Alcocer opened this spot in 2021, he meant to establish a north-of-the-border restaurant for the cuisine of Mexico’s premier wine country, Valle de Guadalupe. Gradually, Mr. Alcocer’s tasting menu evolved to feature dishes from all over the country, for U. S. diners who were looking for a more familiar taste of Mexico. The restaurant has won many accolades for locally caught fish in mole chichilo, a rolled etixtamal set over a red pipián, or a Pueblan Wagyu chancla, all capturing the beauty, grace and diverse ingredients and techniques of Mexico. BILL ESPARZA

Save to your restaurant list:

Detroit

Vecino opened two years ago in Midtown Detroit, but its roots run to the city’s working-class southwest, also known as Mexicantown. That’s where Adriana Jiménez, a co-owner, spent much of her childhood, in a family of restaurateurs who fled violence in Mexico City in the 1990s. Ms. Jiménez didn’t return to the city of her birth until adulthood, after the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program made her a permanent legal resident of the United States. Edgar Torres, a former chef de cuisine at Alinea, in Chicago, was recruited to bring Vecino into conversation with the modern cuisine that has bloomed in Mexico City since Ms. Jiménez’s family left. The results — butterflied whole snapper painted with verde and roja salsas, airy tetelas stuffed with carrot tinga, luscious sikil pak pumpkin seed salsa — carry the thrill of what Ms. Jiménez discovered when she finally returned: a valuable inheritance she didn’t know she had. BRETT ANDERSON

Save to your restaurant list:

Las Vegas

In Vegas, it’s not unusual to sit in the blazing sun beneath a tarp-covered bench, eating over-the-top seafood tostadas ornately stacked with high-end shellfish, and molcajetes chock-full of seafood snacks. What sets Jorge Silva’s ocean-blue trailer apart is a morning specialty: cahuamanta, or stingray soup. A growing number of Sonoran immigrants have relocated to Sin City, a desert locale that feels a lot like back home. Mr. Silva’s cahuamanta is buttery, tangy and comes with springy shrimp and rich tuna fin that add layers of fatty flavors. It tastes like a Sunday in Ciudad Obregón, where Mr. Silva was born. BILL ESPARZA

Save to your restaurant list:

Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. Get regular updates from New York Times Cooking, with recipe suggestions, cooking tips and shopping advice.

Late last year, Bill Esparza and I set out looking for exceptional Mexican food, wherever we could find it – in traditional restaurants as well as food trucks and, in one case in Oklahoma City, served from a modified R. V. Our goal was to find people and places driving the renaissance in Mexican cuisine in the U. S. Our list is a mosaic illustrating a culinary phenomenon that has unfolded over the past 15 years, as Mexican chefs have brought their food to nearly every corner of the country, at the same time Mexican food became a mainstay of American fine dining.

Keep track of where you want to go, where you have been and what you liked, and share your picks with your friends.
