A Candidate Named ‘Count Binface’ Is the Most Normal Part of This Pivotal UK Election

Wired August 12, 2026

A man wearing a trash can on his head dances on the beach, silver cape glinting in the sun as he spins beneath a wheel-topped pier, singing “England needs a new hope” from under an enormous helmet. The scene is Clacton-on-Sea, the centre of one of the east of England’s poorest constituencies and home to around 92,000 people and now the focus of international attention over what locals and observers have dubbed a political circus. The video is part of an extremely online campaign by Count Binface, who is running to represent the Essex town in Parliament. In an ignoble first in British electoral history, he is one of 34 candidates on the ballot.

One of Britain’s most high-profile and perennial candidates, Binface has stood in six previous elections across England over the past decade (UK politicians do not have to live in a constituency in order to represent it in parliament). This Thursday, he faces Clacton incumbent Nigel Farage—leader of the right-wing anti-immigration party Reform UK and a friend of Donald Trump—in a by-election triggered by the latter’s resignation amidst allegations that he and his party accepted and failed to declare financial support, including a £5 million gift from a Thailand-based cryptocurrency tycoon. Reform did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Farage maintains he has done nothing wrong and wants to recontest his seat to let voters judge his actions. Major parties, including governing Labour and the opposition Conservatives, refused to field a candidate in the contest, branding it a “gimmick” and a “circus.” When then chancellor of the exchequer Rachel Reeves accepted Farage’s resignation, she said: “If he wants to spend the summer arguing with a bin, I won't stop him.”

In the vacuum, campaigners have rushed to use a high-profile vote to push their own issues, from psychosexual theory to Bible messaging to white-nationalist conspiracy theories. There are also a number of novelty candidates, three from satirical party Monster Raving Loony Party alone, Nick the Incredible Flying Brick, Baron Von Thunderclap, and Howling Laud Hope, who plans to shrink hospital waiting lists by reducing the font size.

The 34-candidate list is unprecedented; the 3-foot-long ballot papers are reportedly bigger than the tables used to count them on and have proved difficult for organizers to fit into envelopes for postal votes. The parties are fighting frenziedly for voters’ attention. Rosie Morrell of the Everyone Is God party–whose policies include creating a “stable world economy” and “to map and fully comprehend the complete spectrum of human psychology and sexuality”–offers to take off her Union Jack dress so I can snap a photo of her in her matching bikini. That’s what other press have been asking for as her partner contests the by-election, she says, pink feathers dangling from her ears.

In national coverage, Count Binface has broken through. A common figure in British politics, he most recently ran against Prime Minister Andy Burnham in June and has contested several other general and London mayoral elections before. Inside the trash can is comedian and writer Jon Harvey, who has worked on satirical television shows including Last Week Tonight With John Oliver, weekly British news quiz Have I Got News for You, and iconic BBC comedy The Thick of It. With Farage’s popularity collapsing across the country, Britons nationally want a victory for Binface–who pledges to nationalize singer Adele, cap ice cream prices, and hold a referendum on whether Pluto should regain its planet status.

“We did have a giggle, and get that it’s someone just trying to make light of it,” Jaywick resident Angelina Port, who is not a Reform voter, recalls about first reading about Binface in the national press. “But we do have issues that need to be resolved,” she says, standing on the front steps of her bungalow, which has been raised on bricks to avoid flooding. It’s a common feature in the neighborhood, which was built as a summer holiday resort but ended up permanently inhabited due to bomb damage and a housing shortage in London caused by the Second World War. Ten of her neighbors have signs saying “I’m voting Reform,” staked outside. The breakfast and burger van she runs with her partner is parked in her drive.

It’s the first Tuesday of August, 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 Celsius) by midmorning and bin day in Clacton. Garbage trucks heave down quiet cul-de-sacs and flies are buzzing as canvassers armed with leaflets for the Rejoin EU Party’s John Stevens trudge sun-baked tarmac. They are targeting former Conservative voters in the affluent neighbourhood of Holland-on-Sea. Houses with glass fronts, large balconies, and gated, manicured front drives overlook the turquoise sea lapping a sandy beach–where last month a small boat of migrants landed after crossing the English channel from continental Europe.

Once a Conservative member for European Parliament, Stevens is positioning himself as a vote against Farage and his political baby, Brexit. In recent years, national attitudes toward EU membership have shifted, with Brexit being blamed for an annual multibillion-pound hit to the British economy as growth stagnates and living costs climb.

Stevens wants to see if local attitudes have changed, believing that if even those living in Brexit heartlands—around 70 percent of Clacton voted for Brexit in 2016—believe it was a bad idea, it will send a message to Westminster. “The one policy that Farage has been advocating all his political life is widely regarded as a disaster—and that’s how you attack him,” says Stevens, who quit the Conservative party over its increasing Euroscepticism. “You don’t attack him through his money or his morals, because those simply don’t hit.”

Some houses they skip: Those with signs reading “I’m voting Reform” and showing a pointing, smirking Farage staked in the ground. Stevens has learnt from knocking on 2,500 doors so far that staunch Farage fans aren’t concerned by the £5 million. “Everybody knows that Farage is going to win this, because he’s got the place nailed down,” Stevens says.

His view is affirmed when he stops local retiree and Reform voter Jeff Brown, on his sea-view walk. Farage needs the money for security, says Brown, and who wouldn’t accept a £5 million gift? “I don’t think he should have done what he did, resigning and standing again,” he adds, but nevertheless believes Farage has been a good MP in the past couple of years and has voted for him again. Having voted for Brexit, Brown started supporting Farage two years ago when he burst back onto the political scene on Clacton Pier, impressed by the politician’s charisma and speech. Brown already held anti-immigration feelings, saying he had been “pushed” out of London by an influx of immigrants.

It’s a feeling not just Farage is trying to take advantage of. Kai Stephens, 22, is standing for the far-right British Democrats, targeting ex-Londoners living in Jaywick to push his theory that white populations in Western countries are being replaced by nonwhite immigrants. Farage was once a personal hero for 12-year-old Stephens in the run-up to the Brexit referendum and Trump’s first presidency. But since Stephens fell in with Nazi sympathizers and fascist organizations through YouTube and X, he feels that Reform’s immigration policy is too weak. As well as activists from his party, Stephens says he is being assisted in his campaign by people from Restore Britain–which did not submit a candidate for this election and instead has been appealing to Reform to coalesce. Restore did not respond to requests for comment.

Though Farage is polling on top, Irene, 81, thinks he is “ridiculous,” hasn’t done anything in his two years as MP, and finds his closeness with US president Donald Trump “frightening.” “I feel that we've been neglected, really,” she says, frustrated by the focus on Farage. “Somebody's got to stand up against him.” Wheeling her emptied trash can back from the curb, she says she will vote however she needs to to get Farage out.

To retired nurse Sally Hornby, that means voting for Count Binface—even if he “has made it a circus.” Hornby and others like his human alter-ego’s sense of humor, and are impressed by his University of Oxford education. “I would much rather the bin be our MP than Farage,” she says. “I think we just need somebody with intelligence here to actually sort things out,” she adds.

Typically a Labour voter, Hornby would have liked in the last two years to see efforts to keep businesses and shops from closing down in Clacton, as well as to clean up the area and reinvigorate the plain town square. But “I certainly don’t see any evidence whatsoever of Farage doing anything, so I just think people are just sucked into this business of immigration,” she says, adding: “He has used us in Clacton to be a stepping stone for his own power.”

Hornby and her husband Philip have come in from the suburbs to the center of Clacton town, which is steeped in Union Jack flags, in the hopes of getting a glimpse of their hero in a hastily organized hustings, when candidates debate on the campaign trail—advertised by two A4 sheets of paper stuck to a board, one with just “TOMORROW. IMMIGRATION. NOON” scrawled on. But neither he nor 32 of the other candidates, are anywhere to be seen. “Where are they?” she asks. After waiting 20 minutes, she says: “They’re not coming.”

Only the organizer, independent candidate Attieh Fard—plus her government-provided bodyguard—has turned up. This is the second day Fard has attempted to stage a hustings in the town center, trying to turn the concrete square with its metal benches into a “speaker’s corner.” There had been two of them on Monday. Count Binface told WIRED over email he was unable to attend on Tuesday and was not given sufficient notice of the events, noting he visited Clacton the following Thursday and Friday.

The focus on Farage and Count Binface means “it’s not a fair fight,” Fard says. “You can’t have a serious election,” she adds, “there’re no hustings, the media isn’t covering it well, so unfortunately people have been let down.” She says she has paid around £1,800 to make leaflets to post to every household in the constituency to make them aware of her policies on better roads and policing. A solicitor from Surrey, who unsuccessfully contested another by-election last year for the Conservative party, Fard said she decided to stand to give residents a serious alternative to Farage, after the major parties refused to contest the vote. “That’s why I’m standing: I’m saying ‘it’s not funny.’ People have sacrificed their lives for democracy,” says Fard, whose family fled Iran.

But when a woman who has been frantically pacing the square finally kicks over her hustings sign, screaming “fuck you!” at the top of her lungs to nobody in particular, that is enough even for Fard. She decides to go door-knocking in the more affluent area of Frinton, further up the coast, only for about half of the residents who open them to say they don’t intend to vote, disillusioned or calling it a “charade.” Others are pleased to see someone campaigning on local issues and hear about Fard’s parliamentary petition to reform road funding. They want someone to do something about the potholes.

If Farage wins on Thursday, as he is widely expected to, an investigation by Britain's Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards into whether the £5 million donation broke parliamentary standards will resume. As a result, there may then be a second by-election in Clacton if Farage is found guilty of breaching those standards, which the Conservatives and Restore Britain say they would contest.

For that reason, “I would argue that I have done less to create a circus than the MP who resigned,” Count Binface tells WIRED. “You can always vote for a ‘normal party’ next time,” reads one of the 53,800 leaflets he has posted to households across Clacton, just above his manifesto promise to boost the region’s fame.

The Painful Truth of Exactly How ICE’s New Shock Gloves Work

Wired August 13, 2026

With the revelation that ICE will spend up to $20 million by March on gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks to subdue an individual, according to a notice published earlier this week by the Department of Homeland Security, it's worth looking at how this apparel, designated as a nonlethal tool for law enforcement, actually works.

These shock gloves go by the unsubtle acronym of GLOVE (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter) and are manufactured by Compliant Technologies, based in Lexington, Kentucky. The GLOVE, previously used in jails and police departments in the US, looks and functions like a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate an electrical mode.

Classified as a CD3 (conductive distraction and de-escalation device), the gloves don't work like stun guns or Tasers, which shoot out probes or use high voltages to cause neuromuscular incapacitation that overrides the central nervous system. Instead, the GLOVE works using neuro-peripheral interference, essentially shocking the skin to bombard the sensory nerves and temporarily short-circuit the brain's focus.

Compliant Technologies did not respond to WIRED's request for comment.

When activated via a one-second press on a wrist switch, conductive pads embedded on the palm and undersides of the fingers of the gloves can transmit high-frequency electrical pulses directly to the wearer’s point of contact on a subject. A rechargeable battery and microprocessor module tucked inside a zippered pouch on the cuff powers the entire system.

The electrical pulse overstimulates nerve endings in the subject's peripheral nervous system, resulting in pain that inhibits coordinated muscle movement, but without causing systemic muscle lockup. The pain induced is localized to just the area touched by the glove's conductive pads. The manufacturer claims the gloves result in a subject's compliance in less than three seconds and leave no burns, marks, or scars.

Because the current flows only between the contact pads on the device and across the subject's skin, the officer wearing the GLOVE, as well as any assisting officers holding the subject, should not feel electrical shocks. The gloves, capable of operating between 14 and 122 degrees Fahrenheit, come in three versions: Gen 3, 4, and 5. Maximum voltage is capped at 380 V for all, and the minimum voltage for Gen 3 and 4 is 210 V, which rises to 324 V for Gen 5.

Maximum stimulation time on Gen 3 and 4 models is a sobering two hours, though that drops to 90 minutes for Gen 5. The battery is apparently good for 2,000 charge/discharge cycles, and it can recharge to full in two hours. Four LED lights on the gloves display the current charge level, each noting 25 percent battery increments.

Gen 4 and 5 of GLOVE both include mechanisms that record “activation events,” tracking the date, hour, minute, and skin-contact time for audit trails and after-action reporting. Gen 4 stores this data on a removable microSD card, while Gen 5 does away with this in favor of built-in internal memory, accessed via a USB-C cable.

There's a test function on the gloves, too, where operators can verify they are working by tapping an active pad against their own forearm to feel a minor electrical pulse. According to the manuals, GLOVE users must be certified and then recertified every other year to continue using the device.

GLOVE, which can only be sold to verified professional entities such as the military, correctional facilities, and law enforcement agencies—has some clear usage recommendations in Compliant Technologies' instruction manuals:

Crucially, the GLOVE has limitations, chief among them that for the device to work effectively and deliver its restraining pain shock, it must come into contact with the subject's bare skin. According to Compliant Technologies, the gloves won't work through dry clothing or thick hair. The gloves will work, however, if the subject is wearing thin, wet clothing, such as soaked T-shirts or blouses. The GLOVE also does not like being dunked in water and will likely be rendered inoperable if this happens.

Michael Crowley, a senior researcher at Omega Research Foundation—an organization that tracks human rights abuses committed across the world by people using police, security, and military equipment—is concerned that the GLOVE is seemingly designed not to restrain or incapacitate, but to hurt.

“CD3 technology inflicts pain," Crowley says. "The company talks about it as a de-escalation solution, but the whole idea of it is to get control or influence somebody through pain. Omega considers it to be an inherently abusive technology that should not be manufactured, sold, or used by law enforcement officials, including ICE.”

Why This Prediction Market Banned Teens

Wired August 13, 2026

Twenty-eight-year-old Jacob Fortinsky has been busy. “I was a groomsman at two weddings this weekend,” he tells me over Zoom. Also, the sports trading company he runs, Novig, launched its prediction market last week, facilitating $18 million in trading volume on its first day. Today, Novig launches a “responsible trading framework” in its exchange rulebook, codifying its guardrails as part of its effort to be seen as a kinder, gentler prediction market player.

Unlike industry leaders like Polymarket and Kalshi, which allow people 18 and older to participate, you have to be at least 21 to use Novig. Fortinsky says that decision was made in response to “valid concerns” put forth about the susceptibility of younger participants to risky behavior, including lobbying from the NCAA and other professional groups. Fortinsky sees this move as staying ahead of the curve as concerns grow about the negative impact that prediction markets can have on teens. “There’s a broader reckoning coming with the younger traders,” he says. “That group is particularly susceptible to irresponsible behavior and financial ruin.”

Novig’s rulebook also prohibits marketing to minors, and lays out guidelines banning other marketing practices, like ads that claim there’s no risk or ads that try to appeal to a prospective participant’s money troubles. That means when it advertises on TikTok, for example, it uses a setting that allows targeting only people over 21. Fortinsky positions these restrictions as part of Novig’s push to be seen as a “serious, legitimate financial product” as it comes onto the scene. “Some of our competitors, I think, have been seen as being a little bit more cavalier in certain regards,” he says. (He declined to name specific rivals.)

Because Novig only offers sports-themed markets, it doesn’t wade into some of the more hotly contested topics, like US elections and the Iran war. That doesn’t mean it’s avoiding controversy. As a sports-centered platform, the types of speculation opportunities it offers are at the center of an ongoing regulatory war, with prediction markets and federal regulators on one side and state regulators, tribal authorities, and occasionally traditional sportsbooks and casino operators on the other. Dozens of messy legal battles are raging across the US. States are suing Kalshi and other platforms, alleging that they illegally offer gambling; Kalshi is suing right back; the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which oversees the industry, is suing several states, arguing that it alone has jurisdiction over these markets.

Also, Novig isn’t immune to the general cultural distaste for prediction markets; when the New York Mets announced a recent partnership with Novig, the baseball team received a flood of criticism on social media. Sample post: “This is vile.”

If sports-related event contracts offered by prediction markets are banned, big players like Kalshi and Polymarket will be in deep trouble, with the majority of the action on their services gone. But Novig’s position is even shakier, since that’s all it does.

Fortinsky is betting it all on a win, and Novig wasted no time jumping into the legal fray. Within three days of launching, the startup sued New York, Massachusetts, New Mexico, and Washington, all states that have taken an aggressive approach to curbing prediction markets. It is trying to block these states from attempting to apply their gambling laws to federally regulated exchanges, which is what it’s licensed as. Sports betting attorney Daniel Wallach tells WIRED that these complaints are a “great marketing strategy” and a way to announce that Novig has arrived on the scene.

Whether they'll be successful is another matter. Recent court decisions have largely swung toward state attorneys general. A judge in New York denied Novig’s efforts to get a temporary restraining order, on the grounds that doing so would undermine another decision already reached in a case against Kalshi. “It’s increasingly looking more positive for the states,” Wallach notes. But that could change; Wallach and other onlookers expect the fight to get kicked up to the US Supreme Court before anything is definitively resolved.

Until then, Novig is plowing ahead. One of Novig’s appeals to customers is that it offers a different kind of sports speculation experience, one without a house that takes a “vig,” the fee that bookies take for arranging a bet. (“No vig,” get it?) Fortinsky has harsh words for many of the dominant sports gambling players, calling sportsbooks “inefficient, exploitative, and predatory.” He sees the peer-to-peer model that prediction markets facilitate as distinct, since it’s two parties on equal footing going up directly against each other. But if Novig goes how he’d like it to go, those parties won’t always be two average sports fans squaring off. The company is actively courting financial institutions to take sides of wagers, and Fortinsky says Novig is currently onboarding proprietary trading firms and banks. The company is taking steps to make it easier to “trade programmatically,” using algorithms to automate placing money on which team will win the Super Bowl or how many times the Mets will lose, for example.

“Something that's really cool to see,” he says, “is that you have hundreds of these small shops with a couple guys with $100,000 that are now competing against some of the largest Wall Street trading firms in the world and doing quite well.” Good thing the teens aren’t allowed in.

The Best Samsung Galaxy S26 Cases and Accessories

Wired August 13, 2026

A Samsung Galaxy S26 case is probably the first thing you're going to be shopping for once you buy your new phone. Whether you went with the S26, the S26 Plus, or the S26 Ultra, let's face it, you're inevitably going to drop it. A good case and screen protector can help minimize the damage, and I've been testing out a variety to pick the best ones.

You'll find my favorites (so far) below, ranging from rugged and durable cases to razor-thin and minimalist options. Be sure to check out our related guides, including the Best Samsung Phones, the Best Folding Phones, and the Best Phones With a Headphone Jack.

Updated August 2026: I've added new cases from Burga, Mous, and OtterBox, and checked for accuracy throughout.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

How to Enable Qi2 Charging on Your Samsung Galaxy S26

Frustratingly, there's no native Qi2 support on the Samsung Galaxy S26 lineup, so a magnetic phone case is the only way you can take advantage of Qi2 charging speeds and other benefits. I recommend several magnetic options in this guide.

A Note on Magnetic Accessories

It's important to note that due to Samsung's camera bump design, some MagSafe or otherwise magnetic accessories do not play well with the S26 lineup. I didn't have trouble with a PopSockets grip, but I did struggle with most magnetic wallets. Power banks are also hit or miss. Anything square or rectangular might give you some issues due to the camera bump design. This is a frustrating carryover from the Samsung S25 line.

How We Test Cases

WIRED historically has not performed drop tests because we don't have infinite test units. Drop tests are notoriously difficult to control outside of a lab environment, and “dummy” phones aren't usually accurate representations of their working counterparts. However, I am working on standardizing a similar protocol. Remember that while a case or screen protector can offer some protection, neither can guarantee your screen won't shatter.

For now, I'm testing phone cases by assessing fit, comfort, overall look and feel, and checking out the precision and responsiveness of any buttons or additional features.

Spigen

Amazon

This clear case from Spigen is affordable and looks dope. There are 10 different styles to choose from, but I like the classic semi-clear teardown look best. The case is thinner than it is protective, but the printed-on graphics give you a little bit of texture to prevent your phone from feeling as slippery as it would without a case. My only minor complaint is that the volume buttons are a bit difficult to press—not at all impossible, but just not quite as readily responsive as the other cases I tried.

dbrand

Dbrand

We've been fans of Dbrand's Ghost Case 2.0 since its revamp, and I like it for the S26 Ultra as well. The edges feel sturdy and grippy, no matter how my smaller hands are holding this bigger phone, but they aren't too obtrusive or bulky. The clear parts of the case are truly transparent without being magnets for dust or fingerprints. There's also an anti-yellowing guarantee; if your Ghost case turns yellow, Dbrand will replace it for free. The S Pen readily accessible, and the buttons are easy to find with a satisfying clicky response.

This case is available with or without MagSafe. I recommend choosing the option with, because why wouldn't you give yourself the choice?

Pitaka

Amazon (S26)

Amazon (S26 Plus)

Amazon (S26 Ultra)

This aramid fiber case is best for those who prioritze thinness. It offers a little protection, but I wouldn't call it sturdy or particularly substantive. You'll be protected from scuffs and scratches, but probably not any heavy-duty damage. The woven shell has a bit of texture that makes it easy to grip, and it's got a ring of magnets for MagSafe accessories and Qi2 charging. Keep in mind that the buttons on your phone won't be protected at all. These cases also have Aaron buttons, named after late coder and activist Aaron Swartz. The customizable NFC buttons can be used in a myriad of ways, from opening specific apps to turning on a flashlight or starting a playlist. The shell-like case is prone to cracking if you remove it too quickly—so go slowly.

Zagg

Amazon

I am usually a fan of minimalist cases that serve form over function, but this rugged case isn't so overtly tactical that it'll make your phone feel more like a piece of military technology than a pocket-sized sidekick. It's a two-piece case—your phone sits in the lower half and the frame snaps on top to keep it secure. It's still thin and lightweight, with rigid plastic bumpers on the corners and a raised lip around the camera array. It has magnets for MagSafe accessories and Qi2 charging, and I also like that the built-in kickstand is unobtrusive when not in use. The buttons could be easier to press, but I've noticed this is the kind of trade-off you can expect if you want a case that's more protective than pretty.

Casetify

Casetify

There are dozens of designs of this case to choose from for each of the S26 phones, ranging from simple styles to Instagram-worthy prints. There are options for built-in kickstands, too, and the majority of the cases are MagSafe and Qi2 compatible. My favorite is the mirror case, which looks unique and has one well for the camera array rather than cutouts that sit flush with each lens and sensor. There are also custom case options if you want to mix and match features or add in your own photos or text. These aren't the grippiest cases I've tried, but the button cutouts are precise, and I like that the cases feel substantial without adding too much bulk or weight. One thing to note: Casetify has been caught allegedly stealing designs from other companies. Do with that information what you will.

Mous

Mous

Amazon

Anyone on the WIRED Reviews team who tests a Mous Limitless Case usually likes it. I'm partial to this wood finish model, which feels slick and doesn't add much bulk to the phone. It's easy to put on; the textured plastic bumper, in combination with raised buttons and corners, makes the case comfortable to grip despite its slippery wood-feel back. And this might be a bit of a personal touch, but I really like the way the phone case sounds when I tap on the back of it. There are other finishes available, too, like leather and aramid fiber.

Burga

Amazon

Burga

Burga's phone cases all feel like slippery coated plastic. But the hybrid design is flexible enough to put on easily and to protect your phone without being too brittle. The cases are available in dozens of color and pattern options. All of them have slightly raised bezels to protect your screen and you can also pick out matching accessories like phone rings or power banks for select patterns.

dbrand

Dbrand

Dbrand calls its Prism 2.0 screen protectors “idiot-proof," and they truly offer the easiest installation process I've ever experienced. Pop the applicator case on the top, pull the sticker, and your screen protector will be perfectly installed (and you can use the included squeegee to get rid of any air bubbles that you may encounter).

It comes with two tempered glass protectors, plus a cleaning kit that includes alcohol wipes and a microfiber cloth. Unfortunately there are no dust removal stickers, which are commonly included in screen protector kits from other brands.

When you add a new screen protector, you'll probably need to add your fingerprints again. Do this by navigating to Settings > Security and privacy > Screen lock and biometrics > Fingerprints > Add fingerprint. You may also want to increase your display's touch sensitivity by going to Settings > Display > Touch sensitivity.

Spigen Tough Armor ($23) and Nano Pop MagFit ($20) Cases: These affordable cases both look nice and perform well for the price. The Nano Pop case was just a little too slippery for me, and the Tough Armor case's kickstand was flimsier than I'd have liked. But if none of our other recommendations tickle your fancy, these options aren't the worst.

Dbrand Tank Case for $60: This case looks very tactical. If that's the look you're after, it's worth considering. For me, I found the back textures to be a little overstimulating and unpleasant. I wasn't ever able to forget about my phone case. The buttons are swappable, and there are camera covers to help ensure a cohesive aesthetic. The case is durable and sturdy, and it makes it easy to get a good grip on the phone. It just comes down to the kind of design you prefer.

Poetic Spartan ($29), Revolution ($26), and Guardian ($25) Cases: I thought all three of these cases were just fine. I liked the Revolution's built-in camera privacy cover, which also helped to protect the large camera array from bumps and bruises. But I wasn't a fan of the rest of the design—while the built-in kickstand is a neat feature, I found the entirety of the case to be too clunky. The Guardian was the thinnest, and I liked it for the most part, although the black grippy edges were a little bulkier than I wanted them to be. I didn't like the Spartan case's built-in metal ring, tactical design, or rigid bumper corners. Overall, the Poetic cases had appealing prices but their designs just weren't my favorites. All three of these cases come with screen protectors, which work fine (though you'll have to install them the old-fashioned way).

OtterBox Profile Series Case for $40: I initially liked these slim, clear cases, but I didn't love the way the ring of magnets looked on the back. I'm not sure if that's because it was incongruous with the multi-lens cameras of the Samsung Galaxy S26 series or the color, but aesthetically I wasn't a fan. The buttons on this case are also too resistant. But if you want a clear case that has some pizzazz, it might be an option worth checking out.

Spigen AluminaCore Screen Protectors (2-pack) for $20: Installation for this screen protector was easy, with a foolproof frame and a peel-off sticker that leaves it exactly where you want it. I had some initial issues with bubbles (that I was able to remove with the included squeegee), which is why this isn't my top pick. I do like that you get two in case of issues with installation, or as a replacement when you inevitably crack the first one.

Samsung Slim Magnet Case: If this case cost $20, then I'd say sure, go for it. But it's $70 for an exceedingly thin plastic shell with a ring of magnets built in. The build feels flimsy, and the case feels slippery. It's almost easier to grip the phone with no protection rather than to hold it with this case on it. There are simply too many other options on the market for this one to be worthy of a recommendation.

Wireless charging makes a daily task just a little bit easier, and Google’s versatile Pixelsnap Charger with Stand is one of the best wireless chargers at full price. And right now, it's at a 50 percent discount, making it a bargain worth bagging.

Mirroring Google’s curvy Pixel range with a rounded form and soft-touch finish, the Pixelsnap is a regular puck-style Qi2 25W magnetic charger that usually costs $40 on its own. Right now, you can get it and the curvy stand that it pops into for just $35. Perfect if you want to prop your phone up on the nightstand and have it double as an alarm clock, for example.

Google

Amazon (Charger)

Amazon (Stand)

Google Store (Charger)

If you’re not familiar, Qi2 wireless charging is like Apple’s MagSafe; it enables you to stick your phone onto a charger using a ring of magnets, ensuring perfect alignment for the most efficient and speedy wireless charging possible. I love being able to stick my phone onto the charger at night without fumbling around for a cable.

The Pixelsnap sports the very latest Qi2 25W release, so it can charge supported phones, like the Pixel 10 Pro XL, Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, and the iPhone 17 series at up to 25 watts. The Pixelsnap can also charge older iPhones, the rest of the Pixel 10 range, and various other Samsung phones at 15 watts.

Speed might not be the most important thing for you if you charge overnight, like I do, but the Pixelsnap Charger with Stand also has a smart design that’s pretty handy when your phone is running low at the end of the day: you can pop the charger puck out, and it will stick to the back of your phone so you can continue to scroll while it charges.

With the Pixel 11 range just around the corner, Google may be prepping a new charger, but it’s likely that the Pixelsnap will work with the new phones, too. The only thing missing is the power adapter, but if you need one, the Anker Nano 30W ($16) is very affordable.

The Most DangerousDiagnosis in a Heat Wave

Wired August 13, 2026

People with schizophrenia face a perfect storm of dangers on a hotter planet.

By Hilary BeaumontHilary Beaumont is an investigative journalist covering climate change.

Jeff Yoo was working nights as an ER doctor in Vancouver, British Columbia, when weather forecasters started to warn that a heat wave was on its way. Yoo didn’t think much of it, figuring the sun would be down for most of his shift. But when the record-breaking heat dome hit on June 25, 2021, it lasted more than a week, pushing temperatures in the typically mild, maritime city past 102 degrees F. Even after dusk fell at around 8:30 pm, nights refused to cool off. Yoo’s ER was soon hit with a surge of patients it was unprepared to handle.

As the heat dome peaked, 911 calls doubled. There weren’t enough beds, so paramedics lined the hallways, waiting with patients on stretchers instead of responding to emergency calls—a situation called a “bed block.” Yoo felt the kind of adrenaline rush he’d experienced during the first waves of Covid, but this was the first time he’d treated so many patients with heat-related illness. To cool them down, Yoo kept running back and forth to the ER’s ice dispenser. At one point he pressed the button and heard a buzzing noise, indicating there was none left.

“Shit,” he thought to himself …

“what do we do now?”

One night an ambulance rushed a middle-aged man into the ER. He had been found unconscious on the sidewalk, baking in the evening sun. Delirious and suffering from heat stroke, he didn’t know what city he was in or what year it was. He was so dehydrated that his kidneys began to shut down, but he kept yanking his arm away when Yoo’s team tried to insert an IV. So they strapped him down by his wrists and ankles, covered him in ice packs, and eventually inserted a catheter to deliver cool fluids directly to his bladder, stabilizing him and saving his life.

One other thing stuck with Yoo about the man. He was exhibiting the same symptoms as many of the other patients brought in during the heat dome: those of schizophrenia.

Yoo’s hospital, St. Paul’s, serves Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside—a neighborhood with some of the highest rates of mental illness, addiction, and homelessness in Canada. That location gave Yoo a concentrated dose of a widespread epidemiological phenomenon.

People with schizophrenia are estimated to represent about 1 percent of the world’s population …

The root cause of these deaths isn’t just the stigma, social isolation, and lack of decent housing that often accompany life with schizophrenia; nor is it merely the disorganized thinking, altered perceptions, and paranoia that can be symptoms of the disorder.

It’s all of those things—plus an invisible, less popularly understood set of physiological factors that have little to do with behavior. The bodies of people with schizophrenia, especially those on medication, simply regulate temperature very differently than others do.

And for all those reasons, scientists now realize, no other chronic disease appears to put humans at a higher risk of heat-related death.

Source: Modified from Figure 4 in Lee et al., GeoHealth (2023).

In fact, no other chronic condition even comes close.

Long before 2021, front-line doctors like Yoo knew that extreme heat put people with schizophrenia in particular danger. “All of us were quite intimately aware that these patients were going to be at higher risk,” Yoo says. But it wasn’t until researchers studied the BC heat dome that science came to crystallize its understanding of the problem’s true scope.

For years, public health advisories warned that extreme heat was most dangerous to older adults, infants, and people with chronic illnesses like heart disease, respiratory disorders, and diabetes. But in 2023 a study revealed that schizophrenia was associated with a threefold increase in the odds of mortality during the heat dome. “That's when it became very clear that schizophrenia was the outstanding chronic condition in terms of risk,” says Sarah Henderson, scientific director of environmental health at the BC Center for Disease Control, who coauthored the report.

A flurry of studies followed, and in 2025 a group of interdisciplinary experts, including Henderson, published a review of the literature explaining the phenomenon. What they found were layers upon layers of risk factors.

At the most biologically fundamental level, people with schizophrenia have wonky thermoregulation—their bodies are less able to cool themselves for a variety of reasons. They have a harder time regulating dopamine, which is associated with our body’s ability to manage its temperature, explains the study’s coauthor Nathalie Kirby, an applied climate and heat-health scientist.

A related hallmark of schizophrenia, Kirby says, is an imbalance between the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems, often called the “fight or flight” and “rest and digest” systems, respectively. Typically, these systems are in balance, but someone experiencing psychosis is caught up in a vicious cycle: They may experience hallucinations, tied to a dopamine imbalance in the brain, that make neutral experiences seem scary. This suppresses the parasympathetic nervous system, which in turn produces a fight-or-flight response and worsens the initial psychosis.

Along the way, someone with increased fight-or-flight activity is predisposed to adverse cardiovascular events. It becomes harder for them to control the blood vessels and sweating that help with thermoregulation.

“Most deaths during extreme heat are actually cardiovascular in nature,” Kirby says. “So if someone isn't able to control their cardiovascular system very well, they're going to have a much higher risk when it's hot outside.”

Another challenge that faces people with schizophrenia—one that Yoo was already aware of in the ER back in 2021—is that treatment for the disorder can include antipsychotic medications that prevent people from sweating, further depressing their ability to dissipate heat. “A lot of the antipsychotic medications have an anticholinergic effect,” Yoo says, describing physical side effects that include increased heart rate and decreased sweating. “That means they’re going to be at even higher risk of cooking their organs.”

Finally, heat can also cause schizophrenia symptoms to flare up, even for someone whose symptoms are well managed. They may feel increased anxiety, dread, and fear, which further aggravates the fight-or-flight system, Kirby says.

Beyond internal dysregulation, people with schizophrenia often show a lack of insight into their own health (though this can be improved with medication). In a heat wave, they may not be aware that their body is heating up, so they don’t drink water or attempt to cool themselves. They may do just the opposite—wearing multiple layers instead of shedding them.

Paranoia, another marker of schizophrenia, may also cause some people to avoid exposure to media, including news. “They are left in the dark, they don't know that a heat wave is coming,” says Liv Yoon, an assistant professor at the University of British Columbia’s School of Kinesiology. She led a study interviewing dozens of people with schizophrenia who survived the heat dome. “I cannot have news,” one woman told the authors. “News is triggering for me, impacting my mental health a lot. I don't own a radio, I don't watch TV, or the internet or anything.” When the heat dome arrived, the woman had no warning.

Another of Yoon’s research subjects was a Vancouver-based artist named Sandra Yuen, who says she likewise avoids the media. Unless she gets a notification from her weather app, “somebody has to tell me” that a heat wave is coming, she says. Yuen, who in 2010 wrote a memoir about her life with schizophrenia, has been on various antipsychotic medications since she was a teenager—so she can’t really say how her body might regulate temperature differently without them. But Yuen can report this much: “I'm very sensitive to the heat.” She sweats very little, constantly has dry mouth, and has a hard time staying hydrated. “I might perspire a bit, but it’s very hard for me to cool off.”

Yuen wonders what would happen in a major heat wave if the power went out and she had no air-conditioning. In the past when she’s been caught without AC on hot days, she’s felt trapped indoors and fallen asleep. “Hopefully,” she says, “I’ll wake up.”

What can protect people with schizophrenia from extreme heat? None of the experts WIRED interviewed suggest that anyone go off their antipsychotic meds, even though they may exacerbate some risks. (Of the people with schizophrenia who died in the BC heat dome, 80 percent had been dispensed an antipsychotic medication in the past 90 days, compared to 55 percent of those who survived, according to a 2023 article published in the British Columbia Medical Journal.)

There’s a small trade-off, says Kirby, but antipsychotic drugs help manage mental symptoms, and changing medications suddenly can be dangerous. “Keeping people consistent during extreme heat is probably best,” she says, “and someone communicating with their health care provider about what to do is probably the best way forward.”

The experts did emphasize that one entirely preventable risk factor stands out: lack of access to fans, air-conditioning, and other forms of cooling. The BC Coroners Service found that 98 percent of deaths during the heat dome occurred indoors, often in housing that lacked mechanical cooling. “If the people taking the antipsychotics had a safe indoor temperature, they would be fine,” says Henderson. (According to the research, only one predictor of death from extreme heat is stronger than schizophrenia, and that’s another closely related condition: poverty.)

Public cooling centers can help, but only if people actually go. Yoon interviewed one woman who lived in an un-air-conditioned rental apartment that cooked in the afternoon sun during the Vancouver heat dome; she knew cooling centers were open but didn’t want to use them. One reason was that she had hallucinations that made her feel conspicuous around other people. She felt cowed enough by the stigma that she stayed home.

As Yoon interviewed survivors, this kind of experience came up again and again. One participant told Yoon that society had made progress reducing the stigma around anxiety and depression, but not schizophrenia. Yuen, for her part, has encountered strangers who assume people with schizophrenia are violent or use drugs, and others who don’t believe they are truly ill at all. “You doubt yourself,” she says. “You doubt your own brain.”

Another participant in Yoon’s research—one who’d had negative experiences with the health care system—told her outright that neurotypical folk “don’t care if people with schizophrenia die.”

Hearing this “was devastating,” Yoon says. “They learn to have lower expectations of other people.” Over the course of her research, Yoon came to believe that creating new interventions for people with schizophrenia won’t work if they don’t address stigma.

In the years since the heat dome, scientists have pieced together a complex, composite portrait of how the average victim with schizophrenia came to be at such high risk of death. They were likely at home alone, in an older building that heated up easily and lacked mechanical cooling. They were less likely to have a social network to check on them. They likely avoided the news, so they didn’t know a heat wave was coming. When the heat wave hit, their body could not thermoregulate effectively, and antipsychotics further increased heat sensitivity. Even if they were aware of what their body needed, they didn’t feel comfortable going to a cooling center because they faced social stigma. And they didn’t feel safe interacting with the medical system because they’d had bad experiences in the past.

British Columbia’s medical community is determined to prevent the next mass-casualty event and set an example for other places that might be caught off guard by a heat dome. Since 2021, the province has pledged $148 million to hire some 600 more paramedics and increase ambulance services, and BC’s Center for Disease Control placed people with schizophrenia at the top of the list of high-risk conditions during heat waves. The British Columbia Schizophrenia Society developed a check-in program for caregivers, and Kirby and her fellow researchers compiled a guide that includes a checklist of steps to take before a heat wave. BC updated its emergency alert system to push cell phone alerts when extreme heat is coming, as it already did for wildfires and floods. And the province launched a free air conditioner program that enrolls people based on income, delivering AC to 40,000 people. Henderson says the province is also beginning to work on engaging pharmacists to alert people to heat risk when they dispense antipsychotic medications.

Deploying behavioral health workers at cooling centers also seems to help. During the 2021 heat dome in Portland, Oregon—where the heat reached over 110 degrees F, much higher than in Vancouver—a behavioral health specialist named Laurel Wonder was stationed at one of the city’s “weather activation centers.” Without asking about diagnoses, Wonder’s decades of experience allowed her to spot people who likely had schizophrenia.

On day three of the heat dome, a staff member saw a middle-aged man walking down the block in clothing soaked with sweat. Staff could see he was suffering from heat-related illness, and that he was hesitant to come inside. Wonder said they had to actively invite him in by saying, “Please, let us help you. Please, let us get you water.” When he came inside, he was initially only able to utter single words. The man had schizophrenia, Wonder would eventually realize. They called an ambulance, handed him a cooling towel and water, monitored his water consumption, and handed him fresh clothes. It took time for the ambulance to arrive, because the city was experiencing simultaneous heat emergencies. Wonder was concerned that the man might leave, but he stayed. Keeping the man safe until he made it to the hospital felt like a “huge accomplishment,” she says. It may have saved his life.

Back in Vancouver, Yoo says he continues to worry about people with schizophrenia as the planet heats up. “We probably will be seeing more of these extreme heat events in North America every single year,” he said when I first spoke to him in May.

In July, sure enough, a massive heat dome stretched across much of the continent, including large parts of Canada. It didn’t go as far west as Vancouver, but the emergency room at St. Paul’s Hospital is more prepared than it used to be; it now has a chest freezer full of cold packs in addition to the ice machine.

The Best Android Tablets

Wired August 13, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

IPad? Never heard of it.

I have been using Android tablets pretty much since the first one came out, and I've never felt the need for anything made by any fruit companies. Android tablets make great “nice to have” entertainment centers, or they can be complete lightweight laptop replacements for travel.

Whatever your use case, I've tested just about all the Android tablets out there, and these are the best, depending on what you need them for. If you want to see how these stack up next to those iPad things, check out our guide to all the tablets on the market.

Be sure to check out our other buying guides, including the Best Amazon Fire Tablets, Best iPad, and Best iPad Accessories.

Updated August 2026: I've removed the now discontinued (in the US) OnePlus Pad 3 and changed the top pick to the Galaxy Tab S10 FE. I've also added two new tablets from TCL, and removed the discontinued Google Pixel Tablet.

Samsung

Amazon

Samsung

A consequence of OnePlus' exit from the North American and European markets is that we will likely never see the release of its Pad 4, the follow-up to our previous pick for the best Android tablet, the OnePlus Pad 3. While you could buy the international version and get it shipped to you, most people should look toward the Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 FE instead, which does everything you need and comes with a US warranty. I prefer the FE model with its 10.9-inch display, which is a good viewing size for on the couch, in bed, or on the move. There is also the Galaxy Tab S10 FE+ if you prefer a larger 13.1-inch display, but it is heavier.

The Tab S10 FE weighs just over a pound (17.5 ounces), and it's comfortable to hold or prop up in bed with one hand. The 90-Hz refresh rate isn't the fastest among tablets in this guide, but it's plenty smooth for all but the most demanding games. Videos look crisp and sharp, and the 2304 x 1440-pixel LCD screen is bright enough for viewing outdoors in sunlight.

Inside, you get Samsung’s Exynos 1580 midrange mobile processor paired with 8 GB or 12 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage that can be expanded by adding a microSD card. The 8,000-mAh battery will get you about 20 hours of mixed use on a single charge, and the 45-watt charger will get you back to 100 percent in just over an hour and a half.

Samsung includes a stylus in the box with the Tab S10 FE, and it’s handy for writing notes, but it's pretty basic. If you want to draw, there are better tablet options below.

Samsung

Amazon

Best Buy (S11 Ultra)

Samsung (S11)

Samsung (S11 Ultra)

Samsung's Galaxy Tab S11 and Tab S11 Ultra are the Android world's answer to the iPad Pro. They've got the flagship specs, and at a mere 0.20 inches thick (5.1 mm), the Ultra matches the look as well. They are slightly heavier than their iPad Pro counterparts, but not enough that I actually notice the difference. Unlike the prior generation Tab S10 series, there's no middle-of-the-pack “Plus” model anymore. You have the 11-inch Tab S11 and the biggie, the 14.6-inch Tab S11 Ultra. Both run Android 16 out of the box, have 120-Hz AMOLED displays, and can hit a peak brightness of 1,600 nits. Samsung uses a MediaTek processor, the Dimensity 9400+, which is closely matched to the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite. Both models get 12 GB of RAM (if you go for the 1-terabyte Ultra model, the RAM goes up to 16 GB). Storage is expandable via microSD.

While the S11 and S11 Ultra are pretty close specs-wise, I suggest that you go for the Ultra if you can. It's big, and sometimes unwieldy to carry around, but that giant screen is glorious for entertainment, and working in split-screen mode feels like you're on a laptop. While I do like OnePlus's OxygenOS (RIP) better, Samsung's Dex tablet UI is pretty good, turning your tablet into more of a traditional desktop-like user interface, with windowed apps and a dock. The tablet supports an external monitor too, so you can have dual-screen multitasking. The best feature, though, is the workspaces: you set up four different desktops however you like, then quickly cycle between them depending on the workflow at hand. If you do plan to work on your Ultra, get Samsung's Book Cover Keyboard Slim, a keyboard cover that makes it feel more like a 2-in-1 detachable laptop than a tablet.

TCL

Amazon

TCL

TCL’s Tab A1 Plus is a budget tablet that doesn’t feel low-rent. The star here is the very nice 12.2-inch, 2400 x 1600 pixel LCD panel. It’s not an OLED, but it’s sharp, colorful, and bright, and thanks to the 120-Hz screen refresh rate, everything you do feels nice and smooth. The size is nice, too: The A1 Plus has a 3:2 aspect ratio, which makes it feel not so big that it’s hard to hold but not so small that you feel cramped working in split-screen mode. The 2.4K resolution at this size works out to a pixel density of 236 ppi. For comparison, the base model iPad screen is 2360 × 1640 pixels at 264 ppi. Side by side, the two are very close in terms of resolution.

A tablet this cheap—which rivals the iPad in screen size and quality, and currently costs almost $200 less—has some downsides, the biggest being the processor, a Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 2 chip dating back to 2023. This isn't flagship-level performance, but it's plenty fast enough for ordinary tasks, like browsing the web with a dozen tabs open, listening to music, and multitasking—all the typical tablet workloads. I had no trouble playing back 4K video, nor did it falter when live-streaming baseball games (provided the bandwidth was sufficient). Where this tablet falls apart is if you want to game. It’s capable of what I would call casual gaming, but if you really want a tablet for gaming, this is not it. Performance isn't top tier, but it’s adequate for most people. If you’re looking for a budget Android tablet, this is currently the best I’ve tested.

TCL

Amazon

TCL

TCL's Note A1 Nxtpaper tablet straddles between an E Ink digital notebook and an Android tablet. It tries to be the best of both worlds and succeeds to an admirable degree. The matte screen has many of the advantages of an E Ink screen, but it's also a 1440 x 2200-pixel LCD panel with a 120-Hz refresh rate, so it'll happily play back video when you're done using it as an e-reader or note-taking device. The MediaTek G100 processor is par for the course at this price point. It gets paired with 8 GB of RAM and 256 GB of storage, which collectively is enough performance to run all the apps I tested and power some of the AI-driven features that TCL is pushing with this device, including automated meeting summaries, audio-to-text transcription, and handwriting-to-text conversion (also, seldom noted, it can convert complex equations from handwritten to typed).

Surprisingly for a $600 tablet, the Note A1 includes a very nice reversible pen (you can erase with the top) and a keyboard. The unnecessarily complex keyboard case is something only its mother really loves (it's heavy and weirdly designed), but it does a good job of protecting the tablet and the keyboard is nice to type on (and it's included in the price, which is frankly shocking).

The custom UI skews heavily toward note-taking as well as writing and drawing. The home view is a list of notes, with space at the top of the screen allocated for a short to-do list on the right and the Inspiration Space, which is kind of a free-form clipboard area where you can store things you want to highlight (pretty much anything, which is very useful). Click on a note with the pen, and it will open in edit mode with a configuration toolbar shown across the top. Here you can set up pen type, color, line thicknesses, and all the other tools you'd want to use to write or draw. I found the editing interface just about perfect in the sense that it balances keeping it simple but still gives you access to the controls you actually need.

What I was less thrilled with is the file management system that TCL has created. It works, but there are confusing shortcomings. Like, I could not find a way to open a note in reading mode and then switch to editing from within the note. Despite these quirks, the Note A1 Nxtpaper is a really great note-taking device that can also be a regular tablet on the occasions you need it.

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon’s Fire tablets are the cheapest of the cheap. More charitably, you might call them ultra-affordable tablets. They are so cheap—around $85 for the Fire HD 10 during one of Amazon's many sales events— they seem almost like a scam, but Fire tablets are also completely functional, reasonably capable devices. (I've even paired it with a keyboard to work from the beach, although this has become increasingly difficult.)

Amazon sells two models, the aforementioned Fire HD 10 and the smaller Fire HD 8 (see honorable mentions). You'll also find variants made for kids as well as a Harry Potter-edition for the Fire HD 10, but the standard Fire HD 10 is the one to get, as it's the most powerful. The current model dates from 2023, which means it likely will get some kind of update soon, but we don't expect anything more than a processor and RAM upgrade. The current Octa-core processor is plenty fast for everyday tasks like web browsing and watching movies, and the 3 GB of RAM helps in browsing the web with many tabs. The Fire HD 10 also has a full HD (1080p) screen, but it's pretty lackluster by today's standards.

The Fire HD 10 comes with 32 GB of internal storage, with a microSD slot on both, so you can add up to 1 TB if you need more space. (A 64 GB version is currently unavailable through Amazon, but you may find it from a reseller.) Amazon will serve up advertisements on the lock screen. To get rid of that, you'll need to spend $15 to unlock it (via your account settings).

The big downside to the Fire tablets is the Amazon version of Android. It's outdated and slow, with a custom app store that doesn't support many apps (for example, the entire suite of Google Workspace apps won't be available—not even the browser-based versions). You might be able to side-load the Google Play Store (see our guide), but sadly, this hasn't worked reliably for me with the latest models—no more remote work from the beach for me. Still, for less than $100 on sale, the Fire HD 10 is crazy cheap and does work for casual entertainment and web browsing.

There are a lot of Android tablets for sale, so if none of the above seem quite right for your needs, these are also worth considering.

Walmart

Lenovo's Idea Tab Pro has a MediaTek Dimensity 8300 chip, which has proved surprisingly powerful in my testing. It had no trouble playing 4K video or editing some rather large RAW files (using Photoshop Express). The bright LCD screen has 3K resolution spread across a 12.7-inch panel. The speakers sound great, and there's an included stylus to jot down notes or doodle. It's a little more than our top budget pick, and the pre-installed crapware is annoying, but for the price, the Idea Tab Pro is worth considering.

Amazon

The Fire HD 8 makes a good ultra-cheap travel screen if you score one during one of the many sale events where it goes for under $60. It's not a very capable device, but it'll stream movies from Amazon Prime or Netflix, and you can browse the web without bogging down the processor. Don't buy one at full price, though; just wait for the next sale event.

The Best Cooling Mattresses for Hot Sleepers

Wired August 13, 2026

Helix Sleep

Brooklyn Bedding

Birch

Bear

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

It happens to the best of us: You wake up in the middle of the night, clammy and soaked in sweat. If you’re a hot sleeper, a cooling mattress may be for you. Waking up sweaty and hot can be caused by several factors, like sleeping conditions, stress, excessive blankets, the wrong pajamas, and even eating spicy foods before bed. Hot nights can also equate to sleepless nights. According to a study from the Journal of Physiological Anthropology, heat exposure increases wakefulness and decreases time spent in deep sleep and REM sleep.

A cooling mattress is built specifically to help regulate your body temperature by being made of materials that optimize airflow and draw heat away from your body as you sleep. I (and some of my sweatiest colleagues) tested a myriad of cooling mattresses for at least a week each in our homes—to determine which worked best to beat the heat.

Be sure to read our other sleep guides, including the Best Mattresses, Best Organic Mattresses, Best Hybrid Mattresses, and Best Bed Sheets.

Jump to Section

Updated August 2026: We've overhauled this guide with new picks from Bedgear, Helix, Brooklyn Bedding, Birch, Sijo, and Nectar. We've also updated links and prices.

Helix Sleep

Helix Sleep

This is a crowd-pleaser—a medium-firm hybrid mattress that uses six layers to offer all the benefits of both foam and coils. Below the plush cushion top, there are layers of cooling gel foam to regulate body temperature and disperse heat, and then below are several denser foams for support. Individually wrapped coils on the bottom are zoned so that you have firmer coils in areas like your lower spine that need more support to prevent back pain.

The Midnight Luxe comes with a Tencel cover—a semi-synthetic fiber made from eucalyptus—that helps to circulate airflow and regulate temperature. Plus, there's an optional GlacioTex Cooling Cover ($199) or a combination of the GlacioTex Cooling Cover and CoolForce Layer ($399) that uses enhanced cooling technology. Made from Helix's heat-conductive fabric, it draws heat away from the surface of the mattress. The CoolForce Layer is directly on top of the mattress, designed to pull heat away from the body. The company claims it keeps you 4 degrees cooler for over 12 hours while sleeping.

Helix Midnight Luxe ranges from $1,436 for a twin mattress to $2,924 for a California King.

Brooklyn Bedding

Brooklyn Bedding

I haven’t been the biggest fan of hybrid mattresses in the past. I’m a lifelong fussy sleeper and insomniac, and my body prefers soft and sinking, not firm and bouncy—the last hybrid I tested left me feeling like I was sleeping in the backseat of a ’79 Buick. However, the older I get, the more I’m accepting that sinking memory foam is not my friend. It makes it harder to move around at night, and as a stomach sleeper, it provides zero support for my spine. I tested the Aurora Luxe in Soft with the optional pillow top, and it’s the first hybrid I’ve ever tried that I actually like. The pillow top provides the memory-foam feel my body craves while the 8-inch zoned coils give solid support.

Despite arriving tightly compressed in a box, the Aurora Luxe eventually puffed up to an impressive 14.5 inches, and the silky navy blue cover lends a high end aesthetic. Hybrids run cooler in general due to the open-spring design, and the Aurora Luxe’s pillow top contains ThermoPhase “cooling foam.” Though, to be frank, this did not feel overtly cooling to either my husband or me during our three-week test. (The deep dimples on the top, however, do create some extra airflow.) Luckily, Brooklyn Bedding offers a 120-night trial, so you can decide for yourself (returns do cost $99). The Aurora Luxe tends to run firm, so though it comes in Soft, Medium, and Firm, the Soft is more of a medium-firm. I’d only recommend Medium or Firm if you’re looking for firm-firm. —Kat Merck

Brooklyn Bedding’s Aurora Luxe ranges from $1,099 for a twin mattress to $2,099 for an RV king.

Birch

Birch

The Birch Luxe Natural uses organic ways to promote cooling with naturally moisture-wicking materials and enhanced breathability—without the use of chemicals. It has an organic cotton cover, layers of New Zealand wool (a natural fire retardant), and pocketed coils for personalized support and motion isolation. The cotton cover pulls sweat away from your skin to quickly dissipate moisture, and the open-weave design promotes ventilation. The bed's GOLS-certified latex material is naturally hypoallergenic anti-microbal (so you can ensure you're having a healthy sleep), and also breathable for enhanced airflow. The wool is also a naturally hygroscopic fiber, meaning that it is designed to wick moisture away to increase overall airflow and breathability.

Birch Luxe Natural ranges from $1,624 for a twin mattress to $3,124 for a California king.

Bear

Bear

The WIRED Reviews team holds the Bear Elite Hybrid mattress in high regard for multiple reasons. Some of our testers found it excellent for relieving back pain, thanks to pressure-relieving foams and zoned coils that support spine alignment. Testers have also noted that of the three firmness options on offer, Firm didn’t mess around when it came to delivering that unyielding feel.

The Bear Elite Hybrid has breathable, copper-infused memory foam and pocketed coils for airflow. There are two cooling covers available—you can opt for the standard HydroCool cover or the Celliant cover for an upcharge. Celliant textiles are engineered to help absorb heat and moisture while also facilitating better circulation for muscle recovery. We found this to be more or less the case during our tests, where the mattress earned accolades for its support and temperature regulation. So if you’re an athlete or looking to supercharge your sleep, you may want to consider the Celliant upgrade. —Julia Forbes

Bear Elite Hybrid ranges from $1,998 for a twin mattress to $4,282 for a split king.

Bedgear

Bedgear

I've been testing mattresses for the Reviews team for almost three years now, and I always come back to Bedgear. I find its beds feel much more luxurious and cooling than the fair price point suggests. This modular, customizable model is from the brand’s new Night Ice line, which is specifically designed for hot sleepers.

Everything about this hybrid bed is designed for hot sleepers, with a top Bedgear-patented Ver-Tex instant-cooling cover, cooling active core, and cooling boost comfort layer, which all work together as a triple threat on the top layer to effectively dissipate heat. Plus, the sides have Air-X side panels, which are mesh vents to help increase airflow throughout the mattress. Like all Bedgear models I've tried, their proprietary silky blend is literally cool to the touch (and stays cool even during summer). Below is a perforated foam that is designed to react to your body, with conforming pressure relief and airflow channels with gaps and holes for increased breathability. Plus, the M5 is modular, meaning that you can choose the same or different levels of firmness on both sides (the model I tested had both medium firm and medium plush, and the split and differing firmness levels weren't noticeable). This bed is a bit of a splurge, but I find it strikes a great balance of adaptive support while staying cool all night long.

Bedgear M5 Night Ice Performance ranges from $4,500 for a queen mattress to $8,000 for a split California king.

Bedgear

Bedgear

Amazon

Every Bedgear mattress I’ve tested is extremely cooling, comfy, and a super-fair price for the quality. This H Performance Mattress is no different. This cooling mattress is one of the most consistently cooling beds I’ve tested, it feels more expensive than its price tag.

Leesa

The Legend Chill delivered on support, and also had superb cooling qualities, so much so that I found I was significantly less restless at night, falling asleep almost the moment my head hit the pillow. The breathable phase-change fibers draw heat away from the body and release it when your body is cooler to regulate temperature. The airiness is prevalent throughout the bed—right down to the coils, resulting in a deep sleep without sweat. —Nicole Kinning

Leesa Legend Chill ranges from $2,099 for a twin to $3,399 for a California king.

Brooklyn Bedding

Brooklyn Bedding

This comfy bed features a gel foam top, with copper-infused memory foam under, and Variflex IQ memory foam that is specifically designed to conform to your body’s curves. (We also reviewed—and liked—the CopperFlex mattress topper.) The CopperFlex Memory Foam is infused with copper particles to help wick moisture and provide heat regulation and dispersal. Brooklyn Bedding claims that the natural antimicrobial properties promote a cleaner and healthier space to sleep. It's a little on the firmer side, but the comfy and cooling copper-infused pillow top conforms seamlessly to your body's pressure points.

Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex ranges from $665 for a twin to $1,199 for a California king.

Nolah

Nolah

The Nolah Evolution Hybrid supports side sleepers with spinal alignment and pressure relief, while also keeping them cool. When I’m not testing other mattresses, this is what I sleep on. I’m comfortable no matter if I’m on my side or stomach. These sleeping positions have very different support requirements; stomach sleepers need firm and unyielding support, side sleepers need cushy pressure relief. Nolah Evolution Hybrid can pull off both, with a pillow top that conforms around my hips and shoulders and zoned coils that keep my midsection boosted.

The Nolah Evolution Hybrid has a couple of cooling options available. I have the standard model, which has an organic cotton and cooling fiber cover. If you need extra cooling, there is a cool-feeling GlacioTex-fiber pillow top upgrade available. Be advised, if you go this route, you’re also essentially adding another layer of softness and pressure relief. Keep that in mind when picking your firmness level.

Nolah uses AirFoam (its own, supposedly more breathable version of memory foam) and gel-infused foam to prevent the foam layers from trapping heat. Pocketed coils enhance breathability, and there’s a mesh gusset for side ventilation. Altogether, it keeps me sleeping at a neutral temperature and fully supported. —Julia Forbes

How Does WIRED Test Cooling Mattresses?

Mattresses are tested for at least a week, but in many cases for longer. I slept on the majority of these mattresses for half a month or more to really get a feel for the product. I tested them at different times of the season and with different types of sheets and bedding. I sat on the edges to test for edge support, jumped, and performed some other methods to test the bounce and motion transfer of the mattress. Perhaps most important for this guide, I was my normal, perpetually warm (and sweaty) self, and gauged more abstract things like my overall comfort at night, and how well I thought air flowed through the mattress, or how much heat was trapped in.

What Should You Look for in a Cooling Mattress?

When shopping for a cooling mattress, here are a few things to consider:

How Did WIRED Select Models to Be Reviewed?

We have tested over 100 mattresses across all of our guides, like Best Organic Mattresses, Best Mattresses for Back Pain, and Best Mattresses You Can Buy Online, as well as for individual review. We talk with each other, discussing which mattress brands in general we're fans of, and which we aren't. Some mattresses are provided as review samples by the manufacturers, with the understanding that we don't guarantee coverage or type of coverage—we aren't paid for glowing reviews on products we think are just mid. We purchase and expense models we aren't able to get a sample of.

We try to test a range of mattress types, firmness, and brands to ensure we know what's out on the market, so we can best give you our honest, unbiased opinion on which mattresses you should spend your money (and one-third of your life sleeping) on.

What Does WIRED Do With Mattresses After Testing?

We keep top picks for longer-term durability testing in our own homes and the homes of other staffers, friends, and family members, while other models are donated locally.
